questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following best defines the financial system?

options.a: The set of government agencies that collect taxes and spend public revenue
options.b: The network of financial institutions, markets, instruments and regulations that channels funds from surplus units to deficit units in an economy
options.c: The group of commercial banks that accept deposits and grant loans to the public
options.d: The market in which long-term securities such as shares and bonds are traded

questions.explanation: The financial system is the whole network of institutions, markets, instruments and regulators that moves funds from savers (surplus units) to borrowers (deficit units), helping to mobilise savings and allocate capital. Option C is too narrow, because commercial banks are only one type of financial institution within the system. Option D describes the capital market, which is just one of the financial markets, while option A describes the government's fiscal machinery rather than the financial system.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In a financial system, funds are mainly channelled

options.a: from importers to exporters through the foreign exchange market
options.b: from deficit units (borrowers) to surplus units (savers)
options.c: from surplus units (savers) to deficit units (borrowers)
options.d: from the central bank directly to households for their daily spending

questions.explanation: Surplus units are people and organisations that earn more than they spend, and the financial system moves their idle savings to deficit units who need funds for consumption or investment. Option B reverses this flow, since borrowers receive funds rather than supply them. Options D and A describe narrow or incorrect flows that do not capture the basic intermediation role of the financial system.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the financial system?

options.a: Fixing the prices of all goods and services in the economy
options.b: Provision of liquidity to investors and businesses
options.c: Mobilisation of savings from individuals and organisations
options.d: Facilitation of payment and settlement of transactions

questions.explanation: The financial system does not set the prices of goods and services; prices are mostly determined by the market forces of demand and supply. Mobilising savings (option C), providing liquidity (option B) and facilitating payments and settlements (option D) are all genuine objectives of the financial system, alongside efficient allocation of funds and risk management.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The ability of investors to convert their financial assets into cash quickly without significant loss of value reflects which function of the financial system?

options.a: Price discovery
options.b: Monetary policy transmission

questions.explanation: Liquidity provision means the financial system allows investors to turn their investments into cash quickly and at little cost, for example by selling securities in a market. Option D refers to shifting risk to others through insurance or diversification, and option A refers to markets setting fair prices for assets through supply and demand. Option B is the channel through which central bank actions affect the economy, not the ease of converting assets to cash.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An IOU ('I owe you') is best described as

options.a: a written acknowledgement of a debt owed by one party to another
options.b: a document of title to goods shipped by sea
options.c: a certificate showing part-ownership of a company
options.d: an instruction by a customer to his bank to make regular fixed payments to a third party

questions.explanation: An IOU is simply a written acknowledgement that one person owes another a sum of money; it usually shows the parties, the amount and the date, and serves as evidence of the obligation. Option C describes a share certificate, which represents ownership rather than debt. Option B is a bill of lading used in foreign trade, and option D describes a standing order.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The view that financial institutions and services expand in response to the demand created by growth in the real economy is known as

options.a: the financial repression hypothesis
options.b: the demand-following hypothesis

questions.explanation: Under the demand-following view, economic growth comes first and creates demand for financial services, so banks and other institutions develop to meet that demand. Option C is the reverse view, where financial institutions are set up ahead of demand to stimulate growth. Option A refers to government controls such as interest rate ceilings that hold back financial development, and option D explains how banks expand deposits through lending, not how financial development relates to growth.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Under the supply-leading approach to financial development,

options.a: banks lend only to the government and refuse private sector borrowers
options.b: the central bank fixes interest rates below market levels and rations credit to favoured sectors
options.c: financial institutions appear only after the real economy has grown and created a demand for their services
options.d: financial institutions are deliberately set up ahead of demand to mobilise savings and stimulate economic growth

questions.explanation: The supply-leading approach holds that creating financial institutions first can drive growth, because they mobilise savings and provide funds for investment before the economy demands them. Option C describes the demand-following approach, where finance responds to growth instead of leading it. Options B and A describe credit controls and restrictions rather than either view of financial development.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the stages in the evolution of banking?

options.a: The development of central banking systems
options.b: The replacement of money by barter as the main means of exchange
options.c: Goldsmiths accepting deposits of gold and issuing receipts
options.d: Money lending by merchants and money changers

questions.explanation: Banking evolved forward from money changers and merchants to goldsmith bankers, commercial banks and then central banks, so a move back to barter is not a stage in its evolution. Option D describes the earliest money-lending activities from which banking grew. Option C describes goldsmith banking, which led to fractional reserve lending, and option A is a later stage in which central banks came to regulate the banking system.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Goldsmiths began lending out part of the gold deposited with them mainly because they observed that

options.a: the central bank had guaranteed repayment of their loans
options.b: depositors rarely withdrew all their gold at the same time
options.c: gold kept in their vaults steadily lost its value
options.d: the law required them to lend out all deposits received

questions.explanation: Goldsmiths noticed that only a small part of the gold left with them was withdrawn at any one time, so they could safely lend out the rest and earn interest. This idea of keeping only a fraction of deposits as reserves is the basis of modern fractional reserve banking. Option C is wrong because gold holds its value well, option D is wrong because no law forced them to lend, and option A is wrong because no central bank guaranteed goldsmiths' loans.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which statement about goldsmiths and lending is most accurate?

options.a: Goldsmiths' receipts were never accepted by anyone as a means of payment
options.b: Goldsmiths were the first people in history to lend money at interest
options.c: Goldsmiths only stored gold for safekeeping and never lent any of it
options.d: Lending existed before goldsmiths, but their practice of lending out part of deposited gold helped lay the foundation of modern banking

questions.explanation: Money lending is far older than goldsmith banking, but goldsmiths formalised the practice of lending part of the deposits entrusted to them, which is why they are seen as forerunners of modern banks. Option B overstates their role, since merchants and money lenders lent at interest long before them. Options C and A are wrong because goldsmiths did lend part of the deposits, and their receipts came to circulate as a means of payment.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A bank receives a fresh cash deposit of N2,000,000. If the cash reserve ratio is 20% and banks lend out all excess reserves with no cash leakage, what is the maximum total amount of deposits the banking system can create, including the initial deposit?
questions.explanation: The credit multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio, so 1/0.20 = 5, and maximum total deposits are N2,000,000 x 5 = N10,000,000. Option D is only the new deposits created through lending, which leaves out the initial N2,000,000 the question asks you to include. Option C wrongly divides by 0.80 instead of 0.20, and option B is just the reserve the first bank keeps on the initial deposit.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following limits the ability of commercial banks to create credit?

options.a: A steady inflow of fresh cash deposits into the banks
options.b: A low public preference for holding cash

questions.explanation: Banks can only create credit by making loans, so if there are few borrowers who are able and willing to repay, lending and therefore credit creation are held back. Option D actually helps credit creation, because banks keep less in reserve and can lend more. Options B and A also support credit creation, since more cash stays in the banks to be lent out again.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Banking, in its basic sense, is the business of

options.a: issuing currency and regulating the money supply
options.b: buying and selling shares on the stock exchange for clients
options.c: insuring lives and property against loss
options.d: accepting deposits from the public and lending or investing those funds

questions.explanation: At its core, banking means taking deposits from people and organisations and using those funds to make loans and investments, earning a margin between the interest charged and the interest paid. Option A describes central banking, option C describes insurance, and option B describes stockbroking.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The two essential (principal) functions of a commercial bank are:

options.a: Issuing currency and acting as banker to the government
options.b: Accepting deposits from the public and granting loans and advances
options.c: Acting as executor or trustee and keeping customers' valuables in safe custody
options.d: Buying and selling shares on the stock exchange and underwriting new issues

questions.explanation: Accepting deposits and lending them out as loans, overdrafts and discounted bills are the core of banking; through these two activities banks earn interest income and create credit. Option A lists functions of the central bank, not a commercial bank. Option C lists ancillary services a bank may offer, but they are extras rather than its essential business, and option D describes the work of stockbrokers and issuing houses in the capital market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is an agency function performed by a commercial bank for its customers?

options.a: Keeping customers' valuables in safe custody
options.b: Collecting dividends and interest on the customer's behalf
options.c: Granting overdrafts to current account holders

questions.explanation: In its agency functions the bank acts as its customer's agent, doing things on the customer's behalf such as collecting dividends, interest and cheques, paying bills and insurance premiums, buying and selling securities and transferring funds. Options D and C are the bank's principal functions of accepting deposits and lending. Option A is a separate safe-keeping service, where the bank holds the customer's property rather than acting for the customer.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An institution whose main business is accepting deposits from the public and using those funds to give loans and advances is a:

options.a: Stock exchange
options.b: Bank

questions.explanation: A bank is defined by the twin activities of taking deposits and lending them out, which makes it a financial intermediary between savers and borrowers. Option D collects premiums in return for covering risks, not deposits. Option A is a market where shares and bonds are traded, and option C invests contributors' pension savings rather than accepting deposits and granting loans.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A commercial bank accepts deposits and lends at a margin in order to earn profit. Its main source of income is therefore:

options.a: Premiums paid by depositors for insuring their deposits
options.b: Interest earned on the cash reserves it must keep with the CBN
options.c: The issue of new currency and coins
options.d: The difference between the interest it charges on loans and the interest it pays on deposits

questions.explanation: A commercial bank is a profit-seeking firm that takes in funds from depositors at a lower rate and lends them at a higher rate, and this interest margin or spread is its main income. Option C is wrong because only the central bank issues currency. Option A is wrong because deposit insurance premiums are paid by the banks to the deposit insurer, not received by them, and option B is wrong because cash reserves kept with the CBN earn little or no interest.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the assumptions behind the basic theory of credit creation by banks?

options.a: That there is a mandatory reserve proportion the bank has to keep from each deposit
options.b: That only a fraction of each deposit is needed by depositors in the immediate future
options.c: That banks must keep the whole of every deposit as reserves and lend none of it out
options.d: That there must be some initial primary deposit in the form of cash

questions.explanation: The basic credit creation process assumes that banks receive an initial primary deposit in cash, that they must keep a legally required fraction of each deposit as reserves, and that depositors need only part of their deposits in the near future, leaving the rest free to lend. Keeping the whole of every deposit as reserves is the opposite of what the theory assumes, because banks could then lend nothing and no credit would be created. The other three options all describe genuine assumptions of the theory.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The credit creation ability of the banking system is limited by:

options.a: The amount of the initial deposit
options.b: The level of the reserve ratio
options.c: The existence of leakages in the system

questions.explanation: Three things limit how much credit the banking system can create: the size of the initial cash deposit, the cash reserve ratio, and leakages from the system. Total deposits created equal the initial deposit times the money multiplier (1/r), so a smaller deposit or a higher reserve ratio means less credit, and cash withdrawn and kept outside the banks breaks the deposit-lending chain. Since A, B and C are all genuine limits, D is the answer.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In any financial system there are three basic types of institutions. Which of these is NOT included among them?

options.a: Bank Financial Institutions
options.b: Non-bank Financial Institutions

questions.explanation: A financial system is made up of bank financial institutions such as commercial and merchant banks, non-bank financial institutions such as insurance companies and pension funds, and regulatory and supervisory institutions such as the CBN and the NDIC. Reformatory institutions are correctional institutions and play no part in the financial system, so C is the odd one out while A, B and D are all genuine categories.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of these is NOT an example of a non-bank financial institution?

options.a: Pension funds
options.b: Insurance companies

questions.explanation: The NDIC is a regulatory and supervisory body: it insures bank deposits and supervises banks alongside the CBN, instead of mobilising and lending funds as a financial intermediary does. Pension funds (A), insurance companies (B) and finance houses (D) all pool funds from the public and invest or lend them, which is why they are classed as non-bank financial institutions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: What is the basic role of financial intermediaries in the savings-investment process?

options.a: Giving investors information on who has spare funds, while leaving them to raise the funds directly from the owners
options.b: Mobilising funds from surplus units (savers) and channelling them to deficit units (investors)
options.c: Regulating and supervising banks and insurance companies
options.d: Issuing the national currency and controlling the money supply

questions.explanation: Financial intermediaries pool funds from savers and lend or invest them with those who need funds, which lowers the risk and cost of funds and allows longer-term use. Option A describes the slow direct approach that intermediaries replace, because they actually collect and lend the funds themselves. Options D and C describe the work of the central bank and the regulatory bodies, not of intermediaries.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Among the several limitations of trying to source funds directly from the ultimate owners is that:

options.a: The cost of funds would be high
options.b: The period for which the funds can be used would be short
options.c: The risk on releasing funds would be high

questions.explanation: Raising funds directly from fund owners is slow and limiting. The single owner bears all the risk alone, so the risk is high and he charges a high price for his money, and he will usually release it only for a short period, which makes long-term investment difficult. Since A, B and C are all genuine limitations, D is the answer.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a basic advantage of having financial institutions as intermediaries in an economy?

options.a: Investors can now access funds in fairly bulky sums
options.b: The risk on funds is now higher as bulky sums can be accessed
options.c: The cost of funds is reduced
options.d: The term for fund usage is now longer

questions.explanation: Financial intermediaries pool funds from many savers, so the risk carried by each fund owner is lower, not higher. Because risk is spread, the cost of funds falls (C), investors can obtain large sums (A), and funds can be made available for longer periods (D). Option B is therefore not an advantage; it reverses what intermediation actually does.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of these is NOT included among the factors that make for successful financial intermediation?

options.a: Trust and confidence of the public in the financial institutions
options.b: Multilingual ability (ability to speak several languages) of the staff of the financial institutions
options.c: Convenience of accessing the financial institutions by the people
options.d: Price charged by the financial institutions

questions.explanation: Successful financial intermediation depends on public trust and confidence (A), the convenience and ease of dealing with the institutions (C), and the price they charge, such as interest and fees (D). Staff who speak several languages may help customer service, but that is not one of the basic factors that decide whether intermediation succeeds.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of a commercial bank?

options.a: Accepting deposits from members of the public
options.b: Granting its customers loans and advances
options.d: Safe-keeping of wills, jewellery and other important documents for its customers

questions.explanation: Commercial banks accept deposits (A), grant loans and advances (B), and keep wills, jewellery and important documents in safe custody for their customers (D). Writing a will is a legal task for the customer and a lawyer; a bank may keep the finished will safely, but drafting it is not a commercial banking function.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a way in which commercial banks provide credit to their customers?

options.a: Acting as lender of last resort to other banks
options.b: Safe-keeping customers' valuables and documents

questions.explanation: When a bank discounts a bill of exchange, it pays the holder the face value less a discount before the bill matures, which is a form of short-term credit. Safe-keeping of valuables (option B) is a service, not credit, while issuing the currency (option D) and acting as lender of last resort (option A) are functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of commercial banks.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Markets that mobilize funds from the surplus units of society (savers and lenders) to the deficit units (borrowers and investors) are called

options.a: Commodity markets
options.b: Financial markets

questions.explanation: Financial markets channel funds from those who have more than they currently need, the surplus units, to those who need funds to borrow and invest, the deficit units. Commodity markets (A) and product markets (D) deal in goods, and labour markets (C) deal in workers' services, not in the transfer of funds.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a function of the financial system?

options.a: Mobilization of savings and provision of liquidity
options.b: Storage of wealth and provision of payment systems
options.c: Provision of credit and protection against risk

questions.explanation: The financial system mobilizes savings, provides liquidity, stores wealth, provides payment systems, provides credit and offers protection against risk. Every item in A, B and C is therefore a genuine function, so none of them is the odd one out and D is correct.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The capital market can be defined as

options.a: The market for purchasing capital goods otherwise known as equipment and machinery
options.b: The market for raising medium- to long-term funds for investment purposes

questions.explanation: The capital market is the financial market where medium- to long-term funds are mobilised and traded through instruments such as shares, bonds and government stocks. It is not a market for physical machinery and equipment, so option A confuses financial capital with capital goods. Because A is wrong, option C cannot be correct either.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Two principal institutions in the Nigerian capital market are

options.a: The CBN and the Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE)
options.b: The NDIC and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

questions.explanation: The Securities and Exchange Commission is the apex regulator of the capital market, while the stock exchange provides the market where securities are listed, bought and sold, so the NSE and the SEC are its two principal institutions. The NSE was demutualised in 2021 and now operates as the Nigerian Exchange (NGX). Option A is wrong because the CBN's main role is in banking and the money market, and option B is wrong because the NDIC insures bank deposits rather than running the capital market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which body has overall oversight of (is the apex regulator of) the Nigerian capital market?

options.a: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)
options.b: National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)

questions.explanation: The Securities and Exchange Commission is the apex regulator of the Nigerian capital market: it registers securities and market operators, monitors the stock exchange and protects investors. The NDIC (A) insures deposits in banks, NAICOM (B) regulates insurance companies, and PenCom (D) regulates pension fund administrators and custodians, so none of them oversees the capital market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is not a non-bank financial institution?

options.a: Insurance companies
options.b: Pension funds

questions.explanation: The Debt Management Office is a government agency that manages Nigeria's public debt; it does not mobilise funds from savers and lend them out, so it is not a financial intermediary at all. Insurance companies (A), pension funds (B) and primary mortgage institutions (D) all pool funds from the public and channel them into investment without operating as deposit money banks, which is why they are classed as non-bank financial institutions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: There are two major types of insurance. These are

options.a: Life insurance and animal insurance
options.b: Life insurance and non-life insurance

questions.explanation: Insurance business is broadly divided into life insurance, which covers risks to human life such as death, disability or old age, and non-life (general) insurance, which covers other risks. Option C is tempting, but property insurance is only one branch of non-life insurance, which also includes liability insurance, so B is the complete answer. 'Animal insurance' in A is not a major class of insurance.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Under a life insurance policy, the policy holder is mainly protected against financial loss to himself or his family arising from

options.a: Fire or theft affecting his property
options.b: Loss of goods at sea through marine mishaps
options.d: Legal claims against him for negligence

questions.explanation: Life insurance covers risks to the insured person's life, so it protects him or his dependants against financial loss from death, disability or old age, usually in return for regular premiums. Options A and B describe property insurance and option D describes liability insurance, and both of these fall under non-life (general) insurance.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The National Provident Fund (NPF) was established in _______ and was later reformed into the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) in _______ by the NSITF Decree No. 73
questions.explanation: The National Provident Fund was set up in 1961 as a compulsory savings and social security scheme for private sector workers. Because of poor record-keeping and non-remittance of contributions by employers, it was replaced in 1993, under Decree No. 73, by the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund, which took over its assets and liabilities. None of the other pairs of dates, such as 1959 and 1988 in D, matches these two events.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When it was set up in 1993, the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund's areas of operation included

options.a: Retirement pension and survivors' pension
options.b: Retirement grant and survivors' grant

questions.explanation: The NSITF scheme set up in 1993 was a social insurance scheme covering seven benefit areas: retirement pension, retirement grant, invalidity pension, invalidity grant, survivors' pension, survivors' grant and funeral grant. Options A, B and C each list only part of this coverage, so D is the best answer.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The Pension Reform Act of 2004 created a body that is supposed to take oversight of all pension institutions. This body is known as the

options.a: Nigerian Pensions Board
options.b: National Pensions Board

questions.explanation: The Pension Reform Act of 2004 established the National Pension Commission (PenCom) to regulate and supervise pension schemes and to license and supervise pension fund administrators and custodians. Options A and B sound similar but are not the name of any body created by the Act, and D is wrong because a specific regulator was created.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Apart from the National Pension Commission, which two types of pension institutions were created under the Pension Reform Act of 2004?

options.a: Pension Fund Managers and Pension Fund Custodians
options.b: Pension Fund Consultants and Pension Fund Administrators
options.c: Pension Fund Custodians and Pension Fund Administrators

questions.explanation: The 2004 Act created Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs), which open and manage each employee's Retirement Savings Account and invest the contributions, and Pension Fund Custodians (PFCs), which hold the pension fund assets in safe keeping. Option A is close, but 'pension fund managers' is not the name the Act gives to these institutions, and the 'pension fund consultants' in B were not created by the Act.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When primary mortgage institutions (PMIs) were first set up under the Mortgage Institutions Decree No. 53 of 1989, they were answerable to (regulated and supervised by)

options.a: The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
options.b: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)
options.c: The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN)

questions.explanation: Under the 1989 decree, the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria became the apex mortgage institution and was given regulatory and supervisory oversight of the PMIs, which provided housing finance at the retail level. The CBN (A) only took over their regulation and supervision in 1997, so A and D do not describe the original arrangement. The NDIC (B) is a deposit insurer, not the regulator that licensed the PMIs.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The total money created by the banking system is ________ related to the reserve requirement.

options.a: Directly
options.b: Proportionally

questions.explanation: Total money created equals the initial deposit multiplied by the money multiplier, and the multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio. A higher reserve requirement therefore means a smaller multiplier and less money created, while a lower requirement means more, so the relationship is inverse. Options A, B and D all suggest that money created rises when the reserve requirement rises, which is the opposite of what happens.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If the total money (deposits) created by the banking system is N240 million from an initial deposit of N15 million, the reserve requirement ratio is
questions.explanation: Total money created equals the initial deposit divided by the reserve ratio, so the reserve ratio equals the initial deposit divided by the total: N15 million / N240 million = 0.0625, or 6.25%. Option A comes from confusing the money multiplier (240 / 15 = 16) with the ratio itself. Options B and D would give totals of N187.5 million and N120 million, not N240 million.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If a reserve requirement of 6.25% is increased by 100%, determine the total money (deposits) created by the banking system from an initial deposit of N15 million.

options.a: N240 million
options.b: N180 million

questions.explanation: A 100% increase doubles the reserve requirement from 6.25% to 12.5%, so the money multiplier falls to 1 / 0.125 = 8, and N15 million x 8 = N120 million. Option A is the total at the old 6.25% ratio, and option D wrongly doubles the total instead of halving it. A higher reserve requirement always reduces the money the banks can create.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If an initial deposit of N15 million is decreased by 25%, what is the total money (deposits) created by the banking system with a reserve requirement of 6.25%?

options.a: N240 million
options.b: N180 million

questions.explanation: A 25% fall leaves an initial deposit of N11.25 million, and with a 6.25% reserve ratio the multiplier is 1 / 0.0625 = 16, so total money created is N11.25 million x 16 = N180 million. Option A is the total from the original N15 million deposit, and option D wrongly treats the fall in the deposit as a rise. Option C would need a 12.5% reserve ratio on the full N15 million.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If an initial deposit of N15 million is decreased by 25% and a reserve requirement of 6.25% is increased by 100%, determine the total money (deposits) created by the banking system.

options.a: N240 million
options.b: N180 million

questions.explanation: The deposit falls to N15 million x 0.75 = N11.25 million and the reserve ratio doubles to 12.5%, so the multiplier is 1 / 0.125 = 8 and total money created is N11.25 million x 8 = N90 million. Option B applies only the smaller deposit and keeps the old 6.25% ratio, while option C applies only the higher ratio to the full N15 million. Both changes reduce credit creation, so the answer must be lower than either of those.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The three basic types of financial institutions in any financial system are

options.a: Regulatory bodies, financial institutions and insurance companies.
options.b: Regulatory and supervisory institutions, banking financial institutions and insurance companies.
options.c: Regulatory and supervisory institutions, banking financial institutions and non-banking financial institutions.

questions.explanation: A financial system is made up of bank financial institutions (such as commercial and merchant banks), non-bank financial institutions (such as insurance companies, pension funds and finance houses), and the regulatory and supervisory institutions that oversee them (such as the CBN and NDIC). Options A and B are wrong because insurance companies are only one example of non-bank financial institutions, not a separate basic type. Option D cannot be right because A and B are incorrect.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: What general name is given to the institutions whose role is to move funds from surplus units to deficit units?

options.a: Financial intermediaries
options.b: Insurance companies

questions.explanation: Financial intermediaries are the institutions that collect funds from savers (surplus units) and channel them to borrowers and investors (deficit units), and this is their defining role. Options B, C and D each name one particular institution or group, so none of them is the general name for the whole class. The question asks for the overall term, which is financial intermediaries.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The full meaning of NSITF is

options.a: Nigerian Social Insurance and Technical Fund
options.b: National Social Insurance and Technical Fund
options.c: Nigerian Societal Insurance and Trust Fund

questions.explanation: NSITF stands for the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund, a non-bank financial institution set up in 1993 to take over the old National Provident Fund and provide social insurance for workers. Options A and B wrongly expand the "T" as "Technical", and option C wrongly uses "Societal" instead of "Social".

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Given an initial deposit of N5,000 and a reserve ratio of 25%, what is the maximum total deposit that the banking system can create from it?
questions.explanation: With a 25% reserve ratio, each N1 of fresh reserves can support N1 / 0.25 = N4 of deposits, so N5,000 x 4 = N20,000 in total deposits (the original N5,000 plus N15,000 of new deposits created through lending). Option D (N50,000) would only follow from a 10% reserve ratio, and option A (N200,000) from a 2.5% ratio. Option C is smaller than what the deposit multiplier gives.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If commercial banks keep a reserve ratio of 25%, what is the bank deposit multiplier?
questions.explanation: The deposit (credit) multiplier is the reciprocal of the reserve ratio: 1 / 0.25 = 4, so every N1 of new reserves can support up to N4 of deposits. Options C (0.25) and D (25%) simply restate the reserve ratio itself rather than the multiplier. Option A (2.6) does not follow from the formula at all.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The existence of both unorganized and organized financial markets side by side in developing economies is known as

options.a: financial liberalisation
options.b: financial stabilization

questions.explanation: Financial dualism describes an economy where a formal, regulated financial sector (banks, insurance firms, the capital market) operates side by side with an informal one such as esusu, ajo and local moneylenders, as is common in Nigeria. Option D, financial integration, is the opposite idea of the sectors being merged into one linked system. Option A, financial liberalisation, means removing controls on interest rates and entry into banking.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: ________ is the only market segment where capital formation occurs.

options.a: capital market
options.b: money market

questions.explanation: The primary market is where new shares and bonds are sold for the first time, so the money raised goes straight to the issuing company or government to fund new investment, which is capital formation. Option C, the secondary market, only moves existing securities between investors, so no new capital is raised. Option A is partly true because the capital market contains the primary market, but it also includes secondary trading, so it is not the only segment where capital formation happens.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Banks can create more money by

options.a: increasing their cash ratio with the central bank
options.b: issuing more bank charges
options.d: lending out more money from customers' deposits

questions.explanation: Banks create money by lending: when a bank lends out part of a deposit, the loan is spent and redeposited in the banking system, creating new deposits that can be lent again, so total deposits grow to a multiple of the original cash. Option A has it backwards, because a higher cash ratio leaves banks less to lend and reduces credit creation. Option C, accepting deposits, gives banks something to lend from, but by itself it only turns cash into deposits; new money appears when those deposits are lent out.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A market where new shares are traded is known as

options.a: primary market
options.b: stock market

questions.explanation: The primary market is the part of the capital market where new shares are issued and sold for the first time, so the money raised goes to the issuing company. The secondary market (Option C) is for buying and selling shares that already exist. Stock market (Option B) is a general term for share trading as a whole, and the money market (Option D) deals in short-term instruments, not shares.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: _______ is a market for existing issues of securities or claims

options.a: money market
options.b: capital market

questions.explanation: The secondary market is where securities that have already been issued are bought and sold among investors; it makes long-term securities liquid because holders can sell them whenever they need cash. The primary market (Option C) is for new issues. The capital market (Option B) is the whole market for long-term funds, covering both the primary and the secondary market, and the money market (Option A) deals in short-term instruments.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The capital market participants include the following except

options.a: Finance houses
options.b: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

questions.explanation: Finance houses raise short-term placements and lend them out, so they operate mainly in the money market and are the exception here. The Securities and Exchange Commission (Option B) regulates the capital market, the Nigerian Stock Exchange (Option C) is where long-term securities are traded, and underwriters (Option D) guarantee the sale of new share and bond issues, so all three are capital market participants.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Commercial banks can create money in which of the following ways?

options.a: By issuing coins and paper money
options.b: By printing money on the instructions of the Central Bank
options.c: By borrowing money from banks abroad

questions.explanation: Commercial banks create money by granting loans and overdrafts that show up as new deposits in the banking system, and none of Options A to C describes this. Issuing coins and paper money (Option A) or printing money (Option B) is the job of the central bank alone, and borrowing from banks abroad (Option C) is simply taking on a debt, not creating new deposit money.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A commercial bank is able to create money

options.a: by printing it
options.b: by maintaining reserves
options.c: by creating demand deposits as it gives a new loan
options.d: by borrowing from the Central Bank

questions.explanation: When a bank grants a loan it usually credits the borrower's account, creating a new demand deposit that did not exist before, and because demand deposits are part of the money supply, this is how commercial banks create money. Option A is wrong because only the central bank issues currency, Option B (keeping reserves) actually limits how much a bank can lend, and Option D only adds to the bank's reserves without by itself creating deposit money.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A rise in the market price of fixed interest securities is an indication that the

options.a: supply of money has decreased
options.b: liquidity preference has increased
options.c: market rate of interest has risen
options.d: market rate of interest has fallen

questions.explanation: Fixed interest securities pay a set rate, so their prices move opposite to market interest rates: when market rates fall, existing securities paying the older, higher fixed rate become more attractive and their prices rise. Option C is the reverse case, and Options A and B would both push interest rates up and security prices down, because less money in circulation or a stronger wish to hold cash leads people to sell securities.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Given an initial deposit of N500 and a reserve requirement ratio of 15%, what is the money (credit) multiplier?
questions.explanation: The money multiplier is the inverse of the reserve ratio: k = 1/r = 1/0.15 = 6.67, so every naira of fresh deposit can support about 6.67 naira of total deposits. Option C (0.15) is just the reserve ratio itself, and D (1.18) wrongly inverts 0.85, the share of each deposit that is lent out. Option A treats 15% as 15 instead of inverting 0.15.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Given an initial deposit of N500 and a reserve requirement ratio of 15%, what is the total deposit created in the banking system, including the initial deposit?
questions.explanation: Total deposits equal the initial deposit times the money multiplier: 500 x (1/0.15) = N3,333.33. Option A (N75) is only the reserve the first bank must keep, and B (N425) is the amount that first bank can lend out. Option D comes from multiplying 500 by 15 instead of dividing by 0.15.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Given an initial deposit of N500 and a reserve requirement ratio of 15%, how much is the excess reserve of the bank that receives the deposit?
questions.explanation: The bank must keep 15% of N500, which is N75, as its required reserve; what is left, N500 - N75 = N425, is the excess reserve it is free to lend out. Option A is the required reserve, not the excess, and B is simply the original deposit. Option D is the total deposit the whole banking system can eventually create.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: If the total supply of money in the economy is N280 million and the initial deposit is N35 million, what is the reserve requirement ratio?
questions.explanation: Total money created equals the initial deposit divided by the reserve ratio, so r = 35/280 = 0.125, or 12.5%. Option B mixes up the ratio with the money multiplier, which is 280/35 = 8. Option D (87.5%) is the share of each deposit that would be lent out, and C is double the correct ratio.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The total supply of money in an economy is N280 million, created from an initial deposit of N35 million. If the reserve requirement ratio increases by 100% and the initial deposit decreases by 25%, what is the total money supply created in the system?

options.a: N140 million
options.b: N210 million

questions.explanation: The original ratio is 35/280 = 12.5%, so doubling it gives 25% and a multiplier of 4. The new deposit is 75% of N35 million = N26.25 million, so total money created = 26.25 x 4 = N105 million. Option A ignores the fall in the deposit, B ignores the rise in the ratio, and D wrongly raises the deposit by 25% instead of reducing it.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The total supply of money in an economy is N280 million, created from an initial deposit of N35 million. If the reserve requirement ratio increases by 100%, determine the total money created.

options.a: N280 million
options.b: N140 million

questions.explanation: The original reserve ratio is 35/280 = 12.5%, and a 100% increase doubles it to 25%, so the multiplier falls from 8 to 4. Total money created is therefore 35 x 4 = N140 million. Option A is the old total before the change, and C wrongly doubles the money instead of halving it, so D is also wrong.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The total supply of money in an economy is N280 million, created from an initial deposit of N35 million. If the initial deposit increases by 25% (with the reserve ratio unchanged), determine the total money created.

options.a: N210 million
options.b: N180 million

questions.explanation: The reserve ratio is 35/280 = 12.5%, which gives a multiplier of 8. A 25% rise makes the deposit 35 x 1.25 = N43.75 million, so total money created = 43.75 x 8 = N350 million. Option A (N210 million) is what you get if the deposit falls by 25% instead of rising, while B and C do not follow from the multiplier at all.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Mr. Unilag deposited an initial sum of N1,000 in a commercial bank. If the cash reserve ratio fixed by the CBN is 15%, what is the total amount of deposits that the entire banking system can create from it?
questions.explanation: The money multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.67, so the banking system can build total deposits of about 1,000 x 6.67 = N6,667 from the initial N1,000; of this, about N5,667 is new lending on top of the original deposit. Option D (N15,000) comes from multiplying by 15 instead of dividing by 0.15. Options A and C do not follow from the multiplier at all.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The total amount of money that the banking system can create from an initial deposit is determined by the

options.a: Money multiplier
options.b: Deflation

questions.explanation: Total money created equals the initial deposit multiplied by the money (credit) multiplier, which is the inverse of the cash reserve ratio (k = 1/r). Deflation (B) is a general fall in prices, and the accelerator (C) links investment to changes in output, so neither determines how much money banks can create, which also rules out D.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of these will discourage credit creation?

options.a: Leakages in the economy
options.b: The central bank's contractionary monetary policy

questions.explanation: Leakages, such as cash withdrawn and kept outside the banking system, stop deposits from flowing round the banks, so less credit can be created. A contractionary monetary policy, for example raising the reserve requirement or selling securities through open market operations, also cuts the reserves banks can lend. Since both A and B discourage credit creation, C is the best answer and D is wrong.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The relationship between the reserve requirement and the total credit created is

options.a: Direct
options.b: Proportionally direct

questions.explanation: Total credit created equals the initial deposit times 1/r, where r is the reserve requirement, so a higher reserve requirement means less credit and a lower one means more. That is an inverse relationship, which rules out A and B; D is wrong because C correctly describes the link.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The relationship between the reserve requirement and the deposit multiplier is

options.a: Direct
options.b: Proportionally direct

questions.explanation: The deposit multiplier is k = 1/r, so when the reserve requirement rises the multiplier falls; a 10% requirement gives a multiplier of 10, while 20% gives only 5. The two move in opposite directions, so the relationship is inverse, not direct (A) or proportionally direct (B).

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The monetary authority imposes a minimum reserve requirement of 10% and the initial deposit of your bank is N10 million. What is the total amount of money that can be created in the banking system from this deposit?

options.a: N80 million
options.b: N100 million

questions.explanation: The money multiplier is the inverse of the reserve ratio: k = 1/0.10 = 10. Total money created = N10 million x 10 = N100 million. N80 million (A) and the larger figures in C and D do not follow from the 1/r formula.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The monetary authority imposes a minimum reserve requirement of 10% and the initial deposit of your bank is N10 million. If the reserve requirement is increased by 50%, what is the new level of money created?

options.a: N56.37 million
options.b: N66.67 million

questions.explanation: A 50% increase raises the reserve requirement from 10% to 15% (10% x 1.5), not to 60%. The new multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.67, so money created = N10 million / 0.15 = about N66.67 million. Options A and C do not match this calculation, and D is wrong because B is correct.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The monetary authority imposes a minimum reserve requirement of 10% and the initial deposit of your bank is N10 million. If the reserve requirement is instead reduced by 50%, what is the new level of money created?

options.a: N560 million
options.b: N200 million

questions.explanation: Reducing 10% by half gives a new reserve requirement of 5%, so the multiplier becomes 1/0.05 = 20. Money created = N10 million x 20 = N200 million. N150 million (C) and N160 million (D) understate the effect of the lower reserve ratio, and N560 million (A) is far too large.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: How can you describe the deposit multiplier quantitatively?

options.a: It is half of the cash reserve ratio
options.b: It is double the cash reserve ratio
options.c: It is the inverse of the cash reserve ratio

questions.explanation: The deposit (money) multiplier is k = 1/r, the inverse or reciprocal of the cash reserve ratio, so a 25% ratio gives k = 1/0.25 = 4. Halving (A) or doubling (B) the ratio just gives another ratio, not the multiplier, and D is wrong because C is correct.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Bank X receives a primary deposit of N1,000 million and must keep 25% of it as reserves. How much can it lend out at the first stage of the credit creation process?

options.a: N250 million
options.b: N750 million

questions.explanation: The bank keeps 25% of N1,000 million, which is N250 million, as reserves and can lend out the remaining 75%, which is N750 million. N250 million (A) is the reserve, not the loan; N1,000 million (C) ignores the reserve requirement; and N4,000 million (D) is the total deposits the whole banking system can eventually create (N1,000 million x 4), not the first-stage loan.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In the credit creation process, the part of a bank's primary deposit left after it has met the required reserve and expected withdrawals, which it is free to lend out, is called

options.a: Excess reserve
options.b: Required reserve

questions.explanation: Excess reserve is what remains of a primary deposit after the bank has set aside the legally required reserve and what it expects depositors to withdraw; lending it out starts the credit creation chain. The required reserve (B) is the fraction the law says must be kept, the primary deposit (C) is the original cash deposit that starts the process, and a special deposit (D) is a separate central bank control tool.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following does NOT limit the ability of the banking system to create credit?

options.a: Borrowers redepositing their loans in other banks
options.b: The size of the initial cash deposit
options.d: Leakages of cash out of the banking system

questions.explanation: When borrowers redeposit their loan proceeds in other banks, the deposits keep circulating through the system, which is exactly what makes credit creation possible. The size of the initial deposit (B), the reserve requirement (C) and leakages such as cash kept at home (D) are the three factors that limit how much credit the banks can create.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: With an initial deposit of N1,000 million and a reserve ratio of 25%, the banking system can create N4,000 million. If the reserve ratio rises to 40%, the total money that can be created becomes

options.a: N4,000 million
options.b: N2,500 million

questions.explanation: The new multiplier is 1/0.40 = 2.5, so total money created = N1,000 million x 2.5 = N2,500 million. A higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier, so the total must fall, which rules out N4,000 million (A) and N6,400 million (C); N1,600 million (D) comes from wrongly multiplying N4,000 million by 0.40.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An economy is able to create N500 million of money from an initial deposit of N50 million. What is the money multiplier in this economy?
questions.explanation: The money multiplier is total money created divided by the initial deposit: N500 million / N50 million = 10, which also means the reserve ratio is 1/10, or 10%. Option A (0.1) is that reserve ratio, not the multiplier, option B (9) comes from using only the newly created N450 million, and option C (25) has no basis in the figures.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An economy creates N500 million of money from an initial deposit of N50 million. If it increases its reserve requirement by 100%, what is the new reserve requirement?
questions.explanation: The original multiplier is 500/50 = 10, so the reserve requirement is 1/10 = 10%, and increasing it by 100% doubles it to 20%. Option A is the old requirement, option B confuses the size of the increase with the new ratio, and option C wrongly adds 100 percentage points.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An economy creates N500 million of money from an initial deposit of N50 million. If its reserve requirement is increased by 100% while the initial deposit is increased by 40%, what is the total money that can be created?

options.a: N700 million
options.b: N350 million

questions.explanation: The original reserve ratio is 50/500 = 10%, so doubling it gives 20% and a new multiplier of 1/0.20 = 5. The new deposit is N50 million x 1.4 = N70 million, so total money = N70 million x 5 = N350 million. N700 million (A) ignores the higher reserve requirement, N250 million (C) ignores the larger deposit, and N1,400 million (D) wrongly uses 20 as the multiplier instead of 5.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Financial markets are best described as markets that

options.a: Deal only in the shares of quoted companies
options.b: Mobilise funds from surplus units (savers) and channel them to deficit units (borrowers and investors)
options.c: Exist mainly for the central bank to print and issue currency
options.d: Are used for buying and selling goods and services for money

questions.explanation: Financial markets link savers who have more funds than they need with households, firms and governments that need funds, and in doing so they determine the quantity and cost of funds in the economy. Option A describes only one part of the capital market, option C describes a central bank function rather than a market, and option D describes ordinary goods markets.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the money market from the capital market?

options.a: The money market deals in long-term funds, while the capital market deals in short-term funds
options.b: The money market deals in short-term funds and instruments, while the capital market deals in long-term funds
options.c: The money market serves only the government, while the capital market serves only private firms
options.d: The money market deals in shares, while the capital market deals in treasury bills

questions.explanation: The money market is where short-term funds and instruments, such as treasury bills, certificates of deposit and call money, are traded, while the capital market provides long-term funds through shares, bonds and similar securities. Option A reverses the two, option C is wrong because both markets serve government and private users, and option D swaps the typical instruments of each market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions of financial markets?

options.a: Mobilisation of savings
options.b: Fixing the prices of goods and services in the economy

questions.explanation: Financial markets deal in funds and financial assets; they do not fix the prices of goods and services, which are set in goods markets. Mobilising savings (A), providing liquidity by letting people turn financial assets into cash (C) and protecting against risks through instruments like insurance policies (D) are all recognised functions, along with storing wealth, providing credit, providing payment facilities and helping to carry out government policy.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The financial market is commonly divided into two major segments, the money market and the capital market. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

options.a: The money market deals in medium- to long-term funds such as shares and bonds, while the capital market deals in short-term instruments such as treasury bills.
options.b: The money market deals only in foreign currencies, while the capital market deals only in instruments denominated in naira.
options.c: The money market deals in short-term funds and instruments (up to one year), while the capital market deals in medium- to long-term funds such as shares and bonds.
options.d: The money market is open only to the Central Bank of Nigeria, while the capital market is open only to private individual investors.

questions.explanation: The dividing line between the two markets is the maturity of the funds traded. The money market handles short-term borrowing and lending of up to about one year, using instruments like treasury bills and commercial papers, while the capital market raises medium- and long-term funds through shares and bonds. Option A simply swaps the two markets around, and options B and D are wrong because neither market is defined by currency or restricted to one type of participant.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a capital market instrument rather than a money market instrument?

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Bankers' acceptances
options.d: Ordinary shares (equities) of a quoted company

questions.explanation: Ordinary shares are long-term instruments with no fixed maturity, so they are traded in the capital market. Treasury bills (option A), commercial papers (option C) and bankers' acceptances (option B) are all short-term instruments that usually mature within a year, which makes them money market instruments.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes a deposit money bank from a non-bank financial institution such as an insurance company or a pension fund?

options.a: Only banks act as intermediaries between savers and borrowers; non-bank financial institutions do not channel funds to borrowers at all.
options.b: A bank accepts deposits withdrawable on demand by cheque, which serve as money and allow it to create credit; non-bank institutions do not.
options.c: Banks deal only in long-term funds, while non-bank financial institutions deal only in short-term funds repayable within one year.
options.d: Non-bank financial institutions are not regulated by any government agency, while banks are regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria.

questions.explanation: What sets banks apart is that their demand (current account) deposits can be spent by cheque or transfer, so they count as money and allow banks to create credit. Insurance companies, pension funds and finance houses mobilise funds through premiums, contributions or placements, which are not used as money. Option A is wrong because both groups are financial intermediaries, option D is wrong because bodies such as NAICOM and PenCom regulate non-bank institutions, and option C is wrong because banks lend mostly short-term.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: What basic function do bank financial institutions and non-bank financial institutions have in common?

options.a: Both issue the national currency on behalf of the Federal Government.
options.b: Both act as lenders of last resort to the banking system.
options.c: Both mobilise funds from surplus units (savers) and channel them to deficit units (borrowers and investors).
options.d: Both accept current account deposits that customers can withdraw by cheque.

questions.explanation: Banks and non-bank financial institutions are both financial intermediaries: they pool funds from those with surplus money and pass them on to those who need funds for investment or spending. Options A and B describe functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of ordinary financial institutions. Option D is a feature of deposit money banks only, which is exactly what separates them from non-bank institutions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Direct financing means that a borrower raises funds directly from fund owners, without the help of financial institutions. Which of the following is NOT a weakness of direct financing?

options.a: The fund owner is likely to charge a high price to compensate for his risk.
options.b: Much time and effort is needed to find a fund owner who is willing to lend.
options.c: Funds are usually released for only a short period, making long-term investment difficult.
options.d: The risk borne by each lender is low because funds are pooled from many savers.

questions.explanation: Pooling funds from many savers so that the risk per person is low is an advantage that financial intermediaries bring, not a feature of direct financing. Without intermediaries, a borrower must search for a willing lender (option B), pay a high price because that single lender bears all the risk (option A), and usually gets the money for only a short time (option C). These are exactly the weaknesses that financial institutions remove.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Why are savers generally more willing to entrust their funds to a financial institution than to lend directly to an individual borrower?

options.a: The institution promises every saver a share of the profits made by each of its borrowers.
options.b: The institution has a reputation to protect, pays interest and lets savers withdraw their funds when needed.
options.c: The institution is barred by law from lending out any of the funds deposited with it.
options.d: The institution guarantees that savers will never pay any charges on their accounts.

questions.explanation: Financial institutions attract funds because savers trust an established institution more than a private individual, they earn interest on money that would otherwise lie idle, and they can usually get their money back on demand, for example from a demand deposit. Option C is wrong because lending out deposits is how institutions earn their income, and options A and D promise things financial institutions do not offer.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: How do financial intermediaries mainly promote the savings-investment process and capital formation in an economy?

options.a: By printing new money and lending it directly to investors who need funds
options.b: By pooling funds from surplus units and channelling them into productive investment by deficit units
options.c: By taking ownership of every business that borrows money from them
options.d: By transferring funds from investors (deficit units) back to savers (surplus units)

questions.explanation: Financial intermediaries collect savings, including small sums that would otherwise lie idle, and use their expertise to lend them to firms and others with productive investment needs, which raises capital formation and growth. Option A is wrong because only the central bank issues currency, option D reverses the direction in which funds flow, and option C is wrong because lending does not make an intermediary the owner of the borrower's business.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following are the three main factors that make for successful financial intermediation?

options.a: Government ownership, foreign management and a large, impressive head office
options.b: Liquidity, profitability and solvency of the institution's balance sheet
options.c: Public trust and confidence, convenience of dealing with the institution, and the price of its services
options.d: High interest charges on loans, long processing times and few branches

questions.explanation: Intermediaries thrive when the public trusts that their money is safe and can be retrieved at will, when it is convenient and easy to do business with them, and when their prices, such as interest charges and fees, are reasonable. Option B lists the three goals a deposit money bank tries to balance, not the factors behind successful intermediation. Options A and D would not attract customers, and high charges and delays would actually drive them away.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When the public loses confidence in financial institutions and withdraws funds from them in large numbers, the process that follows is known as:

options.a: Bank consolidation
options.b: Credit creation

questions.explanation: Financial disintermediation happens when funds move out of financial institutions, for example when people stop trusting banks and keep their money at home. If it spreads, it can disrupt the payments system and weaken the whole economy. Credit creation (option B) is the expansion of deposits through lending, bank consolidation (option A) refers to mergers and recapitalisation, and financial deepening (option C) is the growth of the financial system, the opposite of what happens here.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of a commercial bank?

options.a: Accepting deposits from members of the public
options.b: Providing safe custody for customers' valuables and documents
options.c: Granting loans and overdrafts and discounting bills for customers
options.d: Issuing the country's legal tender currency

questions.explanation: Issuing legal tender is reserved for the Central Bank of Nigeria, so it is not a commercial bank function. Accepting deposits (option A) and granting advances such as loans, overdrafts and bill discounting (option C) are the two principal functions of a commercial bank, while safe custody (option B) is one of its ancillary services.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A trader holding an N1,000,000 trade bill that matures in three months takes it to his bank, which pays him N950,000 now and collects the full N1,000,000 at maturity. This service is known as:

options.a: Equipment leasing
options.b: A standing order

questions.explanation: In bill discounting, the bank buys a bill before it matures for less than its face value and collects the full amount at maturity; here the N50,000 difference is the bank's earning. An overdraft (option D) lets a current account holder draw more than his balance, a standing order (option B) is an instruction to make regular payments, and equipment leasing (option A) involves renting out an asset.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the capital market from the money market?

options.a: Money market instruments are generally riskier and much harder to sell quickly than capital market securities
options.b: The capital market deals in short-term instruments such as treasury bills, while the money market deals in long-term securities such as shares and bonds
options.c: The capital market mainly provides overnight funds to banks, while the money market finances long-term projects such as factories
options.d: The capital market deals in medium- to long-term funds and securities such as shares and bonds, while the money market deals in short-term instruments such as treasury bills

questions.explanation: The main difference is the maturity of the funds: the capital market mobilises medium- to long-term funds for factories, infrastructure and other long-term projects through shares, bonds and debentures, while the money market handles short-term funds through instruments like treasury bills and commercial papers. Options B and C swap the two markets, and option A is wrong because money market instruments are short-term, highly liquid and generally low-risk.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a capital market instrument rather than a money market instrument?

options.a: Debenture
options.b: Commercial paper

questions.explanation: A debenture is a long-term loan stock issued by a company, which makes it a capital market instrument, like ordinary shares and government bonds. Treasury bills, commercial papers and bankers' acceptances (options B, C and D) are all short-term instruments traded in the money market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of financial markets?

options.a: Providing protection against risk through insurance and diversification
options.b: Mobilising savings from surplus units of the economy
options.c: Issuing the country's legal tender currency
options.d: Providing liquidity by allowing financial assets to be converted into cash

questions.explanation: Issuing legal tender is the exclusive function of the central bank, not of financial markets. Financial markets mobilise savings, provide a store of wealth, liquidity and credit, support the payments system, offer protection against risk and serve as a channel for government's monetary policy, so options A, B and D are all genuine functions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The segment of the capital market in which already-issued securities are bought and sold among investors is called the:

options.a: money market
options.b: interbank market

questions.explanation: The capital market has two arms. The primary market is where new securities are issued and fresh capital flows to the issuing firm or government, while the secondary market, mainly the stock exchange, is where existing securities change hands between investors. By providing this resale outlet, the secondary market makes long-term securities liquid and more attractive. Option D deals only with new issues, and options A and B handle short-term funds.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a major benefit of a capital market to a developing economy such as Nigeria?

options.a: It removes the need for banks to lend to businesses, since firms no longer need loans
options.b: It provides banks with overnight funds to meet their daily cash and clearing needs
options.c: It guarantees investors against any fall in the prices of the shares they buy
options.d: It channels medium- to long-term funds to firms and governments for expansion and development projects

questions.explanation: Development is a long-term process that needs long-term finance, and the capital market supplies it by letting firms and governments raise funds through shares, bonds and loan stocks for factories, infrastructure and other projects. This helps domestic firms expand and supports industrialisation. Option B describes the money market, while options C and A are false, since share prices can fall and banks remain important lenders.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) are described as a 'heterogeneous' group. This means that:

options.a: all NBFIs accept demand deposits and issue cheque books to customers in the same way as commercial banks
options.b: all NBFIs are owned and run by the Federal Government through the Federal Ministry of Finance
options.c: all NBFIs perform exactly the same function, so any one of them can replace another in the financial system
options.d: the group is made up of many different kinds of institutions, such as insurers, pension fund administrators and bureaux de change, each with its own functions

questions.explanation: Heterogeneous means made up of different parts. The NBFI category groups together very different institutions: insurers pool risks, pension fund administrators manage retirement savings, mortgage institutions provide housing finance, finance houses take placements and lend, and bureaux de change deal in foreign exchange. Option C is the opposite of heterogeneous, option B is false since most are privately owned, and option A is wrong because taking demand deposits and issuing cheques is what sets banks apart from NBFIs.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes life insurance from non-life insurance?

options.a: Life insurance covers financial loss from death, disability or old age and is usually long-term, while non-life insurance covers property and liability risks such as fire and theft and is usually short-term
options.b: Non-life insurance policies usually run for twenty years or more, while life policies must be renewed every year
options.c: Life insurance requires no premium payments at all, while non-life insurance requires regular premiums
options.d: Life insurance covers fire, theft and motor accidents, while non-life insurance covers death, disability and old age

questions.explanation: Life insurance (assurance) protects the insured or their dependants against the financial effects of death, disability or old age, and policies such as endowment assurance usually run for many years. Non-life or general insurance covers property and liabilities, for example fire, theft, marine and motor risks, and policies are usually renewed yearly. Options B and D swap the two types, and option C is wrong because both types are paid for with premiums.
