questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A life policy under which the sum assured is paid at the end of an agreed period if the insured person is still alive, or to the beneficiaries if the insured dies before then, is called:

options.a: endowment assurance
options.b: marine insurance

questions.explanation: Endowment assurance combines protection with saving: the policyholder pays premiums for a fixed term and receives the sum assured at the end of it, or the beneficiaries are paid if death occurs earlier. Fire insurance (option C), marine insurance (option B) and liability insurance (option D) are all non-life policies that cover property or legal liabilities, not life.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The National Provident Fund (NPF), set up in 1961 for private-sector workers, was replaced by the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) in 1993. Which problem contributed to this?

options.a: Workers complained that its benefits were too generous for the country to afford
options.b: The fund had accumulated far more money than it could find ways to invest
options.c: Poor performance, including poor record-keeping and the failure of many employers to remit contributions
options.d: It was managed by foreign insurance companies based outside Nigeria

questions.explanation: The NPF was meant to be a compulsory savings scheme protecting workers against retirement, invalidity and death, but its performance was poor: records were badly kept and many employers deducted contributions without paying them in. After a government review, it was converted into the NSITF in 1993. Options A, B and D do not describe the NPF's real problems.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the National Pension Commission (PenCom)?

options.a: Insuring the deposits of bank customers against bank failure
options.b: Licensing and supervising Pension Fund Administrators and Pension Fund Custodians
options.d: Registering securities offered to the public on the stock exchange

questions.explanation: PenCom was created by the Pension Reform Act of 2004 to regulate and supervise pension matters in Nigeria. Its functions include formulating pension policy, licensing and supervising PFAs and PFCs, issuing regulations and guidelines, and keeping a national data bank on pensions. Option A belongs to the NDIC, option C to the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) and option D to the SEC.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Under Nigeria's contributory pension scheme, what is the main difference between a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) and a Pension Fund Custodian (PFC)?

options.a: The PFA opens and manages workers' Retirement Savings Accounts and invests the contributions, while the PFC keeps the pension fund assets in safe custody
options.b: The PFA regulates and licenses all the PFCs operating in Nigeria
options.c: There is no real difference, as the two names refer to the same institution
options.d: The PFC opens workers' Retirement Savings Accounts and invests the contributions, while the PFA only keeps the assets in custody

questions.explanation: The scheme deliberately separates management from custody. The PFA administers each worker's Retirement Savings Account, invests the contributions in permitted assets and pays retirement benefits, while the PFC holds the actual pension fund assets on behalf of the PFA, which protects contributors' money. Option D swaps the two roles, option B wrongly gives the PFA the regulator's job, which belongs to PenCom, and option C ignores the separation altogether.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Under Nigeria's contributory pension scheme, an employee opens his or her Retirement Savings Account (RSA) with:

options.a: a Pension Fund Custodian (PFC)
options.b: a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) of his or her choice

questions.explanation: Each employee chooses a PFA and opens an RSA with it; the contributions of both the employee and the employer are credited to that account, and the PFA manages and invests them. The PFC (option A) only holds the assets in custody, PenCom (option C) is the regulator, and the CBN (option D) plays no direct role in individual pension accounts.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In a defined contribution pension scheme, such as Nigeria's contributory pension scheme, what a worker receives at retirement depends mainly on:

options.a: the profit that the employer makes in the year the worker retires
options.b: the total contributions paid into the worker's Retirement Savings Account and the investment returns earned on them
options.c: an amount the government decides to pay all retirees each year, regardless of contributions
options.d: a fixed formula based on final salary and years of service, which the employer guarantees

questions.explanation: In a defined contribution scheme it is the contribution that is defined, not the benefit: the employee and employer pay set percentages into the RSA, and the final benefit depends on how much has built up and how well it was invested, so the employee bears the investment risk. Option D describes a defined benefit scheme, where the pension is fixed in advance by formula. Options A and C have nothing to do with how benefits are worked out under this scheme.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A pension plan in which the retiree's entitlement is fixed in advance by a formula based on factors such as final salary, years of service and rank is called a:

options.a: defined contribution scheme
options.b: defined benefit scheme

questions.explanation: In a defined benefit scheme the pension promised is set in advance by a formula, so the employer, not the employee, carries the investment risk of meeting that promise. In a defined contribution scheme (option A), only the contributions are fixed and the benefit depends on the fund's growth. A Retirement Savings Account (option D) is the individual account used in the contributory scheme, and an endowment assurance policy (option C) is a life insurance product.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a bureau de change from a discount house in the Nigerian financial system?

options.a: Both are deposit money banks that accept current account deposits and issue cheque books to the public
options.b: A bureau de change deals mainly in short-term government securities, while a discount house buys and sells foreign currency for travellers
options.c: A bureau de change buys and sells foreign exchange mainly for small users, while a discount house deals mainly in short-term government securities in the money market
options.d: A bureau de change trades company shares on the stock exchange, while a discount house grants long-term loans to farmers

questions.explanation: A bureau de change is a non-bank financial institution set up to deal in foreign exchange, mainly for small users such as travellers, while a discount house stands between the CBN and the banks, buying, holding and selling short-term government securities such as treasury bills. Option B simply swaps the two roles. Option A is wrong because neither is a deposit money bank, and option D confuses them with capital market and development finance institutions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the most basic determinants of the success of financial intermediaries, whose loss can lead to financial disintermediation?

options.a: Having branches located far away from customers
options.b: Charging high interest rates on loans and high handling fees
options.c: Public trust and confidence in the institutions
options.d: The number of shareholders who own the institutions

questions.explanation: Financial intermediaries thrive on the confidence of the public: once people believe their funds are safe and can be withdrawn at will, they deposit with them, and once that trust is lost, people withdraw and hoard their money instead. Other success factors are convenience, competitive prices and nearness to customers. Options B and A are the opposite of those factors, since high charges and long distances drive customers away, and option D has no direct bearing on whether the public will use the institutions.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the capital market?

options.a: A market for buying and selling medium- to long-term financial instruments such as shares and bonds
options.b: A market for short-term instruments such as treasury bills and call money
options.c: A market where foreign currencies are bought and sold by small users
options.d: The arrangement through which banks exchange cheques drawn on one another at the clearing house

questions.explanation: The capital market mobilises medium- to long-term funds, for example through shares, debentures and government bonds, to finance long-term investment. Option B describes the money market, which deals in funds of up to about one year. Option D describes the clearing system, and option C describes the work of bureaux de change in the foreign exchange market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the main purposes for introducing bureaux de change in Nigeria?

options.a: To bring the parallel (black) market under official regulation
options.b: To eliminate the parallel market premium by merging the parallel and official exchange rates
options.c: To provide large foreign exchange allocations for big corporate importers
options.d: To cater for small users of foreign exchange

questions.explanation: Bureaux de change were introduced to serve small users of foreign exchange, such as travellers, not to meet the large needs of big corporate importers. Their other purposes were to bring the parallel market into the official net so that government could regulate it, and to close the gap between the parallel and official exchange rates. Options D, A and B therefore state genuine purposes.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The word 'bank' is generally traced to the Italian word 'banco', which referred to

options.a: a strong room in which gold was stored
options.b: a receipt issued by goldsmiths for gold deposited
options.c: the bench or table on which money changers carried on their business
options.d: a temple in which valuables were kept for safety

questions.explanation: Italian money changers did their business on a bench or table, the banco, and the places where they changed money, took deposits and made loans came to be called banks. Option A describes where goldsmiths kept gold, option B describes the goldsmith's receipt that became the bank note, and option D describes how valuables were kept before banking began.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Before modern banking developed, where were gold and other valuables commonly kept for safety in places such as ancient Rome, Greece and Mesopotamia?

options.a: In central banks
options.b: In the vaults of commercial banks
options.c: In temples and other places of worship

questions.explanation: In the ancient world, temples and places of worship were trusted as safe places to keep precious metals and valuables, long before banks existed. Options A, B and D are modern institutions that came into being much later.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Goldsmiths are credited with bringing lending into banking mainly because they

options.a: were the first to issue legal tender currency on behalf of the state
options.b: were required by law to lend a fixed share of their deposits to government
options.c: charged fees for keeping gold and refused to pay interest on deposits
options.d: noticed that depositors did not all withdraw their gold at the same time, so they lent out part of the idle balances at interest

questions.explanation: Goldsmiths found that there were always balances left with them because owners did not all come for their gold at once, so they began lending these balances out at interest, which is the start of bank lending. Option A is wrong because legal tender is issued by the state or central bank, option B has no basis, and option C describes their early safe-keeping practice, not lending; they later paid interest to attract more deposits.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Goldsmiths' receipts for gold deposited with them were later accepted as a means of payment. These receipts were the forerunners of

options.a: treasury bills
options.b: bank notes

questions.explanation: As people began to pay one another with goldsmiths' receipts, the receipts came to be called goldsmiths' notes, the forerunners of the bank note. Option A is a short-term government security, option C is a bank's undertaking used in foreign trade, and option D is evidence of ownership in a company.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When a company raises funds by selling its bonds straight to households in the financial market, with no bank standing in between, this is known as

options.a: indirect finance
options.b: financial intermediation

questions.explanation: In direct finance, borrowers get funds directly from lenders by selling them financial instruments in the market. Options A and B describe the route where an intermediary such as a bank borrows from savers and then lends to borrowers, and option D refers to banks expanding deposits through lending.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the Nigerian financial system?

options.a: To achieve greater mobilisation of savings and channel them efficiently
options.b: To finance government spending without regard to its effect on inflation
options.c: To ensure that no viable project is frustrated simply for lack of funds
options.d: To assist in transforming the rural community

questions.explanation: One stated objective of the financial system is to give non-inflationary support to the economy, so financing spending with no regard to inflation runs against its goals. Options A, C and D are genuine objectives: mobilising and channelling savings, making sure viable projects get funded, and helping rural transformation.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A bank buys an accepted bill of exchange from its customer before maturity for less than its face value, and later collects the full amount from the acceptor. This service is called

options.a: debt factoring
options.b: bill discounting

questions.explanation: In bill discounting the bank pays the customer the face value less a discount and then collects the full value at maturity, the difference being its earnings. Option A is the purchase of a firm's book debts, option C is several banks lending together, and option D is crediting uncleared cheques to an account.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Debt factoring by a bank is essentially

options.a: the lending of money by a group of banks to one large borrower
options.b: the hiring of equipment to a customer for regular rentals
options.c: the purchase of a customer's book debts at an agreed discount, after which the bank collects from the debtors
options.d: the crediting of uncleared cheques to a customer's account

questions.explanation: Factoring is the sale of book debts: the bank pays the customer an agreed part of their value and then collects directly from the debtors. Option A describes loan syndication, option B describes equipment leasing, and option D describes direct credit.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When a lead bank brings together several banks to jointly finance a large project that no single bank could conveniently fund, this is known as

options.a: equipment leasing
options.b: bill discounting

questions.explanation: In loan syndication a lead bank organises a group of banks to share a big loan, often long-term, for a large corporate or government project. Option A is hiring out assets for rentals, option B is buying bills before maturity, and option C is buying a firm's book debts.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The basic distinction between bank and non-bank financial intermediaries is that

options.a: only non-bank intermediaries accept funds from the public
options.b: the liabilities of banks, such as demand deposits, can be spent as money, while the liabilities of non-bank intermediaries cannot
options.c: banks are unregulated, while non-bank intermediaries are regulated
options.d: non-bank intermediaries can create deposits through lending, while banks cannot

questions.explanation: Bank deposits can be used as a means of payment, for example by cheque, while claims on non-bank intermediaries such as insurance policies cannot; this is also why banks can create credit and non-banks really cannot. Option A is wrong because banks accept deposits too, option C is wrong because banks are closely regulated, and option D reverses the credit creation point.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Insurance companies perform two major functions in the economy. These are

options.a: risk transfer and financial intermediation
options.b: currency issue and credit control
options.d: cheque clearing and foreign exchange allocation

questions.explanation: Insurers pool the premiums of many people to cover the losses of a few (risk transfer) and invest the pooled funds in the economy (financial intermediation). Option B describes the central bank, option C describes merchant and commercial banking services, and option D describes the payment and foreign exchange systems.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Why do life insurance companies tend to invest in long-term assets, while non-life insurers keep most of their funds in short-term securities?

options.a: Life insurers are not allowed to buy treasury bills
options.b: Non-life insurers collect much larger premiums than life insurers
options.c: Life insurance is regulated by the CBN, while non-life insurance is not
options.d: Life policies run for long periods, while non-life policies are usually renewed every year

questions.explanation: Insurers match their investments to the length of their liabilities: life policies can run for twenty years or more, so their funds go into long-term investments, while motor, fire and similar policies last about a year. Options A, B and C do not explain the difference and are not true.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is a typical service of a finance company in Nigeria?

options.a: Local purchase order (LPO) financing
options.b: Issuing legal tender currency
options.c: Acting as lender of last resort to banks
options.d: Clearing cheques for deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Finance companies provide services such as LPO financing, equipment leasing, hire purchase, debt factoring and project financing to consumers and businesses. Options B and C are functions of the central bank, and option D is done through the clearing system run for the banks.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Bureaux de change were licensed in Nigeria as a segment of the foreign exchange market mainly in order to:

options.a: Grant medium- and long-term loans to exporters
options.b: Trade treasury bills and other short-term government securities
options.c: Supply foreign exchange in bulk to banks and the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: Retail foreign exchange to small users and reduce the pressure on the official market

questions.explanation: Bureaux de change give small buyers, such as travellers, easy and legal access to foreign currency, and this takes some demand off the official market. They were expected to get their foreign exchange from private suppliers, not to supply banks or the CBN (C). Lending to exporters (A) is bank business, and trading treasury bills (B) is what discount houses do.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the objectives for licensing bureaux de change in Nigeria?

options.a: To accept savings deposits and grant overdrafts to small businesses
options.b: To improve the statistical coverage of foreign exchange flows for better economic management
options.c: To give small buyers free and convenient access to foreign exchange
options.d: To give legal recognition to small dealers in foreign exchange

questions.explanation: A bureau de change only buys and sells foreign currency, so it does not take deposits or grant loans. Legal recognition for small dealers (D), easy access for small buyers (C) and better data on foreign exchange flows (B) were all reasons for licensing them.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a unit trust from a discount house in Nigeria?

options.a: Both are deposit money banks licensed to operate current accounts
options.b: A unit trust pools the funds of many small savers and invests them in a diversified portfolio of securities, while a discount house deals mainly in short-term money market instruments
options.c: A unit trust deals mainly in treasury bills for banks, while a discount house invests small savers' funds in shares
options.d: A unit trust lends mainly to farmers, while a discount house finances housing

questions.explanation: A unit trust is a collective investment scheme: it sells units to small investors and spreads the pooled money across many securities, so each saver gets diversification. A discount house works in the short-term money market with instruments such as treasury bills. Option C swaps the two roles, and A and D describe neither institution.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A financial market can best be defined as:

options.a: A market in which only the Central Bank of Nigeria buys and sells goods
options.b: The department of a bank that handles customers' complaints
options.c: A set of institutional arrangements that brings together surplus and deficit units so that funds can be channelled from savers to users
options.d: A physical building where only bank notes and coins are exchanged

questions.explanation: A financial market is about intermediating funds: it mobilises savings from surplus units and passes them to deficit units for productive use, creating financial assets in the process. It is a network of arrangements and does not need to be a single building (D), and many participants trade in it, not just the CBN (A). Option B has nothing to do with markets.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: What is the difference between the primary market and the secondary market in the financial system?

options.a: The primary market is for government securities only, while the secondary market is for company shares only
options.b: The primary market deals only in short-term funds, while the secondary market deals only in long-term funds
options.c: The primary market is for raising new funds through new issues, while the secondary market is for buying and selling existing securities
options.d: The primary market is controlled by commercial banks, while the secondary market is controlled by insurance companies

questions.explanation: Both the money market and the capital market have primary and secondary segments. New securities are sold and fresh funds raised in the primary market, and existing securities change hands in the secondary market. Option B confuses this with the money market versus capital market split, and A and D invent restrictions that do not exist.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The basic difference between the money market and the capital market is that:

options.a: The money market deals in short-term funds and instruments, while the capital market deals in long-term funds and instruments
options.b: The money market is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission, while the capital market is regulated by the NDIC
options.c: The money market is for individuals only, while the capital market is for companies only
options.d: The money market deals only in foreign currency, while the capital market deals only in naira

questions.explanation: The main distinction is the term and liquidity of the funds. The money market handles short-term, highly liquid claims used for liquidity adjustment, and the capital market channels savings into long-term investment. Both markets serve individuals, firms and governments, so C is wrong. Option B mixes up the regulators, since the CBN oversees the money market and SEC the capital market, and D confuses either market with the foreign exchange market.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A manufacturing company needs funds to build a new factory that will be repaid over 15 years. The most appropriate market to raise these funds is the:

options.a: Inter-bank call money market
options.b: Capital market

questions.explanation: A 15-year project needs long-term finance, and long-term funds, for example through shares or bonds, are raised in the capital market. The money market (C) and the inter-bank call market (A) deal in short-term funds that would have to be repaid long before the factory starts paying for itself. The foreign exchange market (D) is for buying and selling currencies.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The main intermediation role of deposit money banks in the economy is to:

options.a: Mobilise savings from surplus units and channel them as loans to deficit units for productive investment
options.b: Collect taxes on behalf of the government
options.c: Regulate the activities of other banks
options.d: Print currency notes for use by the public

questions.explanation: Financial intermediation means standing between savers and borrowers: banks take deposits from people and firms with spare funds and lend to those who need funds to invest. Printing currency (D) and regulating banks (C) are central bank functions, and tax collection (B) belongs to the tax authorities, even though banks may sometimes collect revenue as agents.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Deposit money banks can finance long-term investments even though many savers deposit money only for short periods. This role is best described as:

options.a: Credit rationing
options.b: Monetary policy formulation
options.d: Bridging different maturity (capital lock-up) periods between savers and borrowers

questions.explanation: Because a bank pools deposits from many customers, it can rely on a stable core of funds and lend for longer periods than any single depositor is willing to commit. This is often called maturity transformation. Credit rationing (A) means restricting loans, window dressing (C) means making accounts look better than they are, and monetary policy (B) is the CBN's job.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Financial inclusion can best be defined as:

options.a: Merging small banks into a few large banks
options.b: Ensuring that all sections of society, especially low-income and vulnerable groups, have access to appropriate and affordable financial products and services
options.c: Requiring every bank to open branches outside Nigeria
options.d: Including all banks in the stock exchange's list of quoted companies

questions.explanation: Financial inclusion is about access: people, including the poor and those in rural areas, should be able to use regulated services such as savings accounts, payments, credit and insurance at a fair cost. Listing banks on the exchange (D), opening foreign branches (C) and consolidation (A) are unrelated policies.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following would most directly help to bring more financially excluded Nigerians into the formal financial system?

options.a: Requiring collateral for every small savings account
options.b: Closing bank branches in rural areas
options.c: Expanding agent banking, mobile money and simple low-cost accounts in rural and underserved areas
options.d: Raising the minimum opening balance for savings accounts

questions.explanation: People are excluded mainly because of distance, cost and complicated requirements, so bringing cheap, simple services closer to them through agents, mobile channels and easy accounts increases inclusion. Higher opening balances (D), closing rural branches (B) and demanding collateral (A) would all push more people out of the system.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes financial innovation from globalisation?

options.a: Financial innovation is the creation of new financial products, services or processes, while globalisation is the growing interconnection of countries through flows of goods, services, finance, people and ideas
options.b: Both terms mean the same thing: the merger of banks across borders
options.c: Financial innovation refers only to printing new currency notes, while globalisation refers only to foreign aid
options.d: Financial innovation is the removal of trade barriers between countries, while globalisation is the creation of new bank products

questions.explanation: Financial innovation is about new things in finance, such as mobile and internet banking, POS payments and new instruments. Globalisation is the wider process of countries becoming linked and interdependent across borders. Option D swaps the two definitions, B wrongly treats them as the same, and C gives definitions that are far too narrow.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: During a sudden wave of withdrawals, a sound Nigerian commercial bank runs short of cash and obtains emergency funds from the Central Bank of Nigeria to meet its depositors' demands. In doing this, the CBN is acting as

options.a: manager of the country's external reserves
options.b: banker and financial adviser to the government
options.c: sole issuer of legal tender currency
options.d: lender of last resort to the banks

questions.explanation: A central bank is the lender of last resort when it provides emergency funds to banks that cannot raise cash elsewhere, especially during a crisis, so that panic does not spread. Option B refers to the CBN's services to the government, not to banks. Options A and C are genuine central bank functions, but neither describes lending to a bank in distress.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional (core) functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: Acting as banker and financial adviser to the federal government
options.b: Accepting savings deposits from and granting loans to members of the public
options.c: Issuing legal tender currency notes and coins in Nigeria
options.d: Maintaining external reserves to safeguard the international value of the naira

questions.explanation: A central bank does not deal with individual customers; taking deposits from and lending to the public is the work of deposit money banks. Options A, C and D are all part of the CBN's core mandate, together with promoting monetary stability and a sound financial system.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Unlike a commercial bank, an investment bank earns its income mainly from

options.a: fees for advisory and underwriting services, commissions on securities trading and profits on its own investments
options.b: the issue of currency notes and coins
options.c: the interest rate spread between loans and customer deposits
options.d: premiums collected from policyholders against stated risks

questions.explanation: Investment banks focus on capital market work, so their income comes from fees, commissions and trading profits rather than from deposit-taking and lending. Option C is where most of a commercial bank's income comes from, not an investment bank. Option B belongs to the central bank and option D describes an insurance company.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: An investment bank agrees to buy the whole of a company's new issue of shares at an agreed price and then resells the shares to investors, bearing the risk of any unsold shares. This service is called

options.a: asset management
options.b: debt factoring

questions.explanation: Underwriting is the process by which an investment bank assesses and prices a new issue of securities, buys it from the issuer and resells it to investors, helping the company raise capital. Option D is a bank buying a bill before maturity at less than face value, and option B is buying a firm's trade debts. Option A means managing investment portfolios for clients, not taking up a new issue.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A member-owned, not-for-profit financial cooperative in which the members are both the owners and the customers, and which usually offers better savings rates and lower fees than commercial banks, is a

options.a: development bank
options.b: discount house

questions.explanation: A credit union is a financial cooperative owned by its members, who also use its savings and loan services; because it does not aim at profit, it can pay better rates and charge lower fees. Option D is a profit-making bank serving mainly corporate clients, option A is a government-sponsored lender for long-term development projects, and option B deals mainly in short-term money market instruments.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Mama Ngozi, a petty trader in Onitsha with no account in any commercial bank, opens a small savings account and later obtains a N50,000 loan to expand her stall from an institution set up to serve low-income people and small businesses. This institution is most likely a

options.a: merchant bank
options.b: development bank

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks provide small loans, savings accounts and financial literacy to low-income people and small businesses who lack access to traditional banks, which is exactly Mama Ngozi's case. Option B provides long-term finance for large development projects such as infrastructure and industry. Options A and C serve corporations and big investors, not petty traders.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Chidi places N2,000,000 with his bank for 12 months at an interest rate agreed at the start, and is told that he will lose part of the interest if he withdraws before the end of the period. Chidi has opened a

options.a: fixed (time) deposit account
options.b: current (demand) deposit account

questions.explanation: A fixed or time deposit is kept for a predetermined period at a fixed rate, earns higher interest than a savings account, and attracts a penalty for early withdrawal. Option B can be withdrawn at any time without notice and earns little or no interest. Option D allows withdrawals with only some restrictions, and option C is a loan facility, not a deposit.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Bisi's current account has a credit balance of N100,000 and her bank has approved an overdraft limit of N500,000. She withdraws N400,000. On what amount will the bank charge overdraft interest?
questions.explanation: Overdraft interest is charged only on the amount actually overdrawn: N400,000 withdrawn minus her own N100,000 balance leaves N300,000 overdrawn. Option B wrongly charges interest on her own money as well, and option A is the approved limit, not the amount used. Option D is her credit balance, which earns no overdraft charge at all.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In one year a Nigerian bank earns 20% interest on loans of N800 million and pays 8% interest on deposits of N1,000 million. What is its net interest income for the year?

options.a: N120 million
options.b: N96 million

questions.explanation: Net interest income is interest earned minus interest paid: 20% of N800 million is N160 million, 8% of N1,000 million is N80 million, so the bank keeps N80 million. Option B applies the 12% rate gap to loans only and option A applies it to deposits only, ignoring that the two balances differ. Option C adds the two interest figures instead of subtracting.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: After severe floods destroy crops in a farming area, many farmers who borrowed from a rural bank are unable to repay their loans. The risk the bank has suffered is

options.a: credit risk
options.b: interest rate risk

questions.explanation: Credit risk is the risk that borrowers will default on their loans, and banks reduce it through careful credit assessment, collateral and spreading loans across many sectors. Option D is the risk of being unable to meet short-term obligations such as withdrawals. Option C arises from internal failures such as fraud or system breakdown, and option B comes from changes in interest rates.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A profitable bank has lent most of its funds on long-term mortgages and, when many depositors come to withdraw on the same day, it does not have enough cash to pay them. This situation illustrates

options.a: market risk
options.b: liquidity risk

questions.explanation: Liquidity risk is the risk of being unable to meet short-term obligations because there are not enough liquid assets, which is why banks keep reserves and liquidity buffers. Option D would require the borrowers to default, which has not happened here. Option A concerns losses from changes in market prices, and option C concerns fraud, error or system failure.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A bank loses N45 million when a cashier collaborates with fraudsters and its computer system fails to flag the suspicious transfers. This type of risk is

options.a: interest rate risk
options.b: liquidity risk

questions.explanation: Operational risk arises from inadequate internal processes, human error, fraud or system failure, and is controlled through strong internal controls and technology. Option D is about borrowers failing to repay, option B is about shortage of cash to meet obligations, and option A is about adverse changes in interest rates; none of these caused this loss.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: In banking regulation, capital adequacy refers to the requirement that a bank must

options.a: maintain a minimum level of capital relative to its risk-weighted assets
options.b: insure all its deposits with the deposit insurance corporation
options.c: keep a fixed percentage of its deposits with the central bank as cash reserves
options.d: lend a minimum share of its loans to priority sectors

questions.explanation: Capital adequacy rules, set out in the Basel Accords, require a bank to hold enough capital in proportion to its risk-weighted assets so that it can absorb losses and protect depositors. Option C describes reserve requirements, which deal with liquidity rather than capital. Option B describes deposit insurance and option D describes sectoral credit allocation.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A regulation requiring banks to disclose all their charges clearly to customers and to provide a system for resolving customer complaints is an example of

options.a: monetary policy regulation
options.b: prudential regulation

questions.explanation: Consumer protection regulation ensures fair treatment of bank customers through transparent fees, truth in lending, disclosure and complaint resolution. Option B focuses on the safety and soundness of each bank through capital, asset quality and liquidity rules, and option C is one part of that prudential framework. Option A concerns reserve ratios and interest rate guidelines set for macroeconomic aims.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The main purpose of a deposit insurance scheme such as the one run by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) is to

options.a: insure banks against losses on all the loans they grant
options.b: protect depositors up to a certain limit if a bank fails, so as to prevent bank runs and maintain confidence
options.c: guarantee that every bank makes a profit each year
options.d: provide long-term loans to the federal government

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance pays depositors up to a stated limit when an insured bank fails; knowing this, depositors are less likely to rush to withdraw, so bank runs are prevented and confidence is kept. Option C is wrong because insurance does not guarantee profits, and option A confuses deposit insurance with protection of the bank's loan book. Option D has nothing to do with deposit insurance.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Financial instruments are commonly grouped as equity, debt, derivative and hybrid instruments. Which of the following is a hybrid instrument?

options.a: A treasury bill
options.b: An ordinary share

questions.explanation: A hybrid instrument combines features of debt and equity; a convertible bond pays interest like debt but can later be converted into shares. Option B is a pure equity instrument and option A is a short-term debt instrument. Option C is a derivative, whose value depends on an underlying asset.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: A Nigerian manufacturing company raises N5 billion by selling its bonds directly to households and firms through the capital market, without borrowing from a bank. This method of moving funds from savers to the borrower is

options.a: financial disintermediation
options.b: direct finance

questions.explanation: In direct finance, borrowers obtain funds straight from lenders in the financial markets by selling them financial instruments such as bonds or shares. Option C would involve an intermediary such as a bank borrowing from savers and then lending to the company. Option A is the mass withdrawal of funds from financial institutions, and option D is the multiple expansion of deposits by banks.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which body regulates insurance business in Nigeria?

options.a: National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)
options.b: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)

questions.explanation: NAICOM is the financial authority that regulates and supervises insurance companies in Nigeria. Option D regulates the capital market and option C regulates pension schemes. Option B insures bank deposits and complements the CBN in supervising banks; despite its name, it does not regulate insurance companies.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the stated objectives of the Nigerian financial system?

options.a: To cut the economy off completely from international trade
options.b: To guarantee a loan to every applicant whether or not the project is viable
options.c: To ensure that no viable project is frustrated simply for lack of funds
options.d: To replace private savings entirely with government funding

questions.explanation: A key objective of the financial system is to mobilise savings and channel them so that sound, viable projects are not abandoned merely because funds are lacking. Option B goes too far, since only viable projects are meant to be financed. Option A is wrong because the aim is to protect the economy from the ups and downs of the international economy, not to isolate it, and option D contradicts the aim of mobilising savings.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an IOU from a promissory note?

options.a: An IOU must always carry interest, while a promissory note never carries interest
options.b: A promissory note is an informal acknowledgement of debt, while an IOU is an order to a bank to pay
options.c: An IOU is negotiable and can be traded in the open market, while a promissory note cannot be transferred
options.d: A promissory note is a negotiable instrument that can be transferred to another person, while an IOU is an informal acknowledgement of debt that is not negotiable

questions.explanation: The key difference is negotiability: a promissory note can be assigned, transferred or sold, while an IOU simply records that a debt exists and cannot be traded. Option C reverses the two. Option A is wrong because an IOU may be with or without interest, and option B wrongly describes an IOU as an order to a bank, which is closer to a cheque.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: When a non-bank financial intermediary buys long-term primary securities from borrowers and in turn offers savers its own indirect securities with different, often shorter, maturities, it is performing

options.a: credit creation through deposit expansion
options.b: financial disintermediation

questions.explanation: Securities or maturity transformation means altering the maturities of primary securities by holding them and issuing indirect securities with various maturities that suit savers. Option D is a related but different service, the collecting of many small savings into one pool. Option B is the withdrawal of funds from intermediaries, and option A is associated mainly with banks, whose deposit liabilities can be spent as money.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Why are the funds of non-life insurance business usually invested in short-term assets such as treasury bills and deposits, while life insurance funds are invested long-term?

options.a: Non-life policies are usually for one year, so the liabilities are short, while life policies run for many years, so the liabilities are long
options.b: Non-life insurers earn no premium income and must stay fully liquid
options.c: Life insurance premiums are paid only once, at the start of the policy
options.d: Non-life insurers are forbidden by law to hold any long-term assets

questions.explanation: Insurers match their investments to the length of their liabilities: non-life covers such as motor and fire are usually renewed yearly, while life and endowment policies may run for twenty years or more. Option D overstates the position, since non-life insurers only rarely hold long-term investments. Options B and C are not true descriptions of how premiums are paid or earned.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: The Bank of Industry (BOI) was formed in 2001 by merging three earlier institutions. Which of the following was one of them?

options.a: Nigerian Industrial Development Bank (NIDB)
options.b: Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Bank of Industry was reconstructed from the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank, the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry and the National Economic Reconstruction Fund (NERFUND). Option D was merged into the agricultural bank that later became the Bank of Agriculture. Option C became the Infrastructure Bank, and option B still exists as the mortgage bank.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Before the shift to market-based monetary management in Nigeria, the CBN relied on direct control instruments. Which of the following is NOT a direct control instrument?

options.a: Credit ceilings on bank lending
options.b: Open market operations in treasury bills

questions.explanation: Open market operations are an indirect, market-based instrument: the central bank buys or sells securities and lets the market adjust bank reserves and interest rates. Options A, C and D are direct controls, because the authority itself fixes how much banks lend, to whom, and at what rate.

questions.topic: The Business of Banking and the Financial System
questions.question: Most of a bank's depositors keep their money with it for only a few months, yet the bank is able to grant a manufacturer a five-year loan for new machinery. This shows that deposit money banks

options.a: remove the need for savers to be paid any interest
options.b: bridge the gap between the short periods for which savers commit funds and the longer periods investors need
options.c: lend only the bank's own share capital to investors
options.d: create legal tender currency for long-term investors

questions.explanation: Because deposits keep flowing in and out while the total stays fairly stable, a bank can turn many short-term deposits into longer-term loans, bridging differing capital blocking periods. Option D is wrong because only the central bank issues currency. Option A is false, since savers still earn interest, and option C ignores that loans are funded mainly from deposits.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of the barter system?

options.a: Indivisibility of some goods
options.b: Difficulty in making deferred payments
options.c: Inflation caused by over-issue of currency
options.d: Lack of double coincidence of wants

questions.explanation: Barter involves no currency at all, so it cannot suffer from inflation caused by issuing too much money; that problem belongs to money economies. Option D is the most serious weakness of barter, since each trader must find someone who has what he wants and wants what he has. Indivisibility (option A) and the difficulty of arranging future payments (option B) are also genuine limitations of barter.

questions.question: A cattle owner wants to obtain a few bags of salt worth far less than one cow, but the cow cannot be split without destroying its value. This illustrates which limitation of barter?

options.a: Lack of double coincidence of wants
options.b: Indivisibility of goods
options.c: Lack of a standard of deferred payment

questions.explanation: Indivisibility means some goods cannot be broken into smaller units without losing their value, so they cannot be used for smaller exchanges; a live cow is the classic example. Option A would apply if the salt seller did not want a cow, which is a different problem. Option D concerns perishable goods losing value over time, and option C concerns arranging payments in the future, neither of which is the issue here.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of money?

options.a: Keeping the general price level constant at all times
options.b: Medium of exchange

questions.explanation: Keeping prices constant is not something money does; prices can rise and erode the purchasing power of money, and price stability is a goal of monetary policy rather than a function of money. Medium of exchange (option B), unit of account (option D) and store of value (option C) are all recognised functions of money, together with standard of deferred payment.

questions.question: When a borrower agrees to repay a bank loan in fixed naira amounts over the next five years, money is serving as a

options.a: standard of deferred payment
options.b: store of value

questions.explanation: Money acts as a standard of deferred payment when debts and contracts to be settled in the future are expressed and paid in money, as in a loan repaid in naira over five years. Option C is related, since the loan is stated in naira, but unit of account refers to pricing and comparing values, while the function that covers future settlement of debts is the standard of deferred payment. Option D applies to buying and selling now, and option B applies to holding money to spend later.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of near money?

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Demand deposits on current accounts
options.c: Currency notes held by the public

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are near money because they can be converted into cash quickly and with little loss, yet they are not themselves generally accepted as a means of payment. Options C and D are cash, which is money proper. Option B, current account deposits, can be spent directly by cheque or transfer, so they are counted as money rather than near money.

questions.question: Near money (quasi-money) is best described as

options.a: financial assets that can be converted into cash quickly with little or no loss but are not generally accepted as a medium of exchange
options.b: foreign currencies held by the central bank as external reserves
options.c: assets such as currency and coins that are generally accepted in payment for goods and services
options.d: money issued by the government that has no intrinsic value

questions.explanation: Near money includes assets such as savings and time deposits, treasury bills and bills of exchange: they are highly liquid stores of value, but people do not normally use them directly to pay for goods. Option C describes money proper, which is generally accepted as a medium of exchange. Option D describes fiat money, and option B describes external reserves, which are a different concept.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way in which money facilitates economic activity?

options.a: Promoting specialisation and division of labour
options.b: Making it necessary for each household to produce all the goods it needs
options.c: Eliminating the need for a double coincidence of wants

questions.explanation: Money does the opposite of forcing self-sufficiency: because goods can be sold for money and the money used to buy other goods, people can specialise in what they do best. Removing the need for a double coincidence of wants (option C), encouraging savings and investment (option D) and promoting specialisation and division of labour (option A) are all ways money makes the economy work better.

questions.question: Other things being equal, which of the following would most likely INCREASE the money supply?

options.a: A greater public preference for holding cash rather than bank deposits
options.b: A reduction in the cash reserve ratio by the central bank
options.c: An increase in the cash reserve ratio by the central bank
options.d: Sale of treasury bills by the central bank to banks through open market operations

questions.explanation: A lower cash reserve ratio frees up reserves that banks can lend, and as loans are redeposited the banking system creates more deposits, so the money supply rises. Option C has the opposite effect because banks must lock up more reserves. Option D withdraws reserves from banks when they pay for the securities, and option A leaves less cash in the banking system to support new lending, so both reduce the money supply.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the origin of money?

options.a: Money was created at a single point in time by one government decree and has not changed form since
options.b: Money arose because barter made it too easy to store wealth
options.c: Money is a social invention that evolved gradually to overcome the inefficiencies of barter
options.d: Money developed only after commercial banks had been established

questions.explanation: Money was not invented in one moment; societies gradually adopted commonly accepted commodities, then metals, paper and bank money, all to escape the problems of barter such as the double coincidence of wants. Option A ignores this long evolution through many forms. Option D reverses the order, since money in forms such as cowries and metal coins existed long before modern banks, and option B is wrong because barter made storing wealth difficult, not easy.

questions.question: Money is best defined as

options.a: any commodity that has intrinsic value
options.b: any financial asset that earns interest
options.c: anything that is generally acceptable as a means of payment for goods and services and in settlement of debts
options.d: only the currency and coins issued by the central bank

questions.explanation: What makes something money is general acceptability: if people widely accept it in exchange for goods and services and to settle debts, it functions as money, whether it is cowries, coins, paper currency or bank deposits. Option D is too narrow, because bank deposits are also money. Option A describes commodity money only, and option B is wrong because many interest-earning assets, such as treasury bills, are near money rather than money.

questions.question: Which pair is usually classified as the primary functions of money?

options.a: Medium of exchange and store of value
options.b: Store of value and standard of deferred payment
options.c: Standard of deferred payment and measure of value
options.d: Medium of exchange and measure of value

questions.explanation: Medium of exchange and measure of value (unit of account) are called primary functions because they are the basic jobs money must perform in any economy. Option B lists the secondary functions, which build on the primary ones. Options A and C each mix one primary function with one secondary function, so neither is the correct pair.

questions.question: The direct exchange of goods and services for other goods and services without the use of money is called

options.a: credit sale
options.b: cheque clearing

questions.explanation: Barter is the oldest form of trade, in which goods are swapped directly for other goods, such as yams for fish, with no money involved. Options C and A are ways of buying goods with money paid later or in instalments. Option B is the process by which banks settle cheques drawn on one another.

questions.question: Money supply refers to

options.a: the total stock of money held by the public in an economy at a particular point in time
options.b: the amount of money the government spends in a year
options.c: the total amount of currency printed by the central bank since it was established
options.d: the total amount of money that households wish to hold

questions.explanation: Money supply is a stock measured at a point in time, made up of currency in the hands of the public and bank deposits. Option C is wrong because much of the currency ever printed has been withdrawn or destroyed, and currency is only one part of the money supply. Option B describes government expenditure, which is a flow over a period, and option D describes the demand for money rather than its supply.

questions.question: Narrow money (M1) consists of

options.a: demand deposits plus treasury bills held by banks
options.b: currency held by the public plus demand deposits with commercial banks
options.c: cash held in bank vaults plus banks' reserves with the central bank
options.d: currency held by the public plus savings and time deposits

questions.explanation: Narrow money covers the most liquid forms of money that are used directly for payments: currency in the hands of the public and demand deposits that can be spent by cheque or transfer. Option D wrongly includes savings and time deposits, which are added only in broad money. Option A includes treasury bills, which are near money, and option C lists bank reserves, which are not money held by the public.

questions.question: In an economy, currency held by the public is N600 billion, demand deposits are N1,400 billion and savings and time deposits are N1,100 billion. What is the narrow money supply (M1)?

options.a: N3,100 billion
options.b: N1,700 billion

questions.explanation: M1 is currency with the public plus demand deposits, so N600 billion + N1,400 billion = N2,000 billion. Option A also adds savings and time deposits, which gives broad money (M2), not M1. Option D counts demand deposits alone, and option B wrongly adds currency to savings and time deposits.

questions.question: In a barter economy, 'double coincidence of wants' means that

options.a: each party to an exchange must have what the other wants and want what the other has at the same time
options.b: two people must want the same good at the same time
options.c: both parties must agree on a price expressed in money
options.d: goods must always be exchanged in equal quantities

questions.explanation: Double coincidence of wants means both sides of a barter deal must match: you must want what I have and I must want what you have, at the same time. Option B describes two people wanting the same good, which is not the matching problem barter faces. Option D is wrong because barter rates can be unequal, and option C is wrong because barter involves no money.

questions.question: A yam farmer wants shoes, but the only shoemaker nearby wants fish, not yams. Under barter, the trade cannot take place mainly because of

options.a: the absence of a standard of deferred payment
options.b: the difficulty of storing value
options.d: the lack of a double coincidence of wants

questions.explanation: The shoemaker has what the farmer wants, but the farmer does not have what the shoemaker wants, so there is no double coincidence of wants and no direct exchange can happen. Option C would apply if the goods could not be split into the right quantities, and option B concerns goods losing value over time. Option A concerns payments to be made in the future, which is not the issue here.

questions.question: Fiat money is best described as

options.a: paper money that can be converted into gold on demand
options.b: money created only by commercial banks in the form of deposits
options.c: money whose value as money equals the value of the metal it contains
options.d: money that is accepted because the government has declared it legal tender, though it has no intrinsic value and is not backed by a commodity

questions.explanation: Fiat money gets its value from government decree and public confidence rather than from what it is made of; the naira today is an example. Option C describes full-bodied commodity money such as gold coins, and option A describes representative or convertible paper money. Option B describes bank deposit money, which is created by banks rather than declared legal tender by the government.

questions.question: Legal tender money is also described as fiat money because

options.a: it is issued by commercial banks rather than the government
options.b: it must be accepted in payment of debts by order of the government
options.c: it is fully backed by gold held by the central bank
options.d: it is accepted only on the basis of personal trust between the parties

questions.explanation: Fiat means 'let it be done', and legal tender is money that the law, on the government's order, says must be accepted in settlement of debts. Option C is wrong because modern legal tender is not backed by gold. Option D describes money accepted voluntarily on trust, which people may refuse, and option A is wrong because legal tender currency is issued by the central monetary authority, not commercial banks.

questions.question: Fiduciary money derives its acceptability mainly from

options.a: trust or confidence in the issuer rather than from any intrinsic value
options.b: its convertibility into gold on demand
options.c: the value of the metal it contains
options.d: the scarcity of the commodity from which it is made

questions.explanation: The word fiduciary comes from the Latin for trust: fiduciary money is accepted because people have confidence that the issuer will honour it, not because the material it is made of is valuable. Option C describes full-bodied commodity money, and option B describes representative or convertible money backed by gold. Option D also points to commodity value, which fiduciary money does not rely on.

questions.question: Money that the law of a country declares must be accepted in settlement of debts, such as the naira currency issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria, is called:

options.a: Commodity money
options.b: Legal tender money

questions.explanation: Legal tender is money that the law says must be accepted in settlement of debts, so a creditor cannot lawfully refuse it; in Nigeria the naira currency issued by the CBN has this status. Option D is the opposite case: money accepted by custom or habit without legal backing. Option C covers assets like time deposits and Treasury bills that can be turned into money but are not themselves legal tender, while option A is money valued for the material it is made of.

questions.question: A trader borrows N500,000 today and agrees to repay N550,000 in two years' time. Which function of money makes it possible to contract this debt now and settle it in money later?

options.a: Transfer of value
options.b: Store of value

questions.explanation: Money acts as a standard of deferred payment when debts are agreed today and repaid in money later, as with loans, bonds and hire purchase; it is one of the secondary functions of money, together with store of value and transfer of value. Option B is about holding wealth in money to spend in the future, not about settling a debt. Option D describes money being used to buy and sell goods on the spot, and option A refers to moving purchasing power from one person or place to another.

questions.question: A barter economy can be defined as:

options.a: An economy where shoes are used as means of exchange
options.b: An economy where goods and services are exchanged for each other directly
options.c: An economy where money is not in use

questions.explanation: A barter economy is one in which goods and services are exchanged directly for one another, which happens because money is not in use, so B and C together give the definition. Option A is wrong because if shoes were generally used as a means of exchange they would be serving as commodity money, not barter. B on its own is true but incomplete, which is why D is the best answer.

questions.question: A basic feature of a barter economy is:

options.a: A producer produces almost all of his needs himself
options.b: The level of surplus is limited
options.c: A producer directly exchanges his products for others' products

questions.explanation: In a barter economy each producer makes almost everything he needs himself, so production and surplus are limited, and whatever he lacks he gets by directly swapping his own goods for someone else's. Options A, B and C each describe one of these features, so picking any single one leaves out the others; D is the best answer.

questions.question: Which statement about relative prices in a barter economy is correct?

options.a: A barter economy needs only one price for each good, just like a money economy
options.b: A barter economy needs fewer relative prices than a money economy
options.c: A barter economy needs a very large number of relative prices, because every good must be valued in terms of every other good
options.d: Relative prices do not exist in a barter economy because goods are swapped directly

questions.explanation: Without a common unit of account, each good must be priced against every other good, so with 1,000 goods there are almost 500,000 exchange ratios to know, and gathering this information wastes time and resources. Options A and B describe the opposite situation, since it is money that reduces the task to one price per good. Option D is wrong because every direct swap still involves an exchange ratio, which is a relative price.

questions.question: That a carpenter who has a table to sell and needs a pair of trousers must necessarily locate a tailor who not only has a pair of trousers to sell but also needs a table creates what is known as:

options.a: Asymmetric problem
options.b: Asymptotic problem

questions.explanation: Barter works only if each trader wants exactly what the other has to offer at the same time, and this requirement is called the double coincidence of wants; the carpenter must find a tailor who both has trousers and wants a table. Options A and B are technical-sounding terms that have nothing to do with this exchange problem, and D is wrong because C names it correctly.

questions.question: Among the many problems or limitations of barter is the fact that:

options.a: Tremendous time is wasted hunting for who needs what one has and has what one needs
options.b: Much cost is involved in trying to gather information as to who needs what
options.c: Divisibility of goods to the proportion needed can sometimes be impossible

questions.explanation: Barter wastes time searching for a trading partner with matching wants, costs a lot in gathering information about who needs what and at what rate, and runs into trouble when goods such as a cow cannot be divided into the small quantities needed. Each of options A, B and C is a genuine limitation, so D is the best answer.

questions.question: Attempts to reduce the cost of transactions under barter create two fresh additional costs, these are:

options.a: Opportunity cost or waiting cost, and storage cost
options.b: Storage cost and advertisement cost

questions.explanation: To avoid searching for a partner every time, a producer may stockpile his output until the surplus is large enough to trade, and this creates two new costs: the waiting or opportunity cost of satisfaction given up while he waits, and the cost of storing the goods. Options B and C each pair one of these with a cost, advertising or marketing, that is not what arises here. D is wrong because A names both costs correctly.

questions.question: A major advantage of a money-economy is:

options.a: It gives the holder pleasure and a sense of well-being
options.b: It acts as a store of value as against the use of perishable commodities in a barter system
options.c: It is divisible to small units and makes purchase of small unit items possible

questions.explanation: Money stores value far better than perishable barter goods, and it can be divided into small units so that even tiny purchases are possible; both are real economic advantages over barter. Option A is about personal feelings rather than an advantage of a money economy over barter. Because B and C are both correct, D is the best answer.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why money came to replace barter?

options.a: The shortcomings of barter, such as the need for a double coincidence of wants, made a generally acceptable medium of exchange necessary
options.b: Barter goods were excellent stores of value, so money was needed only as a unit of account
options.c: Barter made it too easy to find trading partners, so money was introduced to slow trade down
options.d: Specialisation and division of labour reduced the amount of exchange, so barter was no longer needed

questions.explanation: The costs of barter, including the search for someone with matching wants, the huge number of relative prices and the perishability and indivisibility of goods, made it necessary to have one object that everyone would readily accept in exchange. Option D gets it backwards, because specialisation increased the volume of exchange and made barter even more costly. Option B is wrong because many barter goods perish quickly, and option C contradicts the main weakness of barter, which is how hard it is to find a trading partner.

questions.question: Which of these is not a function of money:

options.a: Medium of exchange
options.b: Medium of settling disputes

questions.explanation: Money's functions are economic: it serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, a store of value and a standard of deferred payment. Settling disputes is a job for courts and arbitrators, so B is not a function of money. Options A, C and D are all genuine functions.

questions.question: Token money can be defined as:

options.a: Money that takes the form of cowries
options.b: Money that has no commodity value at all
options.c: Money whose value derives entirely from being generally acceptable

questions.explanation: Token money has no commodity value of its own; it is accepted only because people generally agree to take it in exchange, as with paper money and bank deposits. Option A is wrong because cowries are an example of commodity money. Since B and C together make up the definition, D is the best answer.

questions.question: Near money or quasi-money are:

options.a: Financial assets that can easily be converted into money
options.b: Financial assets like savings and time deposits

questions.explanation: Near money, or quasi-money, consists of financial assets that are not generally used for payment but can be turned into cash quickly with little or no loss; time and savings deposits are the main examples, alongside Treasury bills and bills of exchange. Option A gives the general description and option B gives examples, so both are correct and D is the best answer. C is wrong because both statements are true.

questions.question: The difference between demand deposits on the one hand and time and savings deposits on the other is that:

options.a: Demand deposits can be withdrawn at sight (on demand), whereas time deposits are tied to a fixed period and savings deposits carry withdrawal conditions
options.b: Demand deposits are held by the elites in the society whereas time and savings deposits are held by the ordinary people
options.c: Demand deposits can only be held in the account of development banks while time and savings deposits can be held in the account of merchant banks

questions.explanation: Demand deposits sit on current account and are payable at sight, by cheque or on request, which is why they count as money in M1. Time deposits can only be withdrawn when the agreed period ends and savings deposits come with withdrawal limits, so A is the best statement of the difference. Option B is at most a generalisation about who tends to use each account, C is wrong because these deposits are held with deposit money banks generally, and D is wrong because A states the difference.

questions.question: The monetary aggregate known as M1 is made up of:

options.a: Cash and demand deposits and savings deposit
options.b: Cash and Savings deposits and time deposits
options.d: Cash and demand deposits and savings deposits and time deposit

questions.explanation: Narrow money, M1, is made up of currency in the hands of the public plus demand deposits, the two forms of money that can be used for payment immediately. Options A and D add savings or time deposits, which are quasi-money and are counted only in broad money, M2. Option B leaves out demand deposits altogether.

questions.question: Time and Savings deposits as well as some other liquid financial assets are called:

options.a: Quasi-money or near money
options.b: Quasi-money or far money

questions.explanation: Time and savings deposits, together with other liquid financial assets, are called quasi-money or near money because they can be turned into cash quickly but are not themselves generally used for payment. Option B uses the made-up term 'far money', and option C uses the made-up term 'make-belief money'. D is wrong because A gives the correct names.

questions.question: The monetary aggregate M2 is a summation of M1 and ------------

options.a: Quick-money
options.b: Quasi-money

questions.explanation: Broad money, M2, is narrow money (M1) plus quasi-money, that is, the time and savings deposits held with banks. Option A is not a recognised component of the money supply, and option C, high-powered money, is not the item added to M1 to obtain M2, so D cannot be correct either.

questions.question: Use the table below to answer. Monetary Aggregates in Nigeria 2007-2011 (in billions of naira). Columns: Year | Cash or Currency outside Banks | Demand Deposits | Savings Deposits | Time Deposits. 2007 | 500 | 1000 | 780 | 680; 2008 | 750 | 1550 | 950 | 800; 2009 | 1000 | 2000 | 1450 | 1250; 2010 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600; 2011 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600. From the table, the monetary aggregate M1 for the years 2007 to 2009 is:

options.a: N2280bill ; N2300bill ; N4250bill
options.b: N1500bill ; N2300bill ; N3000bill

questions.explanation: M1 is currency outside banks plus demand deposits: 500 + 1,000 = N1,500 billion for 2007, 750 + 1,550 = N2,300 billion for 2008 and 1,000 + 2,000 = N3,000 billion for 2009. Option A mixes M1 with savings or time deposits, and option C adds demand deposits to savings or time deposits instead of to currency. D is wrong because B matches the table.

questions.question: Use the table below to answer. Monetary Aggregates in Nigeria 2007-2011 (in billions of naira). Columns: Year | Cash or Currency outside Banks | Demand Deposits | Savings Deposits | Time Deposits. 2007 | 500 | 1000 | 780 | 680; 2008 | 750 | 1550 | 950 | 800; 2009 | 1000 | 2000 | 1450 | 1250; 2010 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600; 2011 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600. From the table, quasi-money (near money) for the years 2008 to 2011 is:

options.a: N2280bill ; N3250bill ; N3400bill ; N4300bill
options.b: N2300bill ; N3450bill ; N3900bill ; N4300bill

questions.explanation: Quasi-money is savings deposits plus time deposits: 950 + 800 = N1,750 billion for 2008, 1,450 + 1,250 = N2,700 billion for 2009, and 1,800 + 1,600 = N3,400 billion for both 2010 and 2011. Options A and B give figures that do not match these sums, and D is wrong because C matches the table.

questions.question: The table shows monetary aggregates in Nigeria, 2007-2011 (in billions of naira). Columns: Year | Cash or Currency outside Banks | Demand Deposits | Savings Deposits | Time Deposits. 2007 | 500 | 1000 | 780 | 680; 2008 | 750 | 1550 | 950 | 800; 2009 | 1000 | 2000 | 1450 | 1250; 2010 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600; 2011 | 1125 | 2500 | 1800 | 1600. What are the values of the monetary aggregate M2 for the years 2010 and 2011?

options.a: N7,025 billion; N7,025 billion
options.b: N3,000 billion; N3,400 billion

questions.explanation: M2 (broad money) is M1 plus quasi-money, that is cash outside banks + demand deposits + savings deposits + time deposits.
