For 2010 that is 1125 + 2500 + 1800 + 1600 = N7,025 billion, and because the 2011 figures are identical, 2011 also gives N7,025 billion. The figures in options B, C and D are far too small, since M1 alone (cash plus demand deposits) is already N3,625 billion in each of those years.

questions.question: A decline in the share of currency (cash) in the total money stock is a reflection of the fact that:

options.a: The public have grown more confident in the banking industry
options.b: There is financial distress in the economy
options.c: The structure of the financial system is getting more sophisticated

questions.explanation: When people hold a smaller share of their money as cash, it usually means they trust banks enough to keep more of it as deposits, and that the payment system has become more sophisticated, with cheques, cards, transfers and ATMs reducing the need for cash. Both A and C describe this, so D is the best answer. Option B points the wrong way: financial distress makes people lose confidence in banks and hold more cash, not less.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the components of a country's money stock is correct?

options.a: Only currency notes and coins are money; bank deposits are never part of the money stock
options.b: Each component is regarded as money to the extent that it performs some of the functions of money
options.c: A deposit counts as money only if it pays interest to its holder
options.d: Savings and time deposits are excluded from money at every level of definition

questions.explanation: Money is defined by what it does, so each part of the money stock counts as money to the extent that it performs some of the functions of money. Currency and demand deposits serve as a medium of exchange, while savings and time deposits are a good store of value, which is why they are included in broad money (M2). Options A and D are wrong because bank deposits are part of the money stock, and option C is wrong because demand deposits usually earn no interest yet are still money.

questions.question: In terms of immediate liquidity and general acceptance as a means of payment, which components of the money stock are the most qualified to be called money?

options.a: Savings and time deposits (quasi-money)
options.b: Currency and demand deposits (M1)
options.c: Deposits held with non-bank financial institutions
options.d: Time deposits alone, because they earn the highest interest

questions.explanation: Currency and demand deposits together make up narrow money (M1), and they are the most liquid parts of the money stock because they can be spent at once and are generally accepted in payment. Savings and time deposits (option A) are quasi-money: a good store of value, but they usually have to be converted into cash or demand deposits before they can be spent, and option D confuses earning interest with liquidity. Deposits with non-bank financial institutions (option C) are counted only in the even broader M3 measure.

questions.question: The value of money is best measured by:

options.a: The amount of metal contained in its coins
options.b: Its purchasing power, that is, the quantity of goods and services a given amount of money can buy
options.c: The rate of interest that banks pay on deposits
options.d: The total quantity of money in circulation

questions.explanation: Money is not wanted for itself but for what it can buy, so its value lies in its purchasing power. The more goods and services a given amount of money can obtain, the greater its value; when the same amount buys less, its value has fallen. Option D confuses the quantity of money with its value, and option A describes the commodity value of old metallic coins rather than the value of modern money.

questions.question: That the value of money falls when the prices of goods rise implies that:

options.a: There is a direct relationship between the value of money and the prices of goods
options.b: There is an inverse relationship between the value of money and the prices of goods
options.c: Both (a) and (b) are correct under certain circumstances
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: The value of money and the general price level move in opposite directions: when prices rise, each naira buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls, and when prices fall its value rises. That is an inverse relationship, so B is correct. Option A would mean value and prices rise together, which contradicts the statement in the question, and C cannot be right because the relationship cannot be both direct and inverse at once.

questions.question: Value of money can be described as the worth of money or its _______

options.a: Stock of money
options.b: Face value of money

questions.explanation: The value of money is what a unit of money can buy in goods and services, that is, its purchasing power; when prices rise, the value of money falls. The face value in B is just the amount printed on a banknote or coin, which stays the same even when its purchasing power changes. The stock of money (A) is the total amount of money in the economy, and velocity (C) is how fast money changes hands.

questions.question: Who propounded the view that "money is what money does"?

options.a: Hicks
options.b: Keynes

questions.explanation: Hicks argued that money is defined by its functions: anything that is used as money is money. This is why demand deposits, savings deposits and time deposits are counted in the money stock to the extent that they perform the functions of money. Option C, Fisher, is linked with the equation of exchange (MV = PT), while Keynes (B) and Friedman (D) are known for their theories of the demand for money, not this functional definition.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of good money?

options.a: Acceptability
options.b: Homogeneity

questions.explanation: Acceptability, homogeneity and stability are all qualities that good money must have, so none of options A to C is the odd one out. Acceptability means people readily take it in payment, homogeneity means every unit of the same denomination is identical (N1 in Abuja is the same as N1 in Ibadan), and stability means its value or purchasing power does not swing widely over time. An item lacking any of these would perform poorly as money.

questions.question: Which of the following is not among the types of money?

options.a: Durable money
options.b: Commodity money

questions.explanation: Durability is a quality that good money should possess, not a type of money, so option A is the odd one out. Commodity money (B) has value in itself as a good, such as gold or cowries, token money (C) has little or no commodity value and is accepted because people generally take it in exchange, and fiat money (D) has value because government declares it legal tender.

questions.question: ________ refers to the supply or quantity of money available in an economy

options.a: Price index
options.b: Value of money

questions.explanation: The stock of money, also called money supply, is the total quantity of money available in an economy at a point in time, such as currency held by the public plus deposits with banks (measured as M1, M2 and so on). Option B, the value of money, is its purchasing power, and option C, velocity, is the number of times a unit of money changes hands in a period. Option A, a price index, measures the average level of prices, not the quantity of money.

questions.question: The value of money can be measured by the use of what?

options.a: Paper index
options.b: Price index

questions.explanation: The value of money is its purchasing power, and it moves inversely with the general price level. Because the general price level is measured with a price index (a weighted average of prices), the value of money is found as the reciprocal of the index; for example, if the index rises from 100 to 250, money is worth only 40 percent of its earlier value. Option C, a value index, sounds similar but tracks changes in the total value of goods (price times quantity), and option D, a stock index, tracks share prices on the stock exchange.

questions.question: ______economy does not involve the use of money

options.a: Mixed Economy
options.b: Barter Economy

questions.explanation: In a barter economy, goods and services are exchanged directly for other goods and services without any medium of exchange, which is why it suffers from the problem of double coincidence of wants. Option A, a mixed economy, combines private and public ownership and uses money, and option C, a traditional economy, is organised around custom and tradition rather than being defined by the absence of money. Option D is wrong because B fits exactly.

questions.question: Without money, the ________ would be inoperative.

options.a: Price mechanism
options.b: Resource allocation system

questions.explanation: In a market economy prices are quoted in money, and those money prices signal producers what to make and consumers who gets what, so the price mechanism cannot work without money. Because land, labour and capital are shared out among their uses through that same price mechanism, the allocation system in option B also depends on money. Options A and B are each only half of the answer, and D is wrong because both systems clearly depend on money.

questions.question: The study of money, especially coins and paper currency, is called

options.a: Numeric
options.b: Numerical

questions.explanation: Numismatics is the study and collection of money in its physical forms, such as coins, tokens and paper currency, including their history and design. Options A and B are ordinary words relating to numbers, not to money, and option D is not a real term.

questions.question: ________ is the type of money whose intrinsic value is equal to its face value.

options.a: Subsidiary money
options.b: Representative money

questions.explanation: Standard money, also called full-bodied money, is money whose value as a commodity (for example, the gold in a gold coin) is equal to the value stamped on it. Option A is wrong because subsidiary coins are small change whose face value is higher than the metal they contain. Option B is paper that represents a claim on a commodity but has little value of its own, and option D is too broad, since metallic money can be full-bodied or token.

questions.question: The type of money that has been declared legal tender by the government but is not backed by any physical commodity is

options.a: Token money
options.b: Fiat money

questions.explanation: Fiat money is currency that has value only because the government declares it legal tender, and it cannot be exchanged for gold or any other commodity; the naira is an example. Option A is a broader term for money whose face value is above its commodity value, and it includes convertible paper that is backed by a commodity. Options C and D are wrong because commodity and metallic money draw their value from the material they are made of.

questions.question: The following are functions of money except

options.a: Unit of account
options.b: Standard of deferred payment

questions.explanation: The functions of money are medium of exchange, unit of account (measure of value), store of value and standard of deferred payment. Creating employment is an economic goal that money may help to support indirectly, but it is not one of the functions of money itself. Options A, B and C are all genuine functions of money.

questions.question: Before the advent of the monetary economy, there was in existence a

options.a: Fiscal system
options.b: Barter system

questions.explanation: Before money came into use, people exchanged goods and services directly for other goods and services, which is the barter system. Barter's problems, such as the need for a double coincidence of wants and the difficulty of storing value, led to the development of money. Option A refers to government taxing and spending, and options C and D are not systems of exchange.

questions.question: A persistent rise in the general price level of commodities over a period of time is

options.a: Inflation
options.b: Deflation

questions.explanation: Inflation is a persistent rise in the general level of prices over time, which means each naira buys less than before. Option B, deflation, is the opposite: a sustained fall in the general price level. Option C, stagflation, is a special situation where rising prices come together with stagnant output and high unemployment, so it is narrower than the general definition asked for here.

questions.question: The main limitation of a barter economy is _________

options.a: Inadequate storage of value
options.b: Exchange for cows at the expense of wheat

questions.explanation: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: you must find someone who has what you want and who also wants what you have, which makes trade slow and difficult. Option A, the difficulty of storing value, is also a drawback of barter, but it is not the main one. Option D cannot be right because option B is not a genuine limitation of barter.

questions.question: When, for each good, people know how many units of the object called money must be exchanged for it, money is performing its function as a ________

options.a: Medium of exchange
options.b: Unit of account

questions.explanation: As a unit of account, money is the common measure in which the value of every good is expressed as a price, so people know how many naira a good is worth and can compare values easily. Option A, medium of exchange, is about using money to make payments. Option C, store of value, is about holding money to spend later, and option D is about settling debts in the future.

questions.question: M2 equals

options.a: Cash + quasi money
options.b: M1 + cash + quasi money

questions.explanation: M2, or broad money, is narrow money (M1, which is currency in circulation plus demand deposits) plus quasi money, that is, savings and time deposits. Option B double counts cash, since cash is already part of M1. Option A leaves out demand deposits, and option D is too vague because demand deposits at banks are already inside M1.

questions.question: The system of exchange that requires a double coincidence of wants is known as

options.a: the gold standard
options.b: the barter practice

questions.explanation: Barter is the direct exchange of goods for goods without money, so every trade needs a double coincidence of wants. Under a commodity money system (option C), one generally accepted item such as cowries serves as money, which removes that problem. The gold standard and gold exchange standard (options A and D) are money systems linked to gold, so they do not need a double coincidence either.

questions.question: The value of money varies

options.a: inversely with the price level
options.b: directly with the volume of employment

questions.explanation: The value of money is what it can buy, so when the general price level rises each naira buys less and its value falls, and when prices fall its value rises. That inverse relationship is exactly why option C, which says the value moves in the same direction as prices, is wrong. Options B and D link the value of money to employment and interest rates, which do not define its purchasing power.

questions.question: The most essential attribute of a good currency, without which it cannot function as money at all, is

options.a: scarcity
options.b: homogeneity

questions.explanation: Acceptability is the most essential quality of money: if people will not take something in payment for goods and debts, it cannot work as money however scarce, uniform or recognisable it is. Scarcity, homogeneity and cognizability (options A, B and D) are also desirable qualities of good money, but they only matter once the item is generally accepted.

questions.question: The value of money is generally measured by reference to the

options.a: interest rate charged by banks
options.b: general price level
options.c: size of a country's gold stock

questions.explanation: The value of money is its purchasing power, that is, how much in goods and services a given amount of money can buy. It moves inversely with the general price level: when prices in general rise, each naira buys less, so the value of money falls. Option A, the interest rate, is the price of borrowing money rather than a measure of what money can buy, and Option C mattered only when currencies were tied to gold.

questions.question: To perform its function as a store of wealth and standard for deferred payment, money must be

options.a: portable
options.b: in attractive form
options.d: spent more on capital goods than on consumer goods

questions.explanation: To work as a store of wealth and a standard of deferred payment, money must keep its value over time, so that what is saved or owed today is worth about the same when it is spent or repaid later. Portability (Option A) matters for money as a medium of exchange, not for storing value, and an attractive form (Option B) has nothing to do with these functions. Option D describes spending patterns in the economy, not a quality of money.

questions.question: Money can simply be referred to as a

options.a: medium of exchange
options.b: means for the settlement of debts

questions.explanation: In its simplest form, money is defined as anything that is generally acceptable as a medium of exchange, that is, accepted by everyone in payment for goods and services. Settling debts (Option B) and serving as a standard of value (Option D) are genuine functions of money, but they belong to the fuller definition, while the simplest one rests on the medium of exchange role. Option C is wrong because money is not defined as a durable business asset.

questions.question: A form of money that has gone out of use is

options.a: commodity money
options.b: bank money

questions.explanation: Commodity money, such as cowries, salt or other goods that had value in themselves and were also used in exchange, has gone out of use in modern economies. Paper money (Option C) and bank money, that is, deposits paid out by cheque or transfer (Option B), are the main forms of money today. Foreign money (Option D) is still widely used, especially in international trade.

questions.question: By 'trade by barter', we mean

options.a: trade done by people in villages
options.b: exchange of goods for money
options.c: the trade of the Middle Ages

questions.explanation: Barter is the direct exchange of goods (or services) for other goods without using money, for example swapping yams for cloth. Option B describes a money transaction, which is the system that replaced barter, while Options A and C wrongly tie barter to a place or a period instead of to the method of exchange.

questions.question: The value of money depends primarily on

options.a: the gold backing of the currency
options.b: government decree that it is legal tender

questions.explanation: The value of money is its purchasing power, the quantity of goods and services a unit of money can buy, so it depends mainly on the general price level: when prices rise the value of money falls, and when prices fall it rises. Option A is wrong because modern currencies are not backed by gold, and Option B, legal tender status, makes money acceptable in payment but does not decide how much it can buy.

questions.question: Money becomes a very poor store of value in a period of

options.a: deflation
options.b: harvest

questions.explanation: Money stores value well only if its purchasing power holds over time. During inflation prices keep rising, so the same amount of naira buys less and less, which makes money a poor store of value. Option A, deflation, is the opposite case, because falling prices increase what money can buy, while a harvest or a recession (Options B and C) does not by itself erode money's purchasing power.

questions.question: The function of money as a standard of deferred payments

options.a: makes it possible for an individual to build up stores of many things for future use
options.b: makes it possible for payments to be postponed from the present to a future date

questions.explanation: As a standard of deferred payment, money is the unit in which future payments and debts are stated, so goods can be bought now and paid for later, loans repaid and salaries agreed in advance. Option A describes the store of value function, Option C describes money as a medium of exchange, and Option D describes money as a unit of account.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT belong in respect of the qualities of money?

options.a: Durability
options.b: Portability
options.c: Divisibility into the smallest units of value

questions.explanation: Durability, portability and divisibility are qualities good money must have, so that it lasts, is easy to carry and can be broken into small units for small purchases. Measure of value is not a quality but a function of money, its role as the yardstick for pricing goods and services, so Option D does not belong.

questions.question: An issue of bank notes not backed by gold but by government securities is known as

options.a: fiduciary issue
options.b: guaranteed money

questions.explanation: A fiduciary issue is currency issued on trust: it is backed not by gold but by government securities and the public's confidence in the issuing authority. Option D, legal tender, is money that must by law be accepted in settlement of debts, and Option C, seigniorage, is the profit a government earns from issuing money, so neither describes how the currency is backed.

questions.question: Money performs a number of functions. One of these functions makes it possible for a person to provide for old age. Because of that particular function, money is regarded as a

options.a: medium of exchange
options.b: measure of value

questions.explanation: Money's store of value function lets people save part of their income today and spend it in the future, for example in old age. Option A, medium of exchange, is about using money to buy and sell now, while Options B and C, measure of value and unit of account, are about pricing goods, not keeping wealth for later.

questions.question: The most important characteristic of money is

options.a: portability
options.b: usefulness

questions.explanation: Acceptability matters most because something can only work as money if people generally accept it in exchange for goods and services; if it is refused, its other qualities count for nothing. Portability (A) is helpful, but a portable item that nobody accepts still cannot serve as money. Usefulness (B) and beauty (D) are not required at all, since modern paper money has little use or beauty of its own.

questions.question: The barter system of exchange is noted for many drawbacks, which include the following except

options.a: Lack of double coincidence of wants
options.b: Time wastage
options.c: Lack of a common measure of value
options.d: Direct exchange of goods for goods

questions.explanation: Direct exchange of goods for goods is simply what barter is - its defining feature - not a drawback of it. The lack of double coincidence of wants (A), the time wasted searching for a suitable trading partner (B) and the lack of a common measure of value (C) are all genuine weaknesses of barter that money later solved.

questions.question: Which of the following qualify as near (quasi) money and legal tender respectively?

options.a: Treasury bills and naira notes
options.b: Currency notes and fixed deposits

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are near money because they are not used to make payments but can be turned into cash quickly with little loss, while naira currency issued by the CBN is legal tender that must be accepted in settlement of debts. Option B has the pair the wrong way round, since currency is the legal tender and fixed deposits are the near money. In C, fixed deposits are near money but the second item is not Nigeria's legal tender, and in D gold coins are not near money.

questions.question: Which of the following tools can be used to measure the value (purchasing power) of money?

options.a: Regression method
options.b: Inflation method

questions.explanation: The value of money is its purchasing power, and it is measured with price index numbers, which compare the general price level in one period with a base period. When the price index rises, each naira buys less, so the value of money has fallen. Regression (A) is a general statistical technique and an 'inflation method' (B) is not a recognised measuring tool, so D is also wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following is legal tender in Nigeria, that is, must be accepted by law in settlement of a debt?

options.a: Postal order
options.b: Cheque
options.c: Naira notes issued by the CBN

questions.explanation: Legal tender is money that the law says must be accepted in payment of a debt, and in Nigeria that status belongs to the naira currency issued by the CBN. A postal order (A) is only a payment instrument that has to be cashed or paid into an account, so nobody is legally bound to accept it. A cheque (B) is merely an order on a bank to pay, and a treasury bill (D) is a short-term government security, so neither is legal tender.

questions.question: Which one of the following assets cannot be regarded as quasi money?

options.a: Postal orders
options.b: Deposits in a fixed deposit account

questions.explanation: Current account balances are demand deposits that can be withdrawn or transferred by cheque at once, so they are money itself (part of narrow money, M1), not quasi money. Quasi or near money means assets that are not generally used to make payments but can be turned into cash quickly with little loss. Fixed deposits (B) and treasury bills (C) fit that description, and postal orders (A) likewise have to be cashed before they can be spent.

questions.question: Which of the following describes how trade was actually carried out under the barter system of exchange?

options.a: Traders could always easily find a partner with a double coincidence of wants
options.b: Wealth could easily be stored in a generally acceptable form
options.c: Borrowing and lending could easily be arranged in a common unit of value
options.d: Goods were exchanged directly for other goods

questions.explanation: Barter is the direct exchange of goods for goods, so that is how trade actually took place. Without money it was hard to find someone with a double coincidence of wants (A), and wealth was hard to store (B) because most goods spoil or lose value. Borrowing and lending (C) were also difficult because there was no common unit for measuring what was owed.

questions.question: Which of the following is made legal tender through government decree?

options.a: Fiat money
options.b: Near money

questions.explanation: Fiat money has no intrinsic value and is not backed by any commodity; it is money because the government declares it legal tender, and 'fiat' itself means 'let it be done'. Near money (B) and quasi money (C), such as time deposits or treasury bills, have no legal tender status and are not generally accepted in payment, which also rules out D.

questions.question: One quality of money which makes it possible to be easily carried about is:

options.a: Scarcity
options.b: Durability

questions.explanation: Portability means money must be easy to carry about, with high value relative to its weight and size, which is why paper money and coins replaced bulky commodities like livestock. Scarcity (A) is about keeping money relatively limited so that it holds its value, and durability (B) is about money lasting long without wearing out, so neither describes ease of carrying. Accessibility (D) is not one of the recognised qualities of money.

questions.question: The most important characteristic of money which is not shared by other quasi-money assets is:

options.a: Durability
options.b: Scarcity

questions.explanation: Money is generally acceptable as a medium of exchange, largely because it is legal tender, and this is exactly what near money or quasi-money assets lack. Time deposits, treasury bills and bills of exchange can be durable (A), relatively scarce (B) and fairly stable in value (D), but they must first be converted into money before they can be used to pay for goods and services.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised feature (characteristic) of good money?

options.a: Understandability
options.b: Uniformity

questions.explanation: Uniformity (also called homogeneity) means every unit of the same denomination must be identical and worth exactly the same wherever it is used, so one N100 is as good as any other N100. Understandability (A) is not a feature of money, and uncontrollability (C) is the opposite of what is needed, since the supply of money must be controlled to keep its value. That also rules out D.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic an item must have to serve well as money?

options.a: Divisibility
options.b: Abundance, so that it is as freely available as sand

questions.explanation: Money must be relatively scarce; if it were as plentiful as sand, nobody would give up valuable goods for it, so abundance (option B) is the opposite of what money needs. Divisibility (A), durability (C) and homogeneity (D) are all genuine characteristics of money, along with portability, stability and acceptability.

questions.question: The characteristic of money which requires that N1 in Abuja must be exactly the same as N1 in Ibadan is

options.a: Portability
options.b: Divisibility

questions.explanation: Homogeneity (uniformity) means every unit of money of the same denomination must be exactly alike in size, quality and value wherever it is used. Portability (A) is about being easy to carry, divisibility (B) is about breaking into smaller units for small transactions, and scarcity (C) is about keeping supply limited so that money keeps its value.

questions.question: The quality of money that allows transactions of any size, no matter how small, to be carried out without hindrance is

options.a: Durability
options.b: Stability

questions.explanation: Divisibility means money can be broken into small units, so even tiny purchases can be paid for exactly; this was a real problem under barter, where a cow cannot be split to buy a small item. Durability (A) is about money lasting a long time, stability (B) is about money keeping a steady value, and acceptability (D) is about people being willing to take it in payment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of money?

options.a: Medium of exchange
options.b: Unit of account

questions.explanation: The four functions of money are medium of exchange (A), unit of account (B), store of value and standard of deferred payment (D). Earning interest, option C, is not a function of money; it is a feature of near money such as time and savings deposits, which people hold for income and safety.

questions.question: When the prices of all goods and services in Nigeria are expressed in naira, money is performing its function as a

options.a: Unit of account
options.b: Medium of exchange

questions.explanation: As a unit of account, money is the common measure in which all prices are stated, which makes comparing values and gathering price information easy. Medium of exchange (B) is about actually using money to buy and sell, store of value (C) is about holding wealth for the future, and standard of deferred payment (D) is about settling debts at a future date.

questions.question: A bond contract states that interest and the principal will be paid in naira at specified future dates. Here money is serving mainly as a

options.a: Unit of account
options.b: Standard of deferred payment

questions.explanation: Money acts as a standard of deferred payment when contracts and debts to be settled in the future are stated and paid in money, as with bond interest and principal. Unit of account (A) is closely related, since the future sums are measured in naira, but the main idea here is payment at a later date. Medium of exchange (C) is about present purchases, and store of value (D) is about holding wealth rather than settling debts.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of a barter economy?

options.a: The existence of one common unit in which all prices are quoted
options.b: The need for a double coincidence of wants
options.c: The need to know a very large number of relative prices

questions.explanation: A common unit for quoting all prices (option A) is a benefit of a money economy, so it cannot be a limitation of barter; its absence is actually one of barter's problems. The double coincidence of wants (B), the huge number of relative prices (C) and the indivisibility of goods (D) are all genuine limitations of barter, along with the lack of a good store of value.

questions.question: In a barter economy with 1,000 commodities, roughly how many relative prices would traders need to know?

options.a: About 1,000

questions.explanation: Each pair of goods needs its own rate of exchange, so the number of relative prices is n(n - 1)/2 = 1,000 x 999 / 2 = 499,500, or about 500,000. Option A would be true only if every good were priced in one common unit, as in a money economy, option B counts every pair twice, and option D has no basis in the formula.

questions.question: Under barter, stockpiling one's output while waiting to find a suitable trading partner creates which two additional costs?

options.a: Interest cost and tax cost
options.b: Waiting cost and storage cost

questions.explanation: Storing output to cut search costs means the producer gives up immediate satisfaction while waiting (waiting cost) and must pay to keep the goods safe (storage cost). Interest and tax costs (A) and printing and minting costs (C) belong to a money economy, while transport and advertising costs (D) are not the specific costs that stockpiling creates.

questions.question: A yam farmer who wants palm oil must find someone who not only has palm oil to exchange but also wants yam. This requirement of barter is known as

options.a: Division of labour
options.b: Indivisibility of goods
options.c: Lack of a store of value

questions.explanation: Double coincidence of wants means each party must have what the other wants and want what the other has at the same time; searching for such a partner wastes time and effort and is the biggest drawback of barter. Division of labour (A) is specialisation in production, indivisibility (B) is about goods that cannot be split into small units, and lack of a store of value (C) is about goods that cannot be kept for long.

questions.question: Which quality of money mainly enables a money economy to overcome the double coincidence of wants problem of barter?

options.a: Its intrinsic value as a useful commodity
options.b: Its convertibility into gold on demand
options.c: Its general acceptability, so a seller can accept money and use it to buy from anyone else
options.d: Its ability to earn interest for the holder

questions.explanation: Because money is generally acceptable, a seller no longer needs to find someone who wants exactly what he has; he takes money and spends it with whoever has what he needs. Intrinsic value (A) and convertibility into gold (B) are not needed, since modern paper money has neither, and earning interest (D) is a feature of near money, not of money itself.

questions.question: Which of the following has historically served as commodity money?

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Cheques

questions.explanation: Cowrie shells, like salt, gold and silver, have value of their own and were widely used as money in the past, which makes them commodity money. Treasury bills (A) are near money, a cheque (B) is only an instrument for transferring a bank deposit, and demand deposits (D) are a modern form of token money with no commodity value.

questions.question: Commodity money is best described as money that

options.a: Has an intrinsic value of its own apart from its use as money, such as gold or salt
options.b: Is paper money that can be converted into gold on demand
options.c: Has value only because the government declares it legal tender
options.d: Exists only as entries in bank ledgers

questions.explanation: Commodity money is a medium of exchange that would still be valuable as a commodity even if it stopped being used as money, as with gold used for ornaments or salt used as food. Option B describes representative (convertible) token money, C describes fiat money, and D describes bank deposits, none of which has intrinsic value.

questions.question: Paper money that can be exchanged for a commodity such as gold on demand is known as

options.a: Inconvertible token money
options.b: Representative (convertible) token money

questions.explanation: Representative or convertible token money is a paper claim that promises to pay a commodity, usually gold, on demand, like the old goldsmiths' receipts that people came to accept in payment. Inconvertible token money (A) cannot be exchanged for gold, near money (C) refers to assets like time deposits and treasury bills, and commodity money (D) is the commodity itself, such as gold coins, not paper representing it.

questions.question: Paper money that is not backed by gold or any other commodity, and whose supply is limited only by law, is best described as

options.a: Representative convertible token money
options.b: Commodity money with a design or symbol

questions.explanation: Inconvertible token money cannot be exchanged for gold or any commodity; its scarcity, and so its value, is kept by law rather than by a commodity reserve, and today's naira is of this type. Representative money (A) is convertible on demand, commodity money with a design (B) is something like a gold coin, and near money (C) is not legal tender at all.

questions.question: In Nigeria, narrow money (M1) is defined as

options.a: Currency plus time and savings deposits
options.b: Demand deposits plus savings deposits only
options.c: Currency plus demand, time and savings deposits
options.d: Currency in circulation with the public plus demand deposits

questions.explanation: Narrow money, M1, covers the most liquid forms of money: cash held by the public plus demand (current account) deposits that can be spent by cheque. Option C is broad money (M2), which adds time and savings deposits, while A and B wrongly mix quasi-money into the narrow measure.

questions.question: In the definition of Nigeria's money supply, quasi-money refers to

options.a: Time and savings deposits held by the public with banks
options.b: Currency in circulation with the public

questions.explanation: Quasi-money is the sum of time and savings deposits: they earn interest and are a good store of value, but they are not as readily accepted as a means of payment, and adding them to M1 gives broad money (M2). Currency (B) and demand deposits (C) together make up M1, and cash in bank vaults (D) is not counted as money held by the public.

questions.question: In 2009 an economy's money supply data (N billion) were: currency 150, demand deposits 400, savings deposits 350, time deposits 100, deposits in non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) 600. What was narrow money (M1) in 2009?

options.a: N1,000 billion
options.b: N1,600 billion

questions.explanation: M1 = currency + demand deposits = 150 + 400 = N550 billion. N1,000 billion (A) is M2, which also adds savings and time deposits, N1,600 billion (B) is M3, which further adds NBFI deposits, and N400 billion (C) counts only demand deposits and leaves out currency.

questions.question: In 2008 an economy's money supply data (N billion) were: currency 100, demand deposits 300, savings deposits 280, time deposits 80, deposits in non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) 500. What was broad money (M2) in 2008?

options.a: N400 billion
options.b: N760 billion

questions.explanation: M2 = M1 + quasi-money = (100 + 300) + (280 + 80) = N760 billion. N400 billion (A) is only M1, N1,260 billion (C) is M3 because it includes NBFI deposits, and N660 billion (D) adds up the bank deposits but leaves out currency.

questions.question: In 2007 an economy's money supply data (N billion) were: currency 80, demand deposits 320, savings deposits 300, time deposits 50, deposits in non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) 400. What was the total money supply defined as M3 in 2007?

options.a: N750 billion
options.b: N1,150 billion

questions.explanation: M3 = currency + demand deposits + time and savings deposits + deposits of NBFIs = 80 + 320 + 300 + 50 + 400 = N1,150 billion. N750 billion (A) is M2, N400 billion (C) is M1, and N1,070 billion (D) leaves out the N80 billion of currency.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes a barter economy from a money economy?

options.a: A barter economy uses only coins, while a money economy uses only paper money
options.b: In a barter economy goods are exchanged directly for other goods, while in a money economy goods and services are exchanged for money
options.c: A barter economy has no exchange of any kind, while a money economy has trade
options.d: In a barter economy goods are exchanged for money, while in a money economy goods are exchanged directly for other goods

questions.explanation: Barter is the direct exchange of commodity for commodity, so every trade needs someone who has what you want and wants what you have. In a money economy, money acts as the go-between: goods and services are sold for money, which is then used to buy other things. Option D reverses the two systems, option A is wrong because barter involves no money at all, and option C is wrong because barter is itself a form of trade.

questions.question: The money stock (money supply) of a modern economy such as Nigeria is made up of:

options.a: The external (foreign exchange) reserves held by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: The total market value of shares quoted on the stock exchange
options.c: Only the banknotes and coins issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: Currency (banknotes and coins) held by the public plus bank deposits

questions.explanation: The money stock is the total of cash, meaning banknotes and coins in circulation with the public, and bank deposits, including demand deposits on current account and time and savings deposits. Option C is too narrow because bank deposits are also money, being widely used to settle debts by cheque and transfer. Options A and B are assets held by the CBN and by investors respectively, not part of the money stock.

questions.question: The value of money refers to:

options.a: Its purchasing power, that is, the quantity of goods and services a given amount of money can buy
options.b: The cost of printing and minting the banknotes and coins
options.c: The face value printed on a currency note
options.d: The total amount of money in circulation in the economy

questions.explanation: Money is wanted for what it can buy, so its value lies in the quantity of goods and services a given sum of money can obtain; the more it buys, the higher its value. This is why the value of money moves inversely with the general price level. Option C describes only the face value, which stays the same even when prices rise, option D describes the money supply rather than its value, and option B is a production cost, not a measure of what money will buy.

questions.question: If the general price index rises from 100 to 250, the value of money becomes what percentage of its former value?
questions.explanation: The value of money is the inverse of the price level, so the new value is (100/250) x 100 = 40% of the old value. In other words, a naira now buys only 40% of what it bought before. Option D, 60%, is the size of the fall in value, not what remains, and options C and B wrongly treat the value of money as moving in the same direction as prices.

questions.question: A yam farmer who wants cloth must find a weaver who has the cloth he wants and is also willing to take yams in exchange. This problem of barter is known as

options.a: double coincidence of wants
options.b: lack of divisibility
options.c: lack of a store of value

questions.explanation: Double coincidence of wants means each party must want exactly what the other is offering at the same time, which is what the farmer and the weaver need here. Option B is about goods that cannot be split into small units, option C is about keeping wealth for the future, and option D is about postponing payment, none of which is the problem described.

questions.question: In its general definition, money is

options.a: any commodity that has intrinsic value of its own
options.b: only coins made of gold or silver
options.c: any asset that earns interest for its holder
options.d: anything that is generally acceptable in payment for goods and services and in settlement of debt

questions.explanation: The general definition rests on acceptability: whatever people generally accept in exchange and in settling debts serves as money, which is why items like cowries and tobacco once worked as money. Option A describes commodity money, only one type of money, option B is far too narrow, and option C is wrong because cash itself earns no interest.

questions.question: The monetarist (Chicago) view associated with Milton Friedman defines money as

options.a: only notes and coins that the law declares to be legal tender
options.b: anything that serves as a temporary abode of purchasing power
options.c: whatever the monetary authority declares to be money by law
options.d: only cheques drawn on deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Friedman saw money as a temporary abode of purchasing power, a broad view that takes in cheques, drafts, promissory notes and other bills as well as cash. Option A is the narrow currency school view, option C is the legal definition of money, and option D wrongly limits money to cheques alone.

questions.question: Which school of thought accepted the general definition of money but insisted that bank cheques should also be treated as money?

options.a: The banking school
options.b: The currency school

questions.explanation: The banking school argued that since most deposit money bank transactions are settled by cheque, cheques should count as money alongside cash. Option B, the currency school, restricted money to legal tender currency, while options C and D are best known for their views on the demand for money, not for this definitional debate.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes money from near money?

options.a: Near money is legal tender, while money has no legal status
options.b: Money earns a yield for its holder, while near money earns no return
options.c: Money is legal tender and can be spent directly, while near money mainly stores value and must first be converted into money before it can be spent
options.d: Near money can be spent directly, while money must first be converted

questions.explanation: Money is legal tender, generally acceptable and fully liquid, while near money such as treasury bills or time deposits serves as a store of value and has to be converted, with some delay or cost, before it can be spent. Option A reverses the legal position, option B is wrong because cash earns no yield while near money assets usually do, and option D reverses the liquidity point.

questions.question: When a trader buys goods today and agrees to pay for them in money three months later, money is performing its function as

options.a: a medium of exchange
options.b: a standard of deferred payment

questions.explanation: A standard of deferred payment allows goods and services to be enjoyed now and paid for in money terms later, which is what this credit sale relies on. Option A describes paying at the moment of exchange, option C is about measuring and comparing values, and option D is about holding wealth over time.

questions.question: Money serves as a common measure in which the values of all goods and services are expressed, much as the metre measures distance. This is the function of money as

options.a: a store of value
options.b: a standard of deferred payment

questions.explanation: As a unit of account (standard of value), money lets the worth of every good be stated in one unit, so prices can be compared and accounts kept easily. Option A is about keeping wealth, option B is about settling debts in future, and option C is about moving value from one person or place to another.

questions.question: In Nigeria, narrow money (M1) consists mainly of

options.a: M1 plus time and savings deposits
options.b: currency outside banks plus treasury bills and time deposits
options.c: only the notes and coins held in the vaults of the CBN
options.d: currency outside banks plus demand deposits with deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Narrow money, M1, is made up of currency in circulation outside the banks plus demand (current account) deposits, the money people can spend straight away. Option A describes broad money, M2, option B wrongly adds near money assets, and option C leaves out both the public's cash and bank deposits.

questions.question: Which of the following determinants of money supply is set exogenously by the central bank?

options.a: The minimum cash reserve ratio
options.b: The public's desire to hold cash rather than bank deposits
options.c: Changes in the level of business activity in the economy
options.d: Customers' demand for bank loans and overdrafts

questions.explanation: The cash reserve ratio is fixed by the central bank, so it is an exogenous determinant of money supply that the public cannot change. Options B, C and D all depend on the behaviour of households and firms, which makes them endogenous influences on money supply.

questions.question: Assuming a legal cash reserve ratio of 20% and no cash leakage from the banking system, an initial cash deposit of N2,000 can expand into total bank deposits of
questions.explanation: Total deposits created equal the initial deposit divided by the reserve ratio: N2,000 / 0.20 = N10,000. Option A is the total of new loans (N10,000 minus the original N2,000), option C simply adds 20% to the deposit, and option D is what a 10% reserve ratio would give.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor that limits the ability of banks to create credit?

options.a: The size of the legal cash reserve ratio
options.b: An increase in the cash deposited with banks by the public
options.c: Lack of acceptable collateral security from borrowers
options.d: Fear of cash drain to other banks

questions.explanation: More cash deposits give banks a bigger reserve base, so they increase, not limit, the credit banks can create. Options A, C and D are all limits: a higher reserve ratio cuts lending, banks will not lend without good security, and fear of losing cash to other banks makes them cautious.

questions.question: If the cash reserve ratio is 12.5%, what is the credit creation multiplier, measured as total deposits created divided by the original deposit?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio, so 1 / 0.125 = 8; an original deposit of N1,000 could support N8,000 of total deposits. Option A counts only the new loans created relative to the deposit, option C just repeats the percentage, and option D misplaces the decimal point.

questions.question: A central bank digital currency (CBDC), such as the eNaira, is best defined as:

options.a: A bank deposit held in a commercial bank's savings account
options.b: An electronic form of central bank money that can be used for payments and as a store of value, and that is legal tender
options.c: A foreign currency held by the Central Bank of Nigeria as part of its reserves
options.d: A privately issued cryptocurrency created by computer mining

questions.explanation: A CBDC is money issued directly by the central bank in digital form. The eNaira is simply the naira in electronic form, carrying the same value and legal tender status as cash. Cryptocurrencies (D) are not issued by any central bank, a savings account (A) is a claim on a commercial bank, and external reserves (C) are foreign assets, not a domestic digital currency.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a central bank digital currency (CBDC) from a cryptocurrency?

options.a: A CBDC is issued and backed by the central bank and is legal tender, while a cryptocurrency is not issued by a central bank, is not legal tender and is usually very volatile
options.b: A CBDC has highly volatile value, while cryptocurrencies are fixed in value by law
options.c: A cryptocurrency is issued by the central bank, while a CBDC is created by private users
options.d: Both are legal tender and have equally stable values

questions.explanation: The eNaira is state-backed: it is issued by the CBN, it is legal tender and it is worth the same as the cash naira, so its value is stable. Cryptocurrencies are created on decentralised networks, are not legal tender and swing widely in value. Option C reverses who issues each, D wrongly gives both the same status, and B reverses their volatility.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit expected from the introduction of a central bank digital currency such as the eNaira?

options.a: Reducing the cost of printing and handling naira notes
options.b: Paying holders a high rate of interest on their digital currency balances
options.c: Accelerating financial inclusion by bringing more people into the formal financial system
options.d: Improving the effectiveness of monetary policy through better payment data

questions.explanation: The eNaira was designed as a non-interest-bearing currency, just like cash, so earning interest is not one of its benefits. Wider financial inclusion (C), lower currency printing and handling costs (A) and better data for monetary policy (D) are among the benefits expected, along with safer and cheaper payments.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of the eNaira as designed by the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: Its value floats freely against the cash naira
options.b: It is legal tender with the same value as the cash naira and complements, rather than replaces, physical cash
options.c: It can only be used by people who have a bank account
options.d: It replaces all naira notes and coins completely

questions.explanation: The eNaira is the digital form of the naira. One eNaira equals one naira, it is legal tender, and it was introduced to work alongside cash, not to abolish it (D). Its value does not float against cash (A). The wallet system also allows people without bank accounts to open a basic wallet with their National Identity Number, so C is wrong.

questions.question: Despite its many problems, barter is said to have some advantages. Which of the following is one of them?

options.a: It is free from currency devaluation, over-issue of money and inflation
options.b: It provides a common unit for measuring the value of all goods
options.c: It makes it easy to arrange payments for a future date
options.d: It makes it easy to store wealth for many years

questions.explanation: Because no currency is used under barter, there is no money to be over-issued or devalued, so the economy is free from monetary manipulation and inflation of that kind. Options B, C and D describe things barter lacks: a common measure of value, a means of storing value and a standard for deferred payments are all classic limitations of barter.

questions.question: Two countries agree that one will supply crude oil and the other will supply machinery of equal value in return, with no money changing hands. This modern form of barter is called

options.a: foreign exchange trading
options.b: debasement

questions.explanation: International countertrade is a modern form of barter in which countries exchange goods directly instead of paying in money. Option A involves buying and selling currencies, which is the opposite of avoiding money. Option B is reducing the metal content of coins, and option C is a bank buying a bill of exchange before it matures.

questions.question: In a community that uses grain as money, an unusually large harvest suddenly floods the market with grain and its value as money falls sharply. This illustrates which limitation of commodity money?

options.a: Lack of double coincidence of wants
options.b: Indivisibility

questions.explanation: The supply of commodity money depends on natural events such as harvests, so a bumper harvest or a disaster can change its quantity and cause unpredictable inflation or deflation. Option B is about goods that cannot be split into smaller units, and option A is a problem of barter, not of commodity money. Option C is a deliberate reduction in the metal content of coins by rulers.

questions.question: Two cows offered as payment are of the same breed, but one is healthy and fat while the other is old and thin, so traders argue over what each is worth. This illustrates which limitation of commodity money?

options.a: Variability in quality
options.b: Excessive portability

questions.explanation: Commodity money often varies in size, quality and condition, so units of the same type do not have the same value and pricing becomes difficult; this is the opposite of the uniformity good money needs. Option C concerns changes in the total quantity available, not differences between units. Option D is not the issue here, and option B is wrong because cattle are hard, not easy, to carry.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why gold and silver came to be preferred as money?

options.a: They are naturally scarce, which helps them keep a stable value
options.b: They are durable and do not rust or corrode
options.c: They decay quickly and must be used soon after they are obtained
options.d: They have high value relative to their weight, making them portable

questions.explanation: Precious metals were preferred precisely because they do not decay, so option C describes the opposite of their real quality. Options A, B and D are genuine reasons, alongside divisibility, uniformity, intrinsic value and universal acceptability.

questions.question: The earliest standardised coins, associated with the ancient kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor, were made of electrum, which is

options.a: pure refined gold stamped with the king's seal
options.b: an alloy of iron and nickel
options.c: a mixture of copper and tin, also called bronze
options.d: a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver

questions.explanation: Electrum is a natural mixture of gold and silver, and it was the metal of the early Lydian coins that began the history of standardised coinage. Option C describes bronze, which the Romans used in their early aes money. Option A is wrong because electrum is not pure gold, and option B is not electrum at all.

questions.question: The practice by which a ruler reduces the gold or silver content of coins, for example by mixing in copper, while keeping their face value unchanged, is known as

options.a: debasement
options.b: devaluation

questions.explanation: Debasement means lowering the precious metal content of coins but keeping the same face value, which let rulers mint more coins from the same metal and earn a profit. Option B refers to an official cut in a currency's exchange value against other currencies. Option D means withdrawing a form of money from use as legal tender, and option C is the right to exchange paper money for gold or silver.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a result of rulers debasing their coins?

options.a: Loss of public trust in the currency
options.b: Rejection of debased coins in favour of full-value or foreign coins
options.c: A rise in the purchasing power of each coin
options.d: Inflation, as people raised prices to reflect the lower metal content

questions.explanation: Debasement made each coin worth less in real terms, so its purchasing power fell rather than rose. Options A, B and D are all genuine consequences: prices went up, trust was eroded, and people refused debased coins in favour of better ones.

questions.question: A ruler holds 120 kg of silver. Full-value coins contain 20 g of silver each, but he decides to debase the coins so that each contains only 15 g while keeping the same face value. How many MORE coins can he mint from the same silver?

options.a: 8,000 coins
options.b: 2,000 coins

questions.explanation: At 20 g per coin, 120,000 g of silver makes 6,000 coins; at 15 g per coin it makes 8,000 coins, so debasement yields 2,000 extra coins of the same face value. Option A is the total number of debased coins, not the increase, and option C is the number of full-value coins. Option D wrongly takes 25% of the original 6,000 coins instead of dividing by the new weight.

questions.question: In the development of banking in England, the receipts that goldsmiths issued for gold deposited with them later

options.a: had to be destroyed as soon as the gold was deposited
options.b: circulated as a means of payment and became known as goldsmiths' notes, the forerunners of bank notes
options.c: could be used only by the person who made the deposit
options.d: were treated by law as shares in the goldsmith's business

questions.explanation: People found it convenient to pass the goldsmiths' receipts to others in payment instead of withdrawing the gold, so each receipt came to be called a goldsmith's note, the forerunner of the modern banknote. Option A is wrong because the receipts were evidence of the deposit, and option C contradicts the fact that they changed hands. Option D confuses a deposit receipt with ownership of the business.

questions.question: Bankers noticed that not all depositors demanded their gold at the same time, so they began issuing notes worth more than the metal actually held in their vaults. This practice marked the beginning of

options.a: fractional reserve banking
options.b: debasement of coinage

questions.explanation: Fractional reserve banking means keeping only part of deposits as reserves and lending or issuing paper claims against the rest, relying on the fact that depositors do not all withdraw at once. Option C is direct exchange without money. Option D fixes the value of a currency to gold, and option B reduces the metal content of coins.

questions.question: Why did the earliest bank notes have to be convertible into gold or silver coins on demand?

options.a: Banks wanted to prevent the notes from circulating as money
options.b: People were willing to accept them only because they believed the notes could be exchanged for gold or silver whenever they wished
options.c: Paper was more valuable than gold at that time
options.d: The law required every note to be destroyed once it was converted

questions.explanation: A paper note had no value of its own, so early acceptance rested on the promise that it could be converted into gold or silver coins on demand; such a note was a substitute for money rather than money itself. Option D has no basis, and option C is plainly false. Option A is wrong because convertibility was what made such paper acceptable in circulation.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the gold standard?

options.a: Governments could expand the money supply freely without regard to their gold reserves
options.b: Currencies were defined in terms of a fixed weight of gold
options.c: Exchange rates between countries were fixed by the gold value of their currencies
options.d: Paper money could be exchanged for gold at banks or the treasury

questions.explanation: Under the gold standard the money supply was limited by gold reserves, which is exactly why governments found it hard to respond to crises with monetary policy. Options B, C and D are genuine features: currencies were defined by gold weight, paper money was convertible into gold, and exchange rates were fixed through gold values.

questions.question: The word 'fiat' in fiat money comes from Latin and means

options.a: backed by gold
options.b: made of paper

questions.explanation: Fiat means 'let it be done', reflecting that fiat money has value because the government declares it legal tender, not because it is backed by a commodity. Option A describes representative money, which is the opposite of fiat money. Options B and C are not the meaning of the word, although paper currency can be fiat money.

questions.question: The international link between currencies and gold effectively ended in 1971 when

options.a: the Bank of England was established
options.b: Britain first adopted the gold standard
options.c: the United States suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold
options.d: the first paper banknotes were issued in Europe

questions.explanation: In 1971 the US stopped exchanging dollars for gold, which ended the Bretton Woods gold link and completed the move of the world to fiat currencies. Options A, B and D are events from much earlier in the history of money and banking, and none of them ended the gold standard.

questions.question: Early issuers of paper money added watermarks, intricate designs, special paper and several official signatures to their notes. These features were introduced mainly to deal with the problem of

options.a: overissuance
options.b: counterfeiting

questions.explanation: Paper is easier to copy than metal, so security features such as watermarks, special paper and signatures were added to stop counterfeiting. Option A was a separate problem of printing too much paper money, which needed monetary discipline rather than better designs. Option C relates to the metal content of coins, and option D is a barter problem.

questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct order in which money developed?

options.a: Barter, commodity money, metallic money (coins), paper money, electronic money
options.b: Metallic money (coins), barter, commodity money, electronic money, paper money
options.c: Commodity money, barter, paper money, metallic money (coins), electronic money
options.d: Barter, paper money, commodity money, electronic money, metallic money (coins)

questions.explanation: Money evolved from direct barter, to commodities with their own value, to standardised metal coins, then to paper money and finally to electronic and digital money, each stage solving problems of the one before. Options B, C and D all place at least one stage out of its proper order, for example putting paper money before coins or barter after money had appeared.

questions.question: Services such as M-Pesa in Kenya, which let people send, receive and store money on their mobile phones without a traditional bank account, have mainly

options.a: returned those economies to the barter system
options.b: ended the use of the national currency as a unit of account
options.c: promoted financial inclusion by reaching previously unbanked people
options.d: restored the gold standard in developing countries

questions.explanation: Mobile money uses the phone as a platform for transfers and storage of value, bringing financial services to people who never had bank accounts, which is the essence of financial inclusion. Option A is wrong because mobile money is still money, not direct exchange of goods. Options B and D are false, since balances are still held in and priced in the national currency.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin?

options.a: Legal tender issued by a central bank and backed by gold reserves
options.b: A form of commodity money with intrinsic value as a metal
options.c: A decentralised digital currency built on blockchain technology and not controlled by any government or central bank
options.d: A paper certificate that can be exchanged for silver on demand

questions.explanation: Cryptocurrencies are digital, use blockchain and cryptography, and allow peer-to-peer payments with no central authority in control. Option A describes neither fiat money nor crypto correctly, and option D describes representative money. Option B is wrong because a cryptocurrency has no physical or metallic form.

questions.question: Pierce and Shaw distinguished an abstract from a tangible (concrete) definition of money. Under the abstract definition, money is

options.a: whatever the law of the land declares to be legal tender
options.b: a unit of account, the common denominator in which the exchange value of all goods and services is expressed
options.c: a medium of exchange whose ownership is capable of changing hands
options.d: anything that serves as a temporary abode of purchasing power

questions.explanation: The abstract definition sees money as a measure of exchange value, the unit in which all prices are expressed. Option C is Pierce and Shaw's tangible or concrete definition. Option A is the legal definition of money, and option D is Milton Friedman's view.

questions.question: Which school of thought on the definition of money holds that 'cheque is money and money is cheque', because most bank transactions are carried out with cheques?

options.a: The currency school
options.b: The banking school

questions.explanation: The banking school accepts the general definition of money but objects to leaving out bank cheques, since the bulk of deposit money bank transactions are settled by cheque. Option A limits money to legal tender currency such as naira and kobo. Option D, associated with Milton Friedman, defines money as a temporary abode of purchasing power, and option C is not a school of thought on money.

questions.question: Milton Friedman, often described as the leading monetarist, defined money as

options.a: the table on which money changers carried on their trade
options.b: legal tender currency notes and coins only
options.c: a commodity with intrinsic value equal to its face value
options.d: anything that serves as a temporary abode of purchasing power

questions.explanation: Friedman's monetarist or Chicago view treats money as a temporary abode of purchasing power, which is broad enough to include cheques, drafts, a promissory note and other bills. Option B is the narrower currency school view. Option C describes standard or full-bodied commodity money, and option A refers to the origin of the word 'bank'.

questions.question: Emeka, who works in Lagos, sends N30,000 every month to his parents in Kano, who use it to buy food there. The function of money mainly illustrated here is

options.a: standard of deferred payment
options.b: store of value

questions.explanation: Because money is generally acceptable and its ownership can pass from one person to another, it allows value to be moved from person to person and from one place to another, as Emeka does. Option D is about expressing prices in a common unit, and option A is about settling debts at a future date. Option B is about holding purchasing power over time rather than moving it.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes money held as cash from near-money assets such as treasury bills?

options.a: Cash is legal tender but earns no yield, while near-money assets earn a return but must first be converted, with some delay or cost, before they can be spent
options.b: Near-money assets are legal tender, while cash is not
options.c: Cash cannot be spent directly, while near-money assets are accepted everywhere as payment
options.d: Cash earns interest, while near-money assets earn nothing

questions.explanation: Money is legal tender, fully liquid and generally acceptable, but cash kept idle yields nothing; near money gives a return yet has to be turned into money first, which takes some time or cost. Option D reverses the yield difference. Options B and C reverse the points on legal status and acceptability.

questions.question: The characteristic of good money which requires that every unit of the currency can be identified quickly as genuine money without any technical assistance, so that no time is wasted inspecting it, is

options.a: scarcity
options.b: durability

questions.explanation: Recognisability means each unit of money can be easily and quickly recognised, which speeds up transactions between buyers and sellers. Option C is about dividing money into smaller units for small purchases, option A is about keeping supply limited so money keeps its value, and option B is about money lasting through repeated use.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Nigerian banking system before independence?

options.a: It was dominated by indigenous banks closely supervised by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: Colonial banks channelled most of their credit to Nigerian farmers and small traders
options.c: It was built around a well-developed stock exchange that financed most Nigerian businesses
options.d: It was dominated by foreign-owned banks that served mainly colonial trade and gave little credit to indigenous entrepreneurs

questions.explanation: Before independence, expatriate banks controlled Nigerian banking, concentrating on financing trade between Nigeria and Britain and lending mainly to foreign firms, while regulation was weak. Option A is wrong because indigenous banks were few and many of them failed, and the Central Bank of Nigeria did not begin operations until 1959. Option B is the opposite of what happened, since colonial banks were known for discriminating against indigenous borrowers, and option C is wrong because organised stock market activity only began around independence.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Before the Central Bank of Nigeria was set up, currency in Nigeria was issued by the

options.a: Federal Ministry of Finance
options.b: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation

questions.explanation: The West African Currency Board, set up by the British colonial government in 1912, issued sterling-backed currency for Nigeria and other British West African colonies until the CBN took over this role. Option C is tempting because that bank acted as the Board's agent in distributing currency, but it was not the issuing authority. Option B is a deposit insurer created long after independence, and option A has never been a currency-issuing authority in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor that contributed to the development of the Nigerian financial system?

options.a: Growth in savings and investment activities
options.b: The establishment of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: Technological advancement such as electronic banking
options.d: A return to barter as the main means of exchange

questions.explanation: A return to barter would shrink, not develop, the financial system, because barter removes the need for money, banks and financial markets. The establishment of the CBN (option B) provided leadership and regulation, technology such as electronic banking (option C) widened access to financial services, and rising savings and investment (option A) increased the funds flowing through financial institutions.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Commercial banking in Nigeria began during the colonial era with the establishment of

options.a: foreign-owned (expatriate) banks set up mainly to serve colonial trade
options.b: microfinance banks serving rural communities
options.d: indigenous banks founded by Nigerian nationalists

questions.explanation: The first banks in Nigeria were expatriate institutions, such as the forerunner of today's First Bank, which were set up mainly to finance trade between Nigeria and Britain. Option D is wrong because indigenous banks came later, partly as a reaction to the discrimination Nigerians faced in foreign banks. Option C was not established until 1958, and option B is a much more recent category of bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Bank of British West Africa, one of the earliest banks in Nigeria, eventually became

options.a: First Bank of Nigeria
options.b: United Bank for Africa

questions.explanation: The Bank of British West Africa went through several name changes, including Standard Bank of Nigeria, before becoming First Bank of Nigeria. Option D grew out of Barclays Bank DCO, and option B grew out of the British and French Bank for Commerce and Industry. Option C grew out of the indigenous Agbonmagbe Bank, not a colonial bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the banking consolidation programme announced by the CBN in July 2004, the minimum capital base of Nigerian banks was raised to

options.a: N25 billion
options.b: N10 billion

questions.explanation: In July 2004 the CBN raised the minimum capital base of banks from N2 billion to N25 billion, with a deadline at the end of 2005, and the number of banks fell from 89 to 25 through mergers and acquisitions. Option C was the old requirement in force before the reform. Options B and D do not match the 2004 programme.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason for the collapse of many early indigenous banks in Nigeria?

options.a: Poor management practices
options.b: Excessive regulation and strict supervision by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: Lack of a proper regulatory framework

questions.explanation: Most early indigenous banks failed in the 1940s and early 1950s, when there was little or no banking regulation and the CBN did not yet exist, so excessive CBN supervision cannot have caused their collapse. Inadequate capital (option D), poor management (option A) and the absence of proper regulation (option C) are the main reasons usually given for those failures.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The wave of indigenous bank failures in Nigeria in the late 1940s and early 1950s led the colonial government to

options.a: nationalise all foreign-owned banks
options.b: create the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation to compensate depositors
options.c: introduce banking legislation that required licensing and minimum capital for banks

questions.explanation: Following an enquiry into the failures, the colonial government passed Nigeria's first banking law, which introduced licensing and minimum paid-up capital requirements for banks. Option B is wrong because the NDIC was set up decades later, long after independence. Options A and D did not happen; the response was regulation, not nationalisation or a ban on indigenous ownership.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first commercial bank in Nigeria came in _______ and was known as ________.

options.a: 1892, Barclays Bank
options.b: 1952, Industrial and Commercial Bank

questions.explanation: Commercial banking in Nigeria began in 1892, when the African Banking Corporation opened in Lagos. Its business was taken over in 1894 by the Bank of British West Africa, which later became Standard Bank and is today First Bank of Nigeria.
