Barclays Bank (A) came later, the Industrial and Commercial Bank (B) was an indigenous bank of 1929 rather than 1952, and Standard Bank (D) was a later name, not the first bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The factors that made for the rapid collapse of indigenous commercial banks before the Banking Ordinance of 1952 included:

options.a: Weak capital base
options.b: Untrained and inexperienced managers

questions.explanation: Before the 1952 Banking Ordinance there were no banking rules or bank examiners, and most of the many indigenous banks set up in the 1940s boom collapsed quickly. They had weak capital bases that could not absorb shocks (A), untrained and inexperienced managers who could not analyse balance sheets or forecast bad debts (B), and widespread fraud (C). All three were causes, so D is correct.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Before 1952, only the indigenous commercial banks set up by government or with strong government backing survived the wave of bank failures. Which of these was NOT one of such banks?

options.a: WEMA Bank
options.b: African Continental Bank

questions.explanation: Afribank began as the International Bank for West Africa, a foreign-owned bank that came into Nigeria later, so it was not one of the indigenous banks that survived because of government backing. National Bank (D) was backed by the Western Regional government, African Continental Bank (B) by the Eastern Regional government, and WEMA Bank (A) grew out of Agbonmagbe Bank, which the Western Regional government supported.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: After the Banking Ordinance of 1952, many more banks collapsed because:

options.a: They could not meet the minimum capital requirement set by the Ordinance
options.b: There was no supervisory and regulatory agency to give purposeful direction and leadership

questions.explanation: Many indigenous banks failed after the 1952 Ordinance because they could not meet its new minimum capital requirement (A). There was also no central bank yet to supervise banks and give direction (B), since the CBN only began operations in 1959, and banks without government patronage (C) lacked the support that kept the government-backed banks alive. All three explain the failures, so D is correct.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first Nigerian merchant bank, NAL Merchant Bank, which came on board in 1969, was a merger of two companies that had existed since 1960 and were already performing merchant banking functions. These were:

options.a: Nigerian Acceptances Limited and Peoples Co Limited
options.b: Nigerian Acceptances Limited and Philip Hill (Nigeria) Limited
options.c: Nigerian Acceptances Limited and United African Company

questions.explanation: Merchant banking in Nigeria began in 1960 with Nigerian Acceptances Limited and Philip Hill (Nigeria) Limited. In 1969 the two merged to form NAL Merchant Bank, the first Nigerian merchant bank. Neither Peoples Co Limited (A) nor the United African Company (C), a trading company, was part of this merger.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The colonial government promulgated Nigeria's first Banking Ordinance, based on the Paton Report, in
questions.explanation: Nigeria's first banking law was the Banking Ordinance of 1952, passed after the Paton Report looked into banking practice in the colony. It ended the era of free, unregulated banking by introducing licensing and minimum paid-up capital rules that many weak indigenous banks could not meet. Options A, B and D are wrong because no banking ordinance was passed in 1950, 1951 or 1953; the next major ordinance came in 1958, when the 1952 law was replaced.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In Nigeria's early banking history, the operations of the African Banking Corporation in Lagos were taken over by which bank?

options.a: Barclays Bank DCO
options.b: Bank of British West Africa

questions.explanation: The African Banking Corporation was one of the first banks in colonial Lagos, but it ran into difficulties and its operations were taken over by the Bank of British West Africa, which later became Standard Bank and then First Bank of Nigeria. Option A grew out of the Colonial Bank (option D) and later became Union Bank, while option C later became the United Bank for Africa. None of these took over the African Banking Corporation.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Industrial and Commercial Bank, widely regarded as the first indigenous bank in Nigeria, was established in
questions.explanation: The Industrial and Commercial Bank was set up in Lagos in 1929 as the first bank owned by Nigerians, but it collapsed soon after. Option C, 1930, is the year it failed, not the year it was founded. Option A, 1894, belongs to the era of the foreign-owned Bank of British West Africa, and option D, 1932, does not match the founding date.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The foreign bank that began operating in Nigeria as the Colonial Bank is now known as

options.a: First Bank Plc
options.b: GTB Plc

questions.explanation: The Colonial Bank came to Nigeria during the First World War period, later became Barclays Bank DCO and then Barclays Bank of Nigeria, and is known today as Union Bank of Nigeria Plc. Option A, First Bank, grew out of the Bank of British West Africa, the earlier foreign bank. Option D, UBA, grew out of the British and French Bank, and GTB in option B is a much newer bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Wema Bank Plc, which began as Agbonmagbe Bank, was established in
questions.explanation: Wema Bank started life in 1945 as Agbonmagbe Bank, one of the indigenous banks that sprang up in the post-war banking boom, and it is still operating today under the Wema name. Options A, C and D are nearby years from the same period of indigenous banking, but they are not the year Agbonmagbe Bank was founded.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The former name of United Bank for Africa (UBA) was

options.a: Agbonmagbe Bank
options.b: Barclays Bank

questions.explanation: United Bank for Africa was formed to take over the business of the British and French Bank, so that is its former name. Barclays Bank (Option B) is the forerunner of Union Bank of Nigeria, Agbonmagbe Bank (Option A) became Wema Bank, and Standard Bank of Nigeria (Option D) is a former name of First Bank of Nigeria.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The former name of Wema bank was

options.a: British and French Bank
options.b: Bank of British West Africa

questions.explanation: Wema Bank began as Agbonmagbe Bank, an indigenous bank founded in the Western Region that was later renamed Wema Bank. The Bank of British West Africa (Option B) is the forerunner of First Bank of Nigeria, Barclays Bank (Option C) became Union Bank of Nigeria, and the British and French Bank (Option A) became United Bank for Africa.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Reasons for the collapse of many early indigenous banks in Nigeria during the period of unregulated (free) banking include the following EXCEPT

options.a: poor management
options.b: aggressive competition

questions.explanation: All three of the listed factors were genuine reasons why so many early indigenous banks collapsed, so none of them is an exception and D is correct. Many of these banks were poorly managed and undercapitalised, they faced aggressive competition from larger and better-established expatriate banks, and there was no regulatory authority to set standards or supervise them before banking legislation came in. Choosing A, B or C would wrongly suggest that one of these was not a cause of the failures.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The former name of Union Bank of Nigeria Plc was

options.a: British and French Bank
options.b: Bank of British West Africa

questions.explanation: Union Bank of Nigeria was formerly Barclays Bank (Barclays Bank DCO), a British-owned bank that was later renamed Union Bank. The Bank of British West Africa (Option B) became First Bank of Nigeria, Agbonmagbe Bank (Option D) became Wema Bank, and the British and French Bank (Option A) became United Bank for Africa.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first banking ordinance in Nigeria was passed in the year
questions.explanation: The Banking Ordinance of 1952, based on the 1948 Paton Commission report, was Nigeria's first banking law, passed to check the wave of indigenous bank failures. Option B (1958) is the year that ordinance was replaced by a new Banking Ordinance and the CBN Act was passed. Option D (1912) is when the West African Currency Board was set up, and C (1872) is before modern banking even reached Nigeria.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first legislative measure to tackle the problems associated with the free-for-all banking era was:

options.a: The enactment of the Central Bank of Nigeria Act
options.b: The enactment of the Banking Ordinance in 1952
options.c: The setting up of the Loynes Commission of 1957
options.d: The setting up of the Fisher Commission

questions.explanation: The Banking Ordinance of 1952 was the first law passed to end the era of free, unregulated banking, when many poorly capitalised indigenous banks were collapsing. The Fisher Commission (D) of 1953 and the Loynes Commission (C) of 1957 were enquiries into whether Nigeria should have a central bank, not laws. The CBN Act (A) came later, in 1958.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The West African Currency Board, established in 1912, was criticised on several grounds. Which of the following was NOT one of them?

options.a: Hindering the growth and development of Nigeria's own financial system
options.b: Tying domestic money supply expansion to the balance of trade performance of the economy
options.c: Convertibility of the local currency into the British pound sterling
options.d: Lack of independence for Nigeria in carrying out its own domestic monetary policy

questions.explanation: Easy convertibility into sterling was actually seen as a benefit of the WACB system, because it gave the colonies' currency international recognition and confidence. The real criticisms were that it invested the earnings from Nigeria's trade abroad and so held back the local financial system (A), tied growth in the money supply to balance of trade performance (B), and left Nigeria without an independent monetary policy (D).

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In studying the evolution of commercial banking in Nigeria, the Structural Adjustment Programme adopted in Nigeria in the mid-1980s was responsible for all of the following within the Nigerian banking system from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s except:

options.a: Interest rate deregulation
options.b: Proliferation in the number of banks operating in Nigeria
options.c: Increase in Federal Government deposits in commercial banks

questions.explanation: The Structural Adjustment Programme liberalised banking: interest rates were deregulated and bank licensing was relaxed, so the number of banks grew rapidly. It did not raise Federal Government deposits in commercial banks; in fact, public sector deposits were moved out of the banks to the Central Bank of Nigeria during this period. Options A and B were genuine results of SAP, and D cannot be right because C is the exception.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Some of the reasons for the mass failure of indigenous banks in Nigeria between 1945 and 1952 include all of the following except

options.a: Operational inefficiency
options.b: Discriminating attitude of the colonial masters

questions.explanation: The indigenous banks of the post-war banking boom failed mainly because of poor management and operational inefficiency, inadequate capital, a lack of trained and competent staff, and a discriminating colonial environment. Patronage and encouragement from foreign merchants was not a cause of failure; the indigenous banks actually struggled against competition from the well-established foreign banks. So A, B and C were genuine causes, while D is the exception.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The West African Currency Board was mandated to

options.a: Accept deposits from Nigerians
options.b: Issue and distribute currency in the British West African colonies

questions.explanation: The West African Currency Board, set up in 1912, issued and distributed a sterling-backed currency for the British West African colonies, including Nigeria. It was not a bank and did not take deposits (A), and the naira (C) came much later, issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Since B correctly states its mandate, D is wrong.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of these banks was formerly known as "Agbonmagbe Bank" in Nigeria?

options.a: First Bank of Nigeria
options.b: Access Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: Agbonmagbe Bank was one of the indigenous banks set up in the Western Region during the post-war banking boom, and it later became Wema Bank, which still operates today. First Bank (A) grew out of the Bank of British West Africa, a foreign bank, while Access Bank (B) and Savannah Bank (C) have different histories.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first foreign-owned bank was set up in Nigeria in the year
questions.explanation: Banking in Nigeria began in 1892, when the African Banking Corporation, a foreign bank, opened in Lagos to serve colonial trade; its business was taken over by the Bank of British West Africa (later First Bank) in 1894. The years 1930 (A), 1945 (B) and 1952 (D) all come long after foreign banking had already been established in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Bank of British West Africa (BBWA), which took over the business of the African Banking Corporation in colonial Nigeria, is the forerunner of which present-day bank?

options.a: United Bank for Africa
options.b: Wema Bank

questions.explanation: The Bank of British West Africa later became Standard Bank of Nigeria and was eventually renamed First Bank of Nigeria. Union Bank (option C) grew out of Barclays Bank DCO, while UBA (option A) grew out of the British and French Bank for Commerce and Industry. Wema Bank (option B) is an indigenous bank that began as Agbonmagbe Bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following early indigenous banks survived the wave of bank failures that swept Nigeria before the Central Bank of Nigeria was established?

options.a: Industrial and Commercial Bank
options.b: Nigerian Farmers and Commercial Bank

questions.explanation: The National Bank of Nigeria, founded in 1933, was one of the few indigenous banks to survive, helped by strong backing from the Western Regional Government. The Industrial and Commercial Bank (option A) and the Nigerian Mercantile Bank (option C) both collapsed in the 1930s, and the Nigerian Farmers and Commercial Bank (option B) failed during the crash of the early 1950s.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a cause of the collapse of many indigenous banks in Nigeria before the Central Bank of Nigeria was established?

options.a: Absence of banking regulation and supervision, which allowed fraud to thrive
options.b: Weak capital bases that could not absorb losses or shocks
options.c: Untrained and inexperienced staff and poor management
options.d: Strict cash reserve requirements imposed on them by the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria did not begin operations until 1959, so it could not have caused the bank failures of the 1930s to 1950s. The real causes were weak capital (option B), inexperienced and untrained staff who managed the banks poorly (option C), and the lack of any banking law or supervisory authority before 1952, which allowed fraud and reckless lending (option A).

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which law, passed after the Paton enquiry into bank failures, was the first banking legislation in Nigeria?

options.a: The Central Bank of Nigeria Act of 1958
options.b: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Decree of 1991

questions.explanation: Following the 1948 Paton enquiry into the failures of indigenous banks, the colonial government passed the Banking Ordinance of 1952, which introduced licensing and minimum capital and reserve requirements for banks. The CBN Act of 1958 (option A) created the central bank, the Banking Decree of 1969 (option C) later replaced the earlier banking laws, and the 1991 decree (option B) came much later.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: NAL Merchant Bank, licensed in 1969 as Nigeria's first merchant bank, grew out of which company that had been carrying out merchant banking functions since 1960?

options.a: Nigerian Acceptances Limited
options.b: Industrial and Commercial Bank
options.c: Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry

questions.explanation: Merchant banking in Nigeria began with firms such as Nigerian Acceptances Limited, set up in 1960, which financed trade and acted as an issuing house before becoming NAL Merchant Bank in 1969. The Industrial and Commercial Bank (option B) was an early indigenous commercial bank, the Bank of British West Africa (option D) was a colonial commercial bank that became First Bank, and the NBCI (option C) was a development bank set up in the 1970s.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the banking consolidation programme announced by the CBN in July 2004, deposit money banks were required to raise their minimum capital base to ______ by 31 December 2005.

options.a: N2 billion
options.b: N100 billion

questions.explanation: The 2004 consolidation raised the minimum capital base of every deposit money bank from N2 billion to N25 billion, with a deadline of the end of 2005. Many banks met the target through mergers, acquisitions and public share offers, and the number of banks fell sharply, which left a smaller group of better-capitalised banks. Option A was the old minimum before the exercise, while options B and C were not the 2004 requirement.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following contributed to the development of the Nigerian financial system?

options.a: A return of the economy to trade by barter
options.b: The removal of all regulation of banks at independence
options.c: The establishment of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: The closure of all indigenous banks after independence

questions.explanation: Setting up the CBN was a major step in developing the financial system, because the CBN went on to build money and capital market institutions and regulate the banks; other factors include independence, the oil boom, regulation and deregulation, and the bank reforms. Options A, B and D never happened and would have held the system back rather than developed it.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Bank of British West Africa, established in 1894, is the forerunner of which present-day Nigerian bank?

options.a: Union Bank of Nigeria
options.b: United Bank for Africa

questions.explanation: The Bank of British West Africa took over from the African Banking Corporation, enjoyed a near monopoly of banking for years, and later became First Bank of Nigeria. Option A grew out of Barclays Bank DCO, option B grew out of the British and French Bank, and option D grew out of the indigenous Agbonmagbe Bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Barclays Bank DCO, which came to Nigeria in the 1920s after a merger that included the Colonial Bank, later became

options.a: First Bank of Nigeria
options.b: United Bank for Africa

questions.explanation: The Colonial Bank joined other banks to form Barclays Bank DCO, which later became Union Bank of Nigeria. Option A came from the Bank of British West Africa, option B came from the British and French Bank, and option C came from the indigenous Agbonmagbe Bank.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which bank, established in 1892 and engaged in distributing British currency, marked the beginning of commercial banking in Nigeria?

options.a: Bank of British West Africa
options.b: Colonial Bank

questions.explanation: Commercial banking in Nigeria began with the African Banking Corporation in 1892. Option A came in 1894 and took over its business, option B arrived later, and option D was an indigenous bank founded in the 1930s.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a cause of the collapse of most indigenous banks in Nigeria in the early 1950s?

options.a: Undercapitalisation
options.b: Fraud and bad or inexperienced management

questions.explanation: The early indigenous banks failed because they had too little capital, not too much. Options A, B and D were real causes, along with crude accounting systems and the stricter requirements of the 1952 banking law.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which three indigenous banks survived the banking crisis of the early 1950s?

options.a: National Bank of Nigeria, African Continental Bank and Agbonmagbe Bank
options.b: Industrial and Commercial Bank, Nigerian Mercantile Bank and National Bank of Nigeria
options.c: Bank of British West Africa, Barclays Bank DCO and British and French Bank
options.d: African Continental Bank, Industrial and Commercial Bank and Bank of British West Africa

questions.explanation: Of the many indigenous banks formed during the boom, only National Bank of Nigeria, African Continental Bank and Agbonmagbe Bank (later Wema Bank) survived, with help from their regional governments. Options B and D include the Industrial and Commercial Bank, which had already failed, and options C and D include expatriate banks, which were not indigenous.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first banking legislation in Nigeria was enacted mainly because of:

options.a: The introduction of the naira as Nigeria's currency
options.b: The need to set up the Nigerian Stock Exchange
options.c: The widespread failure of indigenous banks that sprang up during the unregulated free banking era
options.d: The consolidation of banks to a minimum capital of N25 billion

questions.explanation: Before any banking law existed, anyone could set up a bank, and many poorly capitalised and badly managed indigenous banks opened and then collapsed, so depositors lost their savings. The government therefore introduced licensing and minimum capital rules. The stock exchange (B), the naira (A) and the 2004 consolidation (D) all came much later.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The report of which commission led to the enactment of Nigeria's first banking law?

options.a: The Paton Commission
options.b: The Okigbo Financial System Review Committee

questions.explanation: G. D. Paton was asked to study banking in Nigeria and recommend controls, and his report led to the first Banking Ordinance. The Loynes report (D) dealt with setting up a central bank, the Barback Committee (C) recommended a stock exchange, and the Okigbo Committee (B) reviewed the financial system in the 1970s.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a characteristic of the expatriate (colonial) banks that operated in Nigeria before independence?

options.a: They accepted deposits from Africans but were reluctant to lend to them
options.b: They were registered, headquartered and controlled from London
options.c: They mainly financed the trade of British and other foreign firms
options.d: They built wide branch networks in rural areas to give credit to peasant farmers

questions.explanation: Colonial banks concentrated their offices in the commercial centres where British trading interests were strong, so rural credit to peasant farmers was never their focus. Options A, B and C are all genuine features: the banks were London-controlled, served foreign trade and colonial government business, and took African deposits while refusing most African loan requests.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In 1940 a Lagos produce trader keeps his savings with a foreign-owned bank, but his request for a modest loan is refused while a British trading firm with similar business easily obtains credit. This experience best illustrates

options.a: the credit ceilings introduced under the Structural Adjustment Programme
options.b: the conservative cash reserve rules imposed by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: the minimum capital requirement of the 1952 Banking Ordinance
options.d: the discriminatory lending practices of the expatriate banks

questions.explanation: Expatriate banks were happy to take Nigerian deposits but favoured expatriate firms when granting loans, and this discrimination was a major reason Nigerians set up their own banks. Option B is wrong because the CBN did not exist in 1940, and options A and C refer to later laws and policies that came long after this period.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which pair of factors best explains the emergence of indigenous banks in Nigeria during the colonial period?

options.a: The deregulation of interest rates and the liberalisation of bank licensing
options.b: The expansion of African businessmen and the discriminatory lending of expatriate banks
options.c: The 2004 consolidation exercise and the adoption of universal banking
options.d: The establishment of the CBN and the introduction of deposit insurance

questions.explanation: Indigenous banks arose because a growing class of African businessmen needed finance that the expatriate banks were unwilling to give them. Option D describes institutions that came only in 1958-1988, while options A and C describe reforms of the SAP era and the 2000s.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Because the colonial banks in Nigeria were registered and headquartered abroad, they fell mainly under the regulatory jurisdiction of

options.a: Lagos
options.b: Accra

questions.explanation: The colonial banks were registered, headquartered and controlled from London, so they had little need for regulation by the host territory. Lagos (option A) had no banking law at all until 1952, and Accra and Johannesburg (options B and D) were not the home base of these banks.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which group of banks dominated Nigerian banking in the years just before independence?

options.a: Guaranty Trust Bank, Zenith Bank and Access Bank
options.b: Bank of British West Africa, Barclays Bank DCO and the British and French Bank
options.c: Nigerian Industrial Development Bank, Federal Mortgage Bank and NACB
options.d: Spring Bank, Unity Bank and Skye Bank

questions.explanation: Three expatriate banks, the Bank of British West Africa (now First Bank), Barclays DCO (now Union Bank) and the British and French Bank (now UBA), controlled most of the banking business before independence. Option A lists banks set up only after deregulation, option C lists development banks of the post-independence era, and option D lists banks formed during the 2004-2005 consolidation.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The colonial-era banks such as the Bank of British West Africa, Barclays DCO and the British and French Bank are often grouped together as Nigeria's

options.a: third-generation banks
options.b: first-generation banks

questions.explanation: First-generation banks are the earliest banks, set up in the colonial period mainly to serve the colonial administration and foreign trade; today they survive as First Bank, Union Bank and UBA. Option A refers to much later banks of the liberalisation era, while community banks (option D) and non-interest banks (option C) are special categories created long after independence.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: When the West African Currency Board was set up in 1912, the Bank of British West Africa served in Nigeria as the Board's

options.a: agent for the custody and distribution of its currency
options.b: supervisor and examiner of indigenous banks
options.c: lender of last resort to other banks

questions.explanation: The Bank of British West Africa was appointed agent of the Currency Board, holding and distributing the currency the Board issued. Lender of last resort (option C) and bank supervision (option B) are central bank roles that came with the CBN in 1959, and deposit insurance (option D) only began with the NDIC in 1988.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the West African Currency Board system, the West African pound circulating in Nigeria was

options.a: issued by commercial banks and backed by their loans to traders
options.b: issued at a fixed rate against sterling and backed 100 per cent by sterling reserves
options.c: issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria and backed by gold held in Lagos
options.d: issued at a floating rate and backed mainly by Nigerian government bonds

questions.explanation: A currency board issues money only against full reserves of an anchor currency, so the West African pound was tied to sterling at a fixed rate with 100 per cent sterling backing. Option D is wrong because the rate was fixed, not floating, and option C is wrong because the CBN did not exist yet. Option A wrongly treats commercial banks as currency issuers.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Nigerian nationalists in the 1950s argued that the West African Currency Board arrangement had to give way to a central bank. Their main objection was that the Board

options.a: left Nigeria with no room for discretionary monetary management suited to its own needs
options.b: insured bank deposits and so encouraged risky behaviour
options.c: issued too much currency and caused runaway inflation
options.d: lent heavily to indigenous banks and encouraged reckless banking

questions.explanation: A currency board simply exchanges local money for sterling, so it cannot run an independent monetary policy; this lack of local monetary control was the core complaint. Option C is wrong because full sterling backing actually restricted money supply, and options B and D describe roles the Board never performed.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The period before 1952, when anyone could set up a bank in Nigeria without a licence, minimum capital or any form of regulation, is known as the era of

options.a: consolidation
options.b: regulated banking

questions.explanation: Free or laissez-faire banking describes the pre-1952 situation in which there was no banking law, so banks could open and fail without official control. The regulated era (option B) began with the 1952 Banking Ordinance, deregulation (option C) came with SAP in 1986, and consolidation (option A) refers to the 2004-2005 recapitalisation.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The decade from 1945 to 1955, when many indigenous banks were registered and then most of them collapsed, is described in Nigerian banking history as the period of

options.a: banking consolidation
options.b: banking indigenisation

questions.explanation: Between 1945 and 1955 there was a rush to register indigenous banks (the boom), followed by a wave of failures that left only a few survivors (the doom). Consolidation (option A) is the 2004-2005 recapitalisation, universal banking (option D) dates from 2001, and indigenisation (option B) refers to the 1970s ownership decrees.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In 1953 a small indigenous bank in Lagos with very little paid-up capital is forced to close because it cannot satisfy the requirements of the new banking law within the grace period. This bank is a victim of

options.a: the minimum paid-up capital and licensing requirements of the 1952 Banking Ordinance
options.b: the N25 billion recapitalisation directive of the CBN
options.c: the cash reserve requirement set by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: the indigenisation provisions of the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree

questions.explanation: The 1952 Ordinance required every bank to hold a licence and a minimum paid-up capital, and many weak indigenous banks wound up because they could not comply. Option D came in 1972, option B in 2004, and option C is wrong because the CBN did not begin operations until 1959.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was a cause of the collapse of many indigenous banks during the boom of the late 1940s and early 1950s?

options.a: Margin lending to stockbrokers during a stock market bubble
options.b: Removal of their chief executives by the CBN
options.c: Failure to meet the N25 billion minimum capital base

questions.explanation: The early indigenous banks failed largely through malpractice: too little capital, rapid and unplanned branch opening, poor management, fraud and crude accounting. Option A describes the 2009 crisis, option C the 2004-2005 consolidation, and option B the CBN intervention of 2009.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The colonial enquiry into banking practice whose report formed the basis of Nigeria's first banking law was headed by

options.a: G. D. Paton
options.b: Pius Okigbo

questions.explanation: G. D. Paton led the colonial enquiry into banking in Nigeria, and the Paton Report led directly to the Banking Ordinance of 1952. J. B. Loynes (option C) reported in 1957 on setting up a central bank, Pius Okigbo (option B) chaired the 1976 financial system review, and Roy Fenton (option D) was the first CBN Governor.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The main task of the Paton commission set up by the colonial government was to

options.a: design a new Nigerian currency to replace the West African pound
options.b: look into banking business in Nigeria and recommend the form and extent of control to be introduced
options.c: merge the surviving indigenous banks into one national bank
options.d: set up a deposit insurance fund for depositors of failed banks

questions.explanation: Following the boom and crisis in banking, Paton was appointed to study banking business in Nigeria and advise how far the government should control it, which led to the 1952 Ordinance. Options A, C and D describe tasks never given to the commission; currency issue and deposit insurance came much later with the CBN and NDIC.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the Banking Ordinance of 1952?

options.a: The keeping of reserve funds and the examination of banks
options.b: Compulsory insurance of all bank deposits by a deposit insurance corporation
options.c: A minimum paid-up capital for banks
options.d: The requirement to obtain a licence before carrying on banking business

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance did not exist in 1952; it came only when the NDIC was established in 1988. Options A, C and D were all part of the 1952 Ordinance, which introduced licensing, minimum capital, reserve funds and bank examinations to end the free banking era.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the Banking Ordinance of 1952, how did the minimum paid-up capital for banks incorporated in Nigeria compare with that for banks incorporated outside Nigeria?

options.a: It was higher for banks incorporated in Nigeria than for those incorporated abroad
options.b: Only banks incorporated abroad had to meet a minimum capital
options.c: It was the same for all banks wherever incorporated
options.d: It was lower for banks incorporated in Nigeria than for those incorporated abroad

questions.explanation: The 1952 Ordinance set a much smaller minimum capital for locally incorporated (mostly indigenous) banks than for foreign-incorporated banks, which had far more capital. Option A reverses the relationship, option C ignores the two separate levels, and option B is wrong because local banks also had a minimum to meet.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The most important long-term significance of the Banking Ordinance of 1952 was that it

options.a: nationalised the three big expatriate banks
options.b: allowed banks to combine commercial, merchant and insurance business
options.c: transferred currency issue from the Currency Board to the Central Bank
options.d: ended free banking and established the principle of government regulation of banks

questions.explanation: As Nigeria's first banking law, the 1952 Ordinance brought the free-for-all era to an end and set the precedent that banks must be licensed and supervised. Option C happened only with the CBN in 1959, option A wrongly describes the partial government stakes taken in the 1970s, and option B describes universal banking, introduced in 2001.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria was established by the CBN Act of 1958 but began full operations on

options.a: 1 April 1960
options.b: 1 July 1959

questions.explanation: The CBN Act was passed in 1958 and was fully implemented on 1 July 1959, when the Bank came into full operation. Option C is Nigeria's independence day, option D comes before the Act was even passed, and option A falls in 1960, when the CBN issued its first treasury bills.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The 1957 report whose recommendations led the colonial government to agree to set up a central bank for Nigeria is associated with

options.a: Charles Soludo
options.b: J. B. Loynes

questions.explanation: J. B. Loynes produced the 1957 recommendations that led to the CBN Act of 1958. Paton (option C) reported on commercial banking before the 1952 Ordinance, Soludo (option A) was the CBN Governor who announced the 2004 consolidation, and Okigbo (option D) chaired the 1976 financial system review committee.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The first Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, a British banker who served from 1958 to 1963, was

options.a: G. D. Paton
options.b: Roy Pentelow Fenton

questions.explanation: Roy Pentelow Fenton was the first CBN Governor, serving from July 1958 to July 1963. Aliyu Mai-Bornu (option C) succeeded him as the first Nigerian Governor, while Paton (option A) and Loynes (option D) wrote reports that led to the 1952 Ordinance and the CBN respectively.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In 1960 the newly established Central Bank of Nigeria issued its first short-term instruments for government borrowing, which also helped to start a local money market. These instruments were

options.a: certificates of deposit
options.b: development stocks

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term government debt instruments, and the CBN issued the first ones in 1960 to finance government and build the money market. Development stocks (option B) are long-term government securities, while bankers' acceptances (option D) and certificates of deposit (option A) are created by banks, not issued by the central bank for government borrowing.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Lagos Bankers' Clearing House, set up under the CBN in 1961, was mainly designed to

options.a: settle cheques drawn on one bank and paid into another bank
options.b: issue Nigerian currency notes and coins to the banks
options.c: buy non-performing loans from distressed banks
options.d: insure the deposits of customers of banks that fail

questions.explanation: A clearing house is where banks exchange and settle the cheques drawn on each other, so the 1961 Lagos clearing house made cheque collection between banks efficient. Option B is the CBN's currency-issue function, option D is the role of the NDIC from 1988, and option C is the job of AMCON, created in 2010.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The greatest significance of the establishment of the Central Bank of Nigeria in 1958-1959 was that it

options.a: gave Nigeria control over its own currency and monetary policy
options.b: introduced deposit insurance for Nigerian depositors
options.c: ended foreign participation in Nigerian banking
options.d: raised the minimum capital of banks to N25 billion

questions.explanation: With its own central bank, Nigeria could issue its own currency and run monetary policy for local needs instead of relying on the sterling-based Currency Board. Option C is wrong because expatriate banks continued to dominate for years afterwards, option B came with the NDIC in 1988, and option D came with the 2004 consolidation.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which banking law was more comprehensive than the earlier ordinances, added to the CBN's control techniques and extended monetary control to most banking institutions other than commercial banks?

options.a: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1972
options.b: The Banking Decree of 1969

questions.explanation: The Banking Decree of 1969 replaced the colonial-era ordinances and greatly strengthened the CBN's grip on the banking system, including institutions other than commercial banks. The 1952 Ordinance (option D) was a basic first law, the 1972 Decree (option A) dealt with indigenous ownership, and the 1988 Decree (option C) created deposit insurance.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the Banking Decree of 1969, the minimum paid-up capital requirement for commercial banks was set at

options.a: N25,000 for indigenous banks and N200,000 for expatriate banks
options.b: N1.5 million for indigenous banks and N600,000 for expatriate banks
options.c: N600,000 for indigenous banks and N1.5 million for expatriate banks
options.d: N25 billion for all banks regardless of ownership

questions.explanation: The 1969 Decree raised minimum paid-up capital to N600,000 for indigenous banks and N1.5 million for expatriate banks, keeping a higher requirement for foreign banks. Option B reverses the two figures, option A gives figures far below the 1969 levels, and option D is the 2004 consolidation requirement.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Banking Decree of 1969 and all its amendments were repealed and replaced by

options.a: the Banking Ordinance of 1958
options.b: the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1977
options.c: the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria Act of 2010
options.d: the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (Decree) No. 25 of 1991

questions.explanation: During the SAP era, BOFIA No. 25 of 1991, together with the CBN Decree No. 24 of 1991, repealed the 1969 Banking Decree to cover the many new banks and other financial institutions. Option A came before 1969, option B concerned Nigerian ownership of enterprises, and option C set up a bad-loan agency in 2010.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: A government policy of transferring the ownership and control of business enterprises, including banks, from foreigners to Nigerian nationals is called

options.a: deregulation
options.b: indigenisation

questions.explanation: Indigenisation means increasing Nigerian ownership and control of enterprises, and in banking it was carried out through the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decrees of the 1970s. Deregulation (option A) removes government controls, consolidation (option D) reduces the number of banks through mergers, and privatisation (option C) moves government-owned businesses into private hands.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the indigenisation programme that began with the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1972, the Federal Government first acquired an equity interest of

options.a: 60 per cent in the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: 40 per cent in the three largest foreign banks
options.c: 10 per cent in all indigenous banks
options.d: 100 per cent in all foreign banks

questions.explanation: In the first stage of indigenisation, the Federal Government took a 40 per cent stake in the three big expatriate banks, First Bank, Union Bank and UBA. Option D is wrong because the banks were never fully nationalised, option C confuses foreign and indigenous banks, and option A makes no sense because the CBN is wholly government-owned.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Following the 1976-1977 amendments to the indigenisation laws, banking was placed in the category of businesses that had to be

options.a: at least 60 per cent Nigerian-owned
options.b: wholly owned by state governments
options.c: wholly owned by the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The amended indigenisation rules raised required Nigerian ownership of banks to 60 per cent, building on the earlier 40 per cent stake. Option D reverses the aim of the policy, while options B and C are wrong because private Nigerians and foreign partners kept shareholdings.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was an outcome of the indigenisation of banking in Nigeria in the 1970s?

options.a: Foreign banks gained full ownership of all Nigerian banks
options.b: Banks were barred from lending to Nigerian businessmen
options.c: Nigerians moved into top management positions and directorships in the formerly expatriate banks
options.d: The West African Currency Board resumed issuing currency in Nigeria

questions.explanation: Indigenisation gave government and private Nigerians large stakes in the old expatriate banks, opening senior management and board positions to Nigerians. Option A is the opposite of what happened, option D is wrong because the Board had been replaced by the CBN in 1959, and option B contradicts the policy, which pushed banks to lend more to Nigerians.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In the 1970s a Nigerian entrepreneur needs a 10-year loan to build a textile factory. Among the specialised institutions set up by government, the one created to give long-term finance for industrial projects was the

options.a: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
options.b: Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Industrial Development Bank was a development bank meant to provide medium- and long-term finance for industrial projects such as factories. The NACB (option D) financed agriculture and cooperatives, the Federal Mortgage Bank (option B) financed housing, and the NDIC (option A) insures deposits and does not lend to businesses.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches a Nigerian development finance institution with its main purpose?

options.a: Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry - issuing the national currency
options.b: Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria - financing industrial machinery
options.c: Nigerian Agricultural and Cooperative Bank - financing agriculture and rural cooperatives
options.d: Nigerian Industrial Development Bank - insuring bank deposits

questions.explanation: The NACB was set up to finance agricultural development and rural cooperatives. Option B is wrong because the Federal Mortgage Bank provides long-term housing finance, option D is wrong because the NIDB financed industry, not deposit insurance, and option A is wrong because only the CBN issues currency.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry was set up during the indigenisation era chiefly to

options.a: lend to Nigerian businessmen, including for buying shares in foreign firms
options.b: supervise and license the community banks in Nigeria
options.c: manage Nigeria's external reserves on behalf of government
options.d: act as banker and fiscal agent to the Federal Government

questions.explanation: The NBCI was created to lend to indigenous businessmen, especially to help Nigerians acquire equity in foreign-owned firms as the indigenisation decrees required. Options C and D are central bank functions performed by the CBN, and option B wrongly gives it a supervisory role.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In the Nigerian banking system of the 1970s and 1980s, merchant banks differed from commercial banks mainly in that merchant banks

options.a: were owned exclusively by state governments and their agencies
options.b: issued currency notes on behalf of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: were the only banks allowed to open current accounts for individuals
options.d: focused on wholesale, medium- to long-term corporate finance rather than retail deposits

questions.explanation: Merchant banks dealt mainly with large corporate customers, offering wholesale funds, medium- to long-term credit and services such as issuing houses and acceptances, while commercial banks took retail deposits and gave mostly short-term loans. Option C describes commercial banks, option B is a CBN function, and option A is wrong because merchant banks were often joint ventures with foreign and private investors.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In the usual division of Nigerian banking history, the period from 1986 to the mid-1990s is called the

options.a: deregulation era of the Structural Adjustment Programme
options.b: free banking era of the colonial period
options.d: consolidation era of the Soludo reforms

questions.explanation: From 1986 the Structural Adjustment Programme liberalised interest rates, licensing and foreign exchange, so the period is known as the deregulation era. Free banking (option B) was the pre-1952 period, regulated banking (option C) covers roughly 1960-1985, and consolidation (option D) refers to July 2004 to December 2005.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a banking-sector reform of the Structural Adjustment Programme era in Nigeria?

options.a: Liberalisation of bank licensing
options.b: Deregulation of interest rates
options.c: Liberalisation of the foreign exchange market
options.d: Raising the minimum capital base of banks to N25 billion

questions.explanation: The N25 billion capital base was a 2004 consolidation measure, nearly two decades after SAP began. Options A, B and C were all SAP-era reforms: interest rates were freed, it became easier to obtain a bank licence, and the foreign exchange market was liberalised through SFEM and later IFEM.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The foreign exchange market introduced in Nigeria in 1986 under SAP, in which the naira exchange rate was determined largely by market forces, was the

options.a: Lagos Bankers' Clearing House
options.b: West African Currency Board

questions.explanation: SFEM was the market-based foreign exchange window introduced under SAP and later developed into the Inter-Bank Foreign Exchange Market. The Expanded Discount Window (option D) was a CBN liquidity facility of 2009, the clearing house (option A) settles cheques, and the Currency Board (option B) was a colonial currency issuer.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: A situation in which a bank suffers severe financial, operational and managerial weakness that makes it unable to meet its obligations to customers, owners and the economy as and when due is known as

options.a: bank distress
options.b: indigenisation

questions.explanation: Bank distress describes a bank so weakened financially and managerially that it cannot meet its obligations as they fall due. Consolidation (option D) is the merging of banks into fewer and bigger ones, deregulation (option C) is the removal of controls, and indigenisation (option B) concerns ownership by Nigerians.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Nigerian regulators use the CAMEL rating system to determine whether a bank is distressed. Which of the following is NOT one of the CAMEL parameters?

options.a: Asset quality
options.b: Capital adequacy

questions.explanation: CAMEL stands for capital adequacy, asset quality, management competence, earnings strength and liquidity, so market share is not one of the parameters. Options A, B and C are all genuine CAMEL components.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a symptom that a bank is becoming distressed?

options.a: Persistent adverse clearing position and overdraft with the CBN
options.b: Desperate borrowing at interest rates above the market rate
options.c: Being a regular net placer of surplus funds in the interbank market

questions.explanation: A bank that regularly lends its surplus funds to other banks is liquid, which is a sign of health rather than distress. Options A, B and D are classic warning signs of distress, along with window dressing of accounts and customer complaints about unpaid obligations.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The causes of bank distress in Nigeria are usually grouped into internal and external factors. Which of the following is an EXTERNAL cause?

options.a: Fraudulent and corrupt practices of owners and managers
options.b: Poor asset and liability management
options.d: Macroeconomic instability such as high inflation and recession

questions.explanation: External causes arise from the environment outside the bank, such as recession, inflation and currency depreciation, which make borrowers unable to repay. Options A, B and C are internal causes because they come from the bank's own owners, managers and policies.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation, established in 1988, had its origin in a 1983 CBN committee recommendation for the setting up of a

options.a: depositors protection fund
options.b: bankers' clearing house

questions.explanation: The 1983 committee recommended a depositors protection fund, and this led to the NDIC, created by Decree No. 22 of 1988 to insure deposits and help resolve failing banks. A development bank (option D) lends for projects, a clearing house (option B) settles cheques, and a currency board (option C) issues currency.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: After a bank fails in the mid-1990s, a special tribunal is used both to recover the unpaid loans owed to the failed bank and to try its former directors for banking malpractice. This reflects the purpose of the

options.a: Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Decree of 1994
options.b: Central Bank of Nigeria Act of 1958 establishing the CBN
options.d: Banking Ordinance of 1952 based on the Paton Report

questions.explanation: The Failed Banks Decree of 1994 provided for speedy recovery of debts owed to failed banks and speedy trial of bank directors and officials accused of financial malpractice. The 1952 Ordinance (option D) introduced licensing, the 1972 Decree (option C) dealt with indigenous ownership, and the 1958 Act (option B) set up the CBN.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In January 1998, during the distress of the 1990s, the Nigerian authorities liquidated the largest single batch of banks of that decade. How many banks were involved?
questions.explanation: In January 1998, 26 terminally distressed banks (a mix of commercial and merchant banks) lost their licences for failing to recapitalise. Option C, 14, is the number of banks liquidated after the 2004-2005 consolidation, option B, 5, is the number of banks whose chief executives were removed in 2009, and option D, 89, is the number of banks before consolidation.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The banking consolidation programme that raised the minimum capital base of Nigerian banks was announced at a special meeting of the Bankers' Committee on 6 July 2004 by CBN Governor

options.a: Charles Soludo
options.b: Roy Pentelow Fenton

questions.explanation: Professor Charles Soludo announced the consolidation reform in July 2004 in his address on consolidating the banking industry to meet development challenges. Sanusi Lamido Sanusi (option C) led the 2009 reforms, while Fenton (option B) and Mai-Bornu (option D) were the first two CBN Governors.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: The reduction in the number of banks and other deposit-taking institutions, with a simultaneous increase in the size and concentration of the remaining entities, is known as

options.a: universal banking
options.b: indigenisation

questions.explanation: Consolidation means fewer but bigger and more concentrated banks, achieved mainly through mergers and acquisitions. Distress (option D) is a weak bank failing to meet obligations, indigenisation (option B) concerns ownership by Nigerians, and universal banking (option A) concerns the range of business one bank may carry on.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: During the 2004-2005 consolidation, a holding company that owned two small banks proposed to keep them as separate banks within a group and count their combined capital towards the N25 billion. Under the CBN guidelines this was

options.a: acceptable, provided both banks were listed on the stock exchange
options.b: not acceptable, because banks with subsidiaries were to be liquidated
options.c: not acceptable, because only mergers and outright acquisitions were allowed
options.d: acceptable, because group arrangements were the preferred mode

questions.explanation: The CBN guidelines allowed only mergers and outright acquisitions or takeovers, and stated that a mere group arrangement could not be used to meet the N25 billion; banks with common ownership were encouraged to merge. Options A and D wrongly treat a group arrangement as valid, and option B invents a liquidation rule that did not exist.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: For the purpose of the 2004 consolidation guidelines, a bank's 'capital base' meant

options.a: total loans and advances outstanding
options.b: paid-up capital and reserves unimpaired by losses
options.c: total deposits held by the bank
options.d: the market value of the bank's branches

questions.explanation: The CBN defined capital base as paid-up capital plus reserves not impaired by losses, which is the owners' cushion against losses. Deposits (option C) are liabilities to customers, loans (option A) are assets financed largely by deposits, and branch values (option D) are only part of fixed assets.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT among the incentives the CBN offered to banks that met the N25 billion capital base in the 2004-2005 consolidation?

options.a: Permission to take public sector deposits
options.b: Prospects of managing part of Nigeria's external reserves
options.c: Exemption from CBN supervision and examination
options.d: Authorisation to deal in foreign exchange

questions.explanation: The CBN never offered to stop supervising consolidated banks; bigger banks still faced full regulation. Options A, B and D were genuine incentives announced to encourage banks to consolidate early.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: At the end of the 2004-2005 consolidation exercise, the number of banks in Nigeria fell

options.a: from 25 to 14
options.b: from 119 to 89

questions.explanation: The 89 banks that existed in 2004 emerged as 25 banking groups by the end of 2005 through mergers and acquisitions, while 14 banks that could not meet the requirement were liquidated. Option A confuses the number of survivors with the number liquidated, and options B and C give figures that do not describe the outcome of the exercise.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: During the 2004-2005 consolidation, the National Bank of Nigeria, one of the few indigenous banks that survived the colonial bank failures, merged with

options.a: Wema Bank
options.b: Zenith Bank

questions.explanation: In the consolidation, the National Bank of Nigeria combined with Wema Bank, itself the former Agbonmagbe Bank. UBA (option C) merged with Standard Trust Bank, First Bank (option D) merged with MBC International Bank, and Zenith Bank (option B) met the requirement on its own.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In 2009 the special examination that exposed serious problems in five Nigerian banks was carried out by a joint team of officials from

options.a: the NDIC and the Corporate Affairs Commission
options.b: the Federal Ministry of Finance and the Nigerian Stock Exchange
options.c: the CBN and the Securities and Exchange Commission
options.d: the CBN and the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation

questions.explanation: The 2009 special examination was a joint exercise by CBN and NDIC examiners, the two bodies that share responsibility for bank supervision. The SEC (option C) and the Nigerian Stock Exchange (option B) regulate the capital market, and the Corporate Affairs Commission (option A) registers companies.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In August 2009 the CBN removed the chief executives of five banks found to be in grave condition. Which of the following banks was NOT one of the five?

options.a: Intercontinental Bank
options.b: Finbank

questions.explanation: The five banks whose chief executives were removed in August 2009 were Afribank, Finbank, Intercontinental Bank, Oceanic Bank and Union Bank. Zenith Bank was certified fit after the examinations, while options A, B and C were among the five.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Before the 2009 intervention, some troubled Nigerian banks kept borrowing from the CBN's Expanded Discount Window against commercial paper and bankers' acceptances and were almost permanently unable to repay. This pattern was clear evidence that those banks were

options.a: net placers of funds
options.b: illiquid

questions.explanation: A bank that cannot meet maturing obligations without constant support from the CBN or the interbank market is illiquid, and the five banks' heavy reliance on the Expanded Discount Window showed this. Option C is wrong because the banks were in fact undercapitalised, option A is the opposite of their position, and option D conflicts with their huge bad loans.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Which of the following was a major cause of the problems found in Nigerian banks in 2009?

options.a: Inability of most banks to raise their capital from N2 billion to N25 billion
options.b: Heavy exposure to margin loans and oil and gas, with weak risk management and governance
options.c: Excessive government ownership of banks under the indigenisation decrees
options.d: The abolition of the West African Currency Board and its sterling backing

questions.explanation: The 2009 examination found very high non-performing loans driven by margin lending, concentration in oil and gas, and weak risk management and governance. Option A describes the 2004-2005 consolidation challenge, option D refers to colonial history, and option C relates to the 1970s, not 2009.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In the second stage of the 2009 intervention, the CBN removed the managing directors and executive directors of three more banks found to be unhealthy. These banks were

options.a: First Bank, UBA and Stanbic IBTC
options.b: Zenith Bank, Guaranty Trust Bank and Access Bank
options.c: Bank PHB, Equatorial Trust Bank and Spring Bank

questions.explanation: After auditing the remaining banks, the CBN found Bank PHB, Equatorial Trust Bank and Spring Bank unhealthy and sacked their top management. The banks in options A, B and D were among those the CBN certified fit or sound after the examinations.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: In 2010 a new government corporation was created to buy non-performing loans from troubled Nigerian banks, take over the collateral and help recapitalise the banks. This body is the

options.a: Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON)
options.b: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)

questions.explanation: AMCON was established by the AMCON Act of 2010 to acquire bad loans from banks and manage their recovery, cleaning up bank balance sheets after the 2009 crisis. The NDIC (option B) insures deposits and liquidates failed banks, the NIDB (option D) was an industrial development bank, and the WACB (option C) was a colonial currency issuer.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: A banking model, adopted in Nigeria in 2001, under which one bank licence allowed a bank to carry on commercial banking together with merchant (investment) banking and other financial services is called

options.a: correspondent banking
options.b: branch banking

questions.explanation: Universal banking lets a single institution combine commercial banking with investment banking and other financial business. Unit banking (option D) means a bank operates from a single office, branch banking (option B) means one bank runs many branches, and correspondent banking (option A) is one bank acting as agent for another.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: When the CBN reviewed the universal banking model in 2010, banks were required to

options.a: become wholly government-owned development banks funded by the CBN
options.b: divest non-core businesses or adopt a holding company structure, under commercial, merchant or specialised licences
options.c: combine insurance, banking and stockbroking under one universal licence
options.d: convert all their branches into microfinance banks owned by local communities

questions.explanation: The 2010 reform ended the universal banking licence: banks had to divest non-banking subsidiaries or adopt a holding company structure, and licences were split into commercial, merchant and specialised categories. Options A and D were never required, and option C describes the very universal banking practice the CBN was ending.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: Under the commercial banking licensing regulations introduced by the CBN in 2010, the minimum capital for commercial banks depended on their scope of operation. Which set of figures is correct?

options.a: Regional N2 billion, national N10 billion, international N25 billion
options.b: Regional N5 billion, national N15 billion, international N25 billion
options.c: Regional N10 billion, national N25 billion, international N50 billion
options.d: Regional N25 billion, national N50 billion, international N100 billion

questions.explanation: From 2010 a commercial bank needed N10 billion to operate regionally, N25 billion nationally and N50 billion internationally, replacing the single N25 billion minimum of 2004. Options A, B and D mix up these figures with other levels such as the old N2 billion minimum and the N15 billion merchant bank requirement.

questions.topic: Historical Development of Banking in Nigeria
questions.question: How did the Banking Ordinance of 1952 differ from the Banking Decree of 1969?

options.a: The 1952 Ordinance introduced universal banking, while the 1969 Decree abolished it
options.b: The 1952 Ordinance created the CBN, while the 1969 Decree created the NDIC
options.c: The 1952 Ordinance raised capital to N25 billion, while the 1969 Decree reduced it
options.d: The 1952 Ordinance ended free banking under colonial rule, while the 1969 Decree gave the CBN a much wider range of controls over the banking system

questions.explanation: The 1952 Ordinance was Nigeria's first banking law, introducing licensing and minimum capital, while the 1969 Decree was a more comprehensive post-independence law that greatly widened the CBN's powers. Option B is wrong because the CBN came from the 1958 Act and the NDIC from a 1988 Decree, option A describes reforms of 2001 and 2010, and option C describes the 2004 consolidation.

questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria, established under the CBN Act of 1958, commenced operations on

options.a: 1 October 1960
options.b: 1 July 1958

questions.explanation: The CBN Act was passed in 1958, but the Bank formally opened for business on 1 July 1959, taking over currency issue from the West African Currency Board. Option B picks the year the Act was passed, not the year operations started. Option A is Nigeria's independence day, which came more than a year after the CBN began operating, and option D has no connection with the start of the CBN.

questions.question: Which of the following is a developmental, rather than a traditional, function of a central bank in a developing economy?

options.a: Providing special financing schemes for agriculture and industry
options.b: Issuing the national currency
options.c: Acting as lender of last resort to banks
options.d: Acting as banker to the government

questions.explanation: In developing countries central banks often go beyond their classic duties and promote growth directly, for example by running intervention funds and credit schemes for agriculture, industry and small businesses. Options B, D and C are traditional central banking functions that central banks perform in both developed and developing economies.

questions.question: Which of the following has been one of the CBN's development finance initiatives?

options.a: The Anchor Borrowers' Programme
options.b: Open market operations

questions.explanation: The Anchor Borrowers' Programme was a CBN intervention that provided loans to smallholder farmers and linked them with processors, which makes it a development finance initiative. Options B, D and C are monetary policy instruments used to influence liquidity, interest rates and credit across the economy, not schemes aimed at financing particular sectors.

questions.question: The achievements of the CBN include all of the following EXCEPT

options.a: paying insured depositors when a bank fails
options.b: issuing and managing the national currency

questions.explanation: Paying insured depositors of a failed bank is the work of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation, not the CBN. Issuing and managing the naira (option B), regulating and supervising banks (option C) and modernising the payment system (option D) are all achievements credited to the CBN, along with implementing monetary policy and supporting development programmes.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a principle (canon) of central banking?

options.a: Responsibility for the stability of the financial system
options.b: Acting as lender of last resort to the banking system
options.c: Independence of the central bank in conducting monetary policy
options.d: Competing with commercial banks for public deposits in order to maximise profit

questions.explanation: A central bank is meant to serve the public interest and lead the banking system, so it should not compete with commercial banks for ordinary customers or be driven by profit. Independence in monetary policy (option C), acting as lender of last resort (option B) and responsibility for financial stability (option A) are all accepted principles of sound central banking.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Nigeria is chaired by the

options.a: Minister of Finance
options.b: Senate President

questions.explanation: The CBN Act 2007 makes the Governor the chairman of the Board of Directors, which also includes the Deputy Governors and other directors. Option A is wrong because the Minister of Finance does not head the Bank's board, and options C and B are wrong because the President and the Senate take part in appointing the Governor but do not chair the board.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, the Governor of the CBN is appointed by

options.a: the Board of Directors of the CBN from among its members
options.b: the President, subject to confirmation by the Senate
options.d: the Minister of Finance, without reference to the National Assembly

questions.explanation: The Governor, like the Deputy Governors, is appointed by the President of Nigeria and must be confirmed by the Senate before taking office. Option D is wrong because the Minister of Finance does not appoint the Governor, and option A is wrong because the Board is chaired by the Governor rather than choosing the Governor. Option C is a forum of bankers with no power to appoint the head of the CBN.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, which body within the CBN is responsible for formulating monetary and credit policy?

options.a: The Federal Executive Council
options.b: The Monetary Policy Committee

questions.explanation: The Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by the Governor, is the body within the CBN that formulates monetary and credit policy and decides on the Monetary Policy Rate. Option A is the federal cabinet, which handles government policy generally, not CBN monetary policy. Option D is a forum of bankers, and option C is the deposit insurer, neither of which sets monetary policy.

questions.question: A central bank is best defined as

options.a: the commercial bank with the largest branch network in a country
options.b: a privately owned bank that accepts deposits from and lends to the general public
options.c: the apex monetary authority of a country, with the sole right to issue currency and responsibility for regulating the banking system
options.d: a development bank that provides long-term loans to industry

questions.explanation: A central bank sits at the top of the financial system: it has the monopoly of currency issue, controls money and credit, and supervises other banks, as the CBN does in Nigeria. Option A describes a large commercial bank, which is still just one of the banks the central bank regulates. Option D is a development finance institution, and option B describes ordinary commercial banking, which a central bank does not do.

questions.question: Which institution is the apex monetary authority in Nigeria?

options.a: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
options.b: The Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria is the country's central bank and apex monetary authority, responsible for issuing the naira, conducting monetary policy and regulating banks. Option A insures deposits and helps resolve failed banks, and option D regulates the capital market. Option C manages the government's fiscal affairs, while monetary policy is the responsibility of the CBN.

questions.question: In Nigeria, the cash reserve ratio (CRR) is

options.a: the ratio of a bank's capital to its risk-weighted assets
options.b: the minimum percentage of a bank's deposit liabilities that it must hold in liquid assets such as cash and treasury bills
options.c: the minimum percentage of a bank's deposits that it must keep as reserves with the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: the interest rate at which the CBN lends to banks overnight

questions.explanation: The cash reserve ratio requires each bank to keep a set percentage of its deposits with the CBN, which reduces the funds available for lending and is used as a monetary policy tool. Option B is the liquidity ratio, which covers a wider range of liquid assets held by the bank. Option D describes the standing lending facility rate, and option A is the capital adequacy ratio.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: Acting as banker to other banks
options.b: Issuing legal tender currency
options.c: Acting as banker to the government
options.d: Accepting deposits from and granting loans to members of the public

questions.explanation: The CBN does not deal directly with individual members of the public; ordinary deposit-taking and lending are left to commercial and other banks. Issuing legal tender (option B), acting as banker to banks (option A) and acting as banker to the government (option C) are core functions of the CBN, together with managing external reserves and conducting monetary policy.

questions.question: When the CBN provides emergency funds to a solvent bank facing a temporary liquidity shortage, it is acting as

options.a: lender of last resort
options.b: bank of issue

questions.explanation: As lender of last resort, the central bank stands ready to lend to sound banks that run short of cash, preventing a temporary problem from becoming a wider banking crisis. Option B refers to issuing currency, option D refers to managing government accounts and borrowing, and option C refers to managing the country's foreign exchange holdings.

questions.question: If the CBN raises the cash reserve ratio, the most likely effect on deposit money banks is that:
