options.a: Their capacity to grant loans and create credit rises
options.b: Their capacity to grant loans and create credit falls
options.c: Interest rates on their loans automatically fall
options.d: The amount of money in circulation automatically increases

questions.explanation: A higher cash reserve ratio means banks must lock up a larger share of each deposit with the CBN, leaving less to lend; it also lowers the money multiplier, which is 1 divided by the reserve ratio. Option A describes the effect of cutting the ratio, not raising it. Option D is wrong because tighter reserves reduce, not increase, the money in circulation, and option C is unlikely because scarcer loanable funds tend to push lending rates up, not down.

questions.question: The buying and selling of government securities by the central bank in order to influence bank reserves and the money supply is known as:

options.a: Selective credit control
options.b: Moral suasion

questions.explanation: Open market operations (OMO) involve the CBN buying or selling securities such as Treasury bills in the market; a sale drains reserves from banks and a purchase adds to them. Option B is persuasion of banks by the central bank without any market transaction. Option A directs credit to or away from particular sectors, and option D requires banks to lodge extra funds with the central bank rather than trading securities with them.

questions.question: When the CBN sells Treasury bills to banks and the public through open market operations, the likely effect is to:

options.a: Increase the amount of currency issued by the CBN
options.b: Increase bank reserves and the money supply
options.c: Reduce bank reserves and the money supply
options.d: Leave the money supply unchanged because only paper changes hands

questions.explanation: Buyers pay the CBN for the securities out of their bank balances, so money is withdrawn from the banking system and banks have fewer reserves to lend; selling securities is therefore a tightening move. Option B is what happens when the CBN buys securities and pays money into the system. Option D ignores the fact that the money paid for the securities leaves circulation, and option A confuses OMO with currency issue.

questions.question: The apex institution that controls and regulates the banking and monetary system of a country and has the sole authority to issue its currency is the:

options.a: Federal Ministry of Finance
options.b: Central bank

questions.explanation: A central bank sits at the top of the banking system: it issues the currency, acts as banker to the government and to other banks, and conducts monetary policy, which in Nigeria is the role of the CBN. Option A manages government finances and fiscal matters but does not issue currency. Option D insures deposits and helps supervise banks, and option C regulates the capital market.

questions.question: Which of the following is a qualitative (selective) instrument of monetary policy?

options.a: Reserve requirements
options.b: Moral suasion

questions.explanation: Qualitative instruments aim at the direction or use of credit rather than its total volume, and moral suasion, the central bank's use of persuasion and appeals to banks, is a classic example along with selective credit control. Options C, A and D are quantitative instruments, because they work by changing the overall volume and cost of credit and bank reserves.

questions.question: Before the Structural Adjustment Programme of 1986, the CBN issued guidelines directing banks to lend stated proportions of their credit to agriculture and manufacturing at specified interest rates. This tool is known as:

options.a: Open market operations
options.b: Special deposits

questions.explanation: Selective credit control uses administrative directives to channel credit into chosen sectors, in set amounts and at set rates, and it was widely used in Nigeria's regulated era before market-based tools took over. Option C also tries to influence lending, but only through persuasion and appeals, not binding guidelines. Options A and B are quantitative tools that change the total amount of bank reserves rather than steering credit to particular sectors.

questions.question: Which group consists ONLY of quantitative instruments of monetary policy?

options.a: Moral suasion, selective credit control and open market operations
options.b: Moral suasion and selective credit control
options.c: Open market operations, reserve requirements and the discount (bank) rate
options.d: Reserve requirements, moral suasion and the discount (bank) rate

questions.explanation: Quantitative instruments control the total volume and cost of money and credit: open market operations change bank reserves, reserve requirements fix how much of each deposit banks must hold back, and the bank rate sets the cost of borrowing from the central bank. Options A and D each slip in moral suasion, and option B is made up entirely of qualitative tools, which work through persuasion or by directing credit to particular sectors rather than changing its total amount.

questions.question: Temporary advances made directly by the CBN to the Federal Government to cover short-term shortfalls in revenue are known as:

options.a: Ways and Means advances
options.b: Standing Lending Facility

questions.explanation: As banker to the government, the CBN can lend to it directly through Ways and Means advances when revenue falls temporarily short of spending, and the law limits how much may be advanced. Option B is the window through which the CBN lends overnight to banks, not to government. Option D refers to funds banks are made to lodge with the central bank, and option C is a bill accepted by a bank on behalf of its customer.

questions.question: The rate at which the central bank lends to commercial banks by rediscounting their eligible bills is traditionally called the:

options.a: Interbank rate
options.b: Savings deposit rate

questions.explanation: The bank rate, also called the discount or rediscount rate, is what the central bank charges when it provides funds to banks against eligible bills; raising it makes bank borrowing dearer and tends to push up lending rates generally. Option D is the rate a commercial bank charges its best customers. Option A is the rate banks charge one another for short-term loans, and option B is what banks pay depositors on savings accounts.

questions.question: In Nigeria, the CBN's Minimum Rediscount Rate (MRR) was replaced as the main signalling rate of monetary policy by the:

options.a: Prime Lending Rate
options.b: Treasury bill rate

questions.explanation: The MPR replaced the MRR as the CBN's anchor rate, and it is set by the Monetary Policy Committee to signal whether policy is being tightened or eased. Option C is the lower edge of the corridor around the MPR, the rate paid on banks' overnight deposits with the CBN. Option A is set by individual banks for their best customers, and option B is the yield on government Treasury bills, which is determined at auction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of a central bank but NOT of a commercial bank?

options.a: It accepts deposits from and grants loans to members of the public
options.b: Its main objective is to earn profit
options.c: It has the monopoly of issuing the country's currency
options.d: Many of them can operate in the same country

questions.explanation: Only the central bank may issue the national currency; in Nigeria this sole right belongs to the CBN. Options A and B describe commercial banks, which deal directly with the public and are run mainly for profit, while the central bank exists to regulate the monetary and banking system. Option D also fits commercial banks, since a country normally has only one central bank.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the Central Bank of Nigeria with a commercial bank?

options.a: Commercial banks issue the naira, while the CBN only accepts deposits
options.b: The CBN works under the control of commercial banks, which are the apex of the money market
options.c: The CBN deals directly with the general public, while commercial banks deal only with the government
options.d: The CBN controls the availability of credit in the economy, while commercial banks create credit

questions.explanation: Commercial banks create credit by lending out deposits, while the CBN regulates how much credit can be created through tools such as reserve requirements and open market operations. Option C reverses the roles, because commercial banks serve the public and the CBN deals mainly with government and banks. Option A is wrong because only the CBN issues the naira, and option B is wrong because the CBN, not the commercial banks, is the apex institution.

questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) was established by the Central Bank Act of ______.
questions.explanation: The CBN was established by the Central Bank of Nigeria Act of 1958 and began operations on 1 July 1959. Option C, 1960, is the year of Nigeria's independence, not of the CBN Act, and neither 1954 nor 1961 is linked to its creation.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a function expected of the CBN?

options.a: Issuance of currency notes and coins or legal tender to the banking system
options.b: Granting of loans and advances to individuals and households
options.d: Being the lender of last resort to the other banks

questions.explanation: A central bank is banker to the government and to the banks, not to individuals and households, so granting personal loans is the business of deposit money banks and microfinance banks. Issuing currency (A), managing external reserves (C) and acting as lender of last resort to banks (D) are all traditional functions of the CBN.

questions.question: Prior to the establishment of the CBN, the function of issuance of legal tender in Nigeria was performed by the

options.a: Currency Board of Nigeria
options.b: West African Monetary Union

questions.explanation: Before the CBN took over, Nigeria's currency was issued by the West African Currency Board, set up by the colonial government in 1912 to issue currency for the British West African colonies of Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone and The Gambia. There was no 'Currency Board of Nigeria' (A), and the West African Monetary Union (B) was never the body that issued Nigeria's money.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT one of the commissions or missions that examined the setting up of a central bank in Nigeria before 1958?

options.a: Fisher's Commission 1953
options.b: Johnson's Commission 1954

questions.explanation: The Fisher Commission (1953), the World Bank Mission (1955) and the Loynes Commission (1957) all looked into whether Nigeria should have a central bank, and the Loynes Report led directly to the CBN Act of 1958. There was no 'Johnson's Commission' in this process. Fisher and the World Bank Mission did not favour an immediate central bank, but they were still part of the process, so A and C are not the answer.

questions.question: In the years before the CBN Act of 1958, the Nigerian government became persuaded of the need for a central bank for which of the following purposes?

options.a: To provide leadership and direction for the banks and other financial institutions
options.b: To better harness the financial resources of the economy
options.c: To create institutions, instruments, and markets that will ensure the growth and development of the financial system

questions.explanation: Nigerian leaders wanted a central bank that would lead and direct the banks and other financial institutions, harness the economy's financial resources, and create the institutions, instruments and markets the financial system needed to grow. Each of A, B and C was one of these reasons, so D is correct.

questions.question: With the deregulation of the economy, exporters and other customers were allowed to keep foreign exchange in domiciliary accounts with banks in Nigeria. These domiciliary accounts are of two types, namely

options.a: Import domiciliary account and export domiciliary account
options.b: Export domiciliary account and special domiciliary account
options.c: Export domiciliary account and ordinary domiciliary account
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: Domiciliary accounts let customers hold foreign currency with Nigerian banks, and they come in two types: the export domiciliary account, which receives export proceeds, and the ordinary domiciliary account, which receives other foreign currency inflows. Options A and B pair the export account with categories that do not exist (import and special), so they are wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the developmental functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: Accepting savings deposits from members of the public
options.b: Insuring the deposits of customers of failed banks
options.c: Providing the financial infrastructure for the take-off of the money and capital markets

questions.explanation: Beyond its traditional functions, the CBN has a developmental role, and one part of it is providing financial infrastructure: it introduced money market instruments such as treasury bills and encouraged the setting up of the Lagos Stock Exchange in 1961. Taking savings deposits from the public (A) is done by deposit money banks, insuring deposits (B) is the job of the NDIC, and registering companies (D) belongs to the Corporate Affairs Commission.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the schemes/funds established by the CBN or inspired by the CBN?

options.a: The Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme
options.b: National Economic Reconstruction Fund
options.d: Small and Medium Industries Equity Investment Scheme

questions.explanation: The CBN set up or inspired the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme (A), the National Economic Reconstruction Fund or NERFUND (B), and the Small and Medium Industries Equity Investment Scheme (D) to channel credit to important sectors. There has never been a 'National Economic Rejuvenation Fund'; the name is a twist on NERFUND, whose R stands for Reconstruction.

questions.question: Which of these is not one of the broad aims of monetary policy?

options.a: Balance of payments equilibrium
options.b: High growth rate of output

questions.explanation: Monetary policy is aimed at stable prices, a high rate of growth of output, full employment and balance of payments equilibrium. A high growth rate of population is not something the monetary authorities try to achieve, so it is not a policy aim. Options A, B and D are all standard objectives of monetary policy.

questions.question: Monetary policy, like fiscal policy, belongs to the group of policies called

options.a: Management policies
options.b: Strategic economic policies

questions.explanation: Monetary and fiscal policies are known as economic stabilization policies because the authorities use them to bring a misbehaving economy, for example one facing high inflation or unemployment, back to a path of steady growth. 'Management policies' (A) and 'strategic economic policies' (B) are not the standard name for this group, and since C is correct, D is wrong.

questions.question: Monetary policy is best defined as the policy that

options.a: Uses taxation, government expenditure and the public debt to achieve macroeconomic objectives
options.b: Fixes the prices of goods and services sold in the markets
options.c: Regulates the listing and trading of shares on the stock exchange
options.d: Employs monetary instruments to influence the quantity, availability and cost of money and credit in an economy

questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the deliberate action of the monetary authorities, led by the CBN, to influence the quantity, availability and cost of money and credit, using instruments such as the reserve requirement, open market operations and the monetary policy rate. Option A is the definition of fiscal policy, not monetary policy. Options B and C describe price control and capital market regulation, which are different activities.

questions.question: As an objective of monetary policy, full employment means that

options.a: There is a total absence of unemployment, both voluntary and involuntary
options.b: Every adult in the country is employed by the government
options.c: The central bank fixes the number of jobs in each sector of the economy
options.d: All those able and willing to work can find jobs, although some frictional and seasonal unemployment remains

questions.explanation: Full employment does not mean zero unemployment; it means that everyone who is able and willing to work can secure a job. Some frictional unemployment (people moving between jobs) and seasonal unemployment will always exist, so option A sets an impossible standard. Options B and C describe direct government control of jobs, which is not what the objective means.

questions.question: As an objective of monetary policy, 'stable prices' is best understood to mean that

options.a: Prices of all goods and services remain exactly the same from year to year
options.b: The central bank fixes the price of every commodity by law
options.c: The exchange rate of the naira never changes
options.d: The general price level avoids wide fluctuations, changing only at a gradual rate

questions.explanation: Price stability means avoiding wide swings in the general price level, whether sharp rises (inflation) or continuous falls (deflation), so that prices change only gradually. Prices cannot realistically be frozen from year to year, so option A is wrong. Option B describes price control, and C refers to exchange rate stability, which is a separate goal linked to the balance of payments.

questions.question: Which of these is an instrument of monetary policy?

options.a: Reserve requirement
options.b: Open Market Operations

questions.explanation: The CBN controls money and credit through several instruments: the reserve requirement (the share of deposits banks must hold as reserves), open market operations (buying and selling government securities to add or withdraw liquidity) and the monetary policy rate, which anchors other interest rates. Since A, B and C are all monetary policy instruments, D is correct.

questions.question: The two types of monetary policy are:

options.a: Expansionary and fiscal
options.b: Fiscal and contractionary

questions.explanation: Monetary policy is either expansionary (easy), where the central bank increases money supply and lowers the cost of credit to stimulate activity, or contractionary (tight), where it reduces money supply and raises interest rates to curb inflation. Options A and B wrongly pair one type of monetary policy with fiscal policy, which is the government's use of taxation and spending and is a separate policy altogether. Option C, descriptive and inferential, are branches of statistics, not types of monetary policy.

questions.question: ________ is a monetary measure used in controlling inflation.

options.a: Surplus budgeting
options.b: Encouragement of household saving

questions.explanation: Selective credit control is a monetary tool: the central bank issues guidelines on which sectors banks may lend to, how much and at what rates, so it can restrict credit to non-priority or speculative uses and ease inflationary pressure. Option A, surplus budgeting, is a fiscal measure in which government spends less than it earns. Options B and D, encouraging or increasing savings, are general or fiscal measures rather than central bank credit instruments.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-market based instrument

options.a: OMO
options.b: Rediscount rate

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is a qualitative, direct tool: the central bank uses persuasion and friendly appeal to get banks to act in a desired way, for example to lend more to small businesses, without working through market prices. OMO (A), the rediscount rate (B) and the legal reserve requirement (C) are quantitative instruments that work through bank reserves and the cost of funds, which is why they are grouped as market-based or indirect tools.

questions.question: ________ is more or less an appeal by the Central Bank to the commercial banks to behave in certain ways.

options.a: Special deposits
options.b: Special directives

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is the use of persuasion, friendly appeals and meetings by the Central Bank to get banks to act voluntarily in a desired way, for example to lend more to small businesses. Option B is wrong because directives are formal instructions the banks must obey, not appeals. Option A requires banks to lodge funds with the Central Bank, and option D is the buying and selling of government securities.

questions.question: The buying and selling of securities by the Central Bank in order to control the volume of money in the economy is known as

options.a: Moral suasion
options.b: Open market operations (OMO)

questions.explanation: Open market operations are the Central Bank's purchase or sale of government securities: selling them mops up money from the system, while buying them injects money. Option A works through persuasion rather than trading securities, option C is the interest rate the Central Bank charges when it lends to banks, and option D is the share of deposits banks must keep as cash reserves.

questions.question: The discount rate is also known as the

options.a: Liquidity rate
options.b: Cash reserve ratio

questions.explanation: The discount rate, the rate at which the Central Bank lends to or rediscounts bills for commercial banks, is traditionally called the bank rate. Option B is the proportion of deposits banks must hold as reserves, and option C refers to funds banks are required to lodge with the Central Bank, so neither is an interest rate. Option A is not a standard name for this rate.

questions.question: The rate at which the Central Bank charges interest to commercial banks and other financial institutions for discounting bills of exchange or lending to them is known as the

options.a: Bank/discount rate
options.b: Bank/money rate

questions.explanation: When the Central Bank acts as lender of last resort, the interest it charges for lending to banks or discounting their bills is called the bank rate or discount rate. Options B, C and D pair the term with names such as "money rate" or "cash rate", which are not used for this rate. Raising the bank rate makes borrowing from the Central Bank dearer, while lowering it makes borrowing cheaper.

questions.question: If the CBN wants to pump money into the economy, the discount rate will be

options.a: Increased
options.b: Reduced

questions.explanation: Lowering the discount rate makes it cheaper for banks to borrow from the CBN, so they can lend to the public at lower rates, which increases credit and the money supply. Option A is the opposite policy, used when the CBN wants to reduce the money in circulation. Options C and D do not describe any change that can be made to an interest rate.

questions.question: All these are monetary policy measures except

options.a: Open market operations
options.b: Moral suasion

questions.explanation: Budgeting and taxation are tools of fiscal policy, which is handled by the government through its revenue and spending decisions, not by the Central Bank. Open market operations (A), moral suasion (B) and the discount rate (D) are all instruments the CBN uses to influence money supply and credit.

questions.question: A suitable policy to restore equilibrium in an economy during an economic recession is

options.a: Expansionary monetary policy
options.b: Contractionary monetary policy

questions.explanation: In a recession spending and investment are too low, so the Central Bank eases monetary policy, for example by lowering rates or buying securities, to increase credit and encourage spending. Option B would reduce money and credit and deepen the downturn, so it is used against excess demand and inflation instead. Options C and D are vague labels rather than a specific policy stance for fighting a recession.

questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria was established in the year ____ and started operation in the year ____
questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria was created by the CBN Act of 1958 and opened for business on 1 July 1959, so establishment and operations fall in different years. Option C is tempting because it also shows a one-year gap, but both of its dates are a year too early. Options A and B place the bank's creation in 1956, before the CBN Act was even passed.

questions.question: The law establishing the Central Bank of Nigeria (the CBN Act) was passed in
questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria was established by the CBN Act of 1958 and then began operations on 1 July 1959. Option D, 1959, is tempting, but it is the year the bank started work, not the year the law creating it was passed. Options A and B are not linked to the CBN's creation; 1960, for example, is the year of independence.

questions.question: The best way to reduce the supply of money in the economy is to

options.a: increase the liquidity ratio
options.b: increase the number of bank notes and cheques produced

questions.explanation: Raising the liquidity ratio forces banks to hold a larger share of their deposits in cash and other liquid assets, leaving less to lend, so credit creation and the money supply shrink. Producing more currency and cheques (Option B) and liberalising access to credit (Option D) would expand the money supply, not reduce it. Option C is also wrong, because selling fewer treasury bills leaves more money in the hands of banks and the public.

questions.question: The lender of last resort in the banking system is the

options.a: last resort bank
options.b: commercial bank

questions.explanation: The central bank is the lender of last resort: when a basically sound bank faces a temporary cash shortage and cannot borrow elsewhere, the central bank provides emergency funds to stop the problem spreading. In Nigeria this role belongs to the Central Bank of Nigeria. Commercial and mortgage banks (Options B and D) are among the institutions that may need such help, and Option A is not a real type of bank.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct? The Central Bank

options.a: prints the country's currency
options.b: handles the collection of debts owed to the government

questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria has the sole legal authority to issue the country's currency and coins and to control their circulation. Option A is the common trap: the CBN designs and issues the naira, but the actual printing and minting are contracted out to specialised printing companies. Lending to businessmen (Option C) is the work of commercial banks, and Option B is not how the CBN serves the government; it acts as the government's banker and manages its borrowing rather than collecting debts owed to it.

questions.question: Public debt management is one of the functions of

options.a: Merchant Bank
options.b: Central Bank

questions.explanation: Managing the public debt is a central bank function that comes from its role as banker to the government. The Central Bank of Nigeria helps the government borrow by issuing treasury bills and bonds, keeps the register of government debt and handles repayments. Merchant, commercial and development banks (Options A, C and D) may buy government securities, but they do not manage the government's debt.

questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria performs the following functions except

options.a: traditional function
options.b: regulatory function

questions.explanation: The CBN's work is usually grouped into traditional central banking functions such as issuing currency, acting as banker to the government and to banks and running monetary policy; regulatory and supervisory functions over banks and other financial institutions; and developmental functions such as special funds and intervention schemes. A 'cold room function' is not a recognised central bank function at all, so D is the exception. Options A, B and C are all genuine groups of CBN functions.

questions.question: An increase in liquid reserve requirements by the Central Bank of Nigeria will result in

options.a: a reduction in commercial banks' excess reserves
options.b: more commercial bank loans to members of the public
options.c: an increase in commercial banks' excess reserves
options.d: no change in commercial banks' excess reserves

questions.explanation: Excess reserves are the funds a bank holds above the minimum the CBN requires. When the CBN raises the reserve requirement, more of each bank's funds must be held as required reserves, so excess reserves fall and banks have less to lend. Options C and D are wrong because a higher requirement cannot raise or leave unchanged the spare funds banks have, and Option B is the opposite of what happens, since less spare cash means fewer loans.

questions.question: The Central Bank controls the activities of other banks by all but one of the following. Which one?

options.a: The use of bank rate
options.b: The use of directives

questions.explanation: The central bank influences banks through monetary tools such as the bank rate (the rate at which it lends to banks), directives telling banks how to lend, and special deposits that lock up part of their funds. Taxation is a fiscal tool used by government through its tax authorities, not a device the central bank uses to control banks, so Option D is the exception.

questions.question: Which of these alternatives is wrong? Central banks are

options.a: bankers to the government
options.b: bankers to commercial banks

questions.explanation: Central banks act as banker to the government, banker to the commercial banks and sole issuer of the national currency, so Options A, B and D are all true. A central bank is not a merchant bank; merchant banks are profit-seeking institutions that provide wholesale and corporate finance services, which is why Option C is the wrong statement.

questions.question: Which of these financial institutions cannot provide direct loans to individuals?

options.a: The Industrial Bank
options.b: The Agricultural Bank

questions.explanation: The Central Bank is banker to the government and to other banks, not to private individuals, so it does not grant loans directly to members of the public. The industrial, agricultural and co-operative banks in Options A, B and D are development and specialised institutions set up precisely to lend to firms, farmers and members in their sectors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major function of a Central Bank?

options.a: Serving as government's bank
options.b: Serving as bankers' bank
options.c: Acceptance of deposits from the public

questions.explanation: A central bank's major functions include acting as banker to the government, banker to the banks and manager of monetary policy, which covers Options A, B and D. It does not normally take deposits from members of the public; that is the business of commercial and other deposit-taking banks, so Option C is the exception.

questions.question: If the Central Bank intends to increase the money supply through open market operations then it will

options.a: sell securities in the open market
options.b: buy securities in the open market

questions.explanation: In open market operations the CBN buys or sells government securities. When it buys securities it pays with new money that flows into banks' reserves, so the money supply rises; selling securities (Option A) does the opposite by mopping up money. Option C is not an open market operation at all, and Option D is wrong because demand deposits are created by banks through lending, not printed by the central bank.

questions.question: Higher interest rates tend to lead to ________ consumer and business spending, while lower interest rates tend to lead to ________ spending by consumers and businesses.

options.a: higher; lower
options.b: lower; lower

questions.explanation: Interest is the cost of borrowing, so when rates rise, loans for cars, houses or business expansion become dearer and households and firms cut back on spending. When rates fall, borrowing becomes cheaper and spending tends to rise. This is why the CBN raises its policy rate to cool spending and lowers it to stimulate the economy; Options A, B and C each get one or both directions wrong.

questions.question: The government controls the size of the money supply through ________ policies.

options.a: revenue
options.b: monetary

questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the control of the money supply, credit and interest rates, carried out in Nigeria by the CBN through tools such as open market operations, reserve requirements and the policy rate. Option D, fiscal policy, is about government taxation and spending rather than the money supply, while Options A and C are not recognised types of economic policy.

questions.question: All of the following are tools for controlling persistent inflation in an economy except

options.a: Surplus budget
options.b: Sale of treasury bills through Open Market Operations (OMO)
options.c: Decrease in the Monetary Policy Rate

questions.explanation: Cutting the Monetary Policy Rate eases monetary policy: it makes borrowing cheaper and puts more money into circulation, which would worsen inflation rather than control it. Selling treasury bills through OMO (B) mops up excess money from the banking system, and a surplus budget (A) cuts total spending, so both help to fight inflation. Option D is wrong because C is clearly not an anti-inflation tool.

questions.question: The Central Bank of Nigeria performs all but one of the following functions. Which one does it NOT perform?

options.a: Serves as banker to the Federal Government
options.b: Undertakes research on various facets of economic activity
options.d: Administers the country's foreign exchange reserves

questions.explanation: Registering stockbroking firms is the work of the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates capital market operators, not the CBN. Acting as banker to the Federal Government (A), carrying out economic research (B) and managing the country's foreign exchange reserves (D) are all regular CBN functions.

questions.question: To reduce the supply of money, the government (through the central bank) could:

options.a: Reduce interest rates
options.b: Buy back government bonds

questions.explanation: Selling government bonds or other securities draws money out of the system, because buyers pay with cash and bank reserves, so the money supply falls. Buying back bonds (B) does the opposite and injects money into the economy. Reducing interest rates (A) and encouraging banks to lend (D) both expand credit and so increase the money supply.

questions.question: Open Market Operations occur when the central bank

options.a: Reduces spending
options.b: Buys and sells treasury bills

questions.explanation: Open Market Operations are the buying and selling of government securities, mainly treasury bills, by the central bank to influence bank reserves and the money supply. The CBN sells them to mop up excess liquidity and buys them to inject money. Reducing spending (A) and increasing taxation (C) are fiscal actions of government, while D concerns exchange rate policy.

questions.question: All these are "traditional" (quantitative) tools of monetary policy except

options.a: Bank rate
options.b: Open market operations

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is a qualitative tool: the central bank uses persuasion and friendly appeals to get banks to behave in a desired way, instead of directly changing the cost or quantity of money. The bank rate (A), open market operations (B) and cash reserve requirements (C) are the traditional quantitative tools, because each works directly on the cost of funds, the monetary base or the money multiplier.

questions.question: Which of the following was a weakness of the West African Currency Board (WACB) that made the establishment of the Central Bank of Nigeria necessary?

options.a: It invested Nigeria's reserves in local industries instead of in the financial markets of developed countries.
options.b: It lent too freely to Nigerian banks as a lender of last resort, which caused rapid inflation in the colony.
options.c: It gave Nigeria no independent monetary policy, since the local money supply simply moved with the country's sterling earnings.
options.d: It issued a separate, inconvertible currency for Nigeria that was not recognised outside the country.

questions.explanation: The WACB, based in London, issued currency for the British West African colonies fully backed by sterling, so the money supply in Nigeria rose and fell with export earnings and there was no room for an independent monetary policy. It also invested the colonies' reserves abroad and did not act as a lender of last resort, so option B is wrong and option A reverses what it did. Option D is wrong because the WACB currency was freely convertible into sterling and widely recognised.

questions.question: Which report, submitted in 1957, recommended the establishment of the Central Bank of Nigeria and paved the way for the CBN Act of 1958?

options.a: The Paton Report
options.b: The Fisher Report

questions.explanation: J.B. Loynes of the Bank of England was invited to advise on how a central bank for Nigeria should be set up, and his 1957 report led directly to the CBN Act of 1958. The Paton Report (option A) of 1948 dealt with bank failures and led to the 1952 Banking Ordinance. The Fisher Report (option B) advised against a central bank at that time, and the World Bank mission (option C) proposed only an interim state bank.

questions.question: The Fisher Report of 1953 did not support setting up a central bank in Nigeria at that time. What was its main reason?

options.a: Nigeria already had a central bank operating in Lagos under the colonial government.
options.b: The West African Currency Board had already been abolished and replaced by a state bank.
options.c: Nigerian commercial banks were too large and powerful for any central bank to regulate.
options.d: The financial system was too underdeveloped for a central bank to control the money supply, and trained staff were lacking.

questions.explanation: Fisher argued that Nigeria's financial system, with no organised money or capital market, was too narrow for a central bank to carry out its main role of controlling the money supply, and that there were not enough trained people to run one. Option A is wrong because the CBN did not exist until 1959, option B is wrong because the WACB was still operating, and option C is wrong because the indigenous banks of the time were small and weak.

questions.question: Which of the following is a developmental (non-traditional) function of the Central Bank of Nigeria rather than a traditional central banking function?

options.a: Issuing the national currency
options.b: Acting as banker to the government
options.c: Running special credit schemes such as the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund
options.d: Acting as lender of last resort to banks

questions.explanation: Traditional functions are those every central bank performs whatever the level of development, such as issuing currency (option A), banking for the government (option B) and acting as lender of last resort (option D). In a developing economy like Nigeria, the CBN also takes on developmental roles, including building financial markets and instruments, running special funds and credit schemes such as the ACGSF, and providing information and training.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the three main developmental functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: Accepting deposits from the public, granting loans to households, and selling insurance policies
options.b: Issuing currency, acting as banker to the government, and acting as lender of last resort to banks
options.c: Provision of financial infrastructure, provision of special funds and schemes, and provision of information and training
options.d: Collecting taxes, paying civil servants' salaries, and fixing the prices of goods and services

questions.explanation: Beyond its traditional roles, the CBN helps develop the financial system by creating markets and instruments (financial infrastructure), running special funds and credit schemes for sectors like agriculture and small industry, and providing economic information, research and training. Option B lists traditional central banking functions, option A describes commercial bank and insurance business, and option D lists jobs of government, not of a central bank.

questions.question: Under the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund (ACGSF), established in 1977, what does the Fund promise banks that lend to agriculture?

options.a: To repay the full amount of every defaulted loan together with interest
options.b: To repay 25 percent of the net amount in default if a borrower fails to repay
options.c: To repay 75 percent of the net amount in default if a borrower fails to repay
options.d: To repay 50 percent of the net amount in default if a borrower fails to repay

questions.explanation: The ACGSF encourages banks to lend to farmers by guaranteeing 75 percent of the amount in default, net of any security realised. The lending bank still bears the remaining 25 percent, so options B and D understate the cover, while option A is wrong because the guarantee never covers the whole loss.

questions.question: Under the Small and Medium Industries Equity Investment Scheme (SMIEIS), promoted by the CBN through the Bankers' Committee, banks were required to set aside:

options.a: 25 percent of their share capital for the purchase of treasury bills
options.b: 10 percent of their profit before tax for investment in small and medium industries
options.c: 10 percent of their total deposits as interest-free loans to the CBN
options.d: 1 percent of their total loans for the National Housing Fund

questions.explanation: Under SMIEIS, banks set aside 10 percent of their profit before tax to invest in small and medium enterprises, mainly by taking equity stakes, which spares these firms heavy interest payments. Options C, A and D describe requirements that were not part of the scheme. The CBN's role was to initiate the scheme and guide it through the Bankers' Committee.

questions.question: At the apex of the organisational structure of the Central Bank of Nigeria is the:

options.a: Bankers' Committee, chaired by the head of the largest bank
options.b: Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by the Minister of Finance
options.d: Board of Directors, chaired by the Governor

questions.explanation: The CBN is governed by its Board of Directors, which is chaired by the Governor and includes the Deputy Governors and other directors; below it are the directorates and departments that run the bank's daily operations. Option B is wrong because the Monetary Policy Committee sets monetary policy and is chaired by the Governor, not the Minister of Finance. The Bankers' Committee (option A) is a forum where the CBN meets bank chief executives, and the National Assembly (option C) oversees the CBN from outside, so neither sits at the top of its internal structure.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, how many Deputy Governors does the Central Bank of Nigeria have?

options.a: Four
options.b: Two

questions.explanation: The CBN Act 2007 provides for a Governor and four Deputy Governors, all appointed by the President subject to confirmation by the Senate. The Deputy Governors sit on the Board and each oversees a group of directorates. Options B, D and C do not match the number set by the Act.

questions.question: As part of its developmental role of providing information and public enlightenment, which of the following does the Central Bank of Nigeria do?

options.a: It publishes the listing rules that companies must meet before their shares can be quoted on the stock exchange
options.b: It publishes economic and financial information such as Statistical Bulletins, Annual Reports and CBN Briefs, and organises seminars and policy forums
options.c: It insures the deposits of members of the public in banks that fail and pays them compensation
options.d: It sets and conducts the professional examinations that qualify people as chartered bankers in Nigeria

questions.explanation: The CBN keeps government, investors, researchers and the general public informed through regular publications such as its Statistical Bulletin, Annual Report, CBN Briefs and Economic and Financial Review, and it also runs seminars, surveys and policy forums on economic issues. Option D describes the work of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN), not the CBN. Option A relates to the stock exchange and the SEC, while option C is the job of the NDIC.

questions.question: How was the Central Bank of Nigeria involved in the Small and Medium Industries Equity Investment Scheme (SMIEIS)?

options.a: It required commercial banks to open branches in rural areas so as to mobilise rural savings for local lending
options.b: It guaranteed banks against up to 75% of the net losses they suffered on loans granted to farmers
options.c: It initiated the scheme, under which banks, through the Bankers' Committee, set aside 10% of their profit before tax for equity investment in small and medium industries
options.d: It bought shares in small and medium industries directly with its own reserves, without involving the banks at all

questions.explanation: SMIEIS was a CBN initiative adopted through the Bankers' Committee: each bank set aside 10% of its profit before tax to invest as equity in small and medium industries, giving such firms long-term funds without the burden of interest charges. Option B describes the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund and option A describes the Rural Banking Scheme, which are different CBN schemes. Option D is wrong because the money came from the banks' own profits, not from the CBN's reserves.

questions.question: The Rediscounting and Refinancing Facility (RRF) introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria was mainly meant to:

options.a: provide Ways and Means advances to the Federal Government when revenue falls short
options.b: mop up excess liquidity from the banking system in order to bring down inflation
options.c: encourage banks to finance exports by allowing them to rediscount or refinance the export credit they granted
options.d: guarantee banks against losses on loans that they granted to farmers and agricultural firms

questions.explanation: The RRF was an export-promotion facility: banks that granted credit to exporters could rediscount or refinance it, which freed up their funds and encouraged more lending for exports. It was later handed over to the Nigerian Export-Import Bank (NEXIM). Option D describes the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund, option B is the aim of tools such as CBN certificates and open market operations, and option A is part of the CBN's role as banker to the government.

questions.question: The Foreign Input Facility (FIF) introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria was designed to:

options.a: provide long-term housing loans to low-income earners in the cities
options.b: insure the deposits of bank customers in case their bank fails
options.c: help domestic producers obtain foreign exchange to import the capital goods and raw materials they need
options.d: encourage commercial banks to open more branches in rural areas

questions.explanation: The FIF made foreign exchange available so that Nigerian producers could import the machinery and raw materials needed for production. Like the RRF, it was later moved to the Nigerian Export-Import Bank (NEXIM). Option B is the work of the NDIC, option A is the business of mortgage institutions, and option D describes the Rural Banking Scheme.

questions.question: When it is said that the CBN provides 'financial infrastructure' as part of its developmental role, this mainly means that the CBN:

options.a: issues the country's currency notes and coins and manages their distribution to the banks
options.b: helps to create and develop financial markets and instruments, such as treasury bills and the money market, and encouraged the setting up of the stock exchange
options.c: grants loans and overdrafts directly to individuals, households and small traders
options.d: guarantees banks' agricultural loans through the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund

questions.explanation: The basic infrastructure of a financial system is its markets and instruments. When central banking began in Nigeria there was no organised money or capital market, so the CBN introduced instruments such as treasury bills, treasury certificates and bankers' acceptances, later licensed discount houses, and encouraged the setting up of the Lagos Stock Exchange. Option A is a traditional central bank function, option D belongs to the CBN's special funds and schemes, and option C is wrong because the CBN does not lend to the general public.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four major macroeconomic objectives pursued through monetary policy?

options.a: Balance of payments equilibrium
options.b: Price stability (avoidance of inflation)
options.c: Maximising the profits of deposit money banks

questions.explanation: The four major macroeconomic objectives of monetary policy are price stability, a high rate of economic growth, full employment and balance of payments equilibrium. Making banks more profitable is a goal of the banks' own owners and managers, not a national policy objective. Options B, D and A are all among the four objectives, so none of them can be the exception.

questions.question: If the CBN raises the cash reserve requirement for banks from 10% to 20%, what happens to the simple deposit (money) multiplier?

options.a: It stays at 10, because only the discount rate affects credit creation
options.b: It rises from 10 to 20

questions.explanation: The simple deposit multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio, so it is 1/0.10 = 10 at a 10% requirement and 1/0.20 = 5 at 20%. Raising the reserve requirement therefore halves the banks' ability to create credit and slows the growth of money supply. Options B and D get the direction wrong, since a higher reserve ratio always means a smaller multiplier, and option A is wrong because the reserve requirement works directly on the multiplier.

questions.question: If the CBN lowers the discount rate at which it lends to banks, the intended effect is to:

options.a: Withdraw money from circulation by selling government securities
options.b: Encourage banks to borrow more and lend at lower rates, expanding credit and money supply
options.c: Force banks to raise their lending rates, reducing credit and money supply
options.d: Increase the amount of cash banks must hold as required reserves

questions.explanation: The discount rate (also called the bank rate or minimum lending rate) is the price banks pay to borrow from the central bank. Cutting it makes borrowing cheaper, so banks can lower their own lending rates and lend more, which expands credit and money supply. Option C describes the effect of raising the discount rate, while options D and A describe the reserve requirement and an open market sale, which are different instruments.

questions.question: Apart from reserve requirements, the discount rate and open market operations, which of the following is also an instrument of monetary policy?

options.a: Personal income tax
options.b: Selective credit control
options.c: Government spending on roads and bridges

questions.explanation: Selective credit control uses administrative guidelines to direct banks to lend specified amounts to particular sectors, sometimes at set interest rates, and it sits alongside special deposits and moral suasion as an additional monetary policy tool. Options A, C and D are taxation and government spending measures, which belong to fiscal policy rather than to the central bank's control of money and credit.

questions.question: Which monetary policy instrument requires banks to keep cash with the central bank over and above their normal required reserves, with that cash not counted towards the reserve requirement?

options.a: Open market operations
options.b: The discount rate

questions.explanation: Special deposits are extra balances the central bank asks banks to lodge with it on top of their normal required reserves; because they are not counted as reserves, they cut the banks' capacity to create credit, much like a higher reserve ratio. Option D, moral suasion, relies on persuasion and friendly appeal rather than compulsory deposits. Options A and B work through buying or selling government securities and through the cost of borrowing from the central bank.

questions.question: Monetary policy can best be defined as:

options.a: The use of the central bank's control over the quantity, availability and cost of money and credit to achieve general economic objectives
options.b: The lending policy a commercial bank sets for its own customers
options.c: The rules that govern the design and security features of currency notes
options.d: The use of taxation, government expenditure and public debt to influence the economy

questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the deliberate use, by the central bank, of its control over money supply, credit and interest rates to achieve goals such as price stability and economic growth; in Nigeria this is the job of the CBN. Option D is the definition of fiscal policy, which works through the government budget rather than money and credit. Option B is a single bank's internal credit policy, not a national policy, and option C has nothing to do with controlling money and credit.

questions.question: Which of the following is a developmental function of the CBN rather than a traditional central banking function?

options.a: Issuing legal tender currency
options.b: Acting as banker to the government
options.c: Acting as lender of last resort to banks
options.d: Directing commercial banks to open branches in rural areas under the rural banking scheme

questions.explanation: Pushing banks into rural areas is a developmental role, aimed at spreading banking and growth to neglected parts of the economy, much like the CBN's help in setting up development finance institutions. Options A, B and C are traditional functions that central banks perform everywhere.

questions.question: In his 1953 report on establishing a central bank in Nigeria, J. L. Fisher concluded that

options.a: a full central bank should be set up at once to finance rapid development
options.b: all expatriate banks in Nigeria should be nationalised
options.c: the financial environment hardly existed in Nigeria for a central bank to be established
options.d: Nigeria should adopt the US dollar as its official currency

questions.explanation: Fisher felt that Nigeria lacked the financial environment for a central bank and proposed a slow, three-stage approach instead, a view widely criticised as conservative. Option A is the opposite of his conclusion, and options B and D were never part of his report.

questions.question: Whose report favoured the establishment of a central bank in Nigeria and formed part of the draft presented to the House of Representatives in 1958?

options.a: J. L. Fisher
options.b: The IBRD (World Bank) mission

questions.explanation: Loynes reported in favour of a central bank for Nigeria, and his recommendations shaped the 1958 law that set up the CBN. Option A, Fisher, said the environment was not ready, option B also felt it was too early and suggested a State Bank instead, and option C dealt with setting up the West African Currency Board decades earlier.

questions.question: Under the rural banking scheme that the CBN introduced in 1977, commercial banks were

options.a: required to close their rural branches and move to cities
options.b: barred from lending to farmers
options.d: directed to open branches in rural areas

questions.explanation: The rural banking scheme, run in phases from 1977, directed commercial banks to open branches in rural areas to bring banking services to the rural population. Option A is the opposite, option B is wrong because the aim was to increase rural lending, and option C is wrong because community banks were a separate, later scheme.

questions.question: Which grassroots banking scheme, introduced in 1990, replaced the rural banking scheme and later evolved into microfinance banking?

options.a: Merchant banking
options.b: Community banking

questions.explanation: Community banks were introduced in 1990 to serve the grassroots and were later converted into microfinance banks. Option A is wholesale banking for corporate clients, option C removed the line between commercial and merchant banking, and option D is banking based on non-interest principles; none of them was set up to replace rural banking.

questions.question: If the Central Bank of Nigeria wants to reduce the money supply through open market operations, it will:

options.a: Sell government securities to banks and the non-bank public
options.b: Lower the rate at which it lends to banks
options.c: Reduce the cash reserve ratio banks must keep with it
options.d: Buy government securities from banks and the non-bank public

questions.explanation: When the CBN sells securities, buyers pay with money drawn from bank deposits, so bank reserves fall and banks can create less credit, which shrinks the money supply. Buying securities (D) does the opposite and injects money. Options C and B are not open market operations at all, and both would make it easier for banks to lend, not harder.

questions.question: What is the most likely effect when the Central Bank of Nigeria raises the legal (cash) reserve requirement for banks?

options.a: Interest rates on loans tend to fall sharply
options.b: The CBN directly buys more treasury bills from banks
options.c: Banks are able to grant more loans and advances
options.d: Banks are left with less money to lend, so credit and money supply tend to contract

questions.explanation: A reserve requirement is the share of deposits that banks must hold as cash or as balances with the CBN that earn no interest. Raising it ties up more of their deposits, so banks may have to cut loans and investments, and the money supply contracts. Option C is what happens when the ratio is lowered, A is the opposite of the usual effect because tighter credit tends to push lending rates up, and B describes an open market purchase, which is a separate tool.

questions.question: When the Central Bank of Nigeria uses moral suasion as a monetary policy tool, it:

options.a: Fixes the minimum margin of security required for bank advances
options.b: Buys and sells government securities in the open market
options.c: Persuades banks to follow policies it considers in the national interest, without any legal compulsion
options.d: Sets a legal maximum on the total advances each bank may grant

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is persuasion: the CBN appeals to bankers through meetings, letters and dialogue, and the tool has no legal backing behind it. Option D is a credit (loan) ceiling, B is open market operations, and A is a margin requirement. Those three are formal, enforceable controls, unlike moral suasion.

questions.question: Which of the following was a major reason for the banking consolidation exercise announced by the Central Bank of Nigeria in July 2004?

options.a: Nigeria had too few banks to serve the economy
options.b: The NDIC had stopped insuring bank deposits
options.c: Many Nigerian banks were small, fragile and had a weak capital base compared with their expected role in the economy
options.d: Banks were holding too much capital and earning too little

questions.explanation: Before consolidation, Nigeria had 89 banks, many of them tiny and undercapitalised, and the system was too weak to finance big development projects. The CBN therefore required banks to build a much larger capital base, mainly through mergers and acquisitions. The problem was too many weak banks, not too few (A), and banks had too little capital, not too much (D). Deposit insurance (B) did not stop.

questions.question: Which of the following is an argument AGAINST bank consolidation?

options.a: Consolidation removes weak banks from the system
options.b: Bigger banks can achieve cost and revenue efficiency gains
options.c: Larger banks have better opportunities to diversify their risks
options.d: Very large banks can become complex and costly to manage, and may take on more risk

questions.explanation: Opponents of consolidation argue that economies of scale have limits: very big banks are harder and more expensive to manage, and they may increase risk-taking through higher leverage and off-balance-sheet business. Efficiency gains (B), getting rid of weak banks (A) and better diversification (C) are the arguments supporters give in favour of consolidation.

questions.question: In banking, consolidation is best defined as:

options.a: A reduction in the number of banks, with the banks that remain becoming larger and more concentrated
options.b: The closure of all foreign-owned banks in a country
options.c: An increase in the number of small banks in the economy
options.d: The conversion of commercial banks into microfinance banks

questions.explanation: Consolidation shrinks the number of banks while making the survivors bigger, usually through mergers, acquisitions and higher capital requirements. That is why Nigeria's 2004-2005 exercise reduced the number of banks sharply. Option C is the opposite, and D and B describe different policies altogether.

questions.question: Under the CBN's 2004 consolidation guidelines, which of the following could a bank NOT use to meet the new minimum capital requirement?

options.a: An outright acquisition or takeover of another bank
options.b: A mere group arrangement, in which banks stay separate but are linked through common ownership
options.c: A merger with one or more other banks

questions.explanation: The CBN accepted mergers and outright acquisitions as the legal modes of consolidation, and banks could also raise new capital on their own. A loose group arrangement was rejected because it would not create a single, stronger bank. That is why banks with subsidiaries or common owners were encouraged to merge fully. So C, A and D were all acceptable.

questions.question: By the end of the bank consolidation exercise in December 2005, the number of deposit money banks in Nigeria had fallen from 89 to about:
questions.explanation: Mergers and acquisitions cut the number of banks from 89 to 25 bigger banks. The banks that failed to meet the N25 billion capital requirement had their licences revoked, and the 25 later became 24 after one more merger. Options A, B and D do not match the outcome of the exercise.

questions.question: In practice, which objective has become the primary focus of the Central Bank of Nigeria's monetary policy?

options.a: Price stability (low and stable inflation)
options.b: Fixing the share prices of quoted companies
options.c: Financing every budget deficit of the Federal Government
options.d: Maximising the profits of deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Like most central banks, the CBN treats price stability as its main monetary policy goal, because low and stable inflation is an important condition for macroeconomic stability and sustainable growth. Bank profits (D) are the banks' own concern. Automatically financing deficits (C) would undermine price stability, and share prices (B) are set by the market.

questions.question: Which of the following is one way the Central Bank of Nigeria has supported manpower development in the banking industry?

options.a: Requiring all bankers to train abroad
options.b: Supporting the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria and the Financial Institutions Training Centre, and running training programmes for staff
options.c: Banning the employment of graduates in banks
options.d: Taking over the recruitment of staff for every commercial bank

questions.explanation: The CBN has backed banking manpower development by leading the Bankers' Committee, supporting its training institutions, the CIBN and the FITC, running its own training school and guiding banks through its examination reports. There was no rule forcing bankers to train abroad (A), no ban on graduates (C), and the CBN does not recruit staff for commercial banks (D).

questions.question: Which of the following was a major factor behind the stress in the Nigerian banking sector in 2009?

options.a: A sharp rise in the prices of shares on the stock market
options.b: Heavy concentration of bank lending in the capital market (margin loans) and the oil and gas sector, combined with weak risk management and corporate governance
options.c: Banks holding too much capital and too little risk
options.d: Too little lending to the capital market

questions.explanation: After the stock market crash and the global financial crisis, banks that had lent heavily against shares and to oil and gas businesses found many loans going bad, and weak governance and risk management made things worse. Option C is the opposite of the real problem. Share prices fell rather than rose (A), and over-lending to the capital market, not too little lending (D), was part of the trouble.

questions.question: Which of the following was a key finding of the special examination of five Nigerian banks by the CBN and NDIC in 2009?

options.a: The banks were net lenders of large surplus funds to the inter-bank market
options.b: The banks had too much capital and very few bad loans
options.c: The banks had excessively high levels of non-performing loans and were illiquid, depending heavily on CBN support and inter-bank borrowing
options.d: The banks' liquidity ratios were far above the regulatory minimum

questions.explanation: The examination found very high non-performing loans caused by poor credit risk management, and the five banks were persistent borrowers from the CBN and the inter-bank market, which was clear evidence of illiquidity. Their liquidity ratios were below the minimum, not above it (D). Options B and A describe healthy banks, not these ones.

questions.question: Under Nigerian banking law (the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act), a person who wants to carry on banking business in Nigeria must apply in writing for a licence to:

options.a: The Managing Director of the NDIC
options.b: The Director-General of the Securities and Exchange Commission
options.c: The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: The Registrar-General of the Corporate Affairs Commission

questions.explanation: Banking licences are granted by the CBN. The application goes to the CBN Governor together with a feasibility report, the draft memorandum and articles, details of shareholders and directors, and the fee, and the proposed bank must also deposit the minimum paid-up capital. The NDIC (A) insures deposits and SEC (B) regulates the capital market. The CAC (D) only incorporates the company, which is needed but is not a banking licence.

questions.question: Under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, a licensed bank in Nigeria may open or close a branch only:

options.a: Whenever its board decides, without informing any regulator
options.b: With the approval of its customers at a general meeting
options.c: With the prior written consent of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: After notifying the NDIC one week later

questions.explanation: The law requires the CBN's prior written consent before a bank opens or closes any branch, inside or outside Nigeria, so the regulator can control how the banking network expands and contracts. Customers (B) have no say in this, informing the NDIC after the event (D) is not enough, and a board cannot act alone (A).

questions.question: Under the banking licensing regime introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria in 2010, the minimum capital for a commercial bank with international authorisation was:

options.a: N25 billion
options.b: N2 billion

questions.explanation: The 2010 regime ended universal banking and created regional, national and international commercial banks with minimum capital of N10 billion, N25 billion and N50 billion respectively, plus merchant banks at N15 billion. N25 billion (A) was for national banks, N10 billion (C) was for regional banks, and N2 billion (B) was the requirement before the 2004 consolidation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why banks are heavily regulated by the monetary authorities?

options.a: To guarantee that every bank earns a profit every year
options.b: To prevent bank failures and crises that could damage the whole economy
options.c: To promote monetary stability by influencing the cost, volume and availability of credit
options.d: To protect depositors and maintain public confidence in the banking system

questions.explanation: Regulation is meant to keep banks safe and sound, not to guarantee their profits, which depend on how well each bank is managed. Protecting depositors and confidence (D), supporting monetary stability (C) and preventing crises (B) are all genuine reasons, because banks hold the public's money and sit at the centre of the payments system.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the generally accepted principles (canons) of central banking?

options.a: The central bank should grant loans directly to individuals who cannot borrow from commercial banks
options.b: The central bank should keep part of its assets in liquid form so that it can discount short-term commercial and government bills
options.c: The central bank should open retail branches to attract savings deposits from households
options.d: The central bank should aim to earn the highest possible profit on its lending

questions.explanation: A central bank must stay liquid so that it can discount short-term bills and support the banking system when needed, which is one of its recognised canons. Options C and A describe ordinary commercial banking with the public, which a central bank should avoid so that it does not compete with the banks it supervises. Option D is wrong because a central bank serves the economy, not profit maximisation.

questions.question: Which of the following was an ADVANTAGE of the West African Currency Board (WACB) system?

options.a: It allowed Nigeria to run an independent monetary policy suited to its own needs
options.b: It established a unified currency standard that was widely accepted by the people
options.c: It let the colonies invest their currency backing in earning assets at home
options.d: It trained Africans in the art of monetary management

questions.explanation: The WACB gave the British West African colonies one common, generally accepted currency and relieved colonial governments of currency management. Option A is wrong because the WACB gave Nigeria no independent monetary policy. Options D and C are actually its known weaknesses: it failed to train Africans in monetary management, and its sterling backing deprived the colonies of earning assets.

questions.question: Which of the following was a DISADVANTAGE of the West African Currency Board (WACB)?

options.a: Using one currency for four colonies caused problems because the colonies became independent at different dates
options.b: It relieved the colonial governments of the duty of managing currency
options.c: It paved the way for easy acceptance of new currencies at independence
options.d: It established a single currency standard that people accepted

questions.explanation: Because Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone and The Gambia shared one WACB currency but gained independence at different times, the common currency became hard to manage, which was a real weakness of the system. Options B, C and D are all advantages of the WACB, not disadvantages.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, which of the following is the FIRST of the principal objects of the Central Bank of Nigeria, the one monetary policy is mainly built around?

options.a: Achieving full employment of labour
options.b: Ensuring monetary and price stability
options.c: Maximising the rate of economic growth
options.d: Fixing the exchange rate of the naira permanently

questions.explanation: Section 2 of the CBN Act 2007 lists 'ensure monetary and price stability' first among the Bank's principal objects, and the Monetary Policy Committee exists to help achieve price stability. Options A and C are broad aims of economic policy, but they are not stated as the CBN's first object. Option D is not a CBN object at all; the Act speaks of safeguarding the international value of the currency, not fixing it permanently.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, which of the following officials is a member of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: The Managing Director of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation
options.b: The President of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria
options.c: The Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Finance
options.d: The Director-General of the Securities and Exchange Commission

questions.explanation: Section 6 of the CBN Act 2007 makes the Board consist of the Governor (chairman), the four Deputy Governors, the Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Finance, five Directors and the Accountant-General of the Federation. The heads of the NDIC (A) and SEC (D) run separate regulatory bodies and do not sit on the CBN Board, and the CIBN (B) is a professional body.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria is appointed for

options.a: a term of five years in the first instance, and may be reappointed for one more term of not more than five years
options.b: a term of four years, renewable as many times as the President wishes
options.c: life, until the Governor reaches the retirement age of the civil service
options.d: a single term of seven years that cannot be renewed

questions.explanation: The Act appoints the Governor (and each Deputy Governor) for five years in the first instance, with eligibility for one further term of up to five years, so the longest normal tenure is ten years. Options D, B and C describe tenures the Act does not provide; a fixed but renewable term protects the Governor's independence while still allowing a change of leadership.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, the Monetary Policy Committee consists of the Governor (as Chairman), the four Deputy Governors, two members of the Board of Directors, three members appointed by the President and two members appointed by the Governor. How many members does the MPC have in total?
questions.explanation: Adding the groups gives 1 Governor + 4 Deputy Governors + 2 Board members + 3 presidential appointees + 2 Governor's appointees = 12 members. Option B forgets the Governor, who is himself a member and chairs the Committee, while C and A add members who are not in the Act.

questions.question: Under the CBN Act 2007, the Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Nigeria is required to meet

options.a: whenever the Minister of Finance summons it
options.b: at least four times in a year
options.c: only once a year, at the end of the financial year

questions.explanation: The Act's schedule on the MPC says it 'shall meet at least four times in a year'; in practice it has often met more frequently, but four meetings is the legal minimum. Options C and D set lower minimums than the law requires, and A is wrong because the MPC is a committee of the Bank, not one called by the Minister.

questions.question: In the organisational structure of the Central Bank of Nigeria, with four Deputy Governors each overseeing a group of departments, the Banking Supervision Department falls under the Deputy Governor responsible for

options.a: Operations
options.b: Economic Policy

questions.explanation: Supervising banks is about keeping the financial system safe and sound, so Banking Supervision sits with the Deputy Governor for Financial System Stability, along with departments such as Other Financial Institutions Supervision and Consumer Protection. The Economic Policy directorate (B) handles monetary policy, research and statistics; Operations (A) handles currency, banking services and reserves; and Corporate Services (C) handles staffing, finance and legal matters.

questions.question: Nigeria decimalised its currency on 1 January 1973, when the CBN introduced the naira and kobo. The naira replaced the Nigerian pound at the rate of

options.a: N2 to one pound
options.b: N20 to one pound

questions.explanation: When the naira was introduced on 1 January 1973, each Nigerian pound was exchanged for two naira, and the naira was divided into 100 kobo. Option C ignores the conversion, while D and B confuse the conversion rate with the denominations of the new currency, which went up to N10 at the time.

questions.question: The N20 note issued by the CBN was introduced in 1977 to honour a late Head of State whose portrait it still carries. Who is he?

options.a: Sir Ahmadu Bello
options.b: General Murtala Mohammed

questions.explanation: The N20 note honours General Murtala Mohammed, the Head of State assassinated in 1976, and his portrait remains on the green N20 note. Chief Obafemi Awolowo (C) appears on the N100 note, Sir Ahmadu Bello (A) on the N200 note and Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe (D) on the N500 note.

questions.question: From 1973 the CBN began to hold Nigeria's external reserves in as many traded currencies as possible, instead of only US dollars and British pounds. The main aim of this change was to

options.a: make the naira fully convertible into gold
options.b: earn new income and reduce possible losses from a fall in the value of any single reserve currency
options.c: stop exporters from surrendering their foreign exchange earnings to the CBN
options.d: allow commercial banks to keep the country's reserves on behalf of the CBN

questions.explanation: Spreading reserves across several currencies is diversification: it opens up new earning opportunities and limits the loss if one reserve currency is devalued or depreciates. Option A has nothing to do with currency diversification, D is wrong because reserve holdings were centralised in the CBN, and C reverses the policy, which required exporters to surrender their proceeds to the Bank.

questions.question: The Federal Government directs all its ministries, departments and agencies to close their separate revenue accounts in commercial banks and pay all government receipts into one consolidated account kept at the CBN. This arrangement is known as the

options.a: Treasury Single Account (TSA)
options.b: Ways and Means Advance

questions.explanation: The Treasury Single Account pools government revenues into a single account at the CBN, improving transparency and cash management, and the CBN runs it as banker to the government.
