A Ways and Means Advance (B) is a temporary CBN loan to government, FAAC (C) is the committee that shares federally collected revenue among the tiers of government, and the Excess Crude Account (D) holds oil earnings above the budget benchmark.

questions.question: When large government deficits financed by CBN lending, such as Ways and Means advances, pump money into the economy and weaken the CBN's ability to keep prices stable, the problem is described as

options.a: fiscal dominance
options.b: financial inclusion

questions.explanation: Fiscal dominance happens when the government's borrowing needs push the central bank into financing deficits, so monetary policy ends up serving fiscal needs instead of price stability. Moral suasion (D) is informal persuasion of banks, financial inclusion (B) is extending financial services to the unbanked, and regulatory forbearance (C) is a supervisor's decision to delay enforcing rules on a weak bank.

questions.question: At the close of business, Bank A finds it is short of funds to settle its obligations and cannot raise money in the interbank market. It borrows overnight from the CBN against eligible collateral, at a rate set above the Monetary Policy Rate. Bank A has used the

options.a: Treasury Single Account
options.b: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)

questions.explanation: The Standing Lending Facility lets a bank borrow overnight from the CBN, and its rate is set above the MPR so that banks try the interbank market first. The SDF (B) works the other way round, letting banks with surplus funds place them with the CBN at a rate below the MPR. The CRR (D) is a reserve requirement, not a borrowing window, and the TSA (A) is the government's account.

questions.question: Suppose the CBN sets the Monetary Policy Rate at 20% with an asymmetric corridor of +500 basis points and -100 basis points around it. What are the Standing Lending Facility (SLF) and Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rates?

options.a: SLF 25%; SDF 15%
options.b: SLF 21%; SDF 15%

questions.explanation: One hundred basis points equal one percentage point, so the SLF is 20% + 5% = 25% and the SDF is 20% - 1% = 19%. Option B applies the two margins to the wrong facilities, A uses 5 points on both sides as if the corridor were symmetric, and C wrongly puts the lending rate below the deposit rate.

questions.question: In an open market operation, the CBN sells government securities to banks under an agreement to buy them back at a stated price on a future date. What is the effect of this transaction on the banking system?

options.a: It has no effect on bank reserves, because the securities will be bought back
options.b: It temporarily withdraws liquidity from the banking system
options.c: It temporarily injects liquidity into the banking system
options.d: It permanently injects liquidity into the banking system

questions.explanation: When banks buy the securities they pay from their reserve accounts, so liquidity leaves the system, but only until the CBN buys the securities back and the money returns. Option D describes an outright purchase, and C describes the opposite deal in which the CBN buys securities and agrees to sell them back later. Option A is wrong because reserves really are reduced for the life of the agreement.

questions.question: Short-term securities issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria itself, rather than by the Federal Government, specifically to mop up or manage liquidity as part of open market operations, are known as

options.a: Nigerian Treasury Bills
options.b: Federal Government Development Stocks

questions.explanation: CBN Bills are issued by the CBN for monetary policy purposes, so they are a liquidity-management tool, not a way of funding the government. Nigerian Treasury Bills (A) and development stocks (B) are Federal Government debt, even though the CBN manages their issue, and bankers' acceptances (C) are bills accepted by banks to finance trade.

questions.question: Suppose the CBN requires deposit money banks to keep a liquidity ratio of 30%. Ekiti Trust Bank has total deposit liabilities of N600 billion and liquid assets (cash, balances with the CBN and Treasury Bills) of N150 billion. By how much is the bank short of the required liquid assets?

options.a: N45 billion
options.b: N150 billion

questions.explanation: Required liquid assets are 30% of N600 billion = N180 billion, and the bank holds N150 billion, so the shortfall is N180 billion - N150 billion = N30 billion. Option D is the full requirement rather than the shortfall, A wrongly takes 30% of the liquid assets, and B is simply what the bank already holds.

questions.question: Suppose the CBN sets the cash reserve ratio at 40%. A bank receives new deposits of N250 billion. Ignoring all other requirements, what is the most the bank can use for lending out of these deposits?

options.a: N250 billion
options.b: N210 billion

questions.explanation: The bank must keep 40% of N250 billion = N100 billion as reserves with the CBN, leaving N250 billion - N100 billion = N150 billion that it can lend. Option D is the reserve that must be kept, not the amount available, B wrongly subtracts 40 naira-billions instead of 40 percent, and A ignores the reserve requirement altogether.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from the liquidity ratio in Nigerian banking?

options.a: The CRR is kept as balances with the CBN, while the liquidity ratio can also be met with liquid assets such as Treasury Bills and cash in the bank's vaults
options.b: The CRR is fixed by the Bankers' Committee, while the liquidity ratio is fixed by the NDIC
options.c: The CRR applies only to merchant banks, while the liquidity ratio applies only to microfinance banks
options.d: The CRR can be met by holding Treasury Bills, while the liquidity ratio must be met only with deposits at the CBN

questions.explanation: The CRR is a percentage of deposits that must sit as reserves with the CBN, while the liquidity ratio is a wider requirement that a bank can meet with several liquid assets, including cash, CBN balances and Treasury Bills. Option D reverses the two, and C and B are wrong because both ratios are set by the CBN and apply to deposit-taking banks generally.

questions.question: When the CBN moved from direct monetary controls to a market-based approach in the 1990s, which of the following became the main indirect, market-based instrument of monetary management?

options.a: Administratively fixed interest rates
options.b: Credit ceilings on bank lending
options.c: Sectoral credit allocation to priority sectors

questions.explanation: Open market operations work through the market: the CBN buys or sells securities, banks' reserves change, and banks remain free to make their own lending decisions. Options B, C and A are direct controls used mainly before the Structural Adjustment Programme, where the CBN dictated how much banks could lend, to whom, and at what rate.

questions.question: A selective (qualitative) control under which the central bank fixes how much security a borrower must provide for bank advances, so that banks do not lend too much against commodities likely to be hoarded for speculation, is called

options.a: margin requirement
options.b: open market operation

questions.explanation: A margin requirement controls the value of security a borrower must pledge relative to the loan, so raising the margin limits speculative borrowing against particular goods. A loan ceiling (C) caps the total level of advances, a variable cash ratio (D) changes the cash banks keep with the central bank, and an open market operation (B) is the buying and selling of securities.

questions.question: The CBN orders commercial banks not to let their total advances rise above the level they had reached on a date the CBN names. This instrument is

options.a: supplementary reserves
options.b: a margin requirement

questions.explanation: A loan ceiling freezes or caps bank advances at the level reached on a date the central bank fixes, so it directly limits credit growth. A margin requirement (B) deals with the security needed for advances, supplementary reserves (A) require extra holdings of government securities, and the bank rate (D) works through the cost of borrowing from the central bank, not a quantity limit.

questions.question: Under a scheme run in phases from the late 1970s, the CBN directed commercial banks to open a set number of branches in rural areas. This is an example of the CBN's

options.a: function of issuing legal tender currency
options.b: role as lender of last resort to distressed banks
options.c: developmental function of spreading banking services and encouraging rural savings
options.d: function of managing the country's external reserves

questions.explanation: The rural banking scheme was a developmental step: by making banks open rural branches, the CBN sought to bring banking to unbanked areas and mobilise rural savings. Options D, A and B are traditional central banking functions with no direct link to where commercial banks place their branches.

questions.question: Which payment-system reform was launched by the CBN with the Bankers' Committee in February 2014 to give every bank customer a single biometric identity that can be verified across all Nigerian banks?

options.a: The Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system
options.b: The Treasury Single Account (TSA)

questions.explanation: The BVN, launched on 14 February 2014, captures each customer's biometrics so that banks can confirm identity, meet know-your-customer rules and reduce fraud. The TSA (B) consolidates government accounts, RTGS (A) settles large interbank payments in real time, and the cashless policy (C), started in 2012, aimed to reduce cash transactions.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the present-day Nigerian banking structure?

options.a: Deposit money (commercial) banks
options.b: The West African Currency Board

questions.explanation: The West African Currency Board was a colonial currency authority whose role in Nigeria passed to the CBN in 1959, so it is not part of today's banking structure. Deposit money banks (option A), merchant banks (option D) and microfinance banks (option C) all operate in Nigeria today under the regulation of the CBN, alongside development finance institutions and non-interest banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Microfinance banks in Nigeria are mainly intended to

options.a: underwrite share issues for large corporations
options.b: provide financial services to low-income individuals and micro and small enterprises
options.c: provide long-term finance for large industrial projects
options.d: act as lender of last resort to other banks

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks exist to promote financial inclusion by offering small loans, savings and other services to poor households and micro and small businesses that conventional banks often neglect. Option C describes development finance institutions such as the Bank of Industry. Option D is a central bank function, and option A is the work of investment or merchant banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The body that regulates the activities of insurance companies in Nigeria is known as:

options.a: CBN
options.b: NAICOM

questions.explanation: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) is the body that regulates and supervises insurance companies in Nigeria. The CBN (A) regulates banks and other financial institutions under its control, the SEC (C) regulates the capital market, and the NDIC (D) insures bank deposits and helps supervise banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The development bank UDBN (Urban Development Bank of Nigeria) was set up mainly to provide funds for:

options.a: Building houses
options.b: Building networks of bridges
options.c: Providing infrastructural facilities in cities such as public toilets

questions.explanation: The UDBN was created to finance urban infrastructure that conventional banks would not fund, such as motor parks, markets, drainage, street lighting, waste disposal and public conveniences like public toilets. Building houses (A) is the work of housing finance institutions such as the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria. Option B is too narrow and is not what the UDBN was known for; its mandate was the general infrastructure that makes cities work.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When we talk of deposit money banks, we refer to:

options.a: Savings banks and merchant banks
options.b: Development banks and commercial banks

questions.explanation: Deposit money banks are the commercial banks and the merchant banks, the two types of bank that hold the most significant position in the financial system. Option A wrongly includes savings banks, and option B wrongly includes development banks, which are specialised institutions set up mainly to provide long-term finance.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a function of merchant banks?

options.a: Equipment leasing
options.b: Project financing
options.c: Provision of safe-keeping for customers' jewellery and wills
options.d: Provision of investment and advisory services

questions.explanation: Merchant banks deal mainly with corporate and institutional clients, offering services such as equipment leasing (A), project financing (B), and investment and advisory services (D). Safe-keeping of customers' jewellery and wills is a typical retail service of commercial banks, not a merchant banking function.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the universal banking model, which the CBN replaced with a new banking licence regime in 2010, a universal bank was a bank that:

options.a: Could only accept demand deposits and grant short-term loans
options.b: Could carry out both commercial and merchant banking business and also engage in services such as insurance and stockbroking
options.c: Was owned jointly by the Federal government and the CBN to provide long-term development finance

questions.explanation: Universal banking allowed one banking licence to cover commercial banking, merchant banking and other financial services such as insurance and stockbroking. Option A describes a narrow traditional commercial bank, option C describes a development bank, and option D describes a non-interest bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons for setting up development banks?

options.a: To fill the gap left by the DMBs in medium-term and long-term financing
options.b: To fill the gap in funding socially desirable projects (such as housing) which are not commercially attractive
options.c: To provide government officials with an opportunity to raise funds for projects that will be useful to them after retirement
options.d: To accelerate the development of sectors such as agriculture and industry that have heavy multiplier effects in the long run but whose short-run returns may not attract investors

questions.explanation: Development banks were set up to fill gaps left by deposit money banks: medium- and long-term finance (A), socially desirable but commercially unattractive projects such as housing (B), and sectors like agriculture and industry whose long-run benefits are large but whose short-run returns are low (D). Raising money for officials' private retirement projects would be an abuse of office, not a reason for a development bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Development banks in Nigeria have generally been established by:

options.a: The CBN and the Federal government
options.b: The CBN and the DMBs
options.c: The Federal government and the DMBs

questions.explanation: Nigeria's development banks were generally set up and owned jointly by the Federal government and the CBN, because their purpose is national development rather than profit. Deposit money banks (B and C) are privately owned, profit-seeking banks; the very reason development banks exist is that DMBs would not provide the long-term finance these sectors needed.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a development bank in Nigeria?

options.a: Nigerian Industrial Development Bank
options.b: Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry

questions.explanation: The African Continental Bank was a commercial bank with strong Eastern Regional government backing, not a development bank. The NIDB (A), the NBCI (B) and the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (D) were all development finance institutions, set up to provide long-term funds for industry, commerce and housing.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Why were some Nigerian development banks merged in the early 2000s?

options.a: To convert them into deposit money banks that take demand deposits from the public
options.b: Because long-term development finance was no longer needed in Nigeria
options.c: To form bigger, more resilient institutions after the banking crises of the 1990s had weakened them
options.d: To privatise them fully and remove all government ownership

questions.explanation: The crises in Nigerian banking in the 1990s left several development banks weak, so in the early 2000s some were merged into bigger, more resilient institutions, such as the Bank of Industry. The merged banks remained government-owned development banks, so option A (conversion into deposit money banks) and option D (full privatisation) are wrong. Option B is wrong because the merger was meant to strengthen long-term development finance, not end it.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Bank of Industry (BOI), formed in 2001, is an amalgam of:

options.a: The NIDB, the NBCI and the FMBN
options.b: The NBCI, the UDBN and NERFUND
options.c: The NIDB, the NBCI and NERFUND
options.d: The NACB, the NIDB and the NBCI

questions.explanation: The Bank of Industry was formed in 2001 by bringing together the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank, the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry and the National Economic Reconstruction Fund (NERFUND). The FMBN (A) is a housing finance institution, the UDBN (B) financed urban infrastructure, and the NACB (D) went into the new agricultural development bank instead.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is a function of the NIDB?

options.a: To identify and promote projects whose value added to industry was high
options.b: To provide long-term loans to medium- and large-scale industrial enterprises
options.c: To mobilise investible funds as well as skills from both domestic and foreign sources

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Industrial Development Bank was set up to identify and promote projects with high value added to industry (A), to provide long-term loans and equity finance mainly to medium- and large-scale industrial enterprises (B), and to mobilise investible funds and skills both within Nigeria and from abroad (C). Since all three are genuine NIDB functions, D is the answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry (NBCI) was set up mainly to:

options.a: Provide long-term mortgage finance for housing
options.b: Help Nigerians obtain long-term funds to buy shares in enterprises affected by the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree of 1972
options.c: Grant loans to farmers and cooperative societies
options.d: Finance urban infrastructure such as motor parks, markets and drainage

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion (indigenisation) Decree of 1972 required foreign interests in many firms to be sold to Nigerians, but most Nigerians lacked the money to buy the shares. The NBCI was created to give indigenous investors access to long-term funds for this purpose. Option D describes the Urban Development Bank, option A describes housing finance institutions such as the FMBN, and option C describes the agricultural bank (NACB).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The NBCI provided equity capital provided that the promoters of a project were themselves providing at least ____ of the required funds, and its loans were repayable over about ____ years.

options.a: 10%; 10 to 14 years
options.b: 15%; 15 to 20 years

questions.explanation: The NBCI would take up equity in a project only if the promoters themselves provided at least 30% of the required funds, and its loans were usually repayable over about 12 to 15 years. These long repayment periods reflect its role as a development bank providing long-term finance. The figures in options A and B do not match these terms.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: What prompted the government to set up the Nigerian Agricultural and Cooperative Bank (NACB) was:

options.a: A desire to make the country self-sufficient in food production
options.b: A desire to provide a considerable proportion of the country's needed raw materials
options.c: A desire to enable the country to earn more foreign exchange through exports of agricultural produce

questions.explanation: The NACB was set up because government wanted to achieve self-sufficiency in food production (A), increase the domestic supply of raw materials for industry (B), and earn more foreign exchange from exports of agricultural produce (C). Food self-sufficiency is the best-known of these aims, but it was not the only one, so D is the best answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Urban Development Bank of Nigeria (UDBN) came on board the Nigerian financial scene in the:
questions.explanation: The Urban Development Bank of Nigeria was established by Decree 51 of 1992, so it came on the scene in the 1990s. It was created to finance urban infrastructure that conventional banks would not fund. Options A and C give the wrong decade.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the purposes the government specified when it set up the Bank of Industry (BOI) from the merger of the NIDB, the NBCI and NERFUND?

options.a: To act as lender of last resort to the deposit money banks
options.b: To help in the revitalization of the nation's ailing industries through the pumping of fresh funds and ideas
options.c: To help modernize, expand and diversify existing enterprises that are not yet moribund
options.d: To help improve the productive capacity of the economy through the empowerment of small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs)

questions.explanation: Acting as lender of last resort to deposit money banks is a function of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of a development finance institution like the BOI. The government set up the BOI to revive ailing industries with fresh funds and ideas (B), to help existing enterprises modernize, expand and diversify (C), and to boost the economy's productive capacity by empowering SMEs (D). So B, C and D are all genuine BOI purposes.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The need for the Peoples Bank of Nigeria (PBN) arose because the category of people to whom loans were to be granted under the PBN arrangement

options.a: Could not afford collateral security
options.b: Could not afford the high interest rates charged by the DMBs
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: The PBN was created for the rural poor and the urban poor, who were shut out of ordinary bank credit for two reasons: they had no collateral security to pledge, and they could not bear the high interest rates charged by deposit money banks. That is why the PBN lent without collateral and without interest. Options A and B are each only half of the reason, so C is the best answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Community banks in Nigeria performed basically the same functions as commercial banks. The main differences between a community bank and a commercial bank were that

options.a: A community bank was limited to providing financial services to the community where it was located
options.b: A community bank could not deal in foreign exchange transactions without express approval
options.c: A community bank was not admitted into the clearing house system

questions.explanation: Community banks took deposits and granted credit just like commercial banks, but with three restrictions. Their operations were confined to the community where they were located, they could not deal in foreign exchange without express approval, and they were not admitted into the clearing house. Since A, B and C are each true, D is the correct choice.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the community banking system, which body was given the immediate supervision of community banks and was meant to keep a fund from which they could borrow in times of crisis?

options.a: Bank of Industry (BOI)
options.b: National Board for Community Banks (NBCB)

questions.explanation: The National Board for Community Banks was set up to monitor, inspect and supervise community banks, and it was to maintain a fund, built from government contributions, gifts and donations, that the banks could draw on in difficult times. The BOI (A) is a development bank for industry, the FMBN (C) deals with housing finance, and the SEC (D) regulates the capital market, so none of them supervised community banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the Community Banks Decree of 1992, the minimum paid-up capital of a community bank was _________. Before community banks were converted into microfinance banks, this minimum had been raised to __________.
questions.explanation: Community banks started with a modest minimum paid-up capital of N250,000, in line with their role of serving small savers and borrowers in local communities. As weak capital became a problem, the CBN later raised the minimum to N5 million. Option A has the right starting figure but a later figure that is far too high, and option B gets both figures wrong.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In December of which year did the CBN launch the policy under which community banks were to transform, and into what type of institution?

options.a: 2005; Microfinance banks
options.b: 2008; Bank of Industry

questions.explanation: The CBN launched its Microfinance Policy, Regulatory and Supervisory Framework in December 2005, and under it existing community banks were to convert into microfinance banks once they met the new capital and other requirements. Bureaux de change (C) deal only in buying and selling foreign currency, and the Bank of Industry (B) is a development bank formed from earlier mergers, so neither is what community banks became.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an element of the 2005 Microfinance Policy Framework?

options.a: That state governments and local governments set aside not less than 1.0 percent of their annual budgets for microfinancing
options.b: That the federal government makes available 25 percent of its recurrent expenditure for microfinancing
options.c: That a Microfinance Development Fund be established
options.d: That a deposit insurance scheme be set up for microfinance banks to protect depositors

questions.explanation: Nothing in the framework asked the Federal Government to commit 25 percent of its recurrent expenditure to microfinance. The framework did ask state and local governments to set aside at least 1 percent of their annual budgets for on-lending through microfinance banks (A), and it provided for a Microfinance Development Fund (C) and deposit insurance for microfinance banks (D).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the 2005 microfinance policy framework, microfinance banks were to be of two types. These are

options.a: Unit microfinance bank and State microfinance bank
options.b: Regional microfinance bank and State microfinance bank
options.c: Provincial microfinance bank and Unit microfinance bank
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: The 2005 framework created two categories: the unit microfinance bank, with a lower minimum capital, and the state microfinance bank, with a higher one. Regional (B) and provincial (C) microfinance banks were not categories under that framework, and D is wrong because A is correct.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The advantages of bringing microfinance institutions under the supervisory purview of the CBN include that

options.a: It enhances monetary stability
options.b: It expands the financial infrastructure to meet the financial needs of micro-enterprises
options.c: It promotes linkages between universal banks or DMBs, the development banks and the microfinance institutions
options.d: All of the above are correct

questions.explanation: Bringing microfinance institutions under CBN supervision supports monetary stability, because more of the financial activity in the economy comes within the CBN's oversight. It also expands the financial infrastructure serving micro, small and medium enterprises and links universal banks, development banks and microfinance banks together. Each of A, B and C is a real advantage, so D is the best answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the 2005 microfinance policy, which of the following was NOT one of the government's expectations of microfinance banks?

options.a: To provide diversified, affordable and dependable financial services to the active poor in a competitive manner
options.b: To mobilize savings for intermediation and create employment opportunities
options.c: To finance the large-scale industrial projects of multinational companies
options.d: To facilitate payment services such as salaries, gratuities and pensions for the various tiers of government

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks are meant to serve the economically active poor and micro and small enterprises, not to fund big industrial projects for multinationals, which need large long-term finance from commercial and development banks. Providing affordable services to the active poor (A), mobilizing savings and creating jobs (B), and handling payments such as salaries and pensions for governments (D) were all expected of them.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was one of the reasons for setting up the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) in 1988?

options.a: To take over the issue of currency notes and coins from the CBN
options.b: To act as banker to the Federal Government in place of the CBN
options.c: To complement the supervisory work of the CBN as the number of banks grew after financial liberalization
options.d: To fix the lending rates charged by all deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Liberalization in the late 1980s led to a sharp rise in the number of banks, which made supervision much harder for the CBN alone, so the NDIC was created partly to share that oversight work. Issuing currency (A) and acting as banker to the government (B) remain CBN functions, and the NDIC does not fix banks' lending rates (D).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the purposes for setting up the NDIC?

options.a: To protect depositors, especially small depositors, in times of bank failures
options.b: To prevent the government from losing its deposits with the banks
options.c: To prevent banks from failing by coming to their aid as soon as they start to experience difficulties
options.d: In case some banks do fail, to reduce the economic dislocations and disruptions that such failure might cause

questions.explanation: The NDIC was set up to protect depositors, especially small ones (A), to help prevent banks from failing by assisting them early (C), and to reduce the disruption caused when banks do fail (D). Protecting the government's own deposits was not one of its purposes, so B is the odd one out.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which statement about the deposit insurance scheme run by the NDIC is correct?

options.a: It guarantees that no insured bank in Nigeria will ever fail
options.b: It protects only the shareholders of insured banks
options.c: It protects depositors and also helps prevent a massive loss of confidence in the banking system
options.d: It removes the need for the CBN to supervise banks

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance pays depositors up to a set limit when a bank fails, and because people know their money is protected, they are less likely to panic and run on the banks. It cannot guarantee that no bank will fail (A), it is designed for depositors rather than shareholders (B), and the CBN still supervises banks alongside the NDIC (D).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which statement best describes the working relationship between the NDIC and the CBN?

options.a: The NDIC supervises the CBN and can revoke its licence
options.b: They work closely together, sometimes examining banks jointly and sharing reports of their examinations
options.c: The CBN has no role in supervising banks that are insured by the NDIC
options.d: The NDIC issues currency on behalf of the CBN

questions.explanation: The NDIC and the CBN share responsibility for supervising banks, so they carry out joint examinations, set up joint committees for problem banks, and exchange examination reports and other information. The NDIC does not supervise the CBN (A), the CBN remains a main supervisor of insured banks (C), and only the CBN issues currency (D).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the flat-rate deposit insurance scheme introduced by the NDIC Decree of 1988, each insured bank was expected to pay _______ of its total deposit liabilities as annual premium to the NDIC.
questions.explanation: When deposit insurance started, every insured bank paid the same annual premium of 15/16 of one percent of its total deposit liabilities. Banks complained that this was too high and that a uniform rate ignored differences in risk. Rates of 5 percent (A) or 2 percent (B) would be far heavier, and 10/16 of one percent (D) is not the rate that was set.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In case of failure of a deposit money bank, each depositor used to be entitled to a maximum of ________ out of his deposit in the first instance. This figure was later raised to _______ by the year 2010.

options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: When the scheme began, the NDIC paid each depositor of a failed bank up to N50,000 in the first instance, with more paid later on a pro-rata basis as the bank's assets were sold. After complaints that this was too small, the cover was raised in stages and reached N500,000 by 2010; it has been raised again since then. The pairs in A and B do not match these figures.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: According to the decree setting up the NDIC, a bank is regarded as sick (distressed) and may seek NDIC assistance when _______

options.a: It cannot meet its obligations to its depositors/creditors as and when due
options.b: It has accumulated losses that have eroded or are threatening to erode shareholders' funds

questions.explanation: A bank is treated as sick if it cannot meet its obligations to depositors and creditors as they fall due, or if accumulated losses have eroded, or threaten to erode, its shareholders' funds. Either condition qualifies a bank for NDIC assistance, so C is correct; choosing only A or only B leaves one of them out.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The NDIC in its supervisory oversight is concerned with three principal things about deposit money banks, which are

options.a: Capital adequacy, loan collateralization and liquidity ratio
options.b: Cash ratio, loan concentration and capital adequacy
options.c: Loan collateralization, liquidity ratio and capital adequacy
options.d: Capital adequacy, loan concentration and liquidity ratio

questions.explanation: In its supervision, the NDIC pays most attention to capital adequacy (the cushion that absorbs losses), loan concentration (how much risk is tied to a few borrowers) and the liquidity ratio (the ability to meet daily obligations). Options A and C include loan collateralization and option B includes the cash ratio, which are not among the three principal concerns.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: That the capital adequacy ratio is 1:10 means

options.a: That N1 of loans can only be made when there is N10 of capital
options.b: That N1 of capital can only support a maximum of N10 of loans
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: A capital adequacy ratio of 1:10 means capital must be at least one-tenth of loans, so every N1 of capital can support no more than N10 of loans. Option A turns the ratio upside down by requiring N10 of capital for every N1 of loans, so C, which accepts both, is also wrong.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the distress resolution options that the NDIC has applied to distressed banks?

options.a: Imposition of holding actions
options.b: Change of management
options.c: NDIC's assumption of control and management of a distressed bank
options.d: Making the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance buy equity in the distressed bank

questions.explanation: To deal with distressed banks, the NDIC has used holding actions such as restrictions on lending and deposit advertising (A), changes of management through interim boards (B), and taking over the control and management of a sick bank itself (C), with liquidation as the last resort. Making the CBN and the Federal Ministry of Finance buy equity in a distressed bank is not one of its resolution options, so D is the answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a criticism of the NDIC's existence and operations?

options.a: That a premium of 15/16 of one percent of a bank's deposit liabilities is too large
options.b: That the lack of NDIC offices in every state of the federation is not good
options.c: That the maximum payment of N50,000 in the first instance, in case of liquidation, is too small
options.d: That banks should be made to pay premium based on the kind of risk each bank subjects its own deposit liabilities to, rather than a uniform premium

questions.explanation: Critics argued that the 15/16 of one percent premium was too heavy (A), that the N50,000 payout was too small (C), and that premiums should be risk-based instead of uniform (D). The lack of NDIC offices in every state was not one of the criticisms raised, so B is the answer.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: What is the full meaning of FDI?

options.a: Federal Development Initiative
options.b: Federation Developmental Investment

questions.explanation: FDI stands for Foreign Direct Investment, which is investment by foreign firms or individuals that gives them a lasting ownership and control stake in businesses in another country, such as building a factory or buying a controlling share of a local company. It differs from foreign portfolio investment, where the investor only buys shares or bonds without control. Options A, B and C are not real expansions of the abbreviation.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The full name of NEXIM is

options.a: National Export and Import Bank
options.b: National Export and International Bank

questions.explanation: NEXIM is the Nigerian Export-Import Bank, a development finance institution that provides credit, guarantees and insurance to support Nigerian exporters and the import of essential inputs. Options A and B wrongly begin with "National", and option B also replaces "Import" with "International". Option D is not the name of any bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The acquisition of capital assets to enhance productivity is called

options.a: Capital appreciation
options.b: Capital formation

questions.explanation: Capital formation means adding to the stock of real capital assets such as machinery, buildings and equipment so that the economy can produce more, and banks support it by channelling savings into loans for investment. Option A, capital appreciation, is a rise in the value of an asset you already own. Option C, capital structure, is the mix of debt and equity a firm uses, and option D, capital rationing, is limiting investment because funds are scarce.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Community banks in Nigeria came into existence as a result of the

options.a: Community Banks Decree of 1946
options.b: Community Banks Decree No. 46 of 1946

questions.explanation: Community banks were given their legal framework by the Community Banks Decree No. 46 of 1992, to bring small-scale banking to rural communities and micro-entrepreneurs who were not served by the big banks. Options A and B wrongly date the law to 1946, long before community banking existed in Nigeria. Option D has the right year but the wrong decree number.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: _________ banks were designed mainly to take care of the urban poor and the rural masses in order to empower them, by making funds available to them in very small amounts.

options.a: Specialized banks
options.b: Specific banks

questions.explanation: Specialised banks are set up to serve a particular sector or group rather than the general public. In Nigeria, the People's Bank, community banks and microfinance banks make up the group of specialised banks aimed at the urban poor and rural dwellers, giving them access to very small loans. Options B, C and D are not recognised categories of banks; they are just similar-sounding words.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) was established in the year _____
questions.explanation: The NDIC was set up in 1988 by Decree No. 22 of that year to insure deposits and protect depositors in licensed banks, and it started operations in 1989. Options A and B are years before any deposit insurance agency existed in Nigeria. Option D, 1998, is a decade too late.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The NDIC in its supervisory oversight of banks is concerned with one of the following

options.a: fiscal policy
options.b: printing of money
options.c: monitoring the balance of payments of the Nigerian economy

questions.explanation: In supervising insured banks, the NDIC focuses on their soundness, especially capital adequacy, loan concentration and liquidity, because a bank must be able to pay depositors as their claims fall due. Option A, fiscal policy, is handled by the Federal Government. Options B and C, issuing currency and watching the balance of payments, are responsibilities of the CBN, not the NDIC.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: One of these is NOT a distress resolution option of the NDIC

options.a: imposition of holding actions
options.b: moral suasion

questions.explanation: When a bank is in distress, the NDIC working with the CBN can use options such as moral suasion (dialogue to persuade the owners and managers to change their practices), imposition of holding actions and change of management, so 'change of account' is the one that is not a resolution option. Option B is tempting because moral suasion is best known as a CBN monetary policy tool, but it is also used in dealing with sick banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act of 2006, the annual insurance premium paid to the NDIC by an insured deposit money bank could not exceed ____ of 1% of its total deposit liabilities.
questions.explanation: Under the NDIC Act of 2006, an insured deposit money bank paid an annual premium of not more than 15/16 of one per cent of its total deposit liabilities. These premiums build up the deposit insurance fund used to pay depositors when an insured bank fails. Options A, C and D are close-looking fractions, but none of them is the rate set by the law.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Recapitalization policy will enable commercial banks to

options.a: employ more qualified workers
options.b: open more branches
options.d: have a very strong capital base

questions.explanation: Recapitalisation requires banks to raise their minimum capital, giving them a stronger capital base to absorb losses, support bigger loans and protect depositors. Options A, B and C may happen as side effects in some banks, but they are not what the policy is designed to achieve.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The regulatory authority of the capital market in Nigeria is the

options.a: Central Bank
options.b: Securities and Exchange Commission

questions.explanation: The Securities and Exchange Commission is the apex regulator of the Nigerian capital market, registering securities, licensing market operators and protecting investors. Option A, the CBN, regulates banks and the money market, Option C, the NDIC, insures deposits and supervises banks alongside the CBN, and Option D, the stock exchange, is the market where securities are traded under SEC supervision.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The apex regulatory institution of the Nigerian capital market is

options.a: SEC
options.b: NDIC

questions.explanation: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is the apex regulator of the Nigerian capital market: it registers capital market operators, oversees the issue and trading of securities and protects investors. The CBN (C) is the apex authority over banks and the money market, not the capital market. NDIC (B) insures bank deposits, and NAICOM (D) regulates the insurance industry.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation performs the following functions except

options.a: To strengthen the supervisory role of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: Insuring bank deposits against failure
options.c: To implement distress resolution mechanisms in the event of bank failure
options.d: To regulate money supply in the economy

questions.explanation: Regulating the money supply is a monetary policy job of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of NDIC. NDIC insures bank deposits (B), helps to resolve distressed and failed banks (C), and examines insured banks alongside the CBN, which strengthens the CBN's supervisory role (A).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which law, enacted in 2020, replaced the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act of 1991 as the main law regulating banks and other financial institutions in Nigeria?

options.a: The Companies and Allied Matters Act 1990
options.b: The Central Bank of Nigeria Act 2007
options.d: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020

questions.explanation: BOFIA 2020 repealed and replaced the 1991 law and is now the principal law on the licensing, regulation and supervision of banks and other financial institutions. The CBN Act 2007 (option B) deals with the central bank itself, the Companies and Allied Matters Act (option A) governs companies in general, and the 1958 banking ordinance (option C) was a colonial-era law replaced long ago.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Merchant banks are often described as 'wholesale bankers', while commercial banks are called 'retail bankers'. This is because merchant banks:

options.a: mobilise funds mainly from firms and institutions in large amounts and tailor their services to businesses
options.b: sell goods at wholesale prices to traders, distributors and market women
options.c: collect most of their deposits from individuals and households through many branches
options.d: deal only in foreign currencies and never in naira deposits or loans

questions.explanation: Merchant banks deal mainly with corporate and institutional customers, taking large deposits and granting bulkier, often medium-term loans, which is why they are called wholesale bankers. Commercial banks, by contrast, collect funds from all strata of society, which is what option C describes. Option B confuses banking with trading in goods, and option D is wrong because merchant banks also deal in naira.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A merchant bank buys a machine needed by a manufacturing firm and rents it to the firm in return for agreed periodic payments. This service is known as:

options.a: Issuing house service
options.b: A bankers' acceptance

questions.explanation: In equipment leasing, the bank owns the asset and the firm uses it in exchange for rentals, which helps firms that cannot afford to buy expensive machinery outright. Bill discounting (option D) involves buying a bill for less than its face value, an issuing house service (option A) helps a company sell its shares to the public, and a bankers' acceptance (option B) is a bill that a bank has agreed to pay.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When a merchant bank helps a company to sell its new shares and other securities to the public, it is acting as:

options.a: A bureau de change
options.b: An issuing house

questions.explanation: An issuing house manages the offer of a company's shares or other securities to the investing public, which is one of the main services of merchant banks. A discount house (option D) deals in short-term government securities in the money market, a clearing house (option C) settles cheques and other claims between banks, and a bureau de change (option A) deals in foreign currency for small users.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In the Nigerian banking reforms of 2004-2005, 'bank consolidation' mainly involved:

options.a: banks merging with or acquiring one another and raising fresh capital to meet a much higher minimum capital requirement
options.b: the Central Bank of Nigeria taking over the ownership and day-to-day management of all commercial banks in the country
options.c: splitting the large banks into many smaller banks so as to increase competition in the banking industry
options.d: converting all commercial and merchant banks into microfinance banks serving rural communities

questions.explanation: Consolidation strengthens a banking system by creating fewer, bigger and better-capitalised banks, mainly through mergers, acquisitions and fresh capital raised from investors. In Nigeria it reduced the number of banks from 89 to 25 by the end of 2005. Options B, C and D describe nationalisation, break-up and conversion, none of which was the aim of consolidation.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the bank consolidation programme announced by the CBN in July 2004, every Nigerian bank was required to have minimum shareholders' funds of how much by 31 December 2005?

options.a: N25 billion
options.b: N5 billion

questions.explanation: The 2004 consolidation programme raised the minimum capital of banks from N2 billion to N25 billion, with a compliance deadline of 31 December 2005. Option D was the old requirement that the reform replaced, while options B and C were not the figure set in 2004. Banks met the new level mainly through mergers, acquisitions and public offers, and those that could not lost their licences.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A major reason for setting up development banks in Nigeria is that deposit money banks:

options.a: prefer short-term lending because their deposits are mostly short-term, leaving a gap in long-term finance
options.b: are not allowed by law to grant any loans or overdrafts to business customers
options.c: lend mainly long-term to agriculture and housing, leaving no funds for trade
options.d: charge no interest on their loans and so cannot cover their operating costs

questions.explanation: Because most of their deposits can be withdrawn at short notice, deposit money banks concentrate on short- and medium-term lending, yet a developing economy needs long-term finance for industry, agriculture and infrastructure. Development banks are set up to fill this gap. Option C reverses the real situation, while options B and D are simply untrue of deposit money banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The government set up the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria because conventional banks found housing finance unattractive, even though housing is vital to the economy. Which rationale for development banks does this illustrate?

options.a: Financing projects that are socially desirable but commercially unprofitable
options.b: Mobilising short-term funds for trading in the money market
options.c: Issuing currency on behalf of the Federal Government
options.d: Acting as lender of last resort to the deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Development banks are set up to finance projects that benefit society but promise little profit, and housing is a classic example, which is why the government created the FMBN. The other rationales include filling the long-term finance gap, channelling funds from international development banks to local investors, and promoting catalyst sectors like agriculture. Options D and C are central bank functions, and option B is not a reason for setting up development banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Nigerian Industrial Development Bank (NIDB) was set up mainly to:

options.a: finance urban infrastructure such as motor parks, markets and drainage systems
options.b: give small interest-free loans without collateral to petty traders and the rural poor
options.c: provide long-term loans and equity finance to medium- and large-scale industrial enterprises
options.d: grant mortgage loans to individuals building owner-occupier houses

questions.explanation: The NIDB's job was to identify and promote industrial projects with high value added, mobilise funds and skills from home and abroad, and provide long-term loans and equity to industrial firms, mostly medium and large ones. Option B describes the Peoples Bank of Nigeria, option A the Urban Development Bank of Nigeria, and option D the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the services the NIDB provided to promote medium- and large-scale industries in Nigeria?

options.a: Mobilising funds from bodies like the World Bank for on-lending to Nigerian entrepreneurs
options.b: Accepting current account deposits from the general public and issuing cheque books
options.c: Taking up equity shares in large industrial enterprises
options.d: Providing long-term loans to medium and large industrial enterprises

questions.explanation: As a development bank, the NIDB did not run current accounts for the public; that is a deposit money bank activity. Its services included long-term loans (option D), equity participation (option C), mobilising foreign funds from multilateral lenders such as the World Bank and the African Development Bank (option A), and managerial and technical help to firms.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: How did the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry (NBCI) mainly differ from the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank (NIDB)?

options.a: NBCI focused on large-scale industries, while NIDB was set up to help small enterprises and Nigerians buy into businesses under indigenisation.
options.b: NBCI was a foreign-owned commercial bank taking public deposits, while NIDB was a government-owned microfinance bank.
options.c: NBCI focused on small and medium enterprises and on helping Nigerians buy into businesses under indigenisation, while NIDB focused on medium and large industries.
options.d: NBCI financed only agricultural projects in rural areas, while NIDB financed only housing projects in the cities.

questions.explanation: The NBCI was created after the indigenisation decree of 1972 to give Nigerians long-term funds to acquire shares in businesses, with its focus on small and medium enterprises. The NIDB, on the other hand, concentrated on medium- and large-scale industrial projects. Option A swaps the two banks' roles, and options D and B misdescribe both institutions.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an objective for setting up the Nigerian Agricultural and Cooperative Bank (NACB)?

options.a: Financing urban mass transit and motor parks in state capitals
options.b: Increasing the domestic supply of agricultural raw materials for industry
options.c: Increasing the production of export crops to earn foreign exchange

questions.explanation: Financing urban transport facilities was the work of the Urban Development Bank of Nigeria, not the agricultural bank. The NACB was set up to provide finance for agriculture so that Nigeria could feed itself (option D), supply raw materials to its industries (option B), and earn foreign exchange from exported crops (option C).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Urban Development Bank of Nigeria (UDBN), set up in 1992, was established mainly to:

options.a: finance the building and rehabilitation of urban infrastructure such as markets, motor parks and mass transit
options.b: finance farmers and cooperative societies in rural areas
options.c: regulate and supervise community banks across the country
options.d: provide long-term loans for owner-occupier houses under the National Housing Fund

questions.explanation: The UDBN was created to fill the gap left by conventional banks in financing urban infrastructure such as markets, motor parks, mass transit, drainage and waste disposal, and to give technical help to state and local governments on such projects. Option B describes agricultural finance, option C was the role of the National Board for Community Banks, and option D describes the housing role of the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When the National Housing Fund (NHF) scheme was set up in 1992, which institution was given the responsibility of managing the Fund?

options.a: The Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria
options.d: The Urban Development Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The NHF pooled contributions from workers and investments from banks and insurance companies to provide long-term housing finance, and the FMBN was made its manager. This gave the FMBN a steady pool of funds, which it had previously lacked. The CBN (option A) and the NDIC (option C) are banking regulators, and the UDBN (option D) finances urban infrastructure rather than housing loans.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: After primary mortgage institutions (PMIs) were introduced in 1989, how was housing finance in Nigeria shared between the PMIs and the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN)?

options.a: PMIs and FMBN were both stopped from granting any housing loans to the public.
options.b: PMIs lent to the public at the retail level, while FMBN acted as the apex body providing wholesale funds and oversight.
options.c: PMIs financed only urban roads and bridges, while FMBN financed only farm buildings.
options.d: FMBN lent directly to every home buyer, while PMIs only supervised and regulated the FMBN.

questions.explanation: Primary mortgage institutions mobilise savings and grant loans to individuals who want to buy, build or renovate homes, which is retail housing finance. The FMBN became the apex mortgage institution, lending to PMIs and, for a time, overseeing them. Option D reverses the roles, and options C and A misstate what both institutions do.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which development in the 1990s mainly led the Federal Government to merge some development banks in the early 2000s?

options.a: The transfer of all development banking functions to the Nigerian Stock Exchange
options.b: The banks had become so profitable that government wanted to share out their profits
options.c: A court ruling that development banks could no longer lend to industry or agriculture
options.d: Widespread loan defaults and financial distress that left the institutions weak

questions.explanation: During the banking distress of the 1990s, many borrowers of the development banks defaulted, partly because the rising naira cost of imported inputs crippled their businesses, and the banks in turn struggled to repay funds borrowed from international lenders. The government responded by merging the weak institutions into stronger ones, such as the Bank of Industry. Options B, C and A are not what happened.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Nigerian Agricultural Cooperative and Rural Development Bank (NACRDB), formed in 2000, was a merger of the Nigerian Agricultural and Cooperative Bank (NACB) with:

options.a: the Peoples Bank of Nigeria and the Family Economic Advancement Programme (FEAP)
options.b: the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank and the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry
options.c: the National Economic Reconstruction Fund and the Nigerian Export-Import Bank
options.d: the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria and the Urban Development Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The NACRDB brought together three bodies serving rural and low-income borrowers: the NACB, the Peoples Bank of Nigeria and the FEAP. The NIDB and NBCI (option B) were merged with NERFUND to form the Bank of Industry, so options B and C mix up the two mergers. Option D names housing and urban development institutions that were not part of it.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the main purpose of the Bank of Industry (BOI)?

options.a: Providing long-term loans and equity finance to revive, expand and modernise industrial enterprises, including SMEs
options.b: Financing only agricultural cooperatives and individual farmers in rural areas
options.c: Issuing treasury bills and other short-term securities on behalf of the Federal Government
options.d: Regulating and supervising the deposit money banks on behalf of the Federal Government

questions.explanation: The BOI was set up to improve the productive capacity of the economy by giving industrial firms, especially small and medium enterprises, long-term funds in the form of loans and equity, and by reviving and modernising ailing but viable industries. Supervising banks (option D) and issuing treasury bills for the government (option C) are CBN functions, and agricultural finance (option B) was handled by the agricultural development bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Specialised banks such as the Peoples Bank of Nigeria and community banks were set up mainly because:

options.a: large corporations needed banks that could lend them bigger sums in foreign currency
options.b: the Central Bank of Nigeria wanted to stop deposit money banks from operating in cities
options.c: the government wanted banks that would invest mainly in shares on the stock exchange
options.d: the rural poor and small urban entrepreneurs could not get credit from conventional banks, lacking collateral and nearby branches

questions.explanation: In the late 1980s many rural areas had no bank branches, and the poor and micro-entrepreneurs who did live near banks could not meet the collateral demands or afford the interest charged. The Peoples Bank and community banks were created to bring small loans and savings facilities to these groups. Options A, B and C describe goals that have nothing to do with these grassroots banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Peoples Bank of Nigeria granted small loans without collateral. How did it mainly try to ensure that its loans were repaid?

options.a: By requiring each borrower to obtain a repayment guarantee from a commercial bank
options.b: By lending to members of recognised trade or business groups, so that group members pressured one another to repay
options.c: By holding the borrowers' land title documents until the loans were fully repaid
options.d: By deducting repayments directly from borrowers' salaries through their employers

questions.explanation: The Peoples Bank lent to people who belonged to recognised trade or business groups, and if one member defaulted, others in the group could not get loans, so members monitored and pressured each other. This peer pressure took the place of collateral. Options C and A are forms of security that the bank's poor customers could not provide, and option D would not work for traders and artisans who earned no salaries.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a challenge faced by the Peoples Bank of Nigeria?

options.a: A shortage of skilled managerial staff to run its many offices
options.b: The high cost of administering many small loans spread across the country
options.c: Heavy dependence on government funding for its operations
options.d: Excessive demand for its loans by large multinational companies

questions.explanation: The Peoples Bank served the rural poor and petty traders, not large multinationals, so option D was never one of its problems. It did struggle with the cost of managing many tiny loans (option B), a lack of skilled managers (option A) and reliance on government funds (option C), as well as loan defaults and losses on deposits it had placed with failed banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was a main difference between a community bank and a commercial bank in Nigeria?

options.a: A community bank could accept deposits but was not allowed to grant credit.
options.b: A community bank dealt mainly in foreign exchange for importers and exporters.
options.c: A community bank was owned and managed directly by the Central Bank of Nigeria.
options.d: A community bank's operations were limited to the community in which it was located.

questions.explanation: A community bank performed most of the same basic functions as a commercial bank, but it served only the community where it was located and could not deal in foreign exchange without CBN approval. Option A is wrong because community banks did grant credit to their customers, option C is wrong because they were owned by the community rather than the CBN, and option B reverses their restriction on foreign exchange business.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a factor in the collapse of many community banks in Nigeria in the 1990s?

options.a: An excessively large capital base that made them difficult to manage
options.b: Inflation and the rising cost of doing business
options.c: High rates of loan default by their customers
options.d: Loss of funds they had placed with distressed deposit money banks

questions.explanation: Community banks started with very small capital, so an oversized capital base was never their problem. Many failed because the deposit money banks holding their funds became distressed (option D), because customers hit by a harsh economy defaulted on their loans (option C), and because inflation and high operating costs squeezed them (option B).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the Microfinance Policy launched by the CBN in December 2005, what were existing community banks required to do?

options.a: Become discount houses dealing in treasury bills in the money market
options.b: Convert to microfinance banks within 24 months after meeting the new capital and other requirements
options.c: Close down permanently and refund all their depositors' money
options.d: Merge with the Bank of Industry within 12 months to form a single development bank

questions.explanation: The 2005 policy required licensed community banks to transform into microfinance banks within 24 months, mainly by raising their shareholders' funds to the new minimum of N20 million. The policy also brought informal microfinance providers under CBN supervision and introduced measures such as deposit insurance for microfinance banks and a Microfinance Development Fund. Options D, A and C were not part of the policy.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the CBN's 2005 Microfinance Policy, microfinance banks were expected mainly to:

options.a: underwrite large government bond issues in the capital market
options.b: provide diversified, affordable and dependable financial services to the economically active poor
options.c: finance the foreign trade of large multinational corporations
options.d: issue the national currency in rural areas on behalf of the CBN

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks were meant to serve the active poor and micro-entrepreneurs who lacked access to regular banks, by mobilising their savings, giving them small loans, creating jobs and raising household incomes. They were also to serve as channels for government micro-credit programmes. Options C and A describe large corporate and capital market business, and option D is a function reserved for the CBN.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the CBN's 2005 Microfinance Policy framework, how did a unit microfinance bank differ from a state microfinance bank?

options.a: A unit MFB could only grant loans, while a state MFB could only accept deposits.
options.b: A unit MFB needed minimum capital of N20 million, while a state MFB needed N1 billion.
options.c: A unit MFB needed minimum capital of N1 billion, while a state MFB needed N20 million.
options.d: A unit MFB was owned by the Federal Government, while a state MFB was owned by a state government.

questions.explanation: The 2005 framework created two categories: the smaller unit MFB, with minimum paid-up capital of N20 million, and the larger state MFB, serving a whole state, which needed N1 billion. Option C reverses the figures, option D is wrong because the names refer to the scope of operation rather than government ownership, and option A is wrong because both types could take deposits and grant loans. These capital levels applied under the 2005 framework and have since been reviewed.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason for setting up the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)?

options.a: To protect depositors, especially small depositors, when a bank fails
options.b: To guarantee that the shareholders of a failed bank get back their full investment
options.c: To complement the CBN's supervision as the number of banks grew rapidly after liberalisation
options.d: To ensure the orderly exit of failing banks without causing panic in the banking system

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance protects depositors, not shareholders: the owners of a failed bank bear the loss of their capital, and the NDIC can even enforce the liability of shareholders and directors of failed banks. Options A, C and D are all genuine reasons for the NDIC: the boom in bank numbers after deregulation stretched the CBN's supervisory capacity, small depositors needed protection, and failing banks had to exit without triggering a loss of confidence in the whole system.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The establishment of the NDIC in 1988 was closely linked to which development in Nigerian banking?

options.a: The introduction of the naira and kobo as Nigeria's decimal currency
options.b: The deregulation of banking under the Structural Adjustment Programme, which led to a rapid increase in the number of banks
options.c: The banking consolidation of 2004 to 2005, which required banks to raise their capital base to N25 billion
options.d: The replacement of the West African Currency Board by the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: From 1986 the Structural Adjustment Programme liberalised the economy and lowered the barriers to entry into banking, so the number of banks rose sharply. This increased the supervisory burden on the CBN and the risk of bank failures, which led to the creation of the NDIC to help supervise banks and protect depositors. Option C came much later, while options D and A relate to the late 1950s and 1973 respectively.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In the NDIC's supervision of banks, 'off-site surveillance' refers to:

options.a: inviting a bank's owners and managers for dialogue to persuade them to drop unhealthy practices
options.b: sending examiners to a bank's premises to inspect its books, records and operations
options.c: selling off a failed bank's assets and paying its insured depositors
options.d: analysing the periodic returns that banks submit to check whether they are meeting prudential requirements

questions.explanation: Off-site surveillance is done away from the bank: banks send in regular returns on their assets, liabilities, loans and other items, and the NDIC analyses them for signs of weakness in capital, liquidity or loan quality. Option B describes on-site examination, which the NDIC uses to confirm that the returns are accurate. Option A is moral suasion and option C is liquidation, which are distress resolution steps rather than routine surveillance.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually part of the 'holding actions' that the CBN and NDIC impose on a distressed bank?

options.a: Opening new branches and advertising aggressively for more deposits
options.b: Injecting fresh capital funds into the bank
options.c: Stopping the granting of fresh loans and advances
options.d: Embarking on aggressive recovery of debts owed to the bank

questions.explanation: Holding actions place a distressed bank under close supervision and restrictions so that it can restructure itself and stop its position from getting worse. Such a bank is typically told to stop advertising for deposits without approval, stop new lending and new capital projects, recover its debts aggressively and bring in fresh capital, so options B, C and D are all holding actions. Expanding through new branches and deposit campaigns, as in option A, is exactly what holding actions are meant to restrain.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When the NDIC assumes control and management of a distressed bank, the main purpose is to:

options.a: run the bank, usually through an interim management board, and work out a restructuring plan, selling or liquidating it if a turnaround is too costly
options.b: pay all depositors their deposits in full immediately and close the bank down on the same day
options.c: hand the bank straight back to its existing directors and management, without any changes to how it is run
options.d: convert the bank permanently into a government-owned bank run by civil servants, with no plan to sell it

questions.explanation: Assuming control and management is a rescue step: the NDIC takes over the running of the sick bank, usually by appointing an interim management board, to find and carry out a suitable restructuring strategy. If the funds needed for a turnaround are too large, the bank may be put up for sale, and one that finds no buyer may be liquidated. Option B is wrong because closure is the last resort, and even then insured depositors are paid only up to the insured limit; options C and D are not what the takeover aims at.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In the liquidation of a failed insured bank in Nigeria, the NDIC's role is mainly to:

options.a: act as liquidator, paying insured depositors up to the insured limit and sharing the proceeds of the bank's assets among depositors and other creditors
options.b: refund the shareholders' capital in full first, before any depositor or other creditor of the bank is paid
options.c: take over the bank's shares and keep running it as a going concern, with the same staff, for as long as it can
options.d: transfer all the bank's remaining deposits to the CBN, to be kept as part of government revenue

questions.explanation: Liquidation ends a bank's life.
