Once the CBN revokes the licence, the NDIC acts as liquidator: it pays each insured depositor up to the insured limit, then realises the bank's assets and pays depositors and other creditors further sums on a pro-rata basis from the proceeds. Option B reverses the order, because shareholders are the last to receive anything, option C describes a rescue rather than liquidation, and option D is not how liquidation works.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which statement about liquidation as a distress resolution option for banks in Nigeria is correct?

options.a: It is carried out by the NDIC alone, without any role for the CBN
options.b: It is the first step the NDIC takes as soon as a bank shows any sign of weakness
options.c: It guarantees every depositor full repayment of all deposits, whatever their size
options.d: It is usually the last option, used when rescue measures have failed or the bank cannot be saved

questions.explanation: Liquidation is the last resort: the authorities first try options such as moral suasion, holding actions and change of management, and they liquidate only when the bank cannot be saved. A useful side effect is that it warns other bank owners that they can lose their investment if they run their banks badly. Option A is wrong because the licence is revoked by the CBN before the NDIC acts as liquidator, and option C is wrong because insured cover has a limit, with any further payment depending on what the bank's assets fetch.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A distress resolution option in which the CBN and NDIC invite the owners and management of a sick bank for dialogue, to persuade them to drop unhealthy practices and adopt sound banking, is known as:

options.a: moral suasion
options.b: imposition of holding actions

questions.explanation: Moral suasion relies on persuasion rather than force: the regulators meet the owners and managers of the troubled bank and urge them to change their ways and adopt healthy banking practices. Holding actions in option B go further by placing formal restrictions on the bank, such as stopping new loans. Liquidation in option C closes the bank, and purchase and assumption in option D involves a healthy bank taking over the failing bank's assets and deposits.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In a 'purchase and assumption' transaction used to resolve a failing bank:

options.a: regulators hold talks with the failing bank's owners and managers to persuade them to change their practices
options.b: the failing bank is placed under restrictions, such as not granting fresh loans, while it restructures itself
options.c: the failing bank is closed, insured depositors are paid off by the NDIC and the bank's assets are sold piecemeal
options.d: a healthy bank buys all or part of the failing bank's assets and takes over all or part of its liabilities, especially its deposits

questions.explanation: As the name suggests, a healthy institution purchases assets of the failing bank and assumes its liabilities, so depositors move to a sound bank without the disruption of a closure and payoff. Option B describes holding actions, option A describes moral suasion and option C describes liquidation.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In the early years of Nigeria's deposit insurance scheme, which of the following was a criticism raised by banks against the NDIC?

options.a: The maximum amount paid to each depositor of a failed bank was far too generous and encouraged careless banking
options.b: The NDIC had taken over from the CBN the power to issue currency notes and coins
options.c: The flat annual premium of 15/16 of one per cent of deposit liabilities was too heavy for many banks and ignored differences in risk between banks
options.d: Membership of the scheme was voluntary, so too few banks joined and the insurance fund stayed small

questions.explanation: When the scheme started, every insured bank paid the same annual premium of 15/16 of one per cent of its deposit liabilities. Banks complained that this was too heavy, since some earned profits below that figure, and many argued for a risk-based premium instead. Option A reverses the real complaint, which was that the N50,000 cover was too small, option D also reverses it, since critics wanted the scheme to be optional for big banks, and option B is false.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Critics once argued that big, strong banks should be allowed to stay out of Nigeria's deposit insurance scheme. How did the NDIC respond?

options.a: It argued that only big banks needed deposit insurance, so small banks should leave the scheme
options.b: It argued that big banks can also fail, and that their participation helps to keep premiums affordable for smaller, weaker banks
options.c: It agreed with the critics and exempted all big banks from paying any premium
options.d: It said that big banks were already insured directly by the CBN instead

questions.explanation: The NDIC pointed to experience in other countries, where large as well as small banks had failed, so no bank could simply be assumed safe. It also argued that including the big banks spreads the cost of the scheme and effectively subsidises the premium for small and weak banks, which are its most likely beneficiaries. Options A, C and D do not reflect the NDIC's position; membership remained compulsory for licensed deposit money banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Some critics asked the NDIC to exclude banks' investments in government securities from the items it insured. What was the NDIC's reply?

options.a: Excluding them would make the insurance cover for each depositor unlimited
options.b: Such investments are assets of the banks, not deposit liabilities, so they were never part of the insured deposits
options.c: Government securities were the main items covered by deposit insurance, so they could not be excluded
options.d: The CBN would insure banks' government securities in place of the NDIC

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance covers what a bank owes its depositors, which is a liability. Treasury bills and other government securities that a bank buys are assets it holds, so the NDIC replied that they had never been included in the deposit liabilities on which cover and premiums are based. Options A, C and D all miss this difference between a bank's assets and its deposit liabilities.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is an achievement commonly credited to the NDIC since it began operations?

options.a: Taking over from the CBN the issue of currency notes and coins and the conduct of monetary policy
options.b: Completely eliminating bank failures in Nigeria from the time it began operations
options.c: Helping to resolve distressed banks in an orderly way, for example by arranging rescues, sales or mergers and paying insured depositors
options.d: Abolishing deposit insurance premiums, so that insured banks no longer pay anything for the cover

questions.explanation: The NDIC's record includes helping some ailing banks back to health, arranging for others to be bought over or merged with healthier banks, and paying insured depositors when banks were closed, all of which softened the shock of bank failures. Option B overstates its record, since banks still failed, for instance during the distress of the 1990s. Option A is a CBN function and option D is false, because insured banks still pay premiums.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following roles confirms the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as the apex regulator of the Nigerian capital market?

options.a: Registering securities and capital market operators such as stockbrokers and issuing houses, supervising the exchange and protecting investors
options.b: Insuring the deposits of customers whose banks fail and paying them compensation up to a limit
options.c: Licensing and supervising insurance companies, insurance brokers and loss adjusters
options.d: Issuing the national currency, setting the Monetary Policy Rate and acting as banker to government

questions.explanation: The SEC regulates and develops the capital market: it registers securities offered to the public and the operators who deal in them, monitors the stock exchange to keep trading fair and orderly, and protects investors from fraud and misinformation. Option B is the work of the NDIC, option D belongs to the CBN, and option C is the job of the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Primary Mortgage Institutions (PMIs) in Nigeria are best described as institutions that:

options.a: mobilise savings and deposits from the public and grant loans to people to buy, build or improve homes
options.b: deal mainly in buying and selling foreign exchange for small users
options.c: provide wholesale refinancing to mortgage lenders and act as the apex mortgage institution
options.d: insure the deposits of bank customers in case their bank fails

questions.explanation: PMIs provide housing finance at the retail level: they take savings and deposits from the public and lend to individuals for buying, building or renovating houses, then monitor that the loans are used for that purpose. Option C describes the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria, which refinances PMIs, option B describes bureaux de change, and option D is the work of the NDIC.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Today, Primary Mortgage Institutions in Nigeria are licensed and supervised by the:

options.a: National Pension Commission
options.b: National Insurance Commission

questions.explanation: PMIs are deposit-taking institutions, so they fall under the CBN, which licenses and supervises them along with banks, microfinance banks and finance companies. Supervision passed to the CBN in the late 1990s, after widespread distress among PMIs. The SEC (option C) regulates the capital market, NAICOM (option B) regulates insurance, and PenCom (option A) regulates pensions.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In Nigerian banking law, the abbreviation BOFIA stands for:

options.a: Board of Financial Institutions Administration
options.b: Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act
options.c: Bank Owners and Financial Investors Association
options.d: Banking and Offshore Finance Inspection Authority

questions.explanation: BOFIA is the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, the main law under which the CBN licenses, regulates and supervises banks and other financial institutions in Nigeria. It was first enacted in 1991 and was replaced by a new BOFIA in 2020. Options C, D and A are made-up names; BOFIA is a law, not an association, authority or board.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a function of community banks in Nigeria, the forerunners of today's microfinance banks?

options.a: Providing credit facilities to small businesses and members of the community
options.b: Providing auxiliary banking services to their customers
options.c: Issuing the national currency and acting as banker to the Federal Government
options.d: Accepting savings, time and target deposits

questions.explanation: Issuing legal tender currency and acting as banker to the Federal Government are functions of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of community banks. Community banks were set up to take banking to the grassroots, so they accepted savings, time and target deposits, gave small loans and provided auxiliary services, which is why options D, A and B are genuine functions.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In the supervision of Nigerian banks by the CBN and NDIC, moral suasion refers to:

options.a: Selling treasury bills to banks to mop up excess liquidity
options.b: Requiring banks to lodge special deposits with the CBN above their normal reserves
options.c: Revoking the licence of a distressed bank and paying off its depositors
options.d: Using dialogue and persuasion to get the owners and managers of a bank to change unhealthy practices voluntarily

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is an informal tool: rather than issuing formal orders or sanctions, the authorities invite a bank's owners and management to discussions and persuade them to drop unhealthy ways of doing business. The same idea is used in monetary policy, where the CBN appeals to banks to lend in desired directions. Option C describes liquidation, while options B and A are special deposits and open market operations, which work through compulsory deposits or market transactions rather than persuasion.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Broadly, distress resolution for a sick bank in Nigeria involves which two basic options?

options.a: Open market operations or moral suasion
options.b: Rehabilitation of the bank or its liquidation
options.c: Converting the bank into a bureau de change or a discount house
options.d: Increasing the deposit insurance premium or reducing the cash reserve ratio

questions.explanation: When a bank becomes distressed, the authorities first try to rehabilitate it, for example through holding actions, a change of management or fresh capital, so that it returns to health. If the bank cannot be saved, the last option is liquidation, where it is closed and its assets are realised to pay depositors and creditors. Option A lists monetary policy tools, and options C and D are not recognised ways of resolving bank distress.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A bank attracted a corporate fixed deposit of N1,000,000.00 for 3 months at 12% per annum on a non-compound (simple interest) basis. How much will the bank pay the depositor at the end of the 3 months?
questions.explanation: Simple interest is P x R x T = N1,000,000 x 0.12 x 3/12 = N30,000, and at maturity the bank repays the principal plus interest, N1,030,000.00. Option C charges a full year's interest on a 3-month deposit, and option B treats the 3 months as 3 years. Option D is only the interest, not the total amount paid to the depositor.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Nigeria operates a branch banking system. This means that

options.a: each bank is allowed to operate only one office
options.b: banks may operate only in the state where they were registered
options.c: each branch of a bank is a separately owned company
options.d: a single bank runs many offices across the country, one of which serves as its head office

questions.explanation: Under branch banking, one bank operates a network of offices across the country under a single head office and a single legal identity. Option A describes unit banking, option B describes a restriction that does not apply to national banks in Nigeria, and option C is wrong because branches belong to the same bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the indigenisation policy of the 1970s, the Federal Government first acquired what share of the three big expatriate banks, a stake that was raised to 60% in 1976?
questions.explanation: Under the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion (Indigenisation) Decree, government took a 40% interest in the three big expatriate banks, later First Bank, Union Bank and UBA, and raised it to 60% in 1976. Options A, B and D do not match the stake first taken.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which service is regarded as the traditional function that marks merchant banks out from other financial institutions?

options.a: Accepting bills of exchange to finance the trade of others
options.b: Opening savings accounts for individuals

questions.explanation: Acceptance, putting the bank's name on bills of exchange so that others' trade can be financed, is the traditional and distinctive merchant banking function. Option B is retail banking, option C belongs to the central bank, and option D describes commercial banks, since merchant banks need few branches.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A merchant bank that helps a company raise capital from the public through an offer for subscription and advises it on getting a stock exchange quotation is providing

options.a: issuing house services
options.b: equipment leasing

questions.explanation: As an issuing house, a merchant bank guides companies through offers for subscription or sale, places their shares with the public and advises on stock exchange quotation. Option B is hiring out assets, option C is short-term trade finance through accepted bills, and option D is buying book debts.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes merchant banks from commercial banks in Nigeria?

options.a: Commercial banks are wholesale bankers, while merchant banks are retail bankers
options.b: Merchant banks rely on large rural branch networks, while commercial banks have few branches
options.c: Merchant banks issue currency, while commercial banks do not
options.d: Merchant banks are wholesale bankers dealing mainly with corporate and institutional clients, while commercial banks are retail bankers serving the general public

questions.explanation: Merchant banks deal in large sums for firms and institutions, mostly from a few urban offices, while commercial banks serve individuals and businesses of all sizes through wide branch networks. Option A reverses the roles, option B is wrong because it is commercial banks that have branches in rural areas, and option C is wrong because only the CBN issues currency.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The main justification for setting up development banks in developing countries is that they

options.a: provide short-term salary advances to workers
options.b: provide long-term finance to priority sectors whose projects are too large or slow to mature to attract conventional banks
options.c: issue currency and control the money supply
options.d: compete with commercial banks for current account deposits

questions.explanation: Development finance institutions fill gaps that ordinary banks leave, giving long-term loans to real sector and infrastructure projects with long gestation periods or very large funding needs. Option A is a deposit money bank service, option C is a central bank function, and option D is not their purpose.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Bank of Industry was formed through the merger of

options.a: the Nigerian Agricultural and Co-operative Bank, the People's Bank and the Family Economic Advancement Programme
options.b: the Federal Mortgage Bank, the Nigeria Export-Import Bank and the Urban Development Bank
options.c: the Nigerian Industrial Development Bank, the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry and the National Economic Reconstruction Fund
options.d: First Bank, Union Bank and United Bank for Africa

questions.explanation: The Bank of Industry was created by merging NIDB, NBCI and NERFUND, to give financial support to large, medium and small industrial enterprises. Option A is the merger that produced the Bank of Agriculture, option B lists separate institutions that were not merged, and option D lists commercial banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The merger of the Nigerian Agricultural and Co-operative Bank, the People's Bank of Nigeria and the Family Economic Advancement Programme produced the institution now known as

options.a: the Bank of Agriculture
options.b: the Bank of Industry

questions.explanation: These three bodies were merged into the bank now called the Bank of Agriculture, whose main role is lending to farmers to boost food production. Option B came from NIDB, NBCI and NERFUND, option C was set up separately to finance exporters, and option D was formerly the Urban Development Bank.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the problems that undermined development finance institutions in Nigeria?

options.a: Politicisation of lending decisions
options.b: A very high proportion of non-performing loans
options.d: Strict commercial management that was free of political influence

questions.explanation: The trouble with the DFIs was the reverse: non-commercial governance and political interference in lending. Options A, B and C were real problems, together with poor credit discipline, bureaucracy and corruption, which left most of their loans non-performing.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The mortgage finance market set up under the Mortgage Institutions Decree of 1989 has a two-tier structure in which

options.a: primary mortgage institutions are the apex and the Federal Mortgage Bank forms the second tier
options.b: the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria is the apex institution and primary mortgage institutions form the second tier
options.c: insurance companies are the apex and building societies form the second tier
options.d: the stock exchange is the apex and finance houses form the second tier

questions.explanation: The 1989 law made the Federal Mortgage Bank the apex mortgage institution, with a network of primary mortgage institutions below it that take deposits and lend to people buying or building houses. Option A turns the structure upside down, and options C and D name institutions outside the mortgage system.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which institution manages and administers Nigeria's National Housing Fund?

options.a: The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria
options.b: The Bank of Industry

questions.explanation: The Federal Mortgage Bank manages the National Housing Fund, which pools workers' contributions to provide cheap long-term housing loans. Option B finances industry, option C insures bank deposits, and option D regulates the capital market.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a problem holding back mortgage financing in Nigeria?

options.a: Difficulty in obtaining title documents to land
options.b: An abundant supply of cheap long-term funds for mortgage institutions
options.c: The low income of most Nigerians
options.d: Lack of public awareness of mortgage services

questions.explanation: Mortgage institutions actually suffer from a shortage of long-term funds, since they compete for short-term money in the open market. Options A, C and D are real problems, along with weak capital, a shortage of skilled staff and poverty.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which function of the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria was later transferred to the Central Bank of Nigeria, while the Federal Mortgage Bank kept its role in the National Housing Fund?

options.a: Granting long-term housing loans
options.b: Management of the National Housing Fund
options.d: Regulation and supervision of primary mortgage institutions

questions.explanation: The Federal Mortgage Bank's role as regulator and supervisor of mortgage institutions passed to the CBN, while it kept managing the National Housing Fund. Option A is still a lending role, option B is the function it kept, and option C has always belonged to the CBN.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the microfinance policy issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria in December 2005, what was to happen to existing community banks?

options.a: They were to be taken over by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation as its branches
options.b: They were to become discount houses trading in treasury bills
options.c: They were to convert into microfinance banks by meeting the new capital and other requirements
options.d: They were to become merchant banks dealing in wholesale finance

questions.explanation: Community banks had not closed the large gap in financial services for poor and low-income Nigerians, so the 2005 policy phased them out and required them to recapitalise and convert into microfinance banks. Merchant banking (D) and discount house business (B) are wholesale activities, nothing like grassroots banking. The NDIC (A) insures deposits and does not run banks as branches.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the goals of microfinance banks in Nigeria?

options.a: Mobilising savings for intermediation
options.b: Creating employment and raising the productivity and living standards of low-income households
options.c: Dealing in foreign exchange and opening domiciliary accounts for large corporate customers
options.d: Providing affordable and dependable financial services to the economically active poor

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks are meant for grassroots finance. A unit or state microfinance bank is not allowed to offer more sophisticated services such as foreign exchange business, which is left to deposit money banks. Serving the active poor (D), mobilising savings (A) and creating jobs to lift household incomes (B) are all stated goals of microfinance banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In banking, a 'distressed' bank is best described as one that:

options.a: Is owned by the government rather than by private investors
options.b: Has severe financial, operational and managerial weaknesses that make it unable to meet its obligations to customers, owners and others as they fall due
options.c: Has temporarily closed a branch for renovation
options.d: Has more customers than it can serve in its banking hall

questions.explanation: Distress means a bank is in serious trouble. Its capital may be eroded, many of its loans may have gone bad, it may be short of cash and badly managed, so it cannot pay depositors and other creditors as and when due. Closing a branch (C) or having crowded banking halls (D) says nothing about financial health, and ownership (A) does not define distress.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The CAMEL rating system used by Nigerian regulators to judge the health of a bank does NOT include which of the following?

options.a: Capital adequacy
options.b: Asset quality

questions.explanation: CAMEL stands for Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management competence, Earnings strength and Liquidity, the five things regulators check to decide whether a bank is sound or distressed. The C stands for capital, not collateral. Capital adequacy (A), asset quality (B) and earnings (C) are all part of the system.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is an INTERNAL (bank-specific) cause of distress in Nigerian banks?

options.a: Political instability in the country
options.b: Macroeconomic instability such as recession and high inflation
options.c: Weak management, with insider abuse and poor credit control
options.d: A sharp fall in world oil prices

questions.explanation: Internal causes come from inside the bank, such as incompetent management, too little capital, fraud and insider lending, and poor management of assets and liabilities. Recession and inflation (B), political instability (A) and oil price shocks (D) are external factors outside the bank's control. They can still push weak banks into distress.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following measures would help to curb distress in Nigerian banks?

options.a: Granting more unsecured loans to directors and other insiders
options.b: Allowing banks to operate with lower capital
options.c: Improving the quality of bank management and strengthening internal controls against fraud
options.d: Reducing supervision and examination of banks by the regulators

questions.explanation: Poor management and fraud were among the main causes of bank distress, so better management, stronger internal controls, sound credit policies and good liquidity management are the main remedies. Lower capital (B), more insider lending (A) and weaker supervision (D) are the kinds of conditions that cause distress, so they would make it worse.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is a typical early warning sign (symptom) that a bank is becoming distressed?

options.a: A steady rise in customer deposits and profits
options.b: Approval of new branches by the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: Persistent adverse clearing positions and borrowing at rates well above the market rate
options.d: Prompt payment of all customers' withdrawals

questions.explanation: A bank heading for distress often keeps ending up short at clearing, overdraws its account with the CBN and borrows desperately at high rates. Other warning signs include window dressing of accounts, frequent boardroom quarrels and customer complaints about unpaid obligations. Rising deposits and profits (A) and prompt payment of withdrawals (D) point to a healthy bank, and branch approval (B) is a normal business event.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The Bank of Industry (BOI) in Nigeria was formed by merging which institutions?

options.a: The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria and the Urban Development Bank
options.b: The People's Bank of Nigeria, the Nigerian Agricultural and Co-operative Bank and the Family Economic Advancement Programme
options.c: First Bank, Union Bank and United Bank for Africa
options.d: The Nigerian Industrial Development Bank (NIDB), the Nigerian Bank for Commerce and Industry (NBCI) and the National Economic Reconstruction Fund (NERFUND)

questions.explanation: The BOI brought together the three main industrial finance bodies, NIDB, NBCI and NERFUND, to provide medium- and long-term finance to industry. Option B lists the institutions that formed the Bank of Agriculture. Option A names housing and infrastructure finance bodies, and C names commercial banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is a specialised (development) bank in Nigeria rather than a deposit money bank?

options.a: Nigerian Export-Import Bank (NEXIM)
options.b: Access Bank

questions.explanation: NEXIM is a government-owned specialised institution set up to finance and promote exports, alongside development banks such as the Bank of Industry, the Bank of Agriculture and the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria. Zenith (C), GTBank (D) and Access (B) are commercial deposit money banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Before the Pension Reform Act of 2004, the civil service pension scheme in Nigeria was mainly:

options.a: A scheme in which each worker kept his own retirement savings account
options.b: A scheme run by deposit money banks that guaranteed interest on contributions
options.c: A fully funded contributory scheme managed by pension fund administrators
options.d: An unfunded defined benefit scheme, with pensions paid out of annual government revenue

questions.explanation: Under the old scheme the government promised retirees a benefit fixed by formula, but it set no fund aside and paid pensions from each year's budget. This led to huge arrears. Options C and A describe the contributory pension scheme that replaced it, with individual retirement savings accounts managed by PFAs, and B describes no Nigerian pension scheme.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under Nigeria's contributory pension scheme, the main role of the National Pension Commission (PenCom) is to:

options.a: Pay salaries to all federal civil servants
options.b: Fix the interest rates charged by deposit money banks
options.c: Hold workers' pension contributions in its own vaults
options.d: Regulate and supervise pension administration, including licensing and overseeing pension fund administrators and custodians

questions.explanation: PenCom is the regulator of the pension industry. It licenses, monitors and sets rules for pension fund administrators and pension fund custodians so that retirees' money is safe. The funds themselves are held by custodians, not by PenCom (C). Paying salaries (A) is the employer's job, and influencing bank interest rates (B) falls to the CBN.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Nigeria's contributory pension scheme?

options.a: Each worker has an individual retirement savings account (RSA)
options.b: Both the employer and the employee contribute to the scheme
options.c: Pensions are paid out of the government's annual budget, with no fund set aside
options.d: The funds are privately managed by pension fund administrators and kept by pension fund custodians

questions.explanation: The contributory scheme is fully funded: contributions build up in each worker's RSA (A) and are invested, so benefits are not paid from yearly budgets. Payment from the annual budget was the weakness of the old scheme. Joint contributions (B) and private management by PFAs with custody by PFCs (D) are core features of the new scheme.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum monthly contributions to an employee's retirement savings account are:

options.a: 10% of monthly emoluments by the employer and 8% by the employee
options.b: 7.5% by the employer and 7.5% by the employee
options.d: 8% by the employer and 10% by the employee

questions.explanation: The 2014 Act raised the minimum total contribution to 18% of monthly emoluments, made up of 10% from the employer and 8% from the employee. Option B was the arrangement under the 2004 Act, which the 2014 Act replaced. Option D reverses the two shares, and C wrongly leaves the employee out.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The main purpose of establishing the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) was to:

options.a: Replace the Central Bank of Nigeria as the regulator of banks
options.b: Guarantee that every bank will make a profit each year
options.d: Protect depositors, especially small ones, against loss when a bank fails, and so strengthen public confidence in banks

questions.explanation: Deposit insurance means that if an insured bank fails, its depositors are paid up to a set limit. This protects small savers and helps prevent panics and runs on banks. The NDIC does not guarantee bank profits (B). It works alongside the CBN and does not replace it (A), and long-term industrial lending (C) is the work of development banks.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the review announced by the NDIC in 2024, the maximum deposit insurance cover per depositor of a failed deposit money bank was raised to:
questions.explanation: In 2024 the NDIC raised the maximum cover for each depositor of a deposit money bank to N5 million, so that most depositors would be fully protected if their bank failed. N500,000 (D) was the limit set in 2010 and has been overtaken. N50,000 (A) was the original cover when the NDIC started, and N200,000 (C) was an earlier intermediate limit.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When the NDIC began operations in 1989, the maximum amount guaranteed to each depositor of a failed insured bank was:
questions.explanation: At the start of the scheme, each depositor of a failed insured bank was guaranteed up to N50,000. The limit has been raised several times since then as the value of money and the size of deposits grew. N500,000 (B) was introduced in 2010 and N5,000,000 (C) in 2024, while N25,000 (A) was never the NDIC limit.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When the NDIC pays an insured depositor of a failed bank, the depositor's claim against the failed bank to the extent of that payment:

options.a: Remains with the depositor, who can claim the same amount again
options.b: Passes to the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: Passes to the NDIC (subrogation), so the NDIC can recover it from the bank's assets
options.d: Is cancelled, and nobody can recover it

questions.explanation: Subrogation means that once the NDIC has paid a depositor, it steps into that depositor's shoes for the amount paid and can claim it in the liquidation of the failed bank. The claim is not wiped out (D), it does not go to the CBN (B), and the depositor cannot be paid twice for the same amount (A).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation?

options.a: Insuring the deposit liabilities of licensed banks
options.b: Acting as liquidator of failed insured banks
options.c: Issuing legal tender currency notes and coins
options.d: Giving financial or technical assistance to insured banks in difficulty, in the interest of depositors

questions.explanation: Issuing currency is a core function of the Central Bank of Nigeria. The NDIC insures deposits (A), helps troubled insured banks to protect depositors (D), supervises banks alongside the CBN, and winds up failed banks as liquidator (B).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following was a major advantage of the universal banking system practised in Nigeria between 2001 and 2010?

options.a: It stopped banks from granting medium- and long-term loans
options.b: It removed the dichotomy between commercial and merchant banking and created a level playing field for banks
options.d: It made every bank offer all financial services whether it wanted to or not

questions.explanation: Universal banking allowed a bank to choose its own mix of money market, capital market and retail or wholesale services, so the old split between commercial and merchant banks disappeared and competition increased. It gave banks the option, not an obligation, to offer every service (D). It actually let commercial banks lend for longer terms (A), and it increased rather than reduced competition (C).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: What is the main difference between non-interest (Islamic) banking and conventional banking?

options.a: Conventional banks share profits and losses with depositors, while non-interest banks pay fixed interest
options.b: Non-interest banking avoids paying or charging interest (riba) and works on profit-and-loss sharing, while conventional banking is based on interest
options.c: Non-interest banks do not accept any deposits from customers
options.d: Non-interest banks can only lend to the government

questions.explanation: Islamic banking follows the ban on riba (interest), so returns come from sharing the profits, and possibly losses, of the ventures financed, while conventional banks pay and charge agreed interest rates. Non-interest banks do accept deposits (C), option A reverses the two systems, and they lend to businesses and individuals, not only to government (D).

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In a non-interest bank, customers who keep investment (time) deposits are rewarded by:

options.a: A share of the profit earned by the bank, according to a profit-sharing ratio agreed in advance
options.b: A guaranteed bonus equal to the Central Bank's monetary policy rate
options.c: A fixed rate of interest agreed at the time of deposit
options.d: Nothing at all, since all deposits earn no return

questions.explanation: Investment deposits in a non-interest bank work like a partnership: the depositor gets an agreed share of the profit from how the funds are used, so the return is not fixed beforehand. A fixed or rate-linked return (C, B) would be interest, which is not allowed. Option D applies only to demand deposits, which are repayable on demand but earn no return.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Twenty traders at Oshodi market each contribute N5,000 every week, and each week one member collects the whole pool in turn. No licence is held and no regulator supervises the arrangement. This is part of the

options.a: formal financial sector
options.b: capital market

questions.explanation: Rotating savings groups such as Esusu, Ajo or Isusu operate without a licence or formal regulation, which is exactly what defines the informal financial sector. The formal sector (A) and microfinance banks (D) are licensed and supervised, while the capital market (B) deals in long-term securities such as shares and bonds.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A pension fund administrator in Lagos wants approval to manage workers' contributions under the contributory pension scheme. Which body regulates and supervises it?

options.a: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)
options.b: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

questions.explanation: PenCom oversees pension fund administrators and the contributory pension scheme. NAICOM (D) regulates insurance companies, SEC (B) regulates the capital market, and the NDIC (A) insures deposits in banks, so none of them licenses pension fund administrators.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the CBN's banking licence regime, a Nigerian commercial bank that wants to operate across all states of the federation and also run branches or subsidiaries outside Nigeria needs a licence with

options.a: international authorisation
options.b: regional authorisation

questions.explanation: Only a commercial bank with international authorisation may combine nationwide operations with offshore operations. A national licence (D) covers all of Nigeria but not offshore operations, and a regional licence (B) is limited to a specified group of states. Option C is a type of non-interest banking licence with an even narrower scope.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the bank recapitalisation programme announced by the CBN in March 2024 (with a deadline of 31 March 2026), what is the new minimum capital for a commercial bank with international authorisation?

options.a: N25 billion
options.b: N200 billion

questions.explanation: The 2024 programme raised the minimum capital for internationally authorised commercial banks to N500 billion, to be met within 24 months. N200 billion (B) is the figure for national authorisation, N50 billion (C) applies to regional commercial banks and merchant banks, and N25 billion (A) was the minimum set in the 2004-2005 consolidation.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Musa asks a non-interest bank to finance a N4 million delivery van. The bank buys the van, then sells it to Musa for N4.6 million, telling him the N600,000 mark-up openly, and he pays in monthly instalments. This non-interest contract is

options.a: Murabaha
options.b: Ijarah

questions.explanation: Murabaha is a cost-plus sale: the bank buys the asset and resells it to the customer at a disclosed profit margin, usually paid in instalments, so no interest is charged. Mudarabah (C) is a profit-sharing partnership, Ijarah (B) is leasing in which the bank keeps ownership and charges rent, and riba (D) is the interest that non-interest banking forbids.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: The traditional function that first set merchant banks apart from other financial institutions is

options.a: accepting small savings deposits from the general public
options.b: insuring the deposits of failed banks
options.d: accepting bills of exchange to finance the trade of others

questions.explanation: Acceptance business, where the merchant bank adds its name to a bill of exchange so that a trader can obtain short-term finance, is the classic merchant banking function. Option A is retail commercial banking, C belongs to the central bank, and B is the work of the NDIC.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Delta Foods Plc has agreed to raise long-term funds through a share issue in four months' time, but it needs money now to start building a new plant. A merchant bank gives it a short-term loan to be repaid from the issue proceeds. This facility is a

options.a: negotiable certificate of deposit
options.b: debt factoring arrangement

questions.explanation: A bridging loan is temporary finance that 'bridges' the gap until a company completes its permanent funding arrangements, which is exactly Delta Foods' situation. A negotiable certificate of deposit (A) is an interbank deposit instrument, an acceptance credit (C) finances trade through accepted bills, and factoring (B) means selling receivables for immediate cash.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Interbank debt instruments, with maturities of about 3 to 36 months, that are designed mainly to channel commercial banks' surplus funds into merchant banks are called

options.a: unit trust certificates
options.b: bankers' acceptances

questions.explanation: NCDs are issued by banks in exchange for fixed deposits and can be traded, which makes them a convenient way for commercial banks to place surplus funds with merchant banks. Treasury certificates (D) are government debt, bankers' acceptances (B) are trade bills accepted by banks, and unit trust certificates (A) show ownership of units in an investment fund.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states a traditional difference between merchant banks and commercial banks in Nigeria?

options.a: Merchant banks took mostly demand deposits, while commercial banks took only fixed deposits
options.b: Merchant banks mainly served individuals, while commercial banks mainly served large firms
options.c: Merchant banks were not members of the clearing house, while commercial banks took part in the clearing system
options.d: Merchant banks had large rural branch networks, while commercial banks were found only in cities

questions.explanation: Because merchant banks did not run cheque-based retail accounts for the public, they were traditionally not clearing house members, unlike commercial banks. Options D, B and A reverse the real differences: merchant banks were urban-based with few branches, served firms and institutions, and held mostly fixed deposits.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A World Bank review in 2000 traced the decline of Nigeria's federal development finance institutions to several causes. Which of the following was NOT one of them?

options.a: Inappropriate funding vehicles
options.b: Excessive capital and too many highly qualified staff

questions.explanation: The review blamed non-commercial governance, politicised lending, poor credit discipline, lack of quality staff and inappropriate funding vehicles, which left the DFIs with heavy losses and mostly non-performing loans. Option B states the opposite of what happened, since the DFIs suffered from a shortage of quality staff and were short of funds. Options C, D and A were genuine causes.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A Nigerian cashew exporter worries that its buyer in Europe may fail to pay for a shipment because of commercial or political problems. Which development finance institution was set up to provide export credit insurance and guarantees for such risks?

options.a: The Bank of Agriculture (BOA)
options.b: The Bank of Industry (BOI)
options.d: The Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN)

questions.explanation: NEXIM is Nigeria's export credit agency, and it provides export credit guarantees and insurance against commercial and political risks of non-payment by foreign buyers. The BOI (B) finances industry, the BOA (A) finances farmers and rural enterprises, and the FMBN (D) deals in housing finance.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Funmi, who owns a small bakery in Ibadan, wants a loan from the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN), which began operations in 2017. How will she normally obtain DBN funds?

options.a: Through the CBN discount window
options.b: Through a participating financial institution such as a commercial or microfinance bank, which on-lends DBN funds to her
options.c: By applying directly at a DBN retail branch, which lends to individual MSMEs
options.d: By buying DBN shares on the stock exchange

questions.explanation: The DBN is a wholesale development bank: it does not lend directly to small businesses but channels funds through participating financial institutions, which assess the borrower and bear the credit risk. Option C wrongly describes the DBN as a retail lender, A is a facility for banks, not businesses, and D has nothing to do with borrowing.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the National Housing Fund (NHF) Act of 1992, a contributor pays 2.5% of monthly basic salary into the Fund. A public-sector worker in Abuja earns a basic salary of N180,000 a month. How much does she contribute to the NHF in a full year?
questions.explanation: Her monthly contribution is 2.5% of N180,000 = N4,500, and over 12 months this comes to N4,500 x 12 = N54,000. Option B is only the monthly figure, C uses ten months instead of twelve, and A doubles the rate to 5%.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: When discount houses operated in the Nigerian money market, their main role was to

options.a: act as intermediaries between the CBN and licensed banks by trading in and holding Treasury Bills, commercial bills and other short-term securities
options.b: buy and sell foreign currency notes for travellers and small users
options.c: lend long-term funds to manufacturers for plant and machinery
options.d: manage unit trust funds on behalf of small savers

questions.explanation: Discount houses dealt in short-term government and commercial bills and stood between the CBN and the banks in open market operations, which helped the money market grow. Option B describes bureaux de change, C describes development banks such as the Bank of Industry, and D describes unit trust managers.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Bureaux de change were introduced in Nigeria in 1989 to widen the foreign exchange market and serve small users. Under the original guidelines, a licensed bureau de change could deal only in

options.a: the official auction of foreign exchange by the CBN
options.b: letters of credit for importers of capital goods
options.c: domiciliary accounts and foreign currency loans
options.d: foreign bank notes and coins, and the purchase of travellers' cheques

questions.explanation: Bureaux de change were set up to retail foreign exchange to small buyers, so they were limited to foreign cash and coins and cashing travellers' cheques. Options B and C are services offered by banks, which hold full foreign exchange authorisation, and A was the official market from which bureaux were originally expected to stay apart, buying their foreign exchange from private suppliers.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A bank takes thousands of savings deposits that customers can withdraw at short notice, and uses part of them to grant a ten-year loan to a cement factory. Which aspect of financial intermediation does this show?

options.a: Risk diversification
options.b: Maturity transformation

questions.explanation: Turning short-term deposits into long-term loans is maturity transformation, one of the main reasons banks intermediate better than direct lending between savers and borrowers. Risk diversification (A) means spreading loans across many borrowers, which the scenario does not show, moral suasion (C) is a central bank tool, and disintermediation (D) is when savers and borrowers bypass banks altogether.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A bank pays 12% per annum on a savings deposit, while the inflation rate is 21%. Using the approximation that the real interest rate is the nominal rate minus the inflation rate, what is the saver's approximate real rate of return?
questions.explanation: The real rate is about 12% - 21% = -9%, which means the saver's money loses purchasing power even though it earns interest, and this is why high inflation discourages saving. Option B gets the sign wrong, C wrongly adds the two rates, and D ignores the interest earned.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Chidinma keeps N800,000 in a savings account that pays simple interest of 6% per annum. Ignoring taxes and charges, how much interest will she earn after 9 months?
questions.explanation: Simple interest = principal x rate x time = N800,000 x 0.06 x 9/12 = N36,000. Option C uses a full year, D multiplies by 9% instead of 6% for three-quarters of a year, and A misplaces the decimal point.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In May 2024 the NDIC raised its maximum deposit insurance cover for each depositor of a deposit money bank to N5 million. Suppose a depositor has N7.2 million in a deposit money bank that later fails and is liquidated. Under that cover, how will she be paid?

options.a: N7.2 million in full from the NDIC at once
options.b: N500,000 as insured deposit, with N6.7 million claimed from liquidation dividends
options.c: N5 million as insured deposit, with the remaining N2.2 million claimed from liquidation dividends as assets are realised
options.d: N2.2 million only, being the excess over the insured limit

questions.explanation: The NDIC pays the insured amount up to the N5 million limit, and the uninsured balance of N7.2 million - N5 million = N2.2 million becomes a claim paid from liquidation dividends, if and when the failed bank's assets are realised. Option A ignores the limit, B uses the old N500,000 cover that applied before May 2024, and D confuses the uninsured excess with the insured payment.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the flat-rate deposit insurance scheme of the NDIC Decree of 1988, an insured bank paid an annual premium of 15/16 of one per cent of its total deposit liabilities. If a bank's total deposit liabilities were N64 billion, what was its annual premium?

options.a: N9.6 billion
options.b: N600 million

questions.explanation: Fifteen-sixteenths of one per cent is 0.9375%, so the premium is N64 billion x 0.009375 = N600 million. Option C uses a full 1%, D misplaces the decimal point, and A wrongly treats the rate as 15%.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the NDIC Act, when the NDIC pays an insured depositor of a failed bank, the depositor's rights against the failed bank pass to the NDIC to the extent of the amount paid. This legal principle is known as

options.a: subrogation
options.b: lien

questions.explanation: Subrogation means stepping into another person's shoes: having paid the depositor, the NDIC takes over the depositor's claim against the failed bank for that amount and recovers it from the liquidation. Set-off (C) is combining debts owed both ways, a lien (B) is a right to retain property until a debt is paid, and novation (D) replaces an old contract with a new one by agreement.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: In August 2011, after the licences of Afribank, Spring Bank and Bank PHB were revoked, the CBN and NDIC set up Mainstreet Bank, Enterprise Bank and Keystone Bank to take over their assets and liabilities temporarily, keeping services running until buyers could be found. These new banks were

options.a: microfinance banks
options.b: development finance institutions

questions.explanation: A bridge bank is a temporary bank set up by the authorities to take over a failed bank's business so that depositors keep their services until the bank can be sold, and Nigeria used this option for the three banks in 2011. Options A, C and B are permanent categories of licensed institutions, not a failure-resolution tool.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: A microfinance bank in Ibadan plans to start buying and selling US dollars for its customers. Under the CBN's rules for microfinance banks, this plan is

options.a: allowed, because microfinance banks may carry out any service that commercial banks offer
options.b: not allowed, because foreign exchange transactions are a prohibited activity for microfinance banks
options.c: allowed, provided the dollars are sold only to rural customers
options.d: allowed, provided the NDIC insures the foreign currency deposits

questions.explanation: Microfinance banks are not permitted to deal in foreign exchange, a sophisticated service reserved for banks with the proper licence. Option C invents a rural exception, A is wrong because microfinance banks have a much narrower scope than commercial banks, and D is wrong because deposit insurance has nothing to do with permission to deal in foreign exchange.

questions.topic: The Nigerian Banking Structure, Savings and Investment
questions.question: Under the CBN's 2010 regulation on the scope of banking activities, a commercial bank may NOT, without CBN authorisation,

options.a: acquire real estate other than as business premises for its own use
options.b: grant overdrafts and loans to its customers
options.c: accept savings and fixed deposits from the public
options.d: provide payment services such as electronic funds transfers

questions.explanation: The 2010 regulation bars banks from acquiring real estate or immovable property except premises for their own use, unless the CBN authorises it, so that depositors' funds are not tied up in property speculation. Options C, B and D are core commercial banking functions: accepting deposits, giving credit and providing payment services.

questions.question: The Federal Government of Nigeria raises short-term funds, for periods of up to one year, mainly by issuing which instrument through the CBN?

options.a: Commercial papers
options.b: Treasury bills

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term government IOUs issued at a discount for terms such as 91, 182 or 364 days, and the CBN sells them on the government's behalf to banks and other investors. Option D is a long-term government debt instrument. Options A and C are also money market instruments, but commercial papers are issued by companies and bankers' acceptances are bills accepted by banks on behalf of their customers, not government borrowing.

questions.question: The money market can be defined as

options.a: The market where money is traded
options.b: The market where goods and services are exchanged without the use of money
options.c: The market for buying and selling short-term financial instruments or investible funds
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: The money market is the market for buying and selling short-term financial instruments or investible funds, such as treasury bills and commercial papers. Option A sounds close but is too vague, since long-term funds are traded in the capital market instead, and B describes barter, not a money market.

questions.question: The need for a money market arises out of which of the following needs?

options.a: Government's need for accommodation finance to bridge the gap between its expenditure needs and its expected revenues
options.b: Firms' need for working capital purposes
options.c: Traders' need to finance their trade, sometimes on an overnight basis

questions.explanation: A money market is needed because government must bridge the gap between its spending and the timing of its revenue (A), firms need short-term working capital (B), and traders need funds, sometimes overnight, to finance trade (C). All three create demand for short-term funds, so D is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following have operated in the Nigerian money market?

options.a: The Central Bank of Nigeria and commercial, merchant and universal banks
options.b: Discount houses and specialized banks

questions.explanation: Many institutions have taken part in the Nigerian money market: the CBN, which brings government securities such as treasury bills to the market, and the commercial, merchant and universal banks (A), discount houses and specialized banks such as community banks (B), and federal and state governments raising short-term funds (C). Since each group is an operator, D is the correct answer.

questions.question: Which of these are NOT money market instruments?

options.a: Treasury bills and treasury certificates
options.b: Commercial papers and certificates of deposit
options.d: Call-money fund and Bankers' Unit Fund

questions.explanation: Debentures and equities are long-term securities traded in the capital market, so they are not money market instruments. Treasury bills and certificates (A), commercial papers and certificates of deposit (B), and the call-money fund and Bankers' Unit Fund (D) have all been money market instruments in Nigeria.

questions.question: The money market has a lot of benefits; these include

options.a: Reducing the amount of idle barren cash that people hold
options.b: Providing the Central Bank with a ready instrument for gauging the scarcity or relative availability of funds in the economy
options.d: None of the above is correct

questions.explanation: By giving individuals and banks a safe outlet for short-term surplus funds, the money market reduces the amount of idle, barren cash they hold and lets them earn some income on it. Movements in money market interest rates also give the Central Bank a ready gauge of how scarce or plentiful funds are in the economy. Since both A and B are genuine benefits, C is the right choice and D is wrong.

questions.question: Which of these is not one of the major challenges faced by the Nigerian money market?

options.a: Dominance of the market by government securities
options.b: Lack of market space for location of the market in some cities of Nigeria
options.c: Lack of sufficient awareness on the part of the public of the existence and benefits of a money market
options.d: Lack of adequate and effective institutional framework for ensuring probity, integrity and accountability in the market

questions.explanation: The money market is not a building or physical location; it is a network of banks, discount houses, the CBN and other dealers who trade short-term instruments by telephone and electronic means, so lack of market space is not one of its problems. Its real challenges include dominance by government securities (A), low public awareness of the market and its benefits (C), and a weak institutional framework for probity and accountability (D).

questions.question: Which statement best describes the structure of the Nigerian money market?

options.a: It is perfectly competitive, with many small operators and no dominant players
options.b: It has an oligopolistic structure, being dominated (apart from government) by a few large banks
options.c: It is a pure monopoly in which the CBN is the only buyer and seller of instruments
options.d: It is dominated by individual households trading treasury bills directly

questions.explanation: Although many types of operators take part in the Nigerian money market, it has an oligopolistic structure: apart from government, activity has long been dominated by the banks, and among them by a few big banks. Option A is wrong because having many participants does not remove the dominance of a few large players, and C is wrong because the CBN is an important participant, not the only one. D is wrong because low participation by the general public is itself one of the market's weaknesses.

questions.question: Treasury bills, treasury certificates, commercial papers, certificates of deposit and bankers' acceptances are instruments traded in which market?

options.a: Capital market
options.b: Stock market

questions.explanation: All of these are short-term instruments, usually maturing within a year, and the market for short-term funds and instruments is the money market. Options A and B deal in long-term securities such as shares and bonds, and option D is a market for goods and services rather than financial instruments.

questions.question: The market that deals in the buying and selling of short-term financial instruments is the

options.a: Capital market
options.b: Short term market

questions.explanation: The money market is the market for short-term funds and instruments, usually with maturities of one year or less, such as treasury bills, commercial papers and bankers' acceptances. Option A, the capital market, deals in long-term securities like shares and bonds. Option D, financial market, is the broad umbrella covering both, so it is less precise, and 'short term market' in option B is not the standard name.

questions.question: The shortest standard maturity period of a Nigerian treasury bill is

options.a: 81 days
options.b: 61 days

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term Federal Government securities sold at a discount, and their classic and shortest tenor is 91 days (longer issues run for 182 and 364 days). Options A, B and D (81, 61 and 71 days) are not standard treasury bill maturities.

questions.question: All these are money market instruments except

options.a: treasury bills
options.b: bankers' acceptances

questions.explanation: Bonds are long-term debt securities, so they belong to the capital market rather than the money market. Treasury bills, bankers' acceptances and commercial papers (options A, B and D) are all short-term instruments, usually maturing within a year, which is exactly what the money market deals in.

questions.question: The apex institution of the Nigerian money market is the

options.a: NDIC
options.b: CBN

questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Nigeria sits at the top of the money market: it regulates the market, issues treasury bills for the government and acts as lender of last resort to banks. Option A, the NDIC, insures deposits, option C, the SEC, regulates the capital market, and option D, NAICOM, regulates insurance companies.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a money market instrument?

options.a: Certificate of Deposit
options.b: Treasury certificate

questions.explanation: A mortgage is a long-term loan secured on property, so it belongs to the capital (long-term) market, not the money market. Certificates of deposit (A), treasury certificates (B) and call money (D) are all short-term instruments traded in the Nigerian money market.

questions.question: The money market is best described as the market for:

options.a: buying and selling foreign currencies at the official exchange rate
options.b: exchanging goods directly for other goods without the use of money
options.c: short-term funds and financial instruments, usually with maturities of up to one year
options.d: medium- to long-term securities such as shares, bonds and debentures

questions.explanation: The money market is where short-term funds are lent and borrowed, through instruments such as treasury bills, commercial papers and bankers' acceptances, with maturities ranging from overnight to about a year. It helps governments, banks and firms manage temporary cash shortages and surpluses. Option D describes the capital market, option A the foreign exchange market, and option B barter.

questions.question: Which of the following groups consists entirely of operators in the Nigerian money market?

options.a: The stock exchange, the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Central Securities Clearing System
options.b: Stockbrokers, registrars and issuing houses
options.c: The CBN, stockbrokers and the stock exchange
options.d: The CBN, deposit money banks, the Federal Government and large corporations

questions.explanation: Money market operators are those who lend or borrow short-term funds: the CBN, which issues and trades government securities and conducts open market operations; deposit money banks managing their liquidity; governments raising short-term funds through treasury bills; and corporations investing surplus cash or issuing commercial papers. Options A and B list capital market operators and institutions, while option C mixes the CBN with capital market operators.

questions.question: How does the existence of a money market help the CBN to carry out monetary policy?

options.a: It enables the CBN to buy or sell short-term government securities in open market operations to inject or withdraw liquidity from the banking system
options.b: It removes the need for the CBN to set any reserve requirement or liquidity ratio for the banks
options.c: It allows the CBN to fix the prices of goods and services in the economy directly by decree
options.d: It allows the CBN to lend long-term funds directly to manufacturers for building new factories

questions.explanation: Open market operations work through the money market: by selling treasury bills or CBN bills the CBN mops up excess liquidity, and by buying them it injects funds, which in turn influences interest rates and credit. Money market interest rates also show the CBN whether funds are scarce or plentiful. Option C is not how monetary policy works, option D is long-term lending rather than monetary control, and option B is wrong because reserve requirements remain a separate tool.

questions.question: A short-term unsecured promissory note issued by a large, creditworthy company to raise funds, backed only by the issuer's reputation, is called a:

options.a: treasury bill
options.b: bankers' acceptance

questions.explanation: Commercial papers are issued by well-known 'blue-chip' companies to raise short-term funds; they are usually sold at a discount and repaid at face value on maturity, and their only backing is the issuer's good name. A treasury bill (option A) is issued by the Federal Government, a bankers' acceptance (option B) is a bill accepted by a bank, and a certificate of deposit (option D) is issued by a bank against a time deposit.

questions.question: A bill of exchange that is drawn on a bank and accepted by it, so that the bank undertakes to pay it at maturity, is known as:

options.a: a commercial paper
options.b: call money

questions.explanation: By writing 'accepted' on the bill, the bank takes on the obligation to pay at maturity, which makes the bill very safe and easy to discount for cash in the money market; bankers' acceptances are widely used in financing trade. A commercial paper (option A) carries only the issuing company's name, a treasury certificate (option D) is a government security, and call money (option B) is very short-term lending between banks.

questions.question: Which statement about Nigerian Treasury Bills is correct?

options.a: They are time deposits issued by commercial banks to their customers
options.b: They are long-term bonds issued by companies to finance the expansion of their factories
options.c: They are shares in the Central Bank of Nigeria sold to members of the public
options.d: They are short-term Federal Government securities sold at a discount and redeemed at face value on maturity

questions.explanation: Treasury bills are the main money market instrument for the Federal Government's short-term borrowing. Because they are sold below face value and repaid in full at maturity, the difference is the investor's return, and since the government backs them they carry almost no default risk. Option B describes corporate bonds or debentures, option A describes certificates of deposit or fixed deposits, and option C is false.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of having a money market in an economy?

options.a: It is the main channel of long-term funds for building factories, roads and other infrastructure
options.b: It allows banks, firms and individuals to earn income on short-term surplus funds instead of keeping idle cash, while staying liquid
options.c: It guarantees that no bank in the economy will ever face a shortage of liquidity or need help
options.d: It removes the need for the country to have a central bank or any monetary authority

questions.explanation: Through the money market, holders of temporary surplus cash can invest in safe short-term instruments such as treasury bills and earn a return, then get their money back quickly when needed. The market also gives the CBN a gauge of how scarce or plentiful funds are and a channel for monetary policy. Option A describes the capital market, while options C and D overstate what a money market can do.

questions.question: Which of the following is a challenge that has faced the Nigerian money market?

options.a: Dominance of the market by government securities and a narrow range of instruments
options.b: Lack of any role for the CBN, which leaves the market completely unregulated
options.c: Excessive participation by individual small investors, who crowd out the banks
options.d: Too many varieties of instruments, which confuse investors and spread funds too thinly

questions.explanation: The Nigerian money market has long relied heavily on government securities such as treasury bills, so its fortunes are tied to government finances, and the range of instruments has been limited, leaving the market without much depth or breadth. Other challenges include low public awareness and dominance by a few big banks. Options C and D state the opposite of the real situation, and option B is wrong because the CBN regulates the market and is one of its main participants.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually an operator in the Nigerian money market?

options.a: Discount houses
options.b: Stockbroking firms buying and selling company shares on the stock exchange

questions.explanation: Buying and selling company shares is a capital market activity, since shares are long-term securities with no maturity date. The CBN brings treasury bills to the market, discount houses sell short-term securities and discount other short-term instruments, and commercial and merchant banks lend out surplus funds or borrow to meet short-term liquidity needs, so options C, A and D are all money market operators.

questions.question: The main function of a discount house in the Nigerian money market is to:

options.a: Buy and sell shares of quoted companies on the stock exchange
options.b: Accept current account deposits from the public and issue cheque books
options.c: Act as an intermediary between the Central Bank of Nigeria and banks by trading in and holding treasury bills, commercial bills and other short-term securities
options.d: Provide long-term loans for industrial projects

questions.explanation: Discount houses are money market specialists. They buy, hold and sell short-term instruments such as treasury bills, and they stand between the CBN and the banks, which helps the money market grow and work efficiently. Retail current accounts (B) are deposit money bank business, long-term industrial loans (D) belong to development banks, and share dealing (A) is a capital market activity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how discount houses help banks in the money market?

options.a: They issue legal tender currency notes on behalf of banks
options.b: They fix the official exchange rate of the naira
options.c: They give banks a place to invest surplus short-term funds and to get funds back quickly when they need liquidity
options.d: They insure bank deposits against loss when a bank fails

questions.explanation: By taking banks' surplus short-term funds and investing them in instruments such as treasury bills, which can be turned back into cash quickly, discount houses help banks adjust their liquidity at a profit. Deposit insurance (D) is the NDIC's job, while managing the naira exchange rate (B) and issuing currency (A) are CBN functions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a money market instrument in Nigeria?

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Certificates of deposit
options.c: Ordinary shares of a quoted company

questions.explanation: Ordinary shares have no maturity date and are traded on the stock exchange, so they belong to the capital market. Treasury bills (A), treasury certificates (D) and certificates of deposit (B) are all short-term instruments that can quickly be turned into cash, which is what makes them money market instruments.

questions.question: Treasury bills in Nigeria are best described as:

options.a: Shares issued by deposit money banks to raise capital
options.b: Long-term bonds issued by state governments for infrastructure
options.c: Bills of exchange drawn by exporters on foreign buyers
options.d: Short-term debt instruments issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria on behalf of the Federal Government

questions.explanation: A treasury bill is a short-term government IOU. The CBN issues it on behalf of the Federal Government to meet the government's temporary financing needs, and it is the main money market instrument. Long-term state bonds (B) and bank shares (A) are capital market instruments, and a bill drawn by an exporter (C) is a trade bill, not a treasury bill.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the money market?

options.a: Its instruments are generally low-risk and issued by creditworthy borrowers
