options.d: RTGS processes transfers in batches, while NEFT settles each payment in real time

questions.explanation: Real-Time Gross Settlement handles each large-value payment individually and immediately, while NEFT is a batch-processing transfer system. Option D swaps the two, and options C and A describe neither system correctly.

questions.question: The cheque truncation system introduced in Nigeria in 2012 is

options.a: a rule limiting the value of cheques customers can write
options.b: the manual exchange of cheques by bank representatives at the clearing house
options.c: a system that stops banks from issuing cheque books
options.d: electronic image-based cheque clearing that reduces the physical movement of cheques

questions.explanation: Under cheque truncation, the physical cheque stops at the collecting bank and its electronic image and data are used for clearing, so cheques no longer have to be moved around. Option B describes the old manual clearing it replaced, while options C and A are not what truncation means.

questions.question: In the regulatory framework for Nigerian clearing banks, the body that insures deposits and handles the resolution of failed banks is the

options.a: Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
options.b: Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)

questions.explanation: The NDIC insures deposits, takes part in bank supervision and handles failed bank resolution. Option A is the primary regulator that issues licences and prudential guidelines, option D runs inter-bank payment and clearing infrastructure, and option B registers companies.

questions.question: The drawer of a cheque is the

options.a: person who is to be paid
options.b: bank on which the cheque is drawn
options.c: person who writes out the cheque
options.d: bank official who certifies the payment

questions.explanation: The drawer of a cheque is the person who writes and signs it, ordering his bank to pay a sum of money. The person who is to be paid (Option A) is the payee, and the bank on which the cheque is drawn (Option B) is the drawee. Option D does not describe any of the parties to a cheque.

questions.question: An IOU differs from a promissory note mainly because an IOU

options.a: is an informal acknowledgement of a debt and is not a negotiable instrument
options.b: must always be drawn on a bank
options.c: can be freely transferred to another person by endorsement and delivery
options.d: is an unconditional order addressed by one person to another to pay

questions.explanation: An IOU simply records that one person owes another; it cannot be assigned, sold or traded, while a promissory note is a negotiable instrument. Option B describes a cheque, option C describes negotiability, which is a feature of the promissory note, and option D is the definition of a bill of exchange.

questions.question: An unconditional order in writing, addressed by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money to or to the order of a specified person or to bearer, is a

options.a: bill of exchange
options.b: letter of credit

questions.explanation: This is the statutory definition of a bill of exchange: an order from a drawer to a drawee to pay a sum certain to a payee or bearer. Option C is a promise by the maker himself, not an order to someone else. Options B and D are a bank undertaking in trade finance and a government short-term debt security, not orders of this kind.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, a cheque is best defined as

options.a: a written acknowledgement by a bank that a customer owes it money
options.b: a bill of exchange drawn on a banker payable on demand
options.c: a bill of exchange drawn on any person payable at a fixed future date
options.d: an unconditional promise by a banker to pay the bearer on demand

questions.explanation: A cheque is simply a special kind of bill of exchange: the drawee must be a banker and payment must be on demand. Option C describes a time bill, which may be drawn on anyone. Option D is a promise rather than an order, which is the mark of a promissory note or bank note, and A is not a payment instrument at all.

questions.question: An unconditional promise in writing made by one person to another, signed by the maker, engaging to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum certain in money to a specified person or to bearer, is a

options.a: promissory note
options.b: cheque

questions.explanation: A promissory note is a promise by the maker to pay, so it has only two original parties, the maker and the payee. Options C and B are orders addressed to a drawee (a cheque is an order to a banker), not promises. A banker's draft, option D, is an order drawn by a bank on itself or its branch.

questions.question: The basic difference between a bill of exchange and a promissory note is that

options.a: a bill is an order to pay, while a promissory note is a promise to pay
options.b: a bill has only two parties, while a promissory note has three parties
options.c: a bill need not be in writing, while a promissory note must be in writing
options.d: a bill must be payable on demand, while a promissory note is never payable on demand

questions.explanation: A bill of exchange orders a drawee to pay, whereas in a promissory note the maker himself promises to pay. Option D is wrong because bills can be payable at a future time and a promissory note can be payable on demand. Both instruments must be in writing, so C is wrong, and B reverses the parties: a bill has drawer, drawee and payee, a note has maker and payee.

questions.question: In a promissory note, the person who signs the note and undertakes to pay is called the

options.a: maker
options.b: endorsee

questions.explanation: The maker is the party who makes the promise and signs the note, so he is primarily liable on it. A drawee, option D, and an acceptor, option C, belong to a bill of exchange, where an order is addressed to another person who may then accept it. An endorsee, option B, is someone to whom an instrument has been transferred by endorsement.

questions.question: Mr Bello, who keeps a current account with Zenith Bank, writes a cheque for N250,000 in favour of Mrs Adeyemi. In this transaction the drawee is

options.a: the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: Mr Bello

questions.explanation: The drawee is the bank on which the cheque is drawn, the bank that is ordered to pay, which here is Zenith Bank. Mr Bello, option B, signs the order and so is the drawer, while Mrs Adeyemi, option C, is the payee who will receive the money. The Central Bank, option A, is not a party to the cheque at all.

questions.question: The person to whom a cheque is made payable, usually a creditor of the drawer, is the

options.a: drawee
options.b: payee

questions.explanation: The payee is the person named on the cheque to receive payment, and he presents it for settlement. The drawer, option C, writes and signs the cheque, while the drawee, option A, is the bank ordered to pay. An acceptor, option D, is a drawee of a bill who has signified assent to it, which does not arise with cheques.

questions.question: On whom may a bill of exchange be drawn, compared with a cheque?

options.a: A bill may be drawn only on a banker, while a cheque may be drawn on any person
options.b: A bill may be drawn only on a company, while a cheque may be drawn on any individual
options.c: Both a bill and a cheque may be drawn only on the Central Bank
options.d: A bill may be drawn on any person, including a banker, while a cheque may be drawn only on a banker

questions.explanation: A bill of exchange can be addressed to any person, a trader, a company or a bank, but a cheque by definition must be drawn on a banker. Option A reverses the rule. Options C and B invent restrictions that do not exist in law.

questions.question: Which of the following is a SIMILARITY between a cheque and a bill of exchange?

options.a: Both can be drawn on any person
options.b: Both are negotiable instruments
options.c: Both are entitled to days of grace
options.d: Both require formal acceptance by the drawee

questions.explanation: Cheques and bills of exchange are both negotiable instruments: written, signed orders to pay that can be transferred. Option D is wrong because a cheque needs no acceptance. Days of grace in option C apply only to time bills, and option A fails because a cheque can only be drawn on a banker.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares a cheque with a time (usance) bill of exchange?

options.a: A cheque is entitled to days of grace, while a time bill is payable strictly on demand
options.b: A cheque is payable only after a fixed period, while a time bill is payable on demand
options.c: A cheque must be accepted by the paying bank, while a time bill needs no acceptance
options.d: A cheque needs no formal acceptance, while a time bill is presented to the drawee for acceptance

questions.explanation: A cheque is payable on demand and the bank simply pays or refuses, so no formal acceptance is needed, whereas a drawee of a time bill normally signs an acceptance. Options C, A and B all reverse the true positions: days of grace and fixed future payment belong to time bills, not cheques.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, where a bill payable at a fixed period after date does not otherwise provide, how many days of grace are added to the time of payment?

options.a: Three days
options.b: Fourteen days

questions.explanation: The Act adds three days of grace to the time of payment fixed by a time bill, and the bill is due on the last day of grace. Options C and B are not periods used by the Act. Option D describes a bill payable on demand, which gets no days of grace.

questions.question: A bill of exchange dated 1 March is payable 30 days after date. Under the Bills of Exchange Act, three days of grace are added to such a bill. Counting the period by excluding the day of the date and including the day of payment, and assuming none of the relevant days is a weekend or public holiday, the bill falls due on

options.a: 31 March
options.b: 4 April

questions.explanation: Thirty days after 1 March, excluding 1 March itself, is 31 March; adding the three days of grace gives a due date of 3 April. Option A forgets the days of grace. Option D wrongly counts 1 March as the first day, and option B adds one day too many.

questions.question: Mrs Okon holds an accepted bill of exchange for N800,000 which matures in 73 days. Her bank discounts it at 10% per annum on a 365-day year. How much will she receive?
questions.explanation: The discount is N800,000 x 10% x 73/365 = N16,000, so the bank pays her N800,000 - N16,000 = N784,000 now and collects the full face value at maturity. Option A charges a full year's discount, and option C wrongly adds the discount to the face value. Option D deducts the discount twice.

questions.question: Which of the following instruments can a holder discount with a bank to raise cash before its maturity date?

options.a: An accepted usance bill of exchange
options.b: A certified cheque

questions.explanation: A usance bill is payable at a future date, so a bank can pay the holder now, less a discount, and collect the full amount at maturity. Options C, B and D are all cheques, which are payable on demand and have no future maturity date to discount against.

questions.question: The signification by the drawee of a bill of his assent to the order of the drawer is called

options.a: negotiation
options.b: acceptance

questions.explanation: Acceptance is the drawee's written assent to the drawer's order, usually by signing across the face of the bill, and it makes him the acceptor. Endorsement, option C, is the holder's signature for transfer. Noting, option D, records a dishonour, and negotiation, option A, is the transfer of the bill to a new holder.

questions.question: Once the drawee of a bill of exchange has signed his acceptance on it, he becomes known as the

options.a: acceptor
options.b: holder in due course

questions.explanation: By accepting, the drawee takes on primary liability to pay the bill at maturity and is then called the acceptor. The drawer, option C, is the person who wrote the order. An endorser, option D, signs to transfer the bill, and a holder in due course, option B, is a protected transferee, not the person liable to pay.

questions.question: Alhaji Musa is the drawee of a bill for N500,000. He writes on it "Accepted for N300,000 only" and signs. This is

options.a: a qualified acceptance
options.b: a restrictive endorsement

questions.explanation: An acceptance that varies the effect of the bill as drawn, here by agreeing to pay only part of the amount, is a qualified (partial) acceptance. A general acceptance, option D, assents to the order without any qualification. Options B and C are not acceptances at all: one limits transfer, the other records dishonour.

questions.question: A general acceptance of a bill of exchange is one which

options.a: agrees to pay only part of the sum ordered
options.b: assents without qualification to the order of the drawer
options.c: is given by someone other than the drawee
options.d: agrees to pay only if a stated condition is fulfilled

questions.explanation: A general acceptance simply agrees to the drawer's order exactly as drawn. Options A and D describe partial and conditional acceptances, which are forms of qualified acceptance. Option C is wrong because acceptance is the act of the drawee.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, a bill expressed to be payable "at sight" or "on presentation" is treated as

options.a: a usance bill needing acceptance to fix maturity
options.b: a bill payable on demand
options.c: an invalid bill because no date of payment is stated
options.d: a bill payable three days after presentation

questions.explanation: The Act treats a bill payable at sight or on presentation as a demand (sight) bill, payable as soon as it is presented. Option D confuses this with days of grace, which attach to time bills. Option A describes a bill payable after sight, and option C is wrong because the payment time is clear.

questions.question: A bill reads "Ninety days after sight pay Chika Nwosu or order the sum of N1,200,000." This instrument is

options.a: a sight (demand) bill
options.b: a usance (time) bill

questions.explanation: A bill payable a fixed period after sight is a usance or time bill, because payment falls at a determinable future time. A sight bill, option A, is payable immediately on presentation. Option C is a promise by a maker, not an order, and a cheque, option D, must be drawn on a banker and payable on demand.

questions.question: For which of the following bills is presentment for acceptance necessary in order to fix its maturity date?

options.a: A bill payable on demand
options.b: A bill payable 60 days after sight
options.d: A bill payable 60 days after its date

questions.explanation: When a bill is payable a period after sight, the period can only start running once the drawee has seen and accepted it, so presentment for acceptance fixes the maturity. Options A and C are demand bills paid on presentation. In option D the maturity is already fixed by the date on the bill.

questions.question: Which of the following written orders CANNOT be a valid bill of exchange?

options.a: "Pay Kemi Ade N200,000 thirty days after the death of Chief Ade"
options.b: "Pay Kemi Ade N200,000 thirty days after date"
options.c: "Pay Kemi Ade N200,000 on the day she gets married"

questions.explanation: A bill must be payable on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time, and marriage may never happen, so an order payable on a contingency is not a bill. Options B and D are a time bill and a demand bill. Option A is valid because death is an event certain to happen, even though its date is unknown.

questions.question: A customer writes to her bank: "Pay Ola Stores N90,000 provided the attached receipt is signed by the payee." The instruction is addressed to the bank. In law this document is

options.a: not a cheque, because it is a conditional order
options.b: a promissory note made by the customer

questions.explanation: A cheque must be an unconditional order, and an order addressed to the bank that makes payment depend on a signed receipt is conditional. Options D and C are wrong because the condition stops it being a cheque of any kind. Option B is wrong because the document is an order to the bank, not a promise by the customer to pay.

questions.question: A bill of exchange is drawn in Accra by a Ghanaian exporter and is payable in Lagos. Under the Bills of Exchange Act it is

options.a: an inland bill
options.b: a promissory note

questions.explanation: An inland bill is one both drawn and payable within Nigeria; this bill was drawn outside Nigeria, so it is a foreign bill. Option A would need both drawing and payment in Nigeria. Option D refers to a bill signed to lend credit without value, and option B is a promise rather than an order.

questions.question: A foreign bill of exchange, appearing on its face to be such, is dishonoured by non-payment and the holder fails to have it protested. The effect is that

options.a: the bill becomes payable to bearer
options.b: the drawer and endorsers are discharged
options.c: the drawer remains liable but the acceptor is discharged
options.d: nothing happens, because protest is always optional

questions.explanation: For a dishonoured foreign bill, protest is required, and if the bill is not protested the drawer and endorsers are discharged. Option A has nothing to do with dishonour. Option C is wrong because the acceptor's liability is not what protest preserves, and option D confuses foreign bills with inland bills, where noting is optional.

questions.question: The formal certificate drawn up by a notary public, attesting that a bill of exchange has been dishonoured, is called a

options.a: notice of dishonour
options.b: qualified acceptance

questions.explanation: A protest is the notary's formal certificate of dishonour, usually built on an earlier noting of the bill. Notice of dishonour, option A, is the message the holder sends to the drawer and endorsers, which need not be made by a notary. Options B and D concern accepting and transferring a bill, not recording its dishonour.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, when an inland bill has been dishonoured, noting or protest of the bill is

options.a: compulsory, or all prior parties are discharged
options.b: optional, at the holder's discretion
options.d: done only by the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Act says a dishonoured inland bill may be noted or protested if the holder thinks fit, so it is optional. Option A is the rule for foreign bills, not inland ones. Option C is wrong because noting is allowed, and option D is wrong because noting and protest are the work of a notary public, not the Central Bank.

questions.question: A bill of exchange may be dishonoured in which two ways?

options.a: By non-acceptance and by non-payment
options.b: By crossing and by countermand

questions.explanation: A bill is dishonoured when the drawee refuses to accept it or, after acceptance or at maturity, refuses to pay it. Option C lists the ways a bill is transferred. Option D lists ways of recording a dishonour, not the dishonour itself, and option B relates to cheques.

questions.question: When a bill of exchange is dishonoured, the main purpose of giving notice of dishonour to the drawer and endorsers is to

options.a: transfer ownership of the bill to the drawee
options.b: cancel the drawer's liability on the bill
options.c: preserve the holder's right of recourse against them
options.d: convert the bill into a promissory note

questions.explanation: Notice of dishonour tells prior parties that the bill was not accepted or paid, and it keeps their liability alive so the holder can claim from them. Option A is not what notice does. Option D is impossible, and option B is the opposite: it is failure to give notice that discharges them.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, the "holder" of a bill means

options.a: only the drawee who has accepted the bill
options.b: the bank on which the bill is drawn
options.c: the payee or endorsee who is in possession of it, or the bearer of it
options.d: any person who has ever signed the bill

questions.explanation: A holder is the payee or endorsee in possession of the bill, or the bearer of a bearer bill. Option A describes the acceptor. Option D is too wide, since past signers who have parted with the bill are not holders, and option B describes the drawee bank.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a person to be a holder in due course of a bill?

options.a: He took the bill in good faith and for value
options.b: He took the bill complete and regular on the face of it
options.c: He had no notice of any defect in the title of the person who negotiated it
options.d: He must be the original payee named on the bill

questions.explanation: A holder in due course is a transferee who took a complete and regular bill before it was overdue, in good faith, for value and without notice of any defect in title, so being the original payee is not one of the conditions. Options B, A and C are genuine requirements set by the Act.

questions.question: The main advantage of being a holder in due course of a negotiable instrument is that he

options.a: takes a good title free from defects in the title of prior parties
options.b: can never be sued by any later holder
options.c: is excused from presenting the instrument for payment
options.d: is entitled to three extra days of grace

questions.explanation: The special feature of negotiability is that a holder in due course gets a good title even if an earlier party's title was defective, for example where the instrument had been obtained by fraud. Options B, D and C are not privileges of a holder in due course; he must still present the instrument, and days of grace depend on the type of bill.

questions.question: A thief steals an uncrossed bearer cheque and passes it to Ada, a trader, in exchange for goods. Ada takes it in good faith, for value, before it is overdue and without any notice of the theft, and it is complete and regular. Ada's position is that she

options.a: becomes the drawer of the cheque
options.b: has no title, because a thief cannot pass any title
options.c: must return the cheque because it was a bearer cheque
options.d: is a holder in due course with a good title

questions.explanation: Ada meets every condition for a holder in due course, and such a holder takes free of the defect in the thief's title, so she can enforce the cheque. Option B states the rule for ordinary goods and for instruments crossed "not negotiable", not for a negotiable bearer cheque. Option C has no legal basis, and option A is wrong because the drawer is the person who signed the order.

questions.question: A thief steals a cheque crossed "not negotiable" and transfers it to Ada, who takes it in good faith and for value. Compared with an ordinary crossed cheque, the effect of the words "not negotiable" is that Ada

options.a: gets no better title than the thief had
options.b: can cash the cheque over the counter
options.c: becomes liable as drawer of the cheque
options.d: becomes a holder in due course with a perfect title

questions.explanation: A person who takes a cheque crossed "not negotiable" cannot get or give a better title than his transferor had, so Ada takes the thief's defective title and the true owner can recover. Option D is what she would get without those words. Option B is wrong because any crossing stops over-the-counter payment, and option C confuses her with the drawer.

questions.question: The signature of the holder on a negotiable instrument, usually on the back, made for the purpose of transferring it, is called

options.a: endorsement
options.b: crossing

questions.explanation: Endorsement is the holder's signature that, with delivery, transfers title to the instrument. Acceptance, option D, is the drawee's assent to pay a bill. Crossing, option B, is the two parallel lines on a cheque, and countermand, option C, is the drawer's order to stop payment.

questions.question: Kola, the payee of an order cheque, simply signs his name on the back without naming anyone. Under the Bills of Exchange Act, this is

options.a: a restrictive endorsement, stopping further transfer
options.b: a conditional acceptance by the payee
options.c: a special endorsement, making the cheque payable only to Kola
options.d: a blank endorsement, making the cheque payable to bearer

questions.explanation: An endorsement that names no endorsee is a blank endorsement, and the instrument then becomes payable to bearer. A special endorsement, option C, names the person to be paid. Option A requires words such as "pay X only", and option B is wrong because only a drawee can accept.

questions.question: On the back of a cheque payable to her, Bisi writes "Pay Chinedu Okeke or order" and signs. This is

options.a: a general crossing
options.b: a restrictive endorsement

questions.explanation: A special endorsement names the person to whom, or to whose order, the instrument is to be paid, here Chinedu Okeke. A blank endorsement, option D, would be her bare signature. Option B would forbid further transfer, but "or order" allows Chinedu to transfer it again, and option A is made with lines on the front, not words on the back.

questions.question: Which of the following endorsements is a restrictive endorsement?

options.a: "Funke" written alone on the back
options.b: "Pay Musa Ibrahim only" - signed Funke
options.d: "Pay Musa Ibrahim or order" - signed Funke

questions.explanation: A restrictive endorsement prohibits further negotiation, and the word "only" means Musa can receive payment but cannot transfer the instrument. Option D is a special endorsement that allows further transfer. Option A is a blank endorsement, and option C makes the instrument payable to bearer, which makes transfer easier, not harder.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, which of the following is a requirement for a valid endorsement?

options.a: It must be witnessed by a notary public
options.b: It must be approved by the drawee bank in writing
options.c: It must be written on the bill itself and signed by the endorser
options.d: It must state the reason for the transfer

questions.explanation: The Act requires an endorsement to be written on the bill itself and signed by the endorser, and his bare signature is enough. Option A confuses endorsement with noting and protest. Options D and B add conditions the Act does not require.

questions.question: How does a bearer cheque differ from an order cheque?

options.a: A bearer cheque must be paid into an account, while an order cheque can only be cashed over the counter
options.b: A bearer cheque is always crossed, while an order cheque is always open
options.c: A bearer cheque is payable to whoever presents it without endorsement, while an order cheque is payable to the named payee or as he directs by endorsement
options.d: A bearer cheque needs acceptance by the bank, while an order cheque does not

questions.explanation: A bearer cheque can be cashed by anyone holding it and passes by mere delivery, while an order cheque is payable to the named payee or to his order, so it needs his endorsement to be transferred. Option A is about crossing, not bearer or order status. Options D and B are wrong because cheques need no acceptance and either type can be open or crossed.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, where the payee named on a bill or cheque is a fictitious or non-existing person, the instrument

options.a: is void and cannot be paid at all
options.b: may be treated as payable to bearer
options.c: becomes payable only to the drawee
options.d: must first be protested by a notary public

questions.explanation: The Act provides that a bill whose payee is fictitious or non-existing may be treated as payable to bearer. Option A overstates the effect, since the instrument is not void. Options C and D have no basis in the Act.

questions.question: A cheque that is not crossed and can therefore be presented and cashed over the counter of the bank on which it is drawn is

options.a: an open cheque
options.b: a post-dated cheque

questions.explanation: An open cheque carries no crossing, so the paying bank can pay cash over the counter, which also makes it risky if it falls into the wrong hands. A crossed cheque, option D, must be paid through a bank account. Options C and B describe cheques that are too old or dated in the future, not their crossing status.

questions.question: Crossing a cheque involves

options.a: signing the back of the cheque before handing it to the payee
options.b: stamping the cheque "paid" after encashment
options.c: drawing two parallel transverse lines across the face of the cheque
options.d: writing the date on the cheque in red ink

questions.explanation: A crossing is made by drawing two parallel transverse lines across the face of the cheque, with or without words such as "& Co" between them. Option A describes an endorsement. Options D and B have nothing to do with crossing; a paid stamp is what the bank applies after payment.

questions.question: Mr Eze draws two parallel lines across his cheque and writes "& Co" between them. No bank is named. This is

options.a: an account payee crossing
options.b: a restrictive endorsement

questions.explanation: Two parallel lines, with or without "& Co" and with no bank named, form a general crossing, so the cheque can only be paid through a bank account. A special crossing, option D, must name a particular bank between the lines. Option A needs the words "account payee", and option B is written on the back.

questions.question: A cheque has two parallel lines on its face with "Guaranty Trust Bank Plc" written between them. This crossing means the cheque

options.a: can be paid to any bank presenting it
options.b: can be cashed over the counter by the payee
options.c: is not negotiable and cannot be transferred
options.d: can be paid only to Guaranty Trust Bank

questions.explanation: Writing a bank's name in the crossing makes it a special crossing, so the paying bank may pay only to the bank named. Option A describes a general crossing. Option B is impossible for any crossed cheque, and option C is the effect of the words "not negotiable", not of naming a bank.

questions.question: A cheque crossed "Account payee only" operates mainly as

options.a: a direction to the collecting bank to credit the proceeds only to the payee's account
options.b: a notice that the drawer has stopped payment
options.c: an instruction to the paying bank to pay cash only to the payee
options.d: proof that the paying bank has certified the drawer's funds

questions.explanation: "Account payee" tells the collecting bank that only the named payee's account should be credited with the proceeds. Option C is wrong because a crossed cheque is never paid in cash over the counter. Option D describes a certified cheque, and option B describes a countermand.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, who may cross an uncrossed cheque?

options.a: Only the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.b: The drawer, or a holder of the cheque

questions.explanation: The Act allows the drawer to cross a cheque, and also allows a holder to cross an uncrossed cheque generally or specially; a banker may add a special crossing for collection. Options D and C wrongly limit this right to one person, and option A has no role in crossing.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, a crossing on a cheque

options.a: has no legal effect and is only a banking custom
options.b: becomes void after the cheque is endorsed
options.c: may be cancelled by any holder who wants cash
options.d: is a material part of the cheque and may not be unlawfully obliterated or altered

questions.explanation: The Act makes an authorised crossing an essential part of the cheque, and it is unlawful to obliterate it or add to or alter it except as the Act allows. Options C and B wrongly suggest it can simply disappear. Option A is wrong because crossings have statutory force.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of crossing a cheque?

options.a: It helps to trace the person who received payment if the cheque was stolen
options.b: It ensures payment is made through a bank account
options.c: It protects the owner against loss by theft
options.d: It allows the payee to cash the cheque faster over the counter

questions.explanation: Crossing does the opposite of option D: it prevents payment over the counter, so the money must pass through a bank account. Options C, A and B are genuine benefits, because a thief cannot easily get cash and the collecting bank and account can be traced.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of payment by cheque?

options.a: It guarantees that the drawer has enough funds in the account
options.b: It economises the use of currency notes and coins
options.c: It serves as proof of payment
options.d: Payment can easily be stopped to prevent fraud

questions.explanation: An ordinary cheque carries no guarantee of funds, which is why cheques can bounce; only a certified cheque gives that assurance. Options C, B and D are genuine advantages of paying by cheque.

questions.question: Which of the following is a proper precaution when drawing a cheque?

options.a: The drawer should sign any alteration made on the cheque
options.b: The amount should be written in figures only
options.c: The payee's name should be left blank for the bank to fill in
options.d: The cheque should be folded before it is handed over

questions.explanation: The drawer must sign any alteration so the bank knows it was authorised. Options B, D and C are the reverse of good practice: the amount should be in words and figures, the cheque should not be folded, and the payee's name should be written properly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a cheque?

options.a: It is an unconditional order
options.b: It must be in writing
options.d: It must be accepted by the drawee bank before payment

questions.explanation: A cheque is payable on demand and needs no formal acceptance, so option D is not one of its characteristics. Options A, B and C are true: a cheque is an unconditional written order for a specified amount.

questions.question: A cheque that has been in circulation for an unreasonably long time, so that in Nigerian banking practice a bank will refuse it once it is more than six months old, is

options.a: a post-dated cheque
options.b: a stale cheque

questions.explanation: A stale cheque is one presented too long after its date, and banks in Nigeria treat a cheque more than six months old as expired. A post-dated cheque, option A, carries a future date. A countermanded cheque, option D, has been stopped by the drawer, and option C has been confirmed by the bank as funded.

questions.question: Ngozi receives a cheque dated 2 January but forgets it in her drawer and presents it on 10 August of the same year. Under Nigerian banking practice the paying bank will most likely

options.a: refuse payment because the cheque is stale
options.b: refuse payment because the cheque is post-dated
options.c: pay it, since cheques never expire
options.d: pay it only after the drawer accepts it

questions.explanation: More than six months have passed since 2 January, so the cheque is stale and the bank will return it, leaving Ngozi to ask the drawer for a fresh one. Option C ignores the six-month practice. Option D wrongly brings acceptance into cheques, and option B is wrong because the date is in the past, not the future.

questions.question: On 15 November, Tunde is handed a cheque dated 30 November of the same year and presents it at the bank the same day. The bank will

options.a: pay it at once because the date is irrelevant
options.b: pay it only if it is crossed
options.c: refuse to pay it until 30 November because it is post-dated
options.d: treat it as stale and cancel it

questions.explanation: A post-dated cheque bears a later date than the day it was issued, and it cannot be paid before that date, so the bank will return it if presented early. Option A ignores the date written on it. Option D confuses it with a stale cheque, and option B is wrong because crossing does not change when a cheque may be paid.

questions.question: A cheque which the drawee bank has marked to confirm that the drawer has sufficient funds to meet it is

options.a: a bearer cheque
options.b: a dishonoured cheque

questions.explanation: A certified cheque has been confirmed by the bank as covered by the drawer's funds, which makes it much more acceptable to the payee. Options A and D describe who may be paid and whether the cheque is crossed, not any bank guarantee. Option B is a cheque the bank has refused to pay.

questions.question: Under Nigerian banking practice, a customer who wishes to stop payment (countermand) of a cheque should give the bank an instruction that is

options.a: endorsed on the back of the cheque by the payee
options.b: verbal, given to any staff member at any branch
options.c: in writing, clear and signed in line with his mandate, before the cheque is paid
options.d: by telephone, after the cheque has been paid

questions.explanation: A countermand must reach the bank before payment and should be written, unambiguous and signed as the account mandate requires, so the bank can act on it safely. Option D is too late, since a cheque already paid cannot be stopped. Option B lacks the written, signed form, and option A is wrong because the payee cannot stop the drawer's cheque.

questions.question: On Monday, Union Bank receives a death certificate showing that its customer, Mr Okafor, died on Saturday. On Tuesday, a cheque he signed last week is presented for payment. The bank should

options.a: pay the cheque, because it was signed before he died
options.b: pay half the amount and keep the rest for the estate
options.c: pay the cheque if the payee endorses it
options.d: not pay the cheque, because notice of death ends its authority to pay

questions.explanation: Once a bank has notice of its customer's death, its authority to pay his cheques ends, even for cheques he signed while alive. Option A ignores this rule, and option C wrongly suggests endorsement overcomes it. Option B has no basis; the funds belong to the estate and are dealt with by the personal representatives.

questions.question: A court order served on a bank attaching the credit balance in a customer's account to satisfy a judgment debt, so that the bank may not pay the customer's cheques out of that balance, is

options.a: a notice of dishonour
options.b: a garnishee order

questions.explanation: A garnishee order attaches the money a bank owes its customer so that it goes to the judgment creditor, and the bank must not pay cheques against it. Option D gives someone authority to act for the customer. A countermand, option C, comes from the customer himself, and option A is notice that an instrument was not paid.

questions.question: A cheque is paid by a bank, but it later turns out that the drawer's signature was forged by a dismissed employee. The general legal position is that

options.a: the bank cannot debit the customer's account, because a forged signature gives it no mandate
options.b: the customer must bear the loss, because the cheque book was his
options.c: the bank may debit the customer, because the cheque looked regular
options.d: the payee must refund the bank before the customer can complain

questions.explanation: A forged drawer's signature is wholly inoperative, so the customer never gave the bank an order to pay and the bank cannot charge his account. Option C confuses this with the protection given for forged endorsements in some cases, not forged drawer's signatures. Options B and D shift the loss without any legal basis, unless the customer's own conduct caused it.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT end a bank's authority to pay its customer's cheques?

options.a: A valid written countermand by the customer
options.b: Notice of a bankruptcy petition against the customer
options.d: The customer's issue of a new cheque book

questions.explanation: Issuing a new cheque book is routine and has no effect on the bank's authority to pay. Options C, B and A are recognised grounds on which the bank's authority to pay ends or the bank must not pay.

questions.question: Which of the following is a proper reason for a bank to dishonour a customer's cheque?

options.a: The payee is a customer of another bank
options.b: The drawer's account does not have enough funds to cover it
options.c: The cheque is presented by the payee in person
options.d: The cheque is drawn for a large amount

questions.explanation: A bank need not pay a cheque that is not covered by the balance or an agreed overdraft. Option A is normal, since clearing exists for cheques payable to customers of other banks. Options D and C are not grounds for refusing payment on their own.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, where a bill or cheque is materially altered without the assent of all parties liable on it, the instrument is

options.a: valid only if the drawee bank initials the change
options.b: automatically converted into a promissory note
options.c: still fully valid against every party
options.d: avoided, except against a party who made, authorised or assented to the alteration

questions.explanation: An alteration of an essential term, such as the amount, date or payee, made without everyone's assent avoids the instrument, except against the person who made or agreed to the change; this is why banks return cheques with alterations not signed by the drawer. Option C ignores the alteration rule. Options B and A have no basis in the Act, because it is the drawer, not the bank, who must confirm changes.

questions.question: A bank wrongfully dishonours a customer's cheque even though his account was in credit and nothing barred payment. The bank is

options.a: entitled to charge the customer a returned-cheque fee
options.b: liable only to the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: not liable, since a bank may refuse any cheque
options.d: liable to the customer in damages for breach of contract

questions.explanation: A bank's contract with its customer requires it to pay properly drawn cheques when funds are available, so dishonouring one without justification is a breach of contract for which damages can be claimed. Option C wrongly gives the bank a free choice. Options B and A ignore that the injured party is the customer.

questions.question: Under the Bills of Exchange Act, an undated cheque is

options.a: void and of no effect from the start
options.b: treated as a promissory note
options.c: not invalid in law, though bankers by custom usually refuse to pay it until it is dated

questions.explanation: The date is not an essential part of a bill, so an undated instrument is not invalid, but it is a general custom of bankers to refuse undated cheques. Option A overstates the law. Options D and B have no basis.

questions.question: Until a cheque has been endorsed, the only party who is liable on it is the

options.a: drawee bank
options.b: drawer

questions.explanation: No one is liable on a cheque until he signs it, and before any endorsement the only signature is the drawer's. The payee, option D, becomes liable only after he endorses it. The banks in options A and C do not sign the cheque and so are not liable on it as parties.

questions.question: The Bills of Exchange Act protects a paying banker who pays a crossed cheque in accordance with the crossing when he acts

options.a: only when the drawer is present in the banking hall
options.b: only after obtaining a court order
options.c: only if the cheque is less than one month old
options.d: in good faith and without negligence

questions.explanation: Where a banker on whom a crossed cheque is drawn pays it in good faith, without negligence and in line with the crossing, the Act protects him. Options B, A and C are not conditions of that protection.

questions.question: A collecting bank collects a stolen crossed cheque, but it does so for a person who is not its customer and without checking his identity. The bank is most likely to

options.a: be fully protected because it acted only as an agent
options.b: be protected because the cheque was crossed
options.c: lose its statutory protection and be liable to the true owner
options.d: pass all liability to the paying bank

questions.explanation: The collecting banker's protection covers collection for a customer in good faith and without negligence, so collecting for a non-customer without proper checks is negligent and exposes the bank to the true owner. Options A and B forget that the protection depends on care, not just on agency or crossing. Option D has no basis.

questions.question: The procedure through which a bank collects the proceeds of a cheque drawn on another bank in favour of its own customer is called

options.a: countermanding
options.b: discounting

questions.explanation: Clearing is the exchange and settlement of cheques between banks so that a bank can obtain value for cheques drawn on other banks. Discounting, option B, is buying a bill before maturity. Countermanding, option A, is stopping payment, and certification, option C, is confirming the drawer's funds.

questions.question: In the Nigerian cheque clearing system, MICR stands for

options.a: Multiple Interbank Credit Reconciliation
options.b: Manual Interbank Cheque Register

questions.explanation: MICR is Magnetic Ink Character Recognition, a technology in which codes printed in magnetic ink on a cheque are read by machines to speed up sorting and processing. Options B, D and A are made-up names that sound like banking terms but are not what MICR means.

questions.question: In the Nigerian automated cheque clearing system, an indirect participating bank is one that

options.a: exchanges cheques directly at the clearing house with its own equipment
options.b: does not accept cheques from its customers at all
options.c: manages the zonal clearing house for all banks
options.d: takes part in clearing through a direct participating bank

questions.explanation: An indirect participant does not clear on its own account but clears its cheques through a direct participating bank. Option A describes a direct participant. Option C is the role of the clearing house itself, and option B is not a category of clearing participant.

questions.question: Which of the following cheques would NOT need to pass through the interbank clearing system?

options.a: A cheque drawn on Bank C and paid into an account at Bank D
options.b: A cheque drawn on Bank A and paid into another account at Bank A
options.c: A cheque drawn on Bank B and paid into an account at Bank A
options.d: A cheque drawn on Bank A and paid into an account at Bank B

questions.explanation: Clearing is needed to obtain value for non-in-house cheques, those drawn on a different bank from the one collecting them. In option B the same bank is both paying and collecting, so it settles internally. Options D, C and A all involve two different banks and must go through clearing.

questions.question: A person who signs a bill of exchange as drawer, acceptor or endorser without receiving value for it, in order to lend his name to another person, is

options.a: a payee
options.b: a drawee in case of need

questions.explanation: An accommodation party signs a bill without receiving value, purely to lend his name and credit to someone else, and he is liable to a holder for value. Option C is a transferee who took the bill for value. Option B is a person named to be approached if the drawee dishonours the bill, and option A is the person to whom the bill is payable.

questions.question: A bill of exchange contains words prohibiting its transfer, such as "Pay Ade only". Under the Bills of Exchange Act, the bill is

options.a: negotiable by delivery alone
options.b: payable to bearer
options.c: valid between the parties but not negotiable

questions.explanation: Words prohibiting transfer do not destroy the bill; it remains valid between the original parties but cannot be negotiated to anyone else. Option D goes too far. Options A and B describe the opposite of what the words do.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the features normally seen on the face of a completed cheque?

options.a: The date
options.b: The amount in words and in figures

questions.explanation: A completed cheque shows the payee, the drawee bank, the amount in words and figures, the date, the account number and the drawer's signature. Option C does not appear because a cheque is not accepted by the drawee. Options B, A and D are standard features of a cheque.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which payment device looks like a credit card but carries a memory chip that stores value and keeps a record of the transactions made with it, and has been described as a 'cashless wallet'?

options.a: Travellers' cheque
options.b: Smart card

questions.explanation: A smart card is a plastic card with an embedded memory chip that stores value and an up-to-date record of every transaction made with it, which is why it is described as a cashless wallet. Its chip security also helps to reduce fraud and allows secure off-line payments. Options A and C are paper payment instruments, and option D only assures a payee that a cheque up to a stated limit will be honoured, so none of them stores value on a chip.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: SWIFT, the network widely used for electronic fund transfers between banks across the world, mainly provides:

options.a: insurance cover for deposits that customers hold in foreign banks
options.b: a secure system for banks to send payment instructions and other financial messages to one another
options.c: a stock exchange on which the shares of international banks are traded
options.d: a plastic card that bank customers use to withdraw cash from ATMs

questions.explanation: SWIFT stands for the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. It is a messaging network that lets banks exchange standardised, secure instructions for payments, foreign exchange and other transactions, which makes cross-border transfers fast and reliable. Options D, A and C describe a payment card, deposit insurance and a stock exchange, none of which is what SWIFT does.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A plastic card similar to a credit card but with an embedded microchip that stores information and keeps a record of the transactions carried out on it is called a:

options.a: standing order
options.b: traveller's cheque

questions.explanation: A smart card carries a memory chip that stores data and transaction records and can hold security features such as PINs or biometric details, which makes payments secure and helps reduce fraud. A bank draft (option C) is a cheque drawn by a bank on itself, a standing order (option A) is an instruction to a bank to make regular payments, and a traveller's cheque (option B) is a pre-printed cheque meant for travellers.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A customer of your bank, Mr Emeka, has a standing order of N5,000.00 due on the last day of every month. On 1 March 1996 his account had an opening balance of N1,000.00 DR. A local cheque for N8,000.00 was paid into his account on 6 March. On 10 March he was issued a cheque book and his account was debited N100.00 for its cost. On 22 March he issued a cheque of N1,950.00 to Ben, and on 25 March he made a cash lodgement of N920.00. The bank charges 1/2% for standing order services and N50.00 for postage, and he has an overdraft limit of N1,000.00. Which of the following is correct for the standing order due at the end of March?

options.a: The bank will pay the standing order, leaving a balance of N2,795.00 CR after the payment and charges
options.b: The bank will pay the standing order, leaving a balance of N870.00 CR after the payment and charges
options.c: The bank will not pay the standing order, because N5,000.00 is more than his N1,000.00 overdraft limit
options.d: The bank will pay the standing order, leaving a balance of N795.00 CR after the payment and charges

questions.explanation: Before the standing order, the account has N8,920.00 of credits against N3,050.00 of debits (the N1,000.00 opening debit, N100.00 for the cheque book and the N1,950.00 cheque), giving N5,870.00 CR. The standing order and charges total N5,000.00 + N25.00 (1/2% of N5,000.00) + N50.00 = N5,075.00, which the balance covers, leaving N795.00 CR. Option B forgets the commission and postage, option A treats the opening N1,000.00 debit as a credit, and option C is wrong because there are enough funds, so the overdraft is not even needed.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is an international method of payment rather than a domestic one?

options.a: Standing order
options.b: Direct debit

questions.explanation: A documentary letter of credit is used in foreign trade to guarantee that an overseas exporter is paid if he meets the terms of the credit. Options A, B and C are domestic methods used to move funds between accounts within the country.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: The main difference between a direct debit and a standing order is that

options.a: a standing order is started by the beneficiary, while a direct debit is started by the customer
options.b: a standing order can be used only for international payments
options.c: a direct debit is started by the beneficiary (creditor) with the customer's authority, while a standing order is started by the customer
options.d: a direct debit needs no authority from the customer whose account is debited

questions.explanation: With a direct debit, the creditor, such as an insurance company, prepares the claim and the customer signs an authority allowing the bank to debit his account; with a standing order, the customer himself tells the bank to make regular payments. Option A swaps the two, option B is wrong because standing orders are a domestic method, and option D is wrong because the customer's signed authority is essential.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: As methods of payment in Nigeria, a bank cheque differs from a bank draft in that

options.a: a bank draft is used only within the same clearing area, while a bank cheque can be used anywhere
options.b: a bank cheque is used within the same clearing area, while a bank draft is drawn by one branch on another branch or head office and can be used across clearing areas
options.c: a bank cheque is drawn by the customer on his own account, while a bank draft is drawn by the central bank
options.d: a bank draft may be freely dishonoured, while a bank cheque never can be

questions.explanation: Both are bank instruments bought by the customer, but a bank cheque has the narrower use, within one clearing area, while a draft is drawn by a branch on another branch or head office of the same bank for payments elsewhere. Option A swaps them, option C confuses a bank cheque with a personal cheque and wrongly involves the central bank, and option D is wrong because drafts, being bank instruments, are not normally dishonoured.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Electronic banking can best be described as:

options.a: The use of ledger cards and manual files to record customers' accounts
options.b: A system in which only the Central Bank of Nigeria may carry out transactions
options.c: The delivery of banking services through electronic channels such as cards, ATMs, POS terminals, electronic funds transfer, telephone and internet banking
options.d: Banking in which all transactions must be done over the counter with cash

questions.explanation: Electronic banking uses technology so that customers can pay, transfer, withdraw and check balances without handling cash or visiting the banking hall, moving the economy towards cashless payments. Over-the-counter cash (D) and manual ledger records (A) are traditional methods it replaces. E-banking is open to ordinary bank customers, not just the CBN (B).

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a problem that limits the use of cash as an efficient means of payment in Nigeria?

options.a: Cash leaves an electronic record of every transaction
options.b: Carrying large sums of cash exposes people and businesses to robbery
options.c: Large amounts of cash must be carried because of the falling value of the naira
options.d: Banks spend heavily on staff and counting machines to handle cash

questions.explanation: Cash leaves no electronic trail, which is one reason electronic payments are preferred, so this statement is false and is not a problem of cash. The need to carry bulky sums (C), the risk of robbery (B) and the high cost of handling cash (D) are all real problems that pushed banks towards cards and electronic payments.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an electronic banking service?

options.a: Withdrawing cash over the counter with a withdrawal slip signed in the banking hall
options.b: Internet banking

questions.explanation: Withdrawing cash with a paper slip at the counter is a traditional, manual service. Internet banking (B), electronic funds transfer (D) and telephone banking (C) all use electronic channels to deliver banking services, together with smart cards, ATMs and POS terminals.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following services is NOT normally provided through an automated teller machine (ATM)?

options.a: Approving a new loan application
options.b: Transferring funds between accounts
options.c: Checking the current balance on an account

questions.explanation: An ATM is a self-service machine that does a cashier's routine work: cash withdrawals (D), balance enquiries (C), transfers (B), mini-statements and, on some machines, cash deposits. Approving a loan needs a credit officer's appraisal of the borrower, so an ATM cannot do it.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: To carry out most transactions at an ATM, a bank customer must use a card together with:

options.a: A letter of introduction from a referee
options.b: A cheque book

questions.explanation: The PIN shows that the person using the card is the genuine cardholder, so it replaces the signature used in the banking hall. A specimen signature card (C) is checked against paper instruments by bank staff, a cheque book (B) is not used at ATMs, and a referee's letter (A) is needed only when opening an account.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: An instruction given by a customer to his bank to make regular payments of a fixed amount, at weekly, monthly or quarterly intervals, from his account to a named third party is a:

options.a: direct debit
options.b: standing order

questions.explanation: A standing order is the customer's own instruction to his bank to pay a stated amount to a named beneficiary at regular intervals. Option A is a direct debit, which is started by the beneficiary rather than the customer. Option C is a single bank instrument for one payment, and option D is used by banks to pay each other.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Mrs Okafor instructs her bank in Surulere to pay N45,000 to her landlord's account on the first day of every month until further notice. This arrangement is a:

options.a: direct debit
options.b: credit transfer by bank giro

questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor, the payer, gave her own bank a continuing instruction to pay a fixed sum at fixed dates, which is exactly a standing order. Option A would be wrong because in a direct debit the landlord, not Mrs Okafor, would send the claims to the bank. Option B is a one-off transfer made by filling credit slips, and option C relates to collecting bills of exchange.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Standing orders are regularly used to make all the following payments EXCEPT:

options.a: insurance premiums
options.b: a one-off purchase of a used car from a stranger

questions.explanation: Standing orders suit recurring payments of a regular amount, such as premiums, rents, subscriptions, school fees and hire purchase or loan instalments. A one-off payment, option B, does not recur, so it would be made by cheque, draft or transfer instead. Options A, D and C are all typical standing order payments.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: On the due date of a standing order, the customer's account has insufficient funds and no overdraft arrangement. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The bank must pay and charge penal interest on the debit balance
options.b: The bank must pay and recover the amount later from the customer
options.c: The bank must refer the payee to the customer's employer
options.d: The bank is not obliged to pay and incurs no liability for not paying

questions.explanation: A bank carries out a standing order only out of available funds or an agreed credit facility, so when funds are insufficient it may refuse and is not liable for the non-payment. Options B and A wrongly suggest the bank must grant an unarranged overdraft. Option C has no basis in banking practice.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A banker's obligation to carry out a standing order stops in each of the following situations EXCEPT where:

options.a: the balance is insufficient and there is no credit arrangement
options.b: the beneficiary writes directly to the bank asking it to cancel the order
options.c: a garnishee order stops payment out of the account

questions.explanation: A standing order is the customer's mandate, so only the customer (or the law, through a garnishee order) can stop it, while lack of funds also excuses the bank. A request from the payee alone, option B, must be disregarded unless the customer confirms it. Options D, C and A are genuine cases where the bank's duty to pay ends.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Mr Bello's standing order pays N20,000 monthly to his cooperative society. The society's secretary telephones Mr Bello's bank asking why this month's payment was late. The bank should:

options.a: decline to explain and advise the society to contact Mr Bello
options.b: pay the society twice next month to make up
options.c: give the secretary details of Mr Bello's account balance
options.d: cancel the standing order to avoid further complaints

questions.explanation: The bank owes its customer a duty of secrecy, so it should not discuss the reason for the delay with the payee but should refer the payee to the customer. Option C would breach the duty of confidentiality, option D would ignore the customer's mandate, and option B is not authorised by the customer.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: If the beneficiary of a standing order refuses to accept the payments, the paying bank should:

options.a: return the standing order card to the beneficiary
options.b: stop the standing order immediately without telling the customer
options.c: transfer the money to the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.d: continue making each payment as it falls due and notify the customer of each refusal

questions.explanation: The bank acts on its customer's mandate, so it keeps paying as instructed while informing the customer of every refusal, leaving the customer to decide whether to cancel. Option B would act without the customer's authority, and options C and A have no basis in standing order practice.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is a duty of the CUSTOMER in a standing order arrangement?

options.a: To send periodic statements of account to the bank
options.b: To charge commission for the service rendered
options.c: To notify the bank promptly when the standing order is to be discontinued
options.d: To handle the order with diligence and care on behalf of the bank

questions.explanation: The customer must give accurate details, keep enough funds in the account, pay the charges and tell the bank promptly when the order should stop. Option A and option D are duties of the banker, and option B is a right of the banker.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of a standing order to the CUSTOMER?

options.a: The onus of making payment on the due dates rests with the banker
options.b: It widens the range of services the bank offers
options.c: The payee can vary the amount without the customer's consent
options.d: The bank earns commission income from the service

questions.explanation: With a standing order the customer need not remember each due date, because the bank pays automatically and also provides a record of payment. Options D and B are benefits to the bank, not the customer, and option C is false because only the customer can change a standing order.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A bank needs all of the following information before it sets up a standing order EXCEPT:

options.a: the beneficiary's monthly income
options.b: the name and account number of the beneficiary
options.c: the customer's signature in line with the account mandate
options.d: the amount and the intervals of payment

questions.explanation: To set up a standing order the bank needs the customer's signed application, the beneficiary's name, bank and account number, the amount and the payment intervals. The beneficiary's income, option A, is irrelevant to the payment. Options B, D and C are all required particulars.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A method of payment in which the BENEFICIARY (creditor) initiates the process, sending claims to the bank under an authority signed by the paying customer, is called a:

options.a: direct debit
options.b: credit transfer

questions.explanation: Under a direct debit the creditor, with the debtor's signed authority, sends debit claims to the bank, which then debits the debtor's account. Option C is started by the paying customer himself. Options B and D are payments pushed out by the payer, not pulled by the creditor.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: The key difference between a standing order and a direct debit is that:

options.a: a standing order is used only abroad, while a direct debit is used only locally
options.b: a standing order is initiated by the payer, while a direct debit is initiated by the beneficiary
options.c: a standing order needs no signature, while a direct debit needs two
options.d: a standing order is paid in cash, while a direct debit is paid by draft

questions.explanation: In a standing order the payer instructs his own bank to push regular payments out, but in a direct debit the creditor pulls payments from the payer's account under an authority the payer signed. For that reason a direct debit can also handle varying amounts. Options A, C and D describe differences that do not exist.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: An insurance company sends signed debit claims to Union Bank from time to time, under an authority endorsed by its policyholder Mr Musa, so that premiums can be taken from his account. This method of payment is a:

options.a: documentary collection
options.b: banker's payment

questions.explanation: The creditor (the insurance company) initiates each claim using the debtor's endorsed authority, which is the mark of a direct debit; insurance companies and finance houses commonly use it. Option D would be started by Mr Musa himself. Option B is used between banks, and option A belongs to international trade.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A gym in Lekki charges a different amount each month depending on the classes a member attends. Which payment method best suits collecting these monthly fees from members' accounts?

options.a: Standing order
options.b: Direct debit

questions.explanation: A direct debit lets the originator collect variable amounts from the customer's account under the customer's authority, so it fits a fee that changes monthly. Option A pays a fixed amount fixed by the customer, so it would need amending every month. Options C and D are single instruments for one payment each.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A cheque drawn by a branch of a bank on another branch or on the head office of the same bank, signed by the bank's own authorised signatories, is a:

options.a: bank draft
options.b: dividend warrant

questions.explanation: A bank draft is a bank's own instrument drawn by one of its branches on another branch or its head office, so the bank itself is liable on it. Option D is drawn by a customer on his own account, option B is a cheque drawn by a company to pay shareholders, and option C is a prepaid instrument for travel abroad.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Many suppliers insist on being paid by bank draft rather than by personal cheque mainly because:

options.a: a draft does not need to pass through any bank
options.b: a draft is a bank's own instrument and is not normally dishonoured on presentation
options.c: a draft carries interest from the date of issue
options.d: a draft can only be drawn for small amounts

questions.explanation: Because the bank itself is the drawer of a draft, the risk of it bouncing for lack of funds is removed, which is why creditors prefer it to a personal cheque. Option C is false since drafts earn no interest. Option D is wrong because drafts are used for large payments, and option A is wrong because a draft is paid through the banking system.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: When a bank issues a draft, the issuing branch sends the paying branch an advice giving the particulars of the draft. The purpose of this advice is to:

options.a: notify the Central Bank of Nigeria of the transaction
options.b: inform the beneficiary's employer of the payment
options.c: allow the paying branch to confirm that the draft presented is genuine

questions.explanation: The advice, signed by the same signatories as the draft, lets the paying branch check the draft against its details before paying, which guards against forged or altered drafts. Options B, A and D are not functions of a draft advice.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: In banking practice, a bank cheque differs from a bank draft in that a bank cheque:

options.a: can be dishonoured for lack of funds, while a draft cannot
options.b: is drawn by the customer on his own account, while a draft is drawn by the bank
options.c: is used only for international payments, while a draft is used only locally
options.d: is used within the same clearing area, while a draft is used where other clearing areas are involved

questions.explanation: Both are bank instruments, but a bank cheque is cleared within the same clearing locality, so it has a narrower use than a draft, which can be used across clearing areas and even internationally. Option B is wrong because a bank cheque is also issued by the bank, option A is wrong because both are backed by the bank, and option C reverses the scope.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Which of the following is the simplest and most common method of paying a debt within the domestic economy, though creditors may avoid it because of fraud and dishonour?

options.a: Bill negotiation
options.b: A documentary letter of credit

questions.explanation: A personal cheque is the simplest domestic payment method and is used for goods, services, fees and premiums, but because it can bounce or be forged many creditors prefer drafts or standing orders. Options B, C and A are mainly international payment and settlement methods.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: An instrument used by banks to pay EACH OTHER, for example for cash supplied by one bank to another or for the proceeds of a cheque sent for special clearing, is a:

options.a: standing order
options.b: dividend warrant

questions.explanation: A banker's payment is the instrument a bank issues in favour of another bank to settle obligations between them, such as cash exchange or special clearing proceeds. Options A and D are customer payment methods, and option B is a company's cheque to its shareholders.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: After heavy cash withdrawals, Bank X asks Bank Y to supply it with N50 million in cash. Bank X settles by issuing an instrument in favour of Bank Y, and the amount passes through clearing. The instrument issued is a:

options.a: banker's payment
options.b: standing order
options.c: bank draft in favour of a customer

questions.explanation: When one bank pays another for cash supplied, it issues a banker's payment, after which Bank X is debited and Bank Y credited through clearing. Option C is drawn for a customer's beneficiary, option B is a customer's periodic instruction, and option D is used in international trade.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: Chidi writes to his bank to move N200,000 from his savings account to his current account at the same bank so that a cheque he has already issued can be paid. This is an example of:

options.a: a banker's payment
options.b: a direct debit

questions.explanation: Moving funds between accounts of the same customer in the same bank is an intra-bank transfer, often done by letter of instruction. Option C sends funds to another place, option A is a payment between banks, and option B is initiated by a creditor.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: The main advantage of a telegraphic transfer over a mail transfer is that a telegraphic transfer:

options.a: can only be used within the same branch
options.b: moves the payment instruction much faster, by cable, telex or electronic message
options.c: never involves a debit to the customer's account
options.d: does not need the beneficiary's account details

questions.explanation: In both methods the customer gives written instructions and the bank debits his account, but a mail transfer sends the instruction by post while a telegraphic transfer sends it by telegraph or telex, so it is much faster. Option C is false because the remitter is always debited, option A is false because these transfers go to other places, and option D is false because beneficiary details are required.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: To remit funds by mail or telegraphic transfer, a customer gives the bank written instructions stating all the following EXCEPT:

options.a: the name of the beneficiary
options.b: the beneficiary's bank and account number

questions.explanation: A transfer instruction must clearly state the beneficiary's name, bank, account number and the amount, after which the bank debits the customer and pays the beneficiary. The beneficiary's date of birth, option D, is not part of the instruction. Options A, B and C are required particulars.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A system in which a payer completes credit slips (giro slips) at his own bank so that funds are credited directly to payees' accounts at the same or other banks is known as:

options.a: direct debit
options.b: credit transfer (bank giro)

questions.explanation: In a credit transfer the payer pushes funds to the payees by handing in credit slips, with a single cheque or cash, at his bank, which passes the credits to the payees' banks; it is useful for paying several bills or salaries at once. Option A is pulled by the creditor, option D is the purchase of a bill by a bank, and option C lets a customer cash cheques at other branches.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: From the point of view of an exporter, which method of receiving payment for goods shipped abroad is the RISKIEST?

options.a: Payment in advance
options.b: Documentary collection on D/P terms

questions.explanation: Under open account the exporter sends the documents of title straight to the importer, losing control of the goods and relying entirely on the importer's honesty to remit later. Option C gives a bank's guarantee of payment, option B keeps the documents under the bank's control until payment, and option A means the exporter is paid before shipping.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: In bill collection, when only the bill of exchange is sent to the bank for collection WITHOUT commercial documents such as the bill of lading, it is called a:

options.a: clean collection
options.b: documentary credit

questions.explanation: A clean collection involves only the financial document, the bill, while a documentary collection also includes commercial documents like the bill of lading and insurance certificate. Option D is therefore the opposite. Option B is a letter of credit, and option C is the bank buying the bill rather than merely collecting it.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
questions.question: A documentary collection is a bill sent for collection together with:

options.a: a guarantee of payment from the importer's bank
options.b: the importer's tax clearance certificate only
options.c: commercial documents such as the bill of lading and insurance certificate

questions.explanation: In a documentary collection the bill travels with the shipping and commercial documents, and the bank releases them to the importer only against payment or acceptance. Option A describes a letter of credit, which collections do not provide. Options D and B are not features of a collection.

questions.topic: Methods of Payment through the Banking System
