questions.question: Mrs Adeyemi places N5,000,000 with her bank for 180 days at an agreed interest rate of 12% a year and cannot withdraw it early without penalty. This is a

options.a: savings account deposit
options.b: call money borrowing

questions.explanation: A fixed or time deposit carries a fixed maturity (term) and a stipulated interest rate. Option C is withdrawable on demand without interest, A is withdrawable savings with a low rate, and B is short-term money a bank borrows from other banks.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: When a bank raises money through an overnight call deposit or interbank borrowing, the funds can usually be arranged quickly but

options.a: the interest rate is usually very high
options.b: they must be transferred to the statutory reserve
options.c: they carry no obligation to repay
options.d: they become part of the bank's paid-up capital

questions.explanation: Overnight and call borrowing can be arranged in minutes, which makes it useful for short liquidity gaps, but it is expensive. It is a debt the bank must repay, so it is not capital (option D) and certainly carries an obligation to repay (option C).

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a use of a deposit money bank's funds?

options.a: Fees earned from issuing letters of credit
options.b: Payment of interest to depositors
options.d: Repayment of customers' deposits on demand

questions.explanation: Fees from letters of credit, bank drafts and similar services flow INTO the bank, so they bring money in rather than use it. Repaying deposits, paying interest and investing in government securities (options D, B, C) are all ways the bank uses its funds.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Income from the sale of a bank's building or of a subsidiary company is regarded as extraordinary income because it is

options.a: a type of customer deposit
options.b: usually non-recurring

questions.explanation: Sale of assets brings in funds but does not happen every year, so it is treated as extraordinary rather than as regular operating income. Interest on loans (option D) is the bank's main recurring income, not extraordinary income.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: The main reason a banker analyses a customer's balance sheet and profit and loss account before granting an advance is to

options.a: decide the price at which the customer should sell its goods
options.b: audit the accounts on behalf of the shareholders
options.c: judge whether the business can repay the advance and interest from its operations and assets
options.d: calculate the customer's personal income tax

questions.explanation: A lending banker uses the accounts to assess liquidity, profitability, gearing and cash flow, and so the ability to repay and the margin of safety if things go wrong. Auditing (option B) is the auditor's job, and pricing or tax (options D, A) are not the banker's lending concern.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: A banker who wants to know whether a customer can meet its short-term debts as they fall due would look mainly at the

options.a: return on capital employed and net profit margin
options.b: earnings per share and dividend cover

questions.explanation: Current and quick ratios compare liquid resources with short-term liabilities, so they measure short-term liquidity. Option A measures profitability, C measures long-term financial structure and risk, and B matters mainly to shareholders.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Stock is excluded from current assets when calculating the quick (acid-test) ratio because

options.a: it is always valued at more than its cost
options.b: it is the least liquid current asset and may not quickly turn into cash at book value
options.c: it is owed to trade creditors
options.d: it is a fixed asset, not a current asset

questions.explanation: Stock must first be sold and the debts collected before it becomes cash, and in a forced sale it may fetch less than book value. It is still a current asset, so option D is wrong, and option A is false because stock is normally valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: A customer's current ratio is 2.4 : 1 but its quick ratio is only 0.4 : 1. The most likely explanation is that

options.a: it has no current liabilities
options.b: most of its current assets are tied up in stock
options.c: it holds very large cash balances
options.d: its debtors pay immediately in cash

questions.explanation: The gap between the two ratios is caused by stock, the only item the quick ratio leaves out, so a high current ratio with a very low quick ratio points to heavy (possibly slow-moving) stock. Large cash balances (option C) would raise the quick ratio, not lower it.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: From a lending banker's point of view, a HIGHLY geared company is one that

options.a: holds more cash than it needs
options.b: relies heavily on borrowed funds relative to owners' funds, increasing the risk to new lenders
options.c: relies mainly on shareholders' funds and retained profits
options.d: has no long-term borrowing at all

questions.explanation: High gearing means interest-bearing debt is large compared with equity, so fixed interest charges are heavy and the owners have less of their own money at stake. Options D and C describe a low-geared company.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Interest cover tells the lending banker

options.a: how many times the customer's profit before interest and tax covers its interest charges
options.b: what percentage of sales is left as net profit
options.c: how much of the business is financed by borrowing
options.d: how many days customers take to pay their debts

questions.explanation: Interest cover = profit before interest and tax / interest, so a low figure warns that a small fall in profit could leave the borrower unable to pay interest. Option B is net profit margin, D is debtor days, and C is gearing.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Over two years a customer's debtor collection period rises from 35 days to 80 days while sales stay the same. The banker should conclude that

options.a: the business has repaid its overdraft
options.b: stock is selling more quickly
options.c: credit control is weakening and some debts may become bad, putting pressure on cash
options.d: the business is collecting its debts faster

questions.explanation: A longer collection period means customers are taking more time to pay, which ties up cash and raises the risk of bad debts. Option D is the opposite of what the figures show, and B concerns stock days, not debtor days.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: In assessing what could be recovered if a borrower failed, a prudent banker values the borrower's assets on a

options.a: going-concern basis, assuming the business continues trading
options.b: break-up (forced-sale) basis rather than a going-concern basis
options.c: replacement-cost basis, at the cost of buying new assets
options.d: historical-cost basis, exactly as shown in the balance sheet

questions.explanation: Going-concern values assume the business keeps trading, but if it collapses the assets are sold quickly and usually fetch much less, so the banker looks at break-up values for safety. Option A suits a healthy, continuing business, and D ignores that book values may not be realisable.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: When a banker calculates a customer's tangible net worth, goodwill shown in the balance sheet is usually

options.a: treated as a long-term liability
options.b: deducted, because it is likely to have little or no value if the business is wound up
options.c: doubled, because it represents future profits

questions.explanation: Goodwill and similar intangibles depend on the business continuing and rarely realise anything on break-up, so bankers deduct them to see the real asset backing. It is not a current asset (option D) and not a liability (option A).

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Arranging transactions just before the balance sheet date so that the accounts look stronger than the business's normal position is called

options.a: consolidation
options.b: window dressing

questions.explanation: Window dressing makes year-end figures look better, for example by temporarily cutting the overdraft or delaying purchases, so the balance sheet gives a misleading picture. Option D is expanding sales too fast for the available working capital, and A is the combining of group accounts or of banks.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: On 30 December, Bisi Trading Ltd borrows N10 million from a director to clear its bank overdraft, then draws the overdraft again on 3 January to repay the director. This is an example of

options.a: a statutory reserve transfer
options.b: a going-concern valuation

questions.explanation: The company makes its year-end balance sheet show no overdraft even though the borrowing returns a few days later, which is window dressing. Options C and A are reserve movements out of profit, and B is a basis of valuing assets.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of a customer's balance sheet as a basis for lending?

options.a: It is based on historical figures that may be out of date
options.b: It can be affected by window dressing
options.c: It lists the assets and liabilities of the business
options.d: It shows the position at only one date

questions.explanation: Listing assets and liabilities is simply what a balance sheet does, so it is its purpose, not a weakness. Being a snapshot at one date, using historical figures and being open to window dressing (options D, A, B) are recognised limitations, which is why bankers also look at management accounts and cash flow.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: A banker examines a customer's cash flow forecast in addition to its profit because

options.a: profit figures already include all future loan repayments
options.b: cash flow forecasts are audited and so cannot be wrong
options.c: loans are repaid out of cash, and a profitable business can still fail if it runs out of cash
options.d: cash flow shows the break-up value of fixed assets

questions.explanation: Profit is an accounting figure, while repayment needs actual cash; heavy stock or slow debtors can leave a profitable firm short of cash. Forecasts are estimates, not audited facts (option B), and break-up values (D) come from valuing assets, not from cash flow.

questions.topic: Balance Sheet Structure and Interpreting Customers' Accounts
questions.question: A customer's sales have doubled in one year, but its working capital has fallen, its creditors and overdraft have risen sharply and its current ratio has dropped below 1. The banker should suspect

options.a: window dressing
options.b: low gearing

questions.explanation: Overtrading is expanding sales faster than the firm's working capital can support, so it leans increasingly on creditors and the bank. Option A is cosmetic year-end manipulation, and C (too much idle capital) is the opposite problem.

questions.question: In Nigeria, the minimum percentage of its deposit liabilities that a deposit money bank must hold in specified liquid assets, such as cash, balances with the CBN and Treasury bills, is known as the:

options.a: Liquidity ratio
options.b: Loan-to-deposit ratio

questions.explanation: The liquidity ratio requires a bank to keep a minimum share of its deposits in assets that can quickly be turned into cash, such as cash in hand, balances with the CBN and Treasury bills, so that it can meet depositors' withdrawals. Option D is narrower: it is the part of deposits that must be kept as cash reserves with the CBN itself. Option C relates the bank's capital to its risk-weighted assets, and option B compares the bank's loans with its deposits.

questions.question: The percentage of its deposits that a bank is legally required to keep as cash reserves with the Central Bank of Nigeria is called the:

options.a: Monetary policy rate
options.b: Cash reserve ratio

questions.explanation: The cash reserve ratio, also called the legal or required reserve ratio, is the share of deposits that banks must hold as cash with the central bank, and these reserves cannot be lent out. Option D is broader, because it counts a range of liquid assets such as Treasury bills as well as cash. Option A is an interest rate that signals the CBN's policy stance, and option C measures a bank's capital against its risk-weighted assets.

questions.question: Deposit money banks have three major goals. These are:

options.a: Longevity, profitability and solvency
options.b: Liquidity, profitability and solvency

questions.explanation: A deposit money bank must earn profits for its owners, stay liquid enough to meet depositors' withdrawals, and remain solvent so that it can meet all its obligations in the long run. Balancing liquidity, profitability and solvency is the central task of bank management. Longevity (A) and endurability (C) are not recognised banking goals, although a bank that stays liquid, profitable and solvent will naturally survive.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between liquidity and profitability in a deposit money bank?

options.a: The more liquid a bank is, the more profitable it becomes, because cash attracts more depositors
options.b: A bank becomes most profitable by holding all of its deposits as cash in its vaults
options.c: The more liquid a bank is, the less profitable it tends to be, because idle liquid funds earn little or no income
options.d: Liquidity and profitability are unrelated, so a bank can pursue each goal separately

questions.explanation: Liquid assets such as cash earn little or no income, while loans and investments earn interest but tie up funds. So the more liquid a bank keeps itself, the less it can earn, and the more it lends, the less liquid it becomes; managing this trade-off is a core part of banking. Option A reverses the trade-off, option D ignores it, and option B would leave the bank earning nothing on its deposits.

questions.question: The most liquid asset of a bank is _______

options.a: money at call
options.b: bank draft

questions.explanation: Cash is the most liquid asset a bank can hold, because it is already money and can meet withdrawals immediately with no delay or loss of value. Money at call (Option A) is very liquid, since it can be recalled at short notice, but it still has to be called back before it can be used, so it ranks just below cash. Bank drafts and money orders (Options B and C) are payment instruments rather than the liquid assets a bank keeps to meet its obligations.

questions.question: Why is there said to be a conflict between liquidity and profitability for a deposit money bank?

options.a: Loans earn interest but tie up cash, while idle cash keeps the bank liquid but earns no income.
options.b: Staying liquid requires a bank to lend out all its deposits as long-term loans to investors.
options.c: Liquid assets such as cash earn the highest returns, so a more liquid bank is always more profitable.
options.d: A bank's profit depends only on its number of branches, not on the kinds of assets it holds.

questions.explanation: Lending is what earns a bank most of its profit, but every naira lent out is no longer available to meet depositors' withdrawals, so more lending means less liquidity. On the other hand, cash kept to meet withdrawals earns nothing, so a very liquid bank sacrifices profit. Option C is wrong because cash earns no interest, option B reverses the relationship between lending and liquidity, and option D ignores the role of earning assets in producing income.

questions.question: In the context of the goals of a deposit money bank, solvency means the bank's ability to:

options.a: open new branches in every state of the federation
options.b: earn a high return for its shareholders in the current financial year
options.c: meet customers' day-to-day cash withdrawals immediately on demand
options.d: meet all its obligations in the long run, with its assets exceeding its liabilities

questions.explanation: A solvent bank can meet all its obligations in the long run because the value of its assets is greater than its liabilities. Option C describes liquidity, which is about meeting immediate cash demands, and option B describes profitability. A bank needs both liquidity and profitability to remain solvent, while option A has nothing to do with solvency.

questions.question: Which of a commercial bank's assets is the most liquid but earns no income for the bank?

options.a: Loans and advances
options.b: Cash

questions.explanation: Cash is perfectly liquid because it can be paid out immediately, but it earns no interest, which is why holding too much of it reduces profit. Loans and advances (option A) earn the most interest but are much less liquid, government stocks (option C) earn income but must be sold to raise cash, and premises (option D) are fixed assets that are not held for liquidity at all.

questions.question: The 'liquidity versus profitability' problem of a commercial bank arises because

options.a: holding more cash helps the bank meet withdrawals but reduces the income it could earn by lending or investing those funds
options.b: the most profitable loans are always the most liquid assets
options.c: banks are not allowed to hold any cash
options.d: liquidity and profitability always rise together

questions.explanation: Cash is the most liquid asset but earns nothing, while loans and investments earn income but cannot be turned into cash as quickly, so the bank must balance the two to stay both safe and profitable. Option B is wrong because profitable loans are among the least liquid assets, option C is wrong because banks must keep cash and liquid assets, and option D misses the conflict between the two.

questions.question: In banking, liquidity refers to

options.a: the ability of a bank to earn high profits on its loans
options.b: the ability of a bank to meet its customers' demands for cash and its other obligations as they fall due
options.c: the excess of a bank's total assets over its total liabilities
options.d: the share of a bank's capital owned by foreign investors

questions.explanation: A liquid bank can pay depositors on demand and meet its daily cash needs, which keeps public confidence and satisfies the CBN's liquidity ratio. Option A describes profitability, option C describes solvency, and option D is about ownership.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why a deposit money bank keeps an adequate level of liquidity?

options.a: To meet customers' cash withdrawals, since current account holders can demand their money without notice
options.b: To maximise the interest it earns by lending out as much of its deposits as possible
options.c: To maintain public confidence in the bank
options.d: To meet the liquidity requirements prescribed by the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: Lending out as much as possible to earn interest is the profitability objective, and it actually pulls against liquidity because loans cannot be turned into cash quickly. Banks stay liquid to pay depositors on demand (A), to keep the public's confidence (C) and to satisfy the CBN's liquidity ratio (D), so all three of those are genuine reasons.

questions.question: In banking, the term 'liquidity' refers mainly to a bank's:

options.a: Ability to earn enough profit to pay dividends to shareholders
options.b: Excess of total assets over total liabilities
options.c: Total amount of paid-up share capital
options.d: Ability to meet customers' demands for cash and its other obligations as they fall due

questions.explanation: Liquidity is about having cash, or assets that can quickly become cash without much loss, so the bank can pay depositors on demand. Option B describes solvency, and a bank can be solvent but still illiquid if its assets are tied up in long-term loans. Option A is profitability, and C is the bank's capital base, which is a different thing.

questions.question: Under the Basel I Capital Accord of 1988, banks were required to hold capital of at least:

options.a: 25% of their total deposits
options.b: 50% of their loans and advances

questions.explanation: Basel I linked a bank's capital to the riskiness of its assets. Each asset is given a risk weight, for example zero for claims on government and 100% for most corporate loans, and capital must be at least 8% of the resulting risk-weighted total. The other ratios, A, B and D, are not the Basel standard.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the three pillars of the Basel II Accord?

options.a: Market discipline through effective public disclosure
options.b: Abolition of bank supervision
options.d: Fixed interest rates on all loans

questions.explanation: Basel II rests on three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review of a bank's capital adequacy and risk assessment, and market discipline through disclosure, so that investors and depositors can judge the bank. Deposit insurance (C) and fixed loan rates (D) are not Basel pillars. Basel II strengthens supervision rather than abolishing it (B).

questions.question: Ikeja Trust Bank has total deposit liabilities of N100 billion. Its qualifying liquid assets are cash N6 billion, Treasury bills N20 billion and net interbank placements N4 billion. What is its liquidity ratio?
questions.explanation: The liquidity ratio is qualifying liquid assets divided by deposit liabilities: (6 + 20 + 4) / 100 = 30%. Option C leaves out the interbank placements, and option B counts only the Treasury bills. Option D turns the ratio upside down, dividing deposits by liquid assets.

questions.question: A Lagos bank has deposit liabilities of N250 billion and holds N60 billion in qualifying liquid assets. If the required minimum liquidity ratio is 30%, by how much is the bank short of the requirement?

options.a: N18 billion
options.b: N75 billion
options.d: N0, because it already meets the requirement

questions.explanation: The bank must hold 30% x N250 billion = N75 billion in liquid assets, but it holds only N60 billion, so it is N15 billion short. Option B is the total required, not the shortfall. Option A wrongly applies 30% to the N60 billion the bank already holds, and option D ignores that N60 billion is below N75 billion.

questions.question: Assume the Central Bank of Nigeria requires commercial banks to keep a cash reserve ratio of 45% of their eligible deposits. A commercial bank with eligible deposits of N80 billion must keep how much as cash reserves with the CBN?

options.a: N3.6 billion
options.b: N36 billion

questions.explanation: Required cash reserves equal the cash reserve ratio times eligible deposits: 45% x N80 billion = N36 billion. Option C is the 55% of deposits left after the reserve, and option A misplaces the decimal point. Option D divides deposits by the ratio instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Oshodi Bank has deposits of N500 million and total reserves of N130 million. If the required reserve ratio is 20%, what are its excess reserves?

options.a: N130 million
options.b: N100 million

questions.explanation: Excess reserves are total reserves minus required reserves: required reserves are 20% x N500 million = N100 million, so N130 million - N100 million = N30 million. Option B is the required reserve itself, and option A is total reserves. Option D wrongly takes 20% of the reserves instead of 20% of deposits.

questions.question: A single bank receives a fresh cash deposit of N10 million. The required reserve ratio is 25% and the bank had no excess reserves before. What is the maximum amount of new loans this one bank can safely grant out of the deposit?

options.a: N7.5 million
options.b: N40 million

questions.explanation: A single bank can lend only its excess reserves: it must keep 25% x N10 million = N2.5 million, leaving N7.5 million to lend. Option D is the amount it must keep, not lend, and option C ignores the reserve requirement. Option B is the money-multiplier figure (N10 million / 0.25) for the whole banking system, not what one bank can lend.

questions.question: At the end of the year, a deposit money bank reports loans and advances of N420 billion and total deposits of N600 billion. What is its loans-to-deposits ratio?
questions.explanation: The loans-to-deposits ratio is loans and advances divided by deposits: 420 / 600 = 70%. Option B divides deposits by loans, and option A is the share of deposits not lent out. Option D wrongly divides loans by the sum of loans and deposits (420 / 1,020).

questions.question: A bank has rate-sensitive assets of N300 billion and rate-sensitive liabilities of N380 billion for the next 12 months. What is its repricing gap, and how is the bank described?

options.a: -N80 billion; asset-sensitive
options.b: -N80 billion; liability-sensitive

questions.explanation: The repricing gap is rate-sensitive assets minus rate-sensitive liabilities: 300 - 380 = -N80 billion. A negative gap means more liabilities than assets reprice in the period, so the bank is liability-sensitive. Option D reverses the subtraction, option A pairs the right number with the wrong label, and option C adds the two figures together.

questions.question: Yaba Bank has a positive repricing gap of N50 billion over one year. If market interest rates rise by 2 percentage points across the board, the expected change in its net interest income is:

options.a: An increase of N100 million
options.b: An increase of N10 billion

questions.explanation: Change in net interest income = gap x change in rate = N50 billion x 0.02 = +N1 billion. With a positive gap, more assets than liabilities reprice, so rising rates raise interest income faster than interest expense. Option D has the right size but the wrong direction, while options B and A misplace the decimal point.

questions.question: A bank's one-year repricing gap is -N80 billion. If interest rates rise by 1.5 percentage points, its net interest income will change by about:

options.a: -N120 million
options.b: -N12 billion

questions.explanation: Multiply the gap by the change in rates: -N80 billion x 0.015 = -N1.2 billion. A negative gap means the bank's deposits and borrowings reprice faster than its loans, so a rate rise squeezes net interest income. Option D has the wrong sign, and options B and A misplace the decimal point.

questions.question: A bank has capital of N12 billion. Its assets are government securities N40 billion (risk weight 0%), residential mortgages N20 billion (risk weight 50%) and corporate loans N70 billion (risk weight 100%). What is its capital to risk-weighted assets ratio?
questions.explanation: Risk-weighted assets are (40 x 0) + (20 x 0.5) + (70 x 1.0) = N80 billion, so the ratio is 12 / 80 = 15%. Option D divides capital by total unweighted assets of N130 billion. Option B wrongly gives the mortgages a full 100% weight (12 / 90), and option A counts only the corporate loans (12 / 70).

questions.question: Surulere Bank has deposit liabilities of N200 billion and qualifying liquid assets of N70 billion. With a required minimum liquidity ratio of 30%, what is the largest amount of its liquid assets it can switch into new loans and still meet the requirement?

options.a: N10 billion
options.b: N70 billion

questions.explanation: The bank must keep 30% x N200 billion = N60 billion in liquid assets, so only the N10 billion above that can be lent out. Option B would leave it with no liquid assets at all, and option D is the amount it must keep, not the surplus. Option C wrongly takes 70% of its liquid assets.

questions.question: A bank with deposits of N400 million holds exactly the required reserves of N40 million (reserve ratio 10%). A customer then withdraws N20 million in cash. What is the bank's reserve deficiency after the withdrawal?

options.a: N2 million
options.b: Nil, because required reserves also fall

questions.explanation: After the withdrawal deposits are N380 million, so required reserves are 10% x 380 = N38 million, but actual reserves have fallen to N40 - 20 = N20 million, a deficiency of N18 million. Option C ignores that the requirement itself falls by N2 million. Option A is only that fall in the requirement, and option B forgets that reserves fell by the full N20 million.

questions.question: In banking, the conversion of current assets into cash within a short period of time without appreciable loss of value is known as:

options.a: Liquidity
options.b: Profitability

questions.explanation: Liquidity is the ease of turning assets into cash quickly without losing much value; for a bank it means being able to pay depositors on demand. Option C, solvency, is about assets exceeding liabilities in the long run. Option B is about earning income, and option D is about holding enough capital against risk.

questions.question: A bank's total assets exceed its total liabilities by a comfortable margin, but most of its assets are long-term loans, and it cannot pay all the depositors who come to withdraw today. The bank is best described as:

options.a: Insolvent and illiquid
options.b: Solvent but illiquid

questions.explanation: Assets exceeding liabilities means the bank is solvent, but being unable to meet today's withdrawals means it is illiquid. Option C reverses the two ideas. Option D ignores the failed withdrawals, and option A ignores that its assets cover its liabilities.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why a deposit money bank maintains an adequate level of liquidity?

options.a: To meet the statutory liquidity requirements of the CBN
options.b: To meet the daily cash withdrawals of customers
options.c: To pay dividends that satisfy shareholders
options.d: To maintain the unshaken confidence of the public

questions.explanation: Satisfying shareholders with dividends is a reason for pursuing profitability, not liquidity. Options B, A and D are all genuine reasons for holding liquidity: meeting withdrawals on demand, obeying the CBN's liquidity ratio or cash ratio, and keeping public confidence.

questions.question: Which of the following is a reason why a bank pursues profitability?

options.a: Retained profit serves as a source of capital that strengthens the bank
options.b: It keeps the bank within the CBN's cash reserve ratio
options.c: It enables the bank to meet petty cash expenses
options.d: It allows current account holders to withdraw without notice

questions.explanation: Profit ploughed back into the business builds up the bank's capital, which is one of the main reasons banks seek profit. Options D and C describe reasons for holding liquidity, not for earning profit. Option B is a regulatory reserve requirement, which actually reduces earning assets.

questions.question: When a bank keeps more cash in its vaults than it needs, the main cost to the bank is:

options.a: The higher interest it must pay on current accounts
options.b: The interest or investment income it could have earned on those funds
options.c: The rise in its capital adequacy requirement
options.d: The penalty charged by the CBN for holding excess cash

questions.explanation: Idle cash earns nothing, so its cost is the opportunity cost: the interest it would have earned if placed with other banks or invested in government securities. There is no CBN penalty for holding extra cash (option D), and cash carries no capital charge (option C). Current accounts are generally non-interest-bearing, so option A is wrong.

questions.question: The basic problem of asset and liability portfolio management in a commercial bank is best stated as:

options.a: Lending out every naira of deposits to maximise interest income
options.b: Balancing the competing goals of liquidity, profitability and solvency
options.c: Maximising the number of branches the bank operates
options.d: Keeping all deposits as cash so that no depositor is ever turned away

questions.explanation: A bank must earn profit, yet remain liquid enough to pay depositors and solvent enough to absorb losses; striking a balance among these is its central problem. Option D would kill profitability, and option A would destroy liquidity and safety. Option C has nothing to do with the portfolio of assets and liabilities.

questions.question: Bank A moves N20 billion from short-term Treasury bills into three-year corporate loans. Compared with before, the bank is most likely to be:

options.a: Less profitable and less risky
options.b: More liquid and less profitable
options.c: Equally liquid, since both are earning assets
options.d: More profitable but less liquid and more exposed to credit risk

questions.explanation: Corporate loans usually earn more than Treasury bills but cannot be turned into cash quickly and carry default risk, so profit rises while liquidity and safety fall. Options B and A get the trade-off backwards. Option C is wrong because Treasury bills are highly liquid and can be rediscounted with the CBN, while term loans are not.

questions.question: The asset of a deposit money bank that represents its risk assets, generates most of its revenue and earns a higher rate than government securities is:

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Loans and advances

questions.explanation: Loans and advances are the credit facilities a bank grants to customers; they are its risk assets and produce the bulk of its income, which is why their interest rate is higher. Option A is a safe, liquid short-term investment with a lower yield. Option D earns little or nothing, and option C supports operations rather than generating interest.

questions.question: The approach in which a bank treats its deposits and other liabilities as largely given and concentrates on choosing the mix of cash, securities and loans to meet its liquidity and profit goals is known as:

options.a: Credit rationing
options.b: Capital management

questions.explanation: Asset management stores liquidity on the asset side: the bank decides how much to keep in cash, near-cash securities and loans while taking its funding as given. Option D does the opposite, actively buying funds to meet liquidity needs. Option B is about the level of owners' funds, and option A is about limiting loans to borrowers.

questions.question: Faced with a sudden surge in loan requests, a Nigerian bank borrows N15 billion overnight in the interbank market and issues certificates of deposit to companies instead of selling its investments. This practice is:

options.a: Shiftability
options.b: The real bills doctrine

questions.explanation: Liability management means meeting liquidity needs by actively buying funds, for example interbank borrowing and issuing certificates of deposit. Option D would instead involve running down cash or selling securities. Option A relies on selling or shifting assets, and option B is about lending only short-term self-liquidating trade loans.

questions.question: The coordinated management of both sides of a bank's balance sheet, so that the mix, maturity and pricing of assets and liabilities together achieve the bank's liquidity, profitability and risk targets, is called:

options.a: Asset-liability management
options.b: Treasury bill management

questions.explanation: Asset-liability management (ALM) looks at assets and liabilities together, managing their mix, maturities and interest rates to balance liquidity, profit and risk. Option C deals only with granting and monitoring loans, and option B with one type of investment. Option D is a growth decision, not balance sheet risk management.

questions.question: In a bank, the Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO) is best described as:

options.a: A CBN department that inspects banks' liquidity returns
options.b: A unit of the NDIC that pays insured depositors of failed banks
options.c: A committee of shareholders that approves the annual dividend
options.d: A committee of senior management that sets and monitors the bank's balance sheet strategy, including liquidity, interest rate gaps and pricing of loans and deposits

questions.explanation: ALCO is an internal committee of the bank's top managers that reviews the balance sheet and decides how to manage liquidity and interest rate risk and how to price deposits and loans. Option A is an external regulator, not part of the bank. Options C and B describe shareholder and deposit insurance functions that have nothing to do with ALCO.

questions.question: At its monthly meeting, a group of a bank's executive directors reviews the maturity profile of deposits, sets the rates the bank will offer on fixed deposits and decides to reduce the bank's negative repricing gap. This group is the bank's:

options.a: Asset and Liability Committee
options.b: Audit Committee

questions.explanation: Reviewing the maturity mix, pricing deposits and managing the repricing gap are classic tasks of the Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO). Option B checks financial reporting and internal controls. Option C approves individual loans, and option D sets pay for directors.

questions.question: In the traditional priorities for allocating a commercial bank's funds, the FIRST claim on the funds goes to:

options.a: Loans and advances to customers
options.b: Secondary reserves

questions.explanation: Primary reserves (cash in vault, balances with the central bank and cheques in course of collection) come first because the bank must meet legal reserve requirements and daily withdrawals before anything else. Option B comes second, protecting liquidity while earning some income. Options A and C come only after liquidity needs are met.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the traditional priorities in allocating a commercial bank's funds?

options.a: Primary reserves, secondary reserves, loans and advances, investments for income
options.b: Secondary reserves, primary reserves, investments for income, loans and advances
options.c: Loans and advances, primary reserves, secondary reserves, investments for income
options.d: Investments for income, loans and advances, secondary reserves, primary reserves

questions.explanation: Funds go first to primary reserves for legal and day-to-day liquidity, then to secondary reserves as a liquid earning buffer, then to loans to meet customers' credit needs, and only the remainder to investments for income. Option C puts lending ahead of liquidity. Options D and B reverse or scramble the order so that liquidity is not protected first.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical secondary reserve asset of a Nigerian deposit money bank?

options.a: Treasury bills
options.b: Land and buildings

questions.explanation: Secondary reserves are short-term, highly marketable earning assets such as Treasury bills, which can be sold or rediscounted with the CBN when cash is needed. Option C is a primary reserve that earns nothing. Options D and B are illiquid assets that cannot be turned into cash quickly without loss.

questions.question: The theory of bank liquidity which holds that banks should grant only short-term, self-liquidating loans, such as loans to finance goods in the course of production or trade that are repaid when the goods are sold, is the:

options.a: Commercial loan (real bills) theory
options.b: Anticipated income theory

questions.explanation: The commercial loan or real bills theory says a bank stays liquid by lending only for short-term trade purposes, so that each loan repays itself from the sale of the goods it financed. Option D relies on selling assets to other investors, and option B on the borrower's future income. Option C relies on borrowing funds when liquidity is needed.

questions.question: Mama Nkechi, a textile trader at Balogun Market, borrows N3 million for 90 days to buy stock, and the loan is repaid from the proceeds when the fabric is sold. A bank that restricts itself to such loans is following the:

options.a: Commercial loan theory
options.b: Anticipated income theory

questions.explanation: A short-term loan that finances stock and is repaid from the sale of that stock is a self-liquidating loan, the only kind the commercial loan (real bills) theory approves. Option B would justify loans repaid in instalments from future earnings, such as term loans. Option D is about borrowing funds, and option C about selling assets before maturity.

questions.question: A major criticism of the commercial loan (real bills) theory of bank liquidity is that it:

options.a: Depends entirely on the bank's ability to borrow in the money market
options.b: Requires banks to hold all their deposits as cash
options.c: Allows banks to grant too many long-term mortgage loans
options.d: Ignores that a stable core of deposits can safely support some longer-term lending

questions.explanation: Not all depositors withdraw at once, so part of a bank's deposits is stable, and limiting banks to short self-liquidating loans wastes this and starves the economy of term credit. Option C is the opposite of what the theory says. Option A describes liability management, and option B exaggerates: the theory allows short-term lending.

questions.question: The theory which holds that a bank can remain liquid by holding assets that can be sold or transferred to other investors, or to the central bank, before maturity without significant loss is the:

options.a: Commercial loan theory
options.b: Anticipated income theory

questions.explanation: The shiftability theory says liquidity comes from the marketability of assets: as long as the bank holds assets it can shift to others, such as Treasury bills, it can raise cash when needed. Option A relies on loans repaying themselves, and option B on borrowers' future income. Option D relies on borrowing, not selling assets.

questions.question: A key weakness of the shiftability theory of liquidity is that:

options.a: It forbids banks from holding Treasury bills
options.b: It requires every loan to be repaid from the sale of goods
options.c: It assumes banks can borrow unlimited funds overnight
options.d: In a general crisis all banks try to sell assets at once, so assets may not be shiftable without heavy loss

questions.explanation: Shifting assets works for one bank at a time, but when the whole system needs cash together, buyers disappear and prices fall, unless the central bank steps in. Option A is false, because marketable securities like Treasury bills are the core of the theory. Option B describes the commercial loan theory, and option C the liability management theory.

questions.question: According to the anticipated income theory of bank liquidity, a loan is liquid if:

options.a: It is repaid out of the borrower's expected future income, usually in regular instalments
options.b: It is funded by interbank borrowing
options.c: It finances goods that will be sold within 90 days
options.d: It can be sold to another bank before maturity

questions.explanation: The anticipated income theory links liquidity to the borrower's future earnings: a term loan repaid in scheduled instalments gives the bank a steady, predictable cash inflow. Option C describes the commercial loan theory, and option D the shiftability theory. Option B is about the liability side, not the loan itself.

questions.question: A bank grants a civil servant a three-year car loan repaid by equal monthly deductions from her salary, arguing that the predictable instalments keep the bank liquid. This reasoning reflects the:

options.a: Liability management theory
options.b: Anticipated income theory

questions.explanation: Basing liquidity on the borrower's expected income and a fixed repayment schedule is the anticipated income theory, which supports term and instalment lending. Option D would reject a three-year consumer loan as not self-liquidating. Option C depends on reselling assets, and option A on borrowing funds.

questions.question: Which liquidity theory focuses on the LIABILITY side of the balance sheet rather than on the assets a bank holds?

options.a: Shiftability theory
options.b: Commercial loan theory

questions.explanation: The liability management theory says a bank need not store all its liquidity in assets because it can buy funds when needed, for example through interbank borrowing or certificates of deposit. Options A, C and B all look for liquidity in the bank's assets: marketable securities, instalment loans and self-liquidating trade loans respectively.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way a deposit money bank can obtain liquidity at short notice?

options.a: Selling or rediscounting its Treasury bills
options.b: Borrowing in the interbank market
options.c: Borrowing from the CBN through its standing lending facility
options.d: Granting a new five-year loan to a manufacturer

questions.explanation: Granting a new long-term loan uses up cash rather than providing it, so it is not a way of obtaining liquidity. Option A converts liquid assets into cash, while options B and C raise cash by borrowing from other banks or from the CBN.

questions.question: A bank raises cash by (1) letting its maturing Treasury bills run off and (2) borrowing overnight from another bank. Which statement correctly classifies these sources of liquidity?

options.a: Both are asset-side sources
options.b: Both are liability-side sources
options.c: (1) is a liability-side source and (2) is an asset-side source
options.d: (1) is an asset-side source and (2) is a liability-side source

questions.explanation: Maturing Treasury bills turn an asset into cash, so that is liquidity stored on the asset side, while overnight borrowing creates a new liability, so it is purchased liquidity. Options A and B lump the two together, and option C swaps them.

questions.question: The situation in which a bank finances long-term loans with deposits that can be withdrawn on demand or at short notice is known as:

options.a: Maturity mismatch
options.b: Capital adequacy

questions.explanation: Borrowing short and lending long creates a maturity mismatch: the bank's liabilities fall due much sooner than its assets, which exposes it to liquidity and interest rate risk. Option B concerns the size of capital relative to risk assets. Option C is about restricting loans, and option D is not a recognised term for this gap in maturities.

questions.question: A bank holds mainly 10-year fixed-rate mortgage loans funded by 90-day fixed deposits. If market interest rates rise sharply, the bank will most likely suffer because:

options.a: Its capital will rise because of higher interest rates
options.b: Its mortgage income will rise faster than its deposit costs
options.c: Its deposit costs will reprice upward quickly while its mortgage income stays fixed
options.d: Its liquidity ratio will automatically increase

questions.explanation: This is interest rate risk from a maturity mismatch: the 90-day deposits must be renewed at the new, higher rates while the fixed mortgage rates do not change, so net interest income shrinks. Option B gets the direction wrong because the mortgage rate is fixed. Options D and A have no link to a rate rise.

questions.question: The difference between a bank's rate-sensitive assets and its rate-sensitive liabilities over a given period is called the:

options.a: Loans-to-deposits ratio
options.b: Repricing (funding) gap

questions.explanation: The repricing or funding gap measures how much more (or less) of a bank's assets than its liabilities will reprice within a period, and it shows how net interest income will react to rate changes. Option A compares loans with deposits, and option D compares liquid assets with deposits. Option C is net interest income relative to earning assets.

questions.question: A bank whose rate-sensitive assets exceed its rate-sensitive liabilities (a positive gap) will find that its net interest income:

options.a: Falls when interest rates rise
options.b: Is unaffected by any change in interest rates

questions.explanation: With a positive gap more assets than liabilities reprice, so a rate rise lifts interest income more than interest expense and net interest income goes up. Option A describes a negative gap. Option C is the reverse, since a positive-gap bank loses when rates fall, and option B fits only a zero gap.

questions.question: The ALCO of a Nigerian bank expects interest rates to fall over the coming year. Under simple gap analysis, which repricing position would benefit the bank most?

options.a: A zero gap
options.b: A negative gap, with more rate-sensitive liabilities than rate-sensitive assets
options.c: A positive gap, with more rate-sensitive assets than rate-sensitive liabilities
options.d: A gap equal to the bank's paid-up capital

questions.explanation: When rates fall, a negative-gap bank sees its deposit and borrowing costs drop faster than its asset income, so net interest income rises. Option C would lose, because its assets reprice down faster. Option A only protects income rather than gaining from the fall, and option D has no meaning in gap analysis.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of the Basel II Accord?

options.a: Market discipline
options.b: Minimum capital requirements

questions.explanation: Basel II rests on three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review of capital adequacy and market discipline through disclosure. Deposit insurance protects depositors but is a separate safety-net arrangement, run in Nigeria by the NDIC, and not a Basel II pillar. Options B, D and A are the genuine pillars.

questions.question: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which issues the Basel capital accords, operates under the auspices of the:

options.a: World Bank
options.b: Bank for International Settlements

questions.explanation: The Basel Committee was set up by the G10 central banks and works under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel, Switzerland. Options D, A and C are international financial institutions with other mandates, and none of them hosts the Basel Committee.

questions.question: Under Basel III, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is intended to ensure that a bank holds:

options.a: Stable long-term funding for its whole balance sheet
options.b: Enough high-quality liquid assets to cover its net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period
options.c: Cash reserves with the central bank equal to a fixed share of deposits
options.d: Capital of at least 8% of its risk-weighted assets

questions.explanation: The LCR is a short-term liquidity standard: liquid assets must cover the cash a bank would lose over 30 days of stress. Option D is the Basel I capital rule. Option A describes the Net Stable Funding Ratio, which tackles longer-term maturity mismatch, and option C is a cash reserve ratio.

questions.question: A bank's capital is exactly at the minimum required ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets, and it wants to grant many more corporate loans. Without breaching the requirement, it must:

options.a: Reduce its holdings of zero-risk-weight government securities
options.b: Raise more capital or retain more profit before expanding risk assets

questions.explanation: Corporate loans add to risk-weighted assets, so at the minimum ratio the bank must raise capital (or retain profit) to support more lending; this is how capital adequacy limits balance sheet growth. Option D funds loans but adds no capital. Option A does not reduce risk-weighted assets because those securities carry no weight, and option C is set by the CBN, not the bank.

questions.question: In the CAMEL rating system used by Nigerian bank supervisors, the letter 'L' stands for:

options.a: Licensing
options.b: Loan growth

questions.explanation: CAMEL rates a bank on Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings and Liquidity, so 'L' is liquidity, the ability to meet withdrawals and other obligations. Options C, B and A are banking terms but not part of the CAMEL acronym.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a role of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)?

options.a: Upholding professional ethics and codes of conduct in the banking industry
options.b: Granting banking licences to new banks
options.c: Promoting the general advancement of banking practice
options.d: Promoting banking education and awarding professional qualifications to bankers

questions.explanation: The CIBN is the professional body for bankers. It trains and examines bankers, awards professional qualifications, enforces ethical standards and promotes good banking practice (D, A and C). Licensing banks is a regulatory function of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of a professional institute.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: How does the CIBN mainly promote professionalism in the Nigerian banking sector?

options.a: Through rigorous professional examinations and training, codes of conduct, and recognition of distinguished members
options.b: By insuring the deposits of bank customers
options.c: By setting the monetary policy rate
options.d: By buying and selling treasury bills for banks

questions.explanation: The CIBN builds professionalism by training bankers and examining them for professional qualifications, setting and enforcing ethical codes, and honouring outstanding contributions to the profession. Deposit insurance (B) is the NDIC's role, the monetary policy rate (C) is set by the CBN, and trading treasury bills (D) is money market business.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: In Nigeria, the professional body that sets standards of knowledge and skill for persons entering the banking profession, conducts professional banking examinations and promotes ethics among bankers is the

options.a: Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria
options.b: Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The CIBN is the professional body for bankers: it sets entry standards, examines candidates and upholds ethics in the profession. Option B is the regulator of banks and the monetary authority, option C insures deposits, and option D is a training centre, not the body that awards professional banking qualifications.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN) is best described as

options.a: a professional body for banking practitioners
options.b: a deposit insurance agency
options.d: a commercial bank owned by bankers

questions.explanation: The CIBN is a professional institute: it qualifies, registers and disciplines bankers as professionals. It does not license banks (option C, a CBN role), insure deposits (option B, an NDIC role) or carry on banking business itself (option D).

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria first obtained chartered status by

options.a: the CBN Act of 1958
options.b: the Banking Ordinance of 1952

questions.explanation: Chartered status came in 1990 through Act (Decree) No. 12 of 1990, which also gave the Institute its present name. Options A, B and C are banking laws dealing with the central bank and the regulation of banks, not with the professional institute.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The 1990 law that chartered the CIBN has been repealed and replaced. The CIBN is now governed by

options.a: the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, 2023
options.b: the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria Act, 2007
options.c: the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020
options.d: the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, 2020

questions.explanation: The CIBN Act, 2007 repealed the 1990 Act and transferred the Institute's rights and liabilities to the Institute it re-established. Options D and A govern banks and deposit insurance, and option C governs companies generally, so none of them is the Institute's own establishing law.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The CIBN traces its origin to 1963, when bankers in Lagos set up

options.a: a chapter of the American Bankers Association
options.b: a branch of the Central Bank of Nigeria
options.c: a local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London

questions.explanation: In November 1963 bankers meeting in Surulere, Lagos resolved to form a local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London, and this centre became the nucleus of the CIBN. The CBN (option B) is a regulator, a clearing house (option D) settles cheques, and option A has no part in the Institute's history.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Before it became chartered in 1990, the body now known as the CIBN operated under the name

options.a: Nigerian Institute of Bankers
options.b: Institute of Banking and Finance of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The body was registered as the Nigerian Institute of Bankers and changed its name to the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria when it was chartered in 1990. Options C, B and D sound similar but were never the Institute's name.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Before its chartering, the Nigerian Institute of Bankers was registered as

options.a: a public limited company
options.b: a statutory corporation of the CBN

questions.explanation: Professional bodies are commonly formed as companies limited by guarantee because they have members, not shareholders, and do not distribute profit; the Nigerian Institute of Bankers was registered this way. Option A is a profit-making company with share capital, option B would be a government body, and option C is a member-owned business form.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which sequence correctly traces the development of the CIBN?

options.a: Bankers' Committee -> local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London -> CIBN
options.b: CIBN -> Nigerian Institute of Bankers -> local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London
options.c: Local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London -> Nigerian Institute of Bankers -> CIBN
options.d: Nigerian Institute of Bankers -> local centre of the Institute of Bankers, London -> CIBN

questions.explanation: The body began in 1963 as a local centre of the London institute, was then registered locally as the Nigerian Institute of Bankers, and became the CIBN on chartering in 1990. Options D and B reverse the order, and option A wrongly treats the Bankers' Committee, a forum of the CBN and bank chief executives, as the Institute's origin.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, which of the following is NOT a function of the Institute?

options.a: Granting licences to banks to accept deposits
options.b: Maintaining registers of members and corporate members
options.c: Determining the standards of knowledge and skill for persons seeking to become bankers
options.d: Conducting professional examinations leading to certificates

questions.explanation: Licensing banks is a regulatory power of the Central Bank of Nigeria, not of the professional institute. Options C, B and D are all functions given to the CIBN by its Act: setting standards, keeping registers and conducting examinations.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the CIBN under its establishing Act?

options.a: Insuring the deposits of bank customers
options.b: Issuing the national currency
options.c: Ensuring the observance of ethical standards and professionalism among bankers

questions.explanation: Section 3 of the CIBN Act charges the Institute to ensure the furtherance, maintenance and observance of ethical standards and professionalism among practitioners of the banking profession. Option A is a role of the NDIC, while options B and D are central bank functions.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Chiamaka, a graduate trainee in a Lagos bank, wants to sit professional banking examinations that lead to a recognised professional qualification as a banker. The body she should register with is the

options.a: Nigerian Exchange Limited
options.b: Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria

questions.explanation: Conducting professional examinations leading to the award of certificates is a statutory function of the CIBN. The NDIC (option D) insures deposits, the SEC (option C) regulates the capital market, and option A runs the stock exchange; none of them examines bankers.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The CIBN was set up to do all of the following EXCEPT

options.a: conduct open market operations to control money supply
options.b: uphold professional ethics and tradition in the banking industry
options.d: liaise with government in promoting and regulating the banking industry

questions.explanation: Open market operations are a monetary policy tool of the Central Bank of Nigeria. Options C, B and D are all objects of the CIBN: promoting banking education, upholding ethics and tradition, and liaising with government on the development of banking.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: A key benefit of the CIBN's codes of conduct for the banking profession is that they

options.a: guarantee that every bank will make a profit
options.b: fix the interest rates banks charge customers
options.c: replace the supervisory role of the CBN
options.d: enforce self-regulation and compliance among members

questions.explanation: A professional body develops rules and codes of conduct so that members police their own standards, which is self-regulation. Option A is not something any code can guarantee, option C is wrong because the CBN still supervises banks, and option B confuses ethics with pricing.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The CIBN conferring honorary awards on persons for distinguished service or outstanding contributions to banking knowledge is an example of its

options.a: disciplinary procedure
options.b: register of corporate members

questions.explanation: Honorary awards for distinguished service are the Institute's way of recognising and rewarding merit in the profession. Option A deals with misconduct, option C tests candidates for qualifications, and option B is a list of member institutions.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, the administration and general management of the Institute's affairs is the responsibility of the

options.a: Disciplinary Tribunal
options.b: Governing Council
options.d: Board of Directors of the CBN

questions.explanation: The CIBN is governed by a Governing Council chaired by the President, which handles its administration and general management. The Bankers' Committee (option C) is a forum of the CBN and bank chief executives, option D governs the central bank, and the Disciplinary Tribunal (option A) only decides misconduct cases.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The officer of the CIBN who is its Chief Executive, keeps its registers and serves as Secretary to the Governing Council is the

options.a: Governor
options.b: Registrar

questions.explanation: The Registrar/Chief Executive runs the Institute day to day, keeps the registers and acts as Secretary to the Council. The President (option C) chairs the Council, the Second Vice-President (option D) is one of the Council's elected officers, and a Governor (option A) heads the CBN, not the Institute.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Within the CIBN's disciplinary system, the body that conducts the preliminary investigation of an alleged breach of the code of conduct and decides whether the case should go further is the

options.a: Federal High Court
options.b: Body of Past Presidents

questions.explanation: The Investigating Panel does the first-stage inquiry and decides whether there is a case to refer. The Disciplinary Tribunal (option C) hears cases only after referral, the Federal High Court (option A) hears appeals, and option B is an advisory body of former presidents.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: A complaint against a CIBN member has been investigated and referred for hearing. The body that hears the case and decides whether the member is guilty of unprofessional conduct is the

options.a: Investigating Panel
options.b: Bankers' Committee

questions.explanation: The Disciplinary Tribunal determines cases referred to it and can find a member guilty of unprofessional conduct. The Investigating Panel (option A) only carries out the preliminary inquiry, while options B and D are not the statutory body for deciding misconduct cases under the Act.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, the maximum sanction for a member found guilty of unprofessional conduct by the Disciplinary Tribunal is

options.a: a reprimand only
options.b: imprisonment for life
options.c: revocation of his bank's operating licence
options.d: having his name struck off the register of members

questions.explanation: The Act makes striking a name off the register the maximum sanction, which effectively removes the person from the profession. A reprimand (option A) is the lighter sanction, option B is not a power of a professional tribunal, and option C is a CBN power over banks.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which order correctly describes how a misconduct complaint against a CIBN member is handled?

options.a: Council -> Investigating Panel -> Bankers' Committee
options.b: Disciplinary Tribunal -> Investigating Panel -> confirmation by the Council
options.c: Investigating Panel -> Disciplinary Tribunal -> confirmation by the Council
options.d: Federal High Court -> Investigating Panel -> Disciplinary Tribunal

questions.explanation: The Panel first investigates and refers, the Tribunal then hears and decides, and its direction takes effect after confirmation by the Council. Option B reverses the first two stages, option A brings in the Bankers' Committee which has no role here, and option D wrongly puts the court first, when it only hears appeals.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, membership of the Institute is divided into two broad categories, namely

options.a: corporate members and individual members
options.b: practising members and retired members

questions.explanation: The Act recognises corporate members (institutions) and individual members (persons in the various grades). Options D, C and B are not the categories used by the Act.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a grade of individual membership of the CIBN?

options.a: Principal Member
options.b: Honorary Senior Member

questions.explanation: Individual grades include Ordinary, Student, Graduate, Associate, Honorary Senior Member, Honorary Fellow and Fellow, but there is no Principal Member grade. Options C, D and B are genuine grades.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Which of the following can be a corporate member of the CIBN?

options.a: A retired bank manager
options.b: A bank's newly employed cashier

questions.explanation: Corporate membership is for institutions such as the CBN, the NDIC and deposit money, development, mortgage and microfinance banks. Options B, D and A are individuals, who would join in one of the individual grades instead.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: A banker who writes the letters ACIB after her name is, in the CIBN,

options.a: a Fellow
options.b: an Associate

questions.explanation: ACIB stands for Associate of the Chartered Institute of Bankers. A Fellow (option A) uses FCIB, an Honorary Senior Member (option D) uses HCIB, and a Student member (option C) has no such designatory letters.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, the letters FCIB and HCIB respectively denote

options.a: a Fellow and a Holder of a Certificate in Banking
options.b: a Founder and an Honorary Chairman
options.c: a Fellow and an Honorary Senior Member
options.d: an Associate and an Honorary Fellow

questions.explanation: FCIB is used by Fellows and HCIB by persons registered as Honorary Senior Members. Option D wrongly gives FCIB to Associates, who use ACIB, and options A and B invent meanings for the letters.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, a 'chartered banker' is a person who

options.a: has worked in any bank for at least ten years
options.b: has passed the professional examinations and been elected an Associate or Fellow of the Institute
options.c: is a director of a licensed bank
options.d: holds a university degree in banking and finance

questions.explanation: The Act defines a chartered banker by professional qualification and election to the Associate or Fellow grade. Long service (option A), a university degree (option D) or a directorship (option C) do not on their own make anyone a chartered banker.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: A bank wants to appoint Mr Bello to head its Treasury, a technical department. Under the CIBN Act, a key condition is that Mr Bello must

options.a: be a member of the CIBN with valid, current registration
options.b: be approved by the Bankers' Committee
options.d: have been a CBN staff member

questions.explanation: The Act provides that only persons with current registration as members of the Institute may be appointed to head a bank's technical departments. Options C, B and D are not conditions set by the Act.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: Under the CIBN Act, a person who is not a member of the Institute but holds himself out as a professional banker for reward

options.a: commits no wrong if his bank is licensed
options.b: commits an offence
options.c: is automatically made a Student member
options.d: can be sanctioned only by his employer

questions.explanation: The Act makes it an offence to practise or hold oneself out as a banker without being a member, with penalties of a fine, imprisonment or both. Option A confuses the bank's licence with the individual's professional status, and options C and D are not consequences the Act provides.

questions.topic: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN)
questions.question: The Bankers' Committee in Nigeria, a regular meeting of the central bank with the chief executives of banks, is presided over by the

options.a: Managing Director of the NDIC
options.b: Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria

questions.explanation: The Bankers' Committee brings the CBN and bank chief executives together, and the CBN Governor presides over it. The CIBN President (option D) chairs the Institute's own Council, while options C and A do not chair the Committee.
